title: Hike Beehive Loop
shortDescription: This is a 1.4 mile loop trail that ascends a 450 ft cliff face. Exposed cliffs, iron rungs, and granite staircases climb this trail revealing scenic ocean views.

image.altText: person climbing up rocks with a ocean view in the distance

title: Hike Jesup Path and Hemlock Path Loop
shortDescription: This forested path continues to a boardwalk with multiple interpretive signs and benches. It opens up to a meadow before looping back on an old fire road. Views of Dorr Mountain are interspersed in this walk along a birch and hemlock forest.

image.altText: Boardwalk through a forest of white birch trees

title: Waysides at Schoodic Woods Ranger Station
shortDescription: There are two waysides featured on a wall at the Schoodic Woods Ranger Station. "Exploring Schoodic," offers an aerial view of a peninsula with a rugged coastline. The land-mass is partially surrounded by deep blue water. "Summit to Sea," captures the essence of the Schoodic Peninsula in a variety of images -- its rocky landscape, the ocean and its inhabitants, and the decorating of baskets with porcupine quills.

image.altText: Large, narrow building with stone walls, peeled log columns, cedar shingles, and a stone patio

title: Hike Perpendicular and Razorback Loop
shortDescription: The loop features a gravel shoreline path along Long Pond and a steep ascent on granite staircase of over 300 stone steps built by the CCC to reach the summit of Mansell Mountain.

image.altText: Rocky steps through a forested area

title: Hike Bar Island Trail
shortDescription: Walk along a gravel sand bar during low tide to reach Bar Island. Once on the island, hike another mile to the highest point on the island for views of Bar Harbor and Frenchman Bay.

image.title: Bar Island
image.altText: People walking across an exposed sand bar between an island and the mainland
image.caption: Visitors walk between Bar Island and Bar Harbor at low tide

title: Hike Wonderland Trail
shortDescription: This 1.4 out and back trail on an old gravel fire road is family-friendly and provides direct access to the coastline with birding opportunities.

image.altText: Man stands at next to trees on shoreline

title: Hike Ship Harbor Trail
shortDescription: Ship Harbor Trail is a 1.3 mile figure-8 loop near Seawall. Great for families and birders, and a variety of habitats can be seen along the shore.

image.title: Ship Harbor
image.altText: Small harbor with rugged cliffs around edge
image.caption: Ship Harbor

title: Hike Ocean Path Trail
shortDescription: The ocean path is a spectacular 2.2 mile long out and back trail takes you along the bold coast of Maine with ocean views, granite slabs, and rocky cliffs. This trail is a great way to access Thunder Hole and Otter Point from the Sand Beach parking area.

image.altText: View of the ocean and coastline from the ocean path trail

title: Hike Compass Harbor Trail
shortDescription: Explore a historic site near Bar Harbor and enjoy a dramatic shoreline with views of Frenchman Bay and Ironbound Island.

image.altText: Visitor sitting on rocks looking out at the ocean

title: Hike Cadillac Summit Loop
shortDescription: The Cadillac Summit Loop, located on the eastern side of Mount Desert Island, is well known as one of the most scenic paths at Acadia National Park. Starting at the top of Cadillac Mountain, which is accessible via car, this path provides a walk with breathtaking 360-degree views of Frenchman Bay, the Porcupine Islands, and Downeast Maine.

image.title: Cadillac Summit Loop
image.altText: View of a paved trail on a mountain summit with islands and mountains extending to the far horizon.
image.caption: View of Frenchman Bay from the Cadillac Summit Loop

title: Hike Great Head Trail
shortDescription: This 1.7 mile trail has spectacular ocean views along a coastal headland with some wooded sections. This historic trail also includes the ruins of an early 1900's tea house.

image.altText: a wooden sign with in front of ocean view and trees

title: Hike Schoodic Peninsula Trails
shortDescription: This 7.5 mile network of hiking trails leads across the peninsula, from Winter Harbor in the north through spruce-fir forests, pine woodlands, and a shrubland, terminating on the southern end at Blueberry Hill. Enjoy views from the Anvil and Schoodic Head, as well as some challenging steep climbs from the East Trail.

image.altText: Person walking along rocks on a coastline

title: Hike Western Mountain Loop
shortDescription: This 3.8 mile loop travels through forested areas and up the summits of Bernard Mountain and Mansell Mountain, together creating Western Mountain. Although there are not many views, it is a challenging hike with hundreds of cut stone steps and other steep sections along the way.

image.altText: Sunset view over a forest and mountains

title: Hike St. Sauveur and Acadia Mountain Loop
shortDescription: This 3.9 mile challenging loop summits two mountain peaks and offers stunning views of Somes Sound, the surrounding mountains, outlying islands,and the ocean.

image.altText: Visitors overlook islands from a mountain summit

title: Hike Schiff Path
shortDescription: Schiff Path is a popular, relatively steep trail and acts as a connector between Sieur de Monts and the summit of Dorr Mountain. It is one of the memorial trails built between 1924 and 1930.

image.altText: Hiking path with stone steps leading through wooded area

title: Hike Precipice Loop
shortDescription: Rising over 1,000 feet in 0.9 miles, the Precipice Trail requires physical and mental strength. It is a rugged, non-technical climb with open cliff faces and iron rungs, and reaches the summit of Champlain Mountain.
seasonDescription: This trail and associated trails are closed seasonally to public entry to protect peregrine falcons from inadvertent disturbance or harassment during the nesting period. Park staff has observed adults at these sites engaging in courtship and pre-nesting behavior signaling the birds’ intentions to nest and raise chicks during the spring and early summer. Check current conditions for updates on trail closures before hiking.

image.altText: Hikers ascend a cliff with iron rungs

title: Hike Pemetic South Ridge
shortDescription: This hike reaches the summit of Pemetic Mountain from Jordan Pond, providing panoramic views of the ocean and surrounding islands.

image.altText: view of a lake at sunset from a mountain summit

title: Hike Pemetic Mountain Loop
shortDescription: The Pemetic Mountain Loop combines a variety of hiking environments over 4 miles, starting with an easy walk along a scenic pond to a rugged ascent. It culminates at an open granite summit with excellent views of the surrounding landscape, ocean and outlying islands.

image.altText: Hiker ascends a wooden ladder in a ravine

title: Hike Norumbega Mountain Loop
shortDescription: The Norumbega Loop Trail features a steep hike up to the summit of Norumbega Mountain, then a gradual descent in the forest before hiking along the western shore of Lower Hadlock Pond.

image.altText: Visitor hikes down exposed granite section of trail

title: Hike Kurt Diederichs Climb
shortDescription: Kurt Diederichs Climb is a memorial path at Sieur de Monts. It is a .4 mile steep ascent with many granite steps. It is one of the routes to reach Schiff Path, and eventually the summit of Dorr Mountain.

image.altText: Stone steps leading down a trail in a forested area

title: Hike Kebo Brook Trail to Kebo Mountain
shortDescription: This 2 mile out-and-back trail follows a fairly level forest path before a short, steep climb to reach the summit of Kebo Mountain.
seasonDescription: The Park Loop Road is closed from Mid-December to Mid-April. In the winter months, you can access this trail via Kebo St.

image.altText: Rocky granite steps along a trail with a blue blaze

title: Hike Jordan Pond Path
shortDescription: The trail follows the shore of Jordan Pond, providing iconic views of steep, glacially sculpted mountains and the glacially carved valley that is now Jordan Pond.

image.altText: view of lake covered in ice

title: Hike Jordan Cliffs Loop
shortDescription: The Jordan Cliffs Loop offers a challenging 5 mile hike across steep slopes, iron rungs, and a strenuous climb up Sargent Mountain. Hikers are rewarded with panoramic views from two mountain summits and Jordan Pond nestled between the mountains.
seasonDescription: This trail and associated trails are closed seasonally to public entry to protect peregrine falcons from inadvertent disturbance or harassment during the nesting period. Park staff has observed adults at these sites engaging in courtship and pre-nesting behavior signaling the birds’ intentions to nest and raise chicks during the spring and early summer. Check current conditions for updates on trail closures before hiking.

image.altText: View from cliffs of forest and pond below

title: Hike Homans Path
shortDescription: Homans Path is a memorial path at Sieur de Monts. It is a .3 mile steep ascent with impressive examples of intricate rock work. It is one of the routes to reach Schiff Path, and eventually the summit of Dorr Mountain.

image.altText: Rock bridge over a trail cut into granite

title: Hike Hadlock Ponds Loop
shortDescription: Enjoy boardwalks, wooden bridges and some uneven terrain on this 4.1 mile figure eight trail that includes both Lower and Upper Hadlock Ponds.

image.altText: view of a pond with fog rolling in

title: Hike Gorham Mountain Loop
shortDescription: The Gorham Mountain Loop is 3.5 miles featuring mountains and a rocky coastline with panoramic views of Mount Desert Island, Frenchman Bay, and the outlying islands.

image.altText: view of two mountains in the distance from the summit of another mountain

title: Hike Gorge Path
shortDescription: Gorge Path follows a narrow, rocky gorge separating Dorr and Cadillac Mountains. It crosses streams, climbs steep, granite steps, and intersects other trails leading to either summit.

image.title: Gorge Path
image.altText: Rock steps pass a small cascade in a forest
image.caption: Gorge Path

title: Hike Giant Slide Loop
shortDescription: A challenging hike up a rugged ravine to excellent views atop Mount Desert Island's second highest peak, Sargent Mountain, and other summits.

image.altText: Visitor stands on a rock along a forested trail

title: Hike Flying Mountain Loop
shortDescription: This loop hike offers a short, relatively steep hike to the top of a small mountain with spectacular views of Somes Sound and descends to a quiet ocean cove with a rocky beach.

image.altText: a large falcon with pointed wings flying

title: Hike Emery Path
shortDescription: Emery Path is a steep .5 mile memorial path at Sieur de Monts leading up towards Schiff Path and Dorr Mountain.

image.altText: Steps and a passage cut through granite in a forest

title: Hike Dorr Mountain South Ridge Loop
shortDescription: The Dorr Mountain South Ridge Loop is a 3.2 mile loop featuring views of Mount Desert Island from the top of Dorr Mountain after a steep ascent.

image.altText: View of a bay, islands, and a forest below from a mountain ridge line

title: Hike Carriage Roads
shortDescription: Many carriage roads intersect with hiking trails. They can be incorporated into a hike to create a loop, add distance, or provide opportunities for more even terrain to gain or lose elevation.
seasonDescription:
Respect closures during spring mud season while underlying gravel remains vulnerable to ruts, potholes, and erosion.

See Winter Activities for information on carriage roads during the off season.

image.title: Carriage Roads
image.altText: Two people walking along a crushed gravel surfaced road
image.caption: Carriage roads are a great option for hiking or walking

title: Hike Cadillac South Ridge Trail
shortDescription: This out and back trail is the longer option for hiking Cadillac Mountain with spectacular views of the Atlantic Ocean and outlying islands before reaching the summit.

image.altText: Visitor hikes down granite trail marked with cairns

title: Hike Cadillac North Ridge Trail
shortDescription: A moderate out-and-back hike to the highest point both in Acadia and on the eastern seaboard. The trail is mostly exposed, providing hikers with sweeping vistas of Bar Harbor, Frenchman Bay, and the Schoodic Peninsula.

image.altText: Rock cairns leading trail up exposed rock

title: Hike Bubbles Nubble Loop
shortDescription: This hike traverses the summits of North Bubble, South Bubble, and Connors Nubble and crosses varying terrain of forest paths, steep granite sections, and a level carriage road. Visitors can enjoy views of Eagle Lake, Jordan Pond, Pemetic and Sargent Mountains, and the Cranberry Isles.

image.altText: Visitors photographs a sunset over a lake

title: Hike Bubbles
shortDescription: This short 1.5 mile hike offers views of Jordan Pond and the surrounding mountains from the iconic North Bubble, South Bubble, and Bubble Rock.

image.altText: Visitors sitting on a rock ledge overlooking a lake

title: Hike Beech Mountain Trail
shortDescription: This short, moderate loop on the west side of Mount Desert Island provides hikers with views of Long Pond and Mansell Mountain on the way up and access to one of the few remaining fire towers in the area.

image.altText: Golden light through trees along a trail

title: Hike Beech Mountain South Ridge Loop
shortDescription: This loop hike traverses a forest before ascending Beech Mountain, where there is a fire tower and views of Long Pond, Mansell Mountain, and the west side of Mount Desert Island.

image.altText: Fire tower with people on the platform

title: Hike Beachcroft Path
shortDescription: The Beachcroft Path is an historic memorial pathway, constructed in 1915. Take this trail to reach Champlain Mountain for panoramic coastal mountain views of Mount Desert Island, Frenchman Bay, and the outlying islands.

image.altText: Rock cairns mark a trail on exposed rock

title: Hike Bald Peak and Parkman Mountain Loop
shortDescription: A short, challenging loop hike to the summits of Bald Peak and Parkman Mountain, each over 900 feet.

image.altText: Rock cairn on an exposed granite mountain summit

title: Hike Village Green to Sieur de Monts with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: Beginning at the Village Green in Bar Harbor and ending at the Sieur de Mont Area this hike includes the Great Meadow Loop, the Hemlock Road Trail, and the Jesup Path. With virtually no elevation gain it traverses a Bar Harbor neighborhood, crosses the Great Meadow, and finishes with a boardwalk at the Nature Center.

image.title: Hike Village Green to Sieur de Monts
image.altText: Two sunlit green mountains are reflected in a pool of water with grasses under a clear blue sky.
image.caption: Dorr and Cadillac Mountains catch the light of the sun on a late afternoon.
image.credit: Photo courtesy of Maribeth Kambitsch. Used with permission.

title: Hike Pemetic Summit with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: The hike up and over Pemetic takes hikers to the shores of both Bubble and Jordan Pond and summits Pemetic Mountain. Nearly 360-degree views look out over Cadillac, Sargent and Penobscot peaks, the Atlantic Ocean and the Cranberry Isles. Hiking this peak with use of the Island Explorer Bus offers hikers a bus-stop-only starting point for a strenuous hike with minimal mileage.

image.title: Pemetic Summit Hike
image.altText: A hiker stands on an exposed granite peak, looking out at mountains rising across the valley.
image.caption: A hiker admires the view from Pemetic Mountain

title: Hike Double Bubble Nubble Loop with Island Explorer
shortDescription: The trek to summit both Bubbles and Conners Nubble summits three peaks and accesses iconic park locations. Hikers will be treated to views of lakes and mountains while exploring woodlands. By hiking with the use of the Island Explorer Bus, these trails are accessible in a unique way and helps hikers overcome the crowds while exploring popular viewpoints.

image.title: Double Bubble Nubble Loop
image.altText: Two hikers sit on the bald granite summit of North Bubble studying a map.
image.caption: Dorr and Cadillac Mountains catch the light of the sun on a late afternoon.
image.credit: Photo by Ashley L. Conti, Friends of Acadia

title: Hike Gorge/Cadillac Mountain North Ridge Loop with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: This is a great option for hiking to the summit of Cadillac Mountain. It follows Kebo Brook which cuts deeply through the granite bedrock with views of steep canyons walls from the gorge below. The final portion of the path ascends a steep rock face and gives hikers vistas of Dorr Mountain, Frenchman Bay, the Atlantic Ocean, as well the deeply cut gorge itself. The summit of Cadillac Mountain provides a 360-degree view out over Mount Desert Island.

image.title: Hike Gorge/Cadillac Mountain Loop
image.altText: Steep granite mountain face is partially covered with deciduous and evergreen trees in fall color.
image.caption: Fall foliage peppers the ridge of Dorr Mountain from the Gorge Path.
image.credit: Photo be Ashley L. Conti, Friends of Acadia

title: Hike the Acadia Mountain Loop with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: Acadia Mountain Trail follows up the east and west side of the mountain with views of the surrounding mountains and bodies of water. With the Island Explorer bus, visitors won't need to park along the road and can ride to the trailhead stress-free.

image.title: Hike the Acadia Mountain Loop
image.altText: Visitors overlook islands from a mountain summit.
image.caption: View of Sommes Sound and Cranberry Island for Acadia Moutain summit.

title: Hike Sieur de Monts to Jesup Path with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: The trails from Sieur de Monts to Jesup Path are located adjacent to the Nature Center and the Wild Gardens of Acadia in a wooded area.

image.title: Hike Sieur de Monts to Jesup Path and
image.altText: Birch trees and marsh grasses surround a wooden boardwalk with dappled sunlight.
image.caption: View along Jesup Trail Boardwalk with Birch trees and marsh grasses surrounding a wooden boardwalk.
image.credit: Ashley L. Conti, Friends of Acadia

title: Hike Sieur de Monts to Sand Beach Trek with Island Explorer
shortDescription: The trek from Sieur de Monts to Sand Beach connects four trails and summits Champlain Mountain. Hikers will be treated to views of lakes, mountains and ocean while exploring woodlands, ponds and bare summits. By hiking with the use of the Island Explorer Bus, these trails are transformed from out-and-back hikes to a scenic trek across Acadia National Park.

image.title: Hike Sieur de Monts to Sand Beach Trek
image.altText: A clear view of the Porcupine Islands from the summit of Champlain Mountain just after sunrise.
image.caption: The morning sun scatters fog over Frenchman Bay, viewed from the summit of Champlain Mountain.

title: Hike Beech Cliff Trail with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: The Beech Cliff Trail climbs a steep rock face from the southern end of Echo Lake to the top of the cliffs. Continue north along the short and fun Beech Cliff Loop to be treated to even more views from the top of the cliffs. The descent is more gradual and goes down a forested area via the Canada Cliffs Trail back to the beginning of the hike.

image.title: Hike the Beech Cliff Trail
image.altText: Echo Lake and Beach are nestled at the bottom a mountain ridge while granite cliffs rise steeply.
image.caption: View from the top of Beech Cliff Trail onto the deep blue Echo Lake and Beech below.
image.credit: Photo courtesy of Maribeth Kambitsch. Used with permission.

title: Hike Great Head with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: Great Head Trial provides visitors a chance to hike a shorter trail and get amazing views of the ocean and forest in the same hike. Enjoy the views while relaxing on the beach afterward.

image.title: Hike Great Head Trail
image.altText: Two hikers walk along Great Head Trail overlooking Sand Beach.
image.caption: Two hikers walk along Great Head Trail overlooking Sand Beach.
image.credit: Photo by Ashley L. Conti, Friends of Acadia

title: Hike Ocean Path Trail with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: Ocean Path follows atop Acadia’s granite cliffs along the Atlantic Ocean. While exploring the Ocean Path, visitors can enjoy scenic vistas and iconic park locations including Sand beach, Thunder Hole and Otter Cliffs. Combining this hike with Acadia’s Island Explorer bus gives hikers flexibility in trail distance on what would otherwise be an out-and-back hike.

image.title: Otter cliffs
image.altText: A rocky ocean seashore with trees and cliffs in the background.
image.caption: Morning light illuminates Monument Cove off the Ocean Path.

title: Hike Sargent and Penobscot Mountains from JPH with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: The trails up Sargent and Penobscot Mountains are located a short distance from the Jordan Pond House restaurant and gift shop.

image.title: Sargent and Penobscot Mountains from JP
image.altText: Blue skies above Jordan Pond with views of tree lined North and South Bubble Mountains.
image.caption: View from Jordan Cliffs Trail of North and South Bubble across Jordan Pond.
image.credit: Photo by Emma Forthofer, Friends of Acadia

title: Hike Jordan Pond Loop with Island Explorer Bus
shortDescription: If looking for a way to relax, to take in some magnificent views, or to just burn some of the calories from the popovers consumed at the Jordan Pond house, the Jordan Pond Path is a great choice. Even just walking along the eastern shoreline is a certain way to enjoy some scenic vistas of one of Acadia’s iconic locations.

image.title: Hike the Jordan Pond Loop
image.altText: The placid surface Jordan Pond with exposed boulders and a log protruding from the water.
image.caption: View of the Bubbles looking north across Jordan Pond.
image.credit: Photo by Avery Howe, Friends of Acadia

title: Oldfarm Video Tour
shortDescription: George B. Dorr worked tirelessly through the early 1900s to found what we know today as Acadia National Park. His former family estate, known as Oldfarm, is situated along the Compass Harbor Trail, less than a mile from downtown Bar Harbor on State Route 3. The short walk beneath forest canopies leads to foundation remnants of his former cottage, demolished in 1949, and ends at Dorr Point with views of Compass Harbor and the Porcupine Islands.

image.title: Oldfarm
image.altText: View from a covered patio across trees in foreground of a harbor and islands in the distance.
image.caption: View of Compass Harbor from the Oldfarm patio.

title: Explore Historic Carroll Homestead
shortDescription: Head towards the west side of the island to visit an example of 1800s island life at Carroll Homestead, a time capsule of early Euro-american settlement before Mount Desert Island became a tourist destination and Acadia National Park came into being.

image.title: Carroll Homestead
image.altText: A grey, wood-shingle building with two chimneys sits in a grassy field with trees in the background
image.caption: Explore Carroll Homestead on your own or during a ranger program

title: Swim Lake Wood
shortDescription: Lake Wood is a secluded pond with a small beach area, just a short drive away from Hulls Cove Visitor Center. There are no lifeguards and access road does not open until June 1.

image.altText: Visitors swimming in a lake with small beach area

title: Swim Sand Beach
shortDescription: Acadia’s only sandy ocean beach, at the beginning of the Park Loop Road’s coastal section, is one of the park’s most heavily-visited areas. Visitors come to swim in the frigid water, bask and play on the sand, seek intertidal creatures, or view a feature widely publicized as a “must-see.”

image.altText: Sand beach with forest and mountains behind it

title: Swim Echo Lake Beach
shortDescription: Echo Lake Beach is a popular, freshwater swimming area on the southern end of Echo Lake. It is accessible off Route 102 in Southwest Harbor.

image.altText: Child with an inflatable toy in a lake

title: Stargazing on Cadillac Mountain (Vehicle Access Limited)
shortDescription: Gaze in awe at Acadia's night sky from the highest mountain summit in the park.
seasonDescription: Any attempts to hike Cadillac Summit should include significant weather-related preparations. Mountain temperatures and winds are colder and stronger than at at sea level. Cadillac Summit Road is subject to night time road closures and the road closes fully no later than December 1 (with weather-related closures possible throughout the year).

image.altText: Milky way over a mountain summit and trees

title: Tidepooling at Wonderland
shortDescription: Explore rocky tidepools at the far end of this coastal forest trail on the west side of Mount Desert Island.

image.altText: View from a tide pool of surrounding water and forest

title: Drive Cadillac Mountain
shortDescription: Cadillac Mountain is a popular destination for visitors to Acadia National Park. Accessible by car, it is the highest point on the eastern seaboard of the U.S., and offers magnificent views of a glaciated coastal and island landscape. The short, paved Cadillac Summit Loop Trail, interpretive waysides, restrooms, and gift shop are located at the summit.
seasonDescription: Vehicle reservations are required for Cadillac Summit Road from mid-May through mid-October. Weather permitting, the road opens in mid-April and closes no later than December 1st.  The road is also closed for unsafe weather conditions, especially in late fall and early spring Visit our Current Conditions page to up to date closure information.

image.title: Cadillac Summit Road
image.altText: Sun rises over cars driving a mountain landscape with coastal bay in the background.
image.caption: Cadillac Summit Road is a popular drive for sunrise views.

title: Stargazing at Sand Beach
shortDescription: Enjoy stargazing and night photography opportunities from Acadia’s only sandy beach.

image.altText: Saturn, Jupiter and Milky Way viewed from Sand Beach

title: Go Earthcaching At Acadia
shortDescription: Embark on an exciting journey through time to discover how glaciers have shaped Acadia National Park. Using your GPS unit and a set of clues obtained from this website and hidden along the journey, you can guide yourself to a series of sites in the park.
seasonDescription: This is a three season activity. It is not recommended for winter due to ice and snow.

image.title: Sargent Mountain at Acadia
image.altText: a view from a rocky summit looking out to another rocky summit, ocean, and blue sky
image.caption: A view from Sargent Mountain

title: Bike Carriage Roads
shortDescription: Winding through the heart of the park, the 45 miles of historic carriage roads have crushed rock surfaces perfect for miles of bicycling.

image.title: Duck Brook Carriage Road
image.altText: Two people with bicycles looking over a ledge on a bridge
image.caption: Bicyclists can enjoy 45 miles of carriage roads across the park

title: Drive Park Loop Road
shortDescription: Wind your way through forests, past lakes and mountains, and along the shoreline on scenic Park Loop Road. The 27-mile (43 km) road also provides access to popular areas such as Sieur de Monts, Sand Beach, Otter Point, Jordan Pond, and Cadillac Mountain.
seasonDescription:
During winter months:

  • Only one section (Sand Beach Entrance Station to Otter Cliff Road) remains open to vehicles. Check the park Current Conditions page for additional updates.

  • Other portions are open to pedestrians, winter sports, and bicycles. Do not block gates when parking to access the road for recreational activities.

image.title: Park Loop Road
image.altText: A road goes through brightly colored leaves around a mountain above a lake.
image.caption: Drive Park Loop Road in autumn to see spectacular fall foliage.

title: Birding Cadillac Mountain
shortDescription: Enjoy excellent birding opportunities from Acadia's highest point. In the fall (late August-October), join park rangers and volunteers daily at the Cadillac Mountain Hawkwatch.

image.altText: Eagle soars through a blue sky

title: Tour de Wildlife
shortDescription: A few spots with great potential for wildlife viewing, and what you might find there.

image.altText: Three children hold up binoculars to watch wildlife in Acadia National Park.

title: Picnic at Jordan Pond
shortDescription: Eat at Acadia's only restaurant, the historic Jordan Pond House, or bring your own picnic. This popular spot on Park Loop Road is a crossroad for historic carriage roads and hiking trails, as well as a launch point for canoeing and kayaking.

image.title: Jordan Pond House Tea Lawn
image.altText: Groups of people sit on a mowed lawn in front of a lake and distant mountains
image.caption: Jordan Pond House is a popular place to picnic with a view.

title: Paddle Long Pond
shortDescription: Explore Acadia's longest pond by boat.

image.title: Long Pond
image.altText: Large rocks in the foreground of a lake bordered by tree-covered hills
image.caption: Explore four mile long Long Pond

title: Paddle Eagle Lake
shortDescription: Explore Eagle Lake by canoe or kayak.

image.title: Paddle Eagle Lake
image.altText: Trees line a waterway under a cloudy sky
image.caption: Discover the changing colors in the fall at Eagle Lake

title: Paddle Echo Lake
shortDescription: Launch at Ikes Point to explore Echo Lake by boat.

image.title: Paddle Echo Lake
image.altText: Two people in two kayaks, one red and one yellow, examine trees growing along a cliff by the water
image.caption: Get a close up view of the towering granite cliffs.

title: Paddle Jordan Pond
shortDescription: Paddle Jordan Pond in the center of Mount Desert Island.

image.title: Paddling Jordan Pond
image.altText: Two people, wearing jackets and hats, paddle a silver canoe in water surrounded by trees.
image.caption: See Jordan Pond from the water.

title: Birding "with" the Champlain Society
shortDescription: In the early 1880's members if the Champlain Society documented bird species breeding on Mount Desert Island. Follow along the same trails they took and observe what birds we find in those places. Are they the same, or different?

image.title: Champlain Society
image.altText: a group of young men pose in front of a tree
image.caption: Champlain Society group photo in 1881

title: Birding at Otter Point
shortDescription: Enjoy Acadia's rugged coastline along Otter Point and search for passing seabirds and listen for songbirds in the nearby forest.

image.altText: a large black bird with orange throat standing on the rocky coastline

title: Stargazing at Seawall
shortDescription: Explore the night sky from the west side of Mount Desert Island while enjoying the ocean soundscape.

image.altText: Waves and Milky Way at Seawall Picnic Area

title: Tidepooling at Ship Harbor
shortDescription: Explore tidepooling opportunities on the rocky shoreline off this easy figure-8 coastal forest trail.
seasonDescription: This is a summertime activity. Please note that ocean waters can be very cold even in summer.

image.altText: Rocky coast with seaweed covering rocks near the ocean

title: Birding at Thompson Island
shortDescription: Explore migratory shorebirds, terns, and gulls (August-October) on the mudflats of Mt. Desert Narrows.

image.altText: Great blue heron standing in water

title: Tidepooling at the Schoodic Peninsula
shortDescription: Tidepooling locations at the Schoodic Peninsula.

image.altText: Tide pools at Sundew Trail's Cobble Beach.

title: Birding the Carriage Roads
shortDescription: Grab a bike and binoculars and take a ride. Just about everywhere you go you can find a feeding flock of songbirds. Great starting locations and loops: Eagle Lake, Witch Hole Pond Loop, Aunt Betty Pond, Jordan Pond, and Bubble Pond.

image.altText: Bird with red head searches for food in tree

title: Birding Sieur de Monts Springs
shortDescription: Explore the Wild Gardens of Acadia and Great Meadow, or take a walk on Jesup Path, Hemlock Trail and Stratheden Trail for birding opportunities.

image.altText: Two juvenile barred owls rest on a tree branch

title: Stargazing at Jordan Pond
shortDescription: Find opportunities to stargaze and photograph the night sky the shores surrounding Jordan Pond.

image.altText: Milky Way over Jordan Pond

title: Stargazing Ocean Path
shortDescription: Learn about stargazing opportunities along the coast on Ocean Path.

image.altText: Moon-rise and Milky Way from Ocean Path

title: Birding Jordan Pond
shortDescription: Explore Jordan Pond before the crowds by searching for breeding loon and songbirds in the morning at this popular Acadia destination.

image.altText: Adult loon with two chicks in lake

title: Tidepooling at Bar Island
shortDescription: Access the shore from downtown Bar Harbor for a unique tidepooling experience on a natural land bridge.

image.altText: Two people on a sandy gravel area looking at the water

title: Birding the Western Mountains
shortDescription: Explore the rugged side of Acadia National Park to find and listen for boreal breeding songbirds.

title: Birding Schoodic Peninsula

title: Daemonelix Trail
shortDescription: Hike a one-mile trail back in time to the day of the paleocaster, a dry land beaver, and paleosoils, fossilized dirt from the time this landscape was formed. Look out over the vast, open table lands that define the high plaines east of the Rocky Mountains.
seasonDescription: Cooler seasons are best, but the trail can be enjoyed year round. Prepare for the heat with a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water for your entire party. If you have pets please take water for them too.

image.altText: Looking down on trail from an overlook.

title: Fossil Hills Trail
shortDescription: Hike to University (left) and Carnegie Hills. The 2.7-mile Fossil Hills Trail allows visitors to walk up to and see the famed early 1900s quarries. From these quarries, paleontologists recovered some of the world's best preserved and most complete fossilized Menoceras, Moropus, and Dinohyus skeletons.
seasonDescription: Prepare for summer heat with a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water for your entire party.

image.altText: The sun illuminates the fossil hills with a dark, stormy sky in the background.

Even when formal programs are not offered, people are welcome to enjoy the parks after dark on their own.

Many trails use cairns (stacks of rocks) for markers and cross broad rock surfaces, requiring attention to follow. title: Surf Fishing on Assateague
shortDescription: Grab your fishing pole and get comfortable on the beach! Surf fishing is an activity that is not only fun and relaxing, but also has the potential of producing your dinner for the night! Spring, summer and fall are the recommended times of the year to fish.

image.title: Surf Fishing

title: Bird at Toms Cove
shortDescription: The Virginia district of Assateague Island lies within the Atlantic Flyway, providing excellent birding opportunities year-round. No matter what time of year you visit, a great spot to start your birding adventure is along Beach Road overlooking Toms Cove.

image.title: Bird at Toms Cove
image.altText: A volunteer using binoculars to bird from the deck of Toms Cove Visitor Center
image.caption: The deck of the Toms Cove Visitor Center provides excellent birding opportunities year-round

title: See the Wild Horses in the Maryland district
shortDescription: View the wild horses of Assateague Island National Seashore. The wild horses are free roaming and spend time in the various habitats on the island. While they graze in the marshes and find freshwater in the forest, you may even see them out on the beach with you! Remember to observe the horses from no less than 40 feet away because they are wild and will bite and kick.
seasonDescription: Horses are visible year-round.

image.title: Horses in the Grass
image.altText: Horses graze on beach grass
image.caption: Horses graze on beach grass

title: See the Wild Horses in the Virginia District
shortDescription: Assateague Island is well known for the famous wild horses who call the island home. In the Virginia district, the wild horses are commonly referred to as “Chincoteague Ponies”. Unlike the Maryland district where the horses are free to roam, the Chincoteague Ponies are fenced off the road and trails in two separate large management areas of the refuge resulting in a northern herd and a southern herd. Horses may be visible by foot, bike or car.
seasonDescription: Horses are visible year-round. Spring, summer and fall plan for biting insects while viewing the horses.

image.title: View the Wild Horses in Virginia
image.altText: See the wild horses! View horses from a safe distance of at least 40 feet (a bus length) away.
image.caption: See the wild horses! View horses from a safe distance of at least 40 feet (a bus length) away.

title: Crabbing at Assateague Island
shortDescription: Who doesn’t love to eat a blue crab? After all, the literal translation of this Latin name (Callinectes sapidus) is the beautiful (calli) swimmer (nectes) that is savory (sapidus). Crabbing is a great activity for the entire family regardless of age.
seasonDescription: The public crab season varies by state, and by year-to-year. Inquire about public crabbing seasons and regulations at a visitor center or Ranger Station.

title: Badlands Ranger Programs
shortDescription: Many different programs are led by rangers at Badlands National Park. Learn more about wildlife, geology, paleontology, and more by stopping at a ranger program during your visit! Visit this page to find program descriptions, locations, and typical times.

image.altText: a ranger points at a geologic column on a piece of paper in front of a badlands butte.

title: Hiking the Badlands
shortDescription: Interested in hiking at Badlands National Park? Read about rules, official trails, and the park's open hike policy here.
seasonDescription: Weather in the Badlands is often at extremes throughout the year, please plan accordingly and check the weather reports and climate data before heading onto one of the trails.

image.altText: a brown sign with white writing points to door, window, notch, and castle trails.

title: Become a Badlands Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Become a Junior Ranger at Badlands National Park! By completing a fun activity book, you can earn a Junior Ranger badge and pledge to explore, learn about, and protect the parks.

image.altText: a cartoon child stands next to a cartoon range and points at badlands formations

title: Badlands Astronomy Festival
shortDescription: Celebrate the spectacular sights and science of night skies at Badlands National Park's annual Astronomy Festival. Join astronomers, rangers, and visitors for activities, discussions, and programs about the night sky.

image.altText: three people stand silhouetted atop a badlands butte, pointing at the night sky.

title: Visit the Ben Reifel Visitor Center
shortDescription: There's something for everyone at the Ben Reifel Visitor Center in the North Unit of Badlands National Park. Swing by the information desk, watch the park film, check out a working fossil preparation lab, enjoy museum exhibits, or stop by the park bookstore.

image.altText: a sign reading ben reifel visitor center sits in front of jagged badlands formations.

title: Enjoy the Night Sky
shortDescription: Night Sky Viewings are a great way to see the dark skies of the Badlands. Park rangers and astronomy volunteers are available to point out objects in the night sky and help you look through telescopes.
seasonDescription: Night Sky Viewings typically take place May through September. Contact the Ben Reifel Visitor Center for more information on this year's programs.

image.altText: stars whir around the silhouette of a badlands butte in a circular motion

title: Campgrounds
shortDescription: Set up camp at one of Badlands National Park's two official campgrounds. Whether you're seeing views of the Sage Creek Wilderness Area or Cedar Pass, you're sure to enjoy an overnight stay in the park.

image.altText: a cloudy blue sky appears over jagged badlands formations, framed by green grasses in the foreground

title: Visit the White River Visitor Center
shortDescription: The White River Visitor Center is the main facility in the South Unit of the park. Be sure to stop by to pick up maps, enjoy museum exhibits, and chat with rangers about the significance of the Badlands and treaties in Lakota heritage.
seasonDescription: The White River Visitor Center is open seasonally, typically May through October.

image.altText: a squat tan building with a brown porch and a tree.

title: Backcountry Camping
shortDescription: Backcountry camping in the Badlands can be an exciting adventure for prepared and experienced hikers. Read more about rules, safety, and recommendations for backcountry campers here.

title: Pick Your Park Adventure in the Badlands

image.altText: a dirt road meanders through badlands buttes

title: Horseback Riding in the Badlands
shortDescription: Enjoy views of the Badlands from the saddle! Although no commercial horse rental or day rides are available in the park, Badlands invites horse owners to explore the Badlands Wilderness Area, consisting of 64,000 acres of eroded spires and mixed-grass prairie, or other designated areas of the park via horseback.

image.altText: a green rolling prairie melts into a pale blue, cloudy sky.

title: Visit the Fossil Preparation Lab
shortDescription: Visit the Fossil Preparation Lab in Badlands National Park, where visitors have the opportunity to engage with paleontologists and other park staff working on Badlands fossils!
seasonDescription: The Fossil Preparation Lab is typically open from the second week in June through the third week of September.

image.altText: a woman in a white lab coat works on an enormous fossil skull.

title: Spotting Wildlife in the Badlands

image.altText: a bighorn sheep pops its head up and over tall green grasses.

title: Hiking Badlands Back Roads With Your Dog
shortDescription: Back country roads are a great place to escape the everyday with your pet.
seasonDescription: The best time of year is while the daytime temperatures are in the 40s and 50s, late fall, winter, and early spring. These lower temperatures eliminate the chance of running into rattlesnakes, especially at dusk and dawn. You also avoid the potential for heatstroke for both you and your dog.

image.altText: Siberian husky pulls against his leash while walking along a road at Badlands National Park.

title: Drive Around the South Unit of the Badlands
shortDescription: Enjoy stunning views of Badlands National Park's South Unit by driving around its perimeter.
seasonDescription: These roads are open year round, but may be icy and dangerous in winter weather conditions.

image.altText: a large, flat table stands out from similarly brown badlands buttes.

title: Explore Sheep Mountain Table
shortDescription: Sheep Mountain Table is a great place to enjoy stunning views of the Badlands landscape. Whether you’re a hiker looking for a beautiful trail, a photographer scoping out a sunset spot, or simply a visitor seeking to explore the South Unit, Sheep Mountain Table offers incredible vist
seasonDescription: The road up to Sheep Mountain Table is open all year, but should not be driven in snowy or icy conditions. The road may be closed in the winter due to weather. Call the park at (605) 433-5361 for current conditions on this road.

image.altText: a dirt road leads between the low point of two buttes with a vibrant blue sky ahead.

title: Drive Sage Creek Rim Road
shortDescription: Enjoy views of badlands formations and glimpses of wildlife from Sage Creek Rim Road, one of the dirt roads located in the North Unit of Badlands National Park.
seasonDescription: Sage Creek Rim Road is open year-round, but may be closed in the winter due to weather conditions. Contact the park for more information about the current condition of Sage Creek Rim Road at (605) 433-5361.

image.altText: a black car on a dirt road approaches a herd of approximately 20 bison.

title: Drive Badlands Loop Road (Highway 240)
shortDescription: Enjoy the sights of Badlands National Park by driving its most popular road -- Badlands Loop Road, also known as Highway 240. Catch beautiful landscapes, informational exhibits, and glimpses of wildlife on this incredible drive.
seasonDescription: Watch for road conditions in the winter. Badlands Loop Road can be icy and slippery after a storm. The park plows the road when it is safe to do so, but the Loop Road does close due to weather conditions occasionally in the winter. Call the park at (605) 433-5361 to learn more about current road conditions.

image.altText: a paved road descends into a prairie landscape with buttes in the background.

title: Bicycling in the Badlands
shortDescription: Enjoy beautiful views of the Badlands without a windshield! Biking in the park offers a chance to experience scenery firsthand -- from the back of a bike, it almost feels like you can reach out and touch the rugged buttes and twisted spires. Read here to learn more about rules, safety, and suggested routes.

title: Stargazing in Big Cypress
shortDescription: Dark skies are essential natural, scientific, cultural, and economic resources. National Park sites, including Big Cypress National Preserve, are home to some of the last remaining dark skies in the country and are committed to protecting the night sky resource.

image.title: Big Cypress Milky Way
image.altText: The milky way dominating a starry sky over palm trees.
image.caption: Big Cypress is an excellent location to marvel at a dark sky.

title: Florida National Scenic Trail
shortDescription: This 36-mile contiguous section of the Florida National Scenic Trail is the southernmost portion of trail. This moderately strenuous hike can be difficult to traverse at certain times of year. The trail can be under up to 3 to 4 feet of water in the rainy season. During the dry season, there can be little to no water along the trail.

image.title: Florida Trail Backpacker
image.altText: A backpacker crosses over a bridge with poles in hand.
image.caption: Backpacker on the Florida Trail.

title: Nathaniel P. Reed Visitor Center
shortDescription: The Nathaniel P. Reed Visitor Center offers exhibits, bathrooms, picnic areas, a short boardwalk, and visitor information materials that will help orient the first-time visitor and provide the latest information on conditions to returning visitors.

image.title: Nathaniel P Reed Visitor Center
image.altText: Visitor Center illuminated at night with night sky visible and palm trees in the foreground
image.caption: Nathaniel P Reed Visitor Center

title: Fire Prairie Trail
shortDescription: This five-mile long out and back trail is a great way to see the sawgrass prairies of Big Cypress National Preserve. Good for all skill levels, this trail provides unique viewing areas of some of the more elusive wildlife here. Bring plenty of water, sunscreen, and a hat.

image.title: Fire Prairie Trail
image.altText: Trail running through sawgrass prairie with thunderstorm clouds in the distance
image.caption: Fire Prairie Trail

title: The Deep Lake Trail
shortDescription: This one-mile moderate hike to Deep Lake is a unique experiences. Deep Lake is over 95 feet deep, and the deepest lake in south Florida. Leave yourself about an hour to complete the trail. During the wet season (May-October) the trail can be wet and muddy.

image.title: Deep Lake
image.altText: Lake surrounded by plants
image.caption: Deep Lake

title: Turner River/Wagonwheel/Birdon Scenic Drive
shortDescription: This 16-mile loop drive is a great way to get away from the traffic along Highway 41, and take a slower drive through the Preserve. It offers the opportunity to see some of the many plant and animal species that call this place home.

image.title: Canal along Turner River Road
image.altText: Canal with alligator in the foreground and vegetation along both sides
image.caption: Canal along Turner River Road

title: Loop Road Scenic Drive
shortDescription: This 24 mile long drive, on a mostly unpaved gravel road, is a great scenic drive through the cypress swamp. See a variety of plant and wildlife species, while getting a closeup look at the park's namesake cypress trees.

image.title: Sweetwater Strand
image.altText: Cypress trees lining a channel of water.
image.caption: Sweetwater Strand

title: Gator Hook Trail
shortDescription: This moderately strenuous hike is a highly-immersive experience. Journey into the the Gator Hook Strand. Walk through water that is ankle to knee-deep. See alligators, snakes, birds, bromeliads (air plants), and mature cypress trees.

image.title: Gator Hook Trail
image.altText: Cypress trees surrounding a pool of water. Air plants can be seen on cypress trees
image.caption: Gator Hook Trail

title: Oasis Visitor Center Boardwalk
shortDescription: This short boardwalk is a great viewing platform of alligators, birds, turtles, and fish.

image.caption: Oasis Visitor Center Boardwalk

title: H.P. Williams Wayside Park
shortDescription: H.P. Williams Wayside Park is located immediately off of Highway 41. It includes a short boardwalk, picnic areas, and restrooms.

image.caption: H.P. Williams Wayside Park

title: Kirby Storter Roadside Park
shortDescription: This immersive boardwalk will take you into a cypress strand. Good for the whole family, this boardwalk is open daily from an hour before sunrise until an hour after sunset.

image.altText: Two men fishing from a flats boat
image.caption: Enjoying the day in fantastic bonefish habitat

shortDescription: Along with incredible array of marine life, Biscayne National Park is also home to significant populations of birds including protected species. Natural habitats for migratory stopover, feeding, and nesting make the park a wonderful place to watch and enjoy birds particularly in the winter months.

Natural habitats for migratory stopover, feeding, and nesting make the park a wonderful place to watch and enjoy birds particularly in the winter months.

image.title: Royal tern

Natural habitats for migratory stopover, feeding, and nesting make the park a wonderful place to watch and enjoy birds particularly in the winter months.

title: Become a Biscayne Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Join Diego the dolphin, Peter the panther and Aleesha the alligator in exploring three South Florida parks (Big Cypress National Preserve, and Biscayne and Everglades National Park). Pick up a booklet at the park visitor center and complete the required activities to earn a badge. Complete the entire book and earn three badges plus an exclusive South Florida junior ranger patch!

image.title: Become a Biscayne Junior Ranger!
image.altText: A girl and boy wearing ranger hats and badges peering out from a big shark jaw framing their faces
image.caption: Explore! Learn! Protect! Become a Biscayne Junior Ranger!

title: Become a Big Thicket Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Get a free activity booklet from the visitor center and earn a Junior Ranger badge. All ages are welcome!

image.title: Junior Ranger Badge
image.altText: Hand holding a wooden badge that says Junior Ranger, Big Thicket National Preserve.
image.caption: Big Thicket's new wooden badge features a bald cypress tree and cypress knees.

title: Hike the Sundew Trail
shortDescription: 0.3 to 1 mile roundtrip | Search for tiny red carnivorous plants known as sundews on an easy loop hike through a lush wetland pine savannah.
seasonDescription: Sundews produce their small pink blooms from April into early summer. Sundews are most abundant in winter and spring, becoming much harder to find through the summer and fall.

image.title: Sundew Trail
image.altText: A trail meanders through a forest of pines and ferns in the early morning light.
image.caption: Walk through a garden of ferns on the Sundew Trail.

title: Hike to the Sandhill Loop Trail
shortDescription: 4½ to 9.4 miles roundtrip | Look for longleaf pines, cacti, and solitude on this out-and-back and loop hike that leads to an arid sandyland ecosystem.

image.title: Sandhill Loop Trail
image.altText: A pine-needle covered path leads straight through a corridor of tall pine trees.
image.caption: Longleaf pines tower above as you wander on the Sandhill Loop Trail.

title: Hike the Kirby Nature Trail
shortDescription: 1½ to 2½ miles roundtrip | Experience the Big Thicket on a gentle loop hike through different kinds of forest. See majestic bald cypress trees and knees and Village Creek.

image.title: Village Creek
image.altText: An iron bridge spans a calm murky creek with dense forest along its banks.
image.caption: The iron bridge over Village Creek connects the Kirby and Turkey Creek trails.

title: Hike the Longleaf Pine Trail
shortDescription: 1 mile roundtrip | Stroll through a longleaf pine forest near the visitor center on Big Thicket's newest trail.

image.title: Longleaf Pine Trail
image.altText: A wooden platform set in a clearing in a pine forest.
image.caption: Observation platform in the longleaf pine savannah

title: Backcountry Camp at Big Thicket National Preserve
shortDescription: You can camp for free in much of the Big Thicket backcountry! Pick up a permit at the visitor center.

image.title: Backcountry Camping
image.altText: A camper builds a small fire while another camper sits on a fallen log with a tent in background.
image.caption: Camp in the Big Thicket backcountry with a free permit.

title: Bike the Big Sandy Trail
shortDescription: Take your mountain bike on a 14.7-mile roundtrip trail through the woods of the Big Sandy Creek Unit. See different kinds of forest habitats along the way.
seasonDescription: Hunting is allowed in the area from Oct 1 to Feb 28. Wear orange if you go during hunting season.

image.title: Biking Big Sandy
image.altText: low angle view of a mountain bike on a trail in the forest
image.caption: Ride through the woods on old logging roads.

title: Hike the Big Sandy Trail
shortDescription: 14.7 miles roundtrip | The Big Sandy Trail follows old logging roads through the woods. This is the only trail in the preserve open to bicycles and horses.
seasonDescription: Hunting is allowed in this area Oct–Feb; wear orange if you hike Big Sandy Trail during hunting season.

image.title: Big Sandy Trail
image.altText: A wide curving path lined with grass leads into a dense green forest on a sunny spring day.
image.caption: Hike the Big Sandy Trail to explore the backcountry of the Big Sandy Creek Unit.

title: Hike the Turkey Creek Trail
shortDescription: 14 miles one-way | The Turkey Creek Trail leads into the backcountry of the Turkey Creek Unit. Several trailheads at road crossings provide options for shorter hikes.

image.title: Turkey Creek Trail
image.altText: A trail leads through a forest of dense green shrubs and trees.
image.caption: The Turkey Creek Trail offers plenty of shade.

title: Hike the Beaver Slide Trail
shortDescription: 1 mile roundtrip | The Beaver Slide Trail is a hidden gem. This short hike leads hikers past several scenic ponds and sloughs. Keep an eye out for beaver dams along the way!
seasonDescription: The cypresses and beeches display bright fall colors in late November and early December. April is a great time to see bright green foliage. Mosquitoes are common in late spring and summer.

image.title: Beaver Slide Trail
image.altText: Pond reflecting the bright green trees growing from within and along its banks.
image.caption: See tranquil ponds on the Beaver Slide Trail.

title: Hike the Birdwatchers Trail
shortDescription: ¾ mile roundtrip | This short hike leads to views of Menard Creek and the Trinity River, an important migration route for birds.
seasonDescription: Winter and early spring are best for views of the Trinity River.

image.title: Menard Creek
image.altText: A wide, curving creek with trees and green shrubs lining its banks.
image.caption: See Menard Creek on the Birdwatchers Trail.

title: Explore the Rugged Lance Rosier Unit
shortDescription: The Lance Rosier Unit is the largest, wildest area of the Big Thicket. Discover its secrets on this scenic, unpaved auto tour.
seasonDescription: Hunting is allowed in the Lance Rosier Unit from October 1 to February 28. Wear orange if you visit during hunting season.

image.title: Road to Nowhere
image.altText: rutted dirt road leading into green forest
image.caption: This unnamed road leads to the "Bridge to Nowhere."

title: Hike the Woodlands Trail
shortDescription: 5 miles roundtrip | The Woodlands Trail loops through different kinds of forest landscapes and some hilly terrain. Find a scenic pond near the beginning of the trail.

image.title: Woodlands Trail
image.altText: A leaf-covered path leads straight through shrubs and thick forest on a late fall day.
image.caption: The Woodlands Trail loops through different kinds of forest.

title: Hike the Beech Woods Trail
shortDescription: 1½ miles roundtrip | See a forest of American beeches on this pleasant loop hike in the northeastern corner of the preserve.
seasonDescription: See bright green foliage in spring; fall colors in late November and early December.

image.title: Beech Woods Trail in Fall
image.altText: Colorful beech trees displaying red-orange-yellow colors along a trail leading through the forest.
image.caption: Beech Woods Trail is great in late fall, when the beeches display fall colors.

title: Hike the Pitcher Plant Trail
shortDescription: 1 mile roundtrip | Follow an easy loop that leads to a boardwalk through a pitcher plant bog where you can look for carnivorous plants in spring and summer.
seasonDescription: See pitcher plants' large yellow flowers in late March and April. The pitcher plants are usually small in the spring and reach their peak size in summer and early fall. The plants dry up in fall and winter.

image.title: Fly and Pitcher Plant
image.altText: fly sitting on the lip of a carnivorous pitcher plant
image.caption: A fly is tempted to go down the funnel of a pitcher plant.

title: Picnic by the Bayou
shortDescription: Have a picnic next to Pine Island Bayou at Edgewater Day-Use Area. A short trail starts here and follows the bank of the bayou.

image.title: Edgewater picnic table
image.altText: picnic table and metal grill in a forest next to a river
image.caption: Have a picnic next to Pine Island Bayou at Edgewater.

title: Birdwatch in a Wetland Pine Savannah
shortDescription: Grab your binoculars and birdwatch in a popular spot for our local and migratory birds.
seasonDescription: Birds are present year-round, but the annual spring migration is the recommended time of year for this activity.

image.title: birdwatcher
image.altText: woman in the woods looking upward with binoculars
image.caption: Remember to bring your binoculars!

title: Watch the Big Thicket Park Film
shortDescription: Watch a 16-minute film about the story of Big Thicket National Preserve at the visitor center or online.

image.title: Big Thicket Video
image.altText: foggy river view with text that reads "Big Thicket: America's First National Preserve"
image.caption: Watch the film online or at the visitor center.

title: Paddle Village Creek
shortDescription: Whether you want to go 2.1 miles or 21 miles, Village Creek is a great place for a paddle trip. Tall trees along the creek provide shade and white sand beaches invite paddlers to stop and relax for awhile.

image.title: Village Creek Canoeists
image.altText: 2 people paddling a green canoe on a creek
image.caption: Canoeists on Village Creek

title: Paddle Through a Cypress Slough
shortDescription: Paddle from one river to another through a cypress slough! Explore quiet oxbow lakes and bayous along the way on this 4.8-mile paddling trail.

image.title: Paddling a cypress slough
image.altText: a person kayaking on a creek in the woods
image.caption: Paddle past tupelos and cypresses growing out of the water.

title: Tour the South Rim Drive
shortDescription: The South Rim Drive is a scenic paved road that follows the canyon rim for 7 miles from Tomichi Point to High Point and features 12 overlooks.
seasonDescription: In winter and early spring, the South Rim Drive is closed to vehicles just past the visitor center. During this time, it is open only for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. The South Rim Drive generally opens to vehicular access in mid- to late April, but this is entirely dependent on weather conditions.

image.title: Gunnison Point in the fog
image.altText: An overlook lined with wooden fencing leading towards a canyon edge
image.caption: Gunnison Point in the fog

title: Cross-country Skiing at Black Canyon
shortDescription: In winter, South Rim Drive is closed to vehicles beyond the visitor center at Gunnison Point. As staffing and snow conditions allow, rangers groom the remainder of the road for cross-country skiing (skate and classic) and snowshoeing.

image.title: Cross-country skiing
image.altText: Two large signs behind a gate where people can cross-country ski
image.caption: South Rim Ski and Snowshoe Trail

title: Snowshoeing at Black Canyon
shortDescription: Although services and access are limited during winter, the park provides recreation opportunities for winter enthusiasts.

image.title: Snowshoeing at Black Canyon
image.altText: A line of people in different colored clothing snowshoeing on a snow-covered road
image.caption: Snowshoeing along the South Rim Drive

title: Hike Rim Rock Trail - South Rim
shortDescription: This 1-mile (1.6 km) trail, which meanders along the canyon rim, connects the South Rim Visitor Center to the South Rim Campground.

image.title: Hike the Rim Rock Trail
image.altText: Hike the Rim Rock Trail
image.caption: The Rim Rock Trail is moderately strenuous and offers great views of the canyon.

title: Hike Uplands Trail - South Rim
shortDescription: This .9-mile (1.4 km) trail links the Rim Rock Trail (near the campground) to the upper Oak Flat Loop Trail near the South Rim Visitor Center.

image.title: Uplands Trail
image.altText: Uplands Trail
image.caption: Uplands Trail

title: Stargazing at Black Canyon
shortDescription: Black Canyon has exceptional opportunities to view the night skies. Choose overlooks far from the road for optimal stargazing and astrophotography or join one of the park's telescope viewing programs during summer.

image.title: Telescope programs
image.altText: People standing around telescopes with red headlamps underneath a night sky
image.caption: Visitors can attend telescope programs scheduled throughout the summer.

title: Hike North Vista Trail - North Rim
shortDescription: Constructed by the Volunteers for Outdoor Colorado, the North Vista Trail offers some of the best scenic views and birding in the park. Difficulty varies from moderate to strenuous based on distance.
seasonDescription: North Rim of the Black Canyon is closed during winter.

image.title: View from Green Mountain
image.altText: Green and blueish canyon cliffs with mountains in the background
image.caption: View from Green Mountain

title: Hike Deadhorse Trail - North Rim
shortDescription: Deadhorse Trail takes hikers into the Black Canyon of the Gunnison Wilderness Area. It offers good views of Deadhorse Gulch and East Portal on the Gunnison River, as well as good birding.
seasonDescription: North Rim of the Black Canyon is closed during winter.

image.title: Deadhorse Trail
image.altText: Deadhorse Trail
image.caption: Deadhorse Trail

title: Drive East Portal Road

seasonDescription: The road is closed in winter, typically from November to April.

image.title: East Portal Road
image.altText: A view of a steep canyon and greyish river
image.caption: Views of Black Canyon from the East Portal Road

title: Tour the North Rim Road
shortDescription: The North Rim is reached by taking a gravel road from the east end of Crawford State Park. The North Rim Road provides access to 6 overlooks. The canyon walls on the North Rim are almost vertical, offering impressive views.
seasonDescription: The North Rim is closed to vehicles in the winter and early spring.

title: Hike Chasm View Nature Trail - North Rim
shortDescription: This short loop trail breaks out of the pinyon/juniper forest at the North Chasm View to provide excellent views of Painted Wall and Serpent Point.

image.title: Chasm View Nature Trail
