shortDescription: Are you a "Passport to Your National Parks" cancellation collector? Bryce Canyon has a cancellation stamp to commemorate your visit in your passport book.

image.title: Stamp Your Passport
image.altText: A merchandise display between two windows reads Passports with many stickers and stamps.
image.caption: Stamp your "Passport to Your National Parks" book in the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center.

title: Navajo/Peekaboo Combination Loop
shortDescription: Combine two of our most iconic trails, the Navajo and Peekaboo Loop trails, into a a mini Figure-8 combination loop. Start the hike at Sunset Point, descend down either side of the Navajo Loop (Two Bridges in winter), connect to the Peekaboo Loop (we recommend hiking it in a clockwise direction), and ascend Navajo back to Sunset Point.

image.title: Thor's Hammer from Navajo Loop
image.altText: A view over a landscape filled with red rock formations with the iconic thor's hammer formation.
image.caption: The Thor's Hammer hoodoo can be seen from Sunset Point and the Navajo Loop portion of this trail.

title: Navajo Loop Trail
shortDescription: The iconic Navajo Loop Trail begins and ends at Sunset Point. Its switchbacks wind between narrow walls of colorful limestone with views of towering Douglas-fir trees and the park's most famous hoodoo: Thor's hammer. The loop has two sides: Two Bridges and Wall Street. The Two Bridges side is open year-round, however, the Wall Street side is closed during the winter months. During this time Two-Bridges can be hiked as an out-and-back trail or combined with other trails.

image.title: Hiking Navajo Loop
image.altText: Hikers descend sandy switchbacks heading into a canyon of red rock with trees
image.caption: The famous Wall Street switchbacks on the Navajo Loop Trail.

title: Swamp Canyon Loop
shortDescription: Swamp Canyon appears relatively small and sheltered from the overlook, allowing the viewer to develop a more intimate connection with the landscape than some of the grander viewpoints in the park. The Swamp Canyon Loop, which starts at the viewpoint, is more rugged than the Bryce Amphitheater trails, taking hikers into a more forested backcountry hike. There is less signage on this hike and hikers are encouraged to carry a map.

image.title: Swamp Canyon Loop
image.altText: A large formation of red rock partially in shadow with threatening storm clouds above it
image.caption: The Swamp Canyon Loop takes you into the forested backcountry wilderness area of the park.

title: Figure-8 Combination
shortDescription: The Figure-8 Combination combines three amphitheater hikes, Queen's Garden, Navajo Loop, and the Peekaboo Loop, into one ultimate hike! We recommend a clockwise direction descending Queen's Garden, connecting to the Peekaboo Loop (we recommend hiking it in a clockwise direction), and ascending either side of the Navajo Loop (Two Bridges in winter). From there you can complete the trail by hiking back to Sunrise Point along the Rim Trail.

image.title: Hoodoos along Peekaboo Connector
image.altText: Red rock formations on top of a steep sandy slope with distant red rock formations in the background
image.caption: Views along the connector trail between the Queen's/Navajo trails and the Peekaboo Loop.

title: Queen's/Navajo Combination Loop
shortDescription: Our most popular hike in the park and the one we most recommend to first-time visitors. The Queen's/Navajo Combination Loop combines the open views and unique hoodoos of the Queen's Garden Trail with the iconic switchbacks and towering canyon walls of the Navajo Loop Trail. Descend Queen's Garden at Sunrise Point, ascend the Navajo Loop to Sunset Point, and then complete the loop back to Sunrise Point via the Rim Trail, enjoying views into the Bryce Canyon Amphitheater below.

image.title: Hikers on Queen's Garden
image.altText: Hikers walk along a trail towards an open archway in the red rock
image.caption: Hikers approach an archway on the Queen's Garden side of the Combination Loop

title: Queen's Garden Trail
shortDescription: The Queen's Garden Trail is the least difficult of the trails descending from the rim into the Bryce Canyon Amphitheater. Hike this out-and-back trail to the Queen Victoria hoodoo at the end of a short spur trail and experience the splendor of hiking amongst the hoodoos. This trail is commonly combined with the Navajo Loop to create a 2.9 mile round trip trail where you can descend at Sunrise Point and ascend at Sunset Point.

image.title: Queen's Garden from the Rim
image.altText: An overhead shot of a landscape with irregular red rock formations
image.caption: The view of the Queen's Garden Trail from the Rim.

title: Bryce Canyon Evening Program
shortDescription: Evening programs, typically offered from Memorial Day through Labor Day, offer topics that go beyond the rim! Check the calendar for daily times and locations. This is a Ranger’s Choice program offering an exploration into compelling stories, interesting themes, and unique resources that make Bryce Canyon special.
seasonDescription: Evening programs are presented from Memorial Day (May 29) to Labor Day (Sept. 4).

image.title: Bryce Canyon Evening Program
image.altText: A ranger stands in front of a screen before a seated audience.
image.caption: Bryce Canyon Evening Programs now take place in the Lodge Auditorium.

title: Riggs Spring Loop
shortDescription: The Riggs Spring Loop is a backcountry trail that begins and ends at Yovimpa Point. This trail travels through spruce, fir, and bristlecone forests offering beautiful views of distant cliffs. The western section of the trail is steeper and more heavily forested. Permits are not required to hike this trail, but all overnight stays require a permit.

image.title: Riggs Spring Loop Trail
image.altText: Forested hills with rock formations in the background
image.caption: Views from the Riggs Spring Loop

title: Rim Walk with a Ranger
shortDescription: Typically offered Memorial Day through Labor Day at Sunset Point at 2:00 p.m. Join a Ranger and experience the enchantment of the hoodoos, the history of the people who have passed through the amphitheaters for thousands of years, and the many ways the animals and plants have adapted to the unique ecosystems of Bryce Canyon National Park.

image.title: Rim Walk with a Ranger
image.altText: A landscape of red rocks at sunrise.
image.caption: Join a ranger for a half mile walk along the Rim Trail.

title: Hoodoo Geology Talk
shortDescription: Typically offered year-round at Sunset Point at 11 a.m. Geologists have spent years studying the unique geologic story of Bryce Canyon and its amphitheaters of hoodoos. Join the Ranger along the rim at Sunset Point to explore the evolution of the hoodoos and the groups of people who have passed through this magical terrain.

image.title: Hoodoo Geology Talk
image.altText: A ranger in uniform stands in front of a crowd with a background of red rock formations
image.caption: Ranger Anne gives a Hoodoo Geology Talk along the rim at Sunset Point.

title: Sunset Point to Sunrise Point Hike
shortDescription: The Rim Trail hike meanders along the rim of the iconic Bryce Canyon Amphitheater, giving you views of the hoodoos below. This portion of the Rim Trail, from Sunset Point to Sunrise Point, is the only paved section of this trail and is the easiest walk in the park. Pets are allowed on this trail but must remain on paved surfaces.

image.title: Sunset Point at Sunrise
image.altText: Looking down from above over a scenery of irregular red rocks with the sun rising behind them
image.caption: A view from Sunset Point at sunrise

title: Fairyland Loop
shortDescription: The Fairyland Loop is a quiet 8 mile hike that combines hiking along the plateau rim near Boat Mesa with a hike in the canyon with long views of the Bryce Amphitheater surrounded by unique hoodoos. You can start this hike at Fairyland Point or on the rim trail north of Sunrise Point at the Tower Bridge trailhead. We recommend hiking in a counter-clockwise direction. There is no shuttle pick-up at Fairyland Point, so you will need to hike to your starting point.

image.title: Fairyland Loop
image.altText: An overhead photo of red rock formations that appear to be glowing in the sun
image.caption: Unique hoodoo formations and long views can be seen along the Fairyland Loop.

title: See the Night Sky
shortDescription: Bryce Canyon is a sanctuary for natural darkness. Bryce Canyon's skies are so dark, that in 2019 the park was designated as a Gold Tier International Dark Sky Park. Since the park is open 24 hours a day, whether you head off to a viewpoint yourself or join a night sky ranger program, we welcome you to the dark side!

image.title: Sunrise Point Milky Way
image.altText: A silhouetted figure stands at a fenced overlook with the milky way arching above
image.caption: Sunrise Point is an easily accessible view with a 360 view of the night sky

title: Birdwatching
shortDescription: 175 different species of birds have been documented to frequent Bryce Canyon National Park. Some are just passing through. Others stay for an entire season. Fewer still make this their year-round home, but those that do are charming and charismatic.

image.title: Steller's Jay
image.altText: A blue and black bird with a black crest sits perched on a pine branch among green pine needles
image.caption: Steller's Jays are one of the park's most common year-round bird species.

title: Bristlecone Loop Trail
shortDescription: The Bristlecone Loop, an easy 1 mile hike, meanders through the forest atop this highest portion of the park, reaching elevations over 9,100 feet (2778 m). Here you will pass by bristlecone pines up to 1,800-years-old and experience vistas reaching into the Four Corners area.
seasonDescription: This trail may be inaccessible during mid-winter due to snow depths ranging from 2-15 ft. (.7-5 m)

image.title: View from the Bristlecone Loop Trail
image.altText: Red rocks topped with dark green trees slope down into a canyon of red rocks
image.caption: Views from the Bristlecone Loop Trail

title: Plan a Picnic
shortDescription: Looking for a good place to enjoy a picnic? Here is a list of Bryce Canyon picnic areas.

image.title: Rainbow Point
image.altText: A raven sits atop a brown sign that says Rainbow Point Elevation 9115.
image.caption: Rainbow Point, at the end of the Southern Scenic Drive, is a great place to stop for a picnic.

title: Go Cross-Country Skiing
shortDescription: A great way to explore Bryce Canyon in winter is on cross-country skis. Though it is illegal to ski off of the rim into the canyon, you can enjoy a variety of routes above the rim. These include sections of the Rim Trail along the edge of the Main Amphitheater, the Bristlecone Loop Trail; Paria Ski Loop; and the unplowed Paria View and Fairyland Point roads.

image.title: Cross-country skiing
image.altText: Two skiers ski amongst the trees.
image.caption: You can enjoy a variety of cross-country skiing routes above the rim.
image.credit: Photo courtesy of Jay Dash Photography

title: Bryce Amphitheater Traverse
shortDescription: The Bryce Amphitheater Traverse is a one-way hike combining the Peekaboo Loop with the Queen's Garden trail. Hikers descend from Bryce Point, turning left (clockwise) on Peekaboo Loop and then connecting to the Queen's Garden trail to ascend to Sunrise Point.

image.title: Hikers on Queen's Garden
image.altText: Two hikers descend down a trail from right to left with red rock formations in the background
image.caption: Hikers enjoying the views along the Queen's Garden trail.

title: The Rim Trail
shortDescription: The Rim Trail stretches from its beginning in the south at Bryce Point 5.5 miles (8.9 km) north to Fairyland Point. As it follows the edge of the Bryce Amphitheater area of the park, it connects to the park's most popular viewpoints: Inspiration Point, Sunset Point, and Sunrise Point. This relatively easy hike (depending on how much of it you do) offers spectacular views of the park's most popular area.

image.title: HIkers along the Rim Trail
image.altText: Two hikers pause along a path to view a red rock landscape of badlands and spires at a cliff's edge
image.caption: The Rim Trail provides views along the edge of the Bryce Amphitheater and connects viewpoints.

title: Tower Bridge
shortDescription: The Tower Bridge hike consists of the southern portion of the Fairyland Loop trail. This is an out-and-back trail that descends to a shady 1/4-mile spur trail leading to the Tower Bridge hoodoo. From there, hikers can return the way they came or continue to hike the entirety of the Fairyland Loop Trail.

image.title: Tower Bridge in snow
image.altText: A pale red rock formation covered in snow surrounded by green trees
image.caption: The Tower Bridge hoodoo is at the end of a 1/4-mile spur trail.

title: Peekaboo Loop
shortDescription: The Peekaboo Loop descends 670 feet (204 meters) from Bryce Point to this hoodoo-filled loop trail before ascending back up to Bryce Point. In summer months, hikers will encounter horses/mules on this trail. We recommend hiking this trail in a clockwise direction.

image.title: Peekaboo Loop
image.altText: An overhead view of red rock formations with a blue sky in the background
image.caption: Views from the Peekaboo Loop trail

title: Hat Shop
shortDescription: The Hat Shop trail descends from Bryce Point into the backcountry using the Under-the-Rim trail, offering views of the colorful cliffs of the Grand Staircase. This strenuous out-and-back hike leads down 1,380 feet (421 meters) over two-miles to a cluster of balanced-rock hoodoos before hikers turn around to return to Bryce Point. These narrow, orange pinnacles wear "hats" of large gray boulders, giving them a distinct appearance.

image.title: Hat Shop Overlook
image.altText: A landscape of red rocks in the foreground with hazy mountains on the horizon
image.caption: Views along the Hat Shop trail.

title: Stargazing at Bryce Canyon
shortDescription: Bryce Canyon's high elevation, clean air, and remote location creates some of the darkest skies in the country. In fact, in 2019 Bryce Canyon officially gained International Dark Sky status. During a new Moon on a clear weather night, you can see thousands of stars and the spectacular band of the Milky Way Galaxy shooting across the sky. We take pride in our ability to protect the night skies for the present and future generations.

image.title: Stargazing at Bryce Canyon
image.altText: The black silhouette of a person standing at a viewpoint with the milky way in the backgroundn
image.caption: Bryce Canyon is an International Dark Sky Park with some of the darkest skies in the U.S.

title: Snowshoe Hikes
shortDescription: Here at 8,000 feet (2,438 m) the scenery changes dramatically in the colder months. Come experience this magical season by taking a snowshoe-hike! Snowshoeing is allowed throughout the park on all trails so you can head out on your own or join a ranger-led snowshoe hike. These hikes are offered in winter as weather and snow conditions permit and are designed for all levels of experience, from beginner to expert.

image.title: Visitors Snowshoeing
image.altText: A group of people snowshoeing amongst the trees.
image.caption: Snowshoe Hikes

title: Mossy Cave Trail
shortDescription: Mossy Cave trail is one of the lowest elevation hikes in the park as well as one of the only hikes that begins with a climb and ends with a descent. This trail provides access to Water Canyon in one direction and to a sheltered overhang known as Mossy Cave in the other. This area is filled with mosses in the summer and icicles in the winter. Please stay on the main trail and respect all posted signs. Pets are not permitted on this trail.

image.title: Mossy Cave Trail
image.altText: A creek meanders through red rocks with red rock formations in the background.
image.caption: See a waterfall in the summer and icicles in the winter on one of the park's easier hikes.

title: Go Horseback Riding
shortDescription: Horseback riding is a great way to slow down and experience Bryce Canyon National Park. Horses have been used to explore Bryce Canyon National Park since before it was set aside for federal protection. To support this activity, the National Park Service completed 4.5 miles of foot and horse trails in 1931 that are still in use today.

image.title: Horseback Tour along Peekaboo Loop
image.altText: Three riders on horseback descend a trail bordered by pine trees and large rocks
image.caption: Horseback rides take riders within the Bryce Amphitheater and along the Peekaboo Loop

title: View Wildlife
shortDescription: The canyons and plateau of Bryce Canyon National Park are home to many animals. Park boundaries mean little to the migratory hummingbirds, nesting Peregrine Falcon, Rocky Mountain Elk and Pronghorn which daily cross through the forested plateau and amphitheaters. The search for food and water leads them to the best place to find sustenance and shelter. Many animals share habitats. Ebb and flow of populations is interdependent on all the members of the wildlife community.

image.title: Pronghorn
image.altText: Three male pronghorns stand together in a field of grass
image.caption: Pronghorn are seen in warmer months in meadows within and around the park.

title: Go For a Winter Hike
shortDescription: Many hikes are available to visitors during the winter season, in both the front and backcountry, but might require some additional equipment. For much of the winter the most popular trails are so icy that steep sections cannot be safely traversed without some sort of additional traction device for your hiking shoes or boots.

image.title: Hikers Along Queen's Garden in Winter
image.altText: Two hikers walk on a snow covered trail with mountains in the background.
image.caption: Two visitors enjoy a winter hike along the Queen's Garden trail.

title: Walk the Rim Trail
shortDescription: The Rim Trail stretches from its beginning in the south at Bryce Point 5.5 miles (8.9 km) north to Fairyland Point. As it follows the edge of the Bryce Amphitheater area of the park, it connects to Inspiration Point, Sunset Point, and Sunrise Point providing a relatively easy hike (depending on how much of it you do) that offers spectacular views of the park's most popular area.
seasonDescription: Those visiting in winter may find icy or snowy conditions and should dress accordingly. Footwear traction devices are highly recommended for all areas of the park in winter.

image.title: HIkers along the Rim Trail
image.altText: Two hikers pause along a path to view a red rock landscape of badlands and spires at a cliff's edge
image.caption: The Rim Trail provides views all along the edge of the Bryce Amphitheater and connects viewpoints

title: Backcountry Hiking and Camping
shortDescription: Experience the solitude of Bryce's forested backcountry! To preserve this experience, backcountry camping is permitted only in designated campsites. A backcountry permit must be obtained at the Visitor Center prior to any overnight trips.
seasonDescription: While permitted year-round, these trails may be difficult to access during mid-winter due to snow depths ranging from 2-15 ft (0.7-5 m).

image.title: Bryce Canyon Backcountry Hikers
image.altText: Two hikers wearing backpacks and using poles along a red rock path surrounded by forested cliffs.
image.caption: Hikers along the Under-the-Rim Trail near Rainbow Point.

title: See the Park Film
shortDescription: "A Song of Seasons" plays in the Visitor Center theater every half hour when the Visitor Center is open.

image.title: A Song of Seasons
image.altText: Title screen for A Song of Seasons film reads Bryce Canyon National Park
image.caption: "A Song of Seasons" explores the park in all four seasons.

title: Day Hikes
shortDescription: From easy walks along the edge of the famous Bryce Amphitheater using the Rim Trail to more strenuous adventures surrounded by the hoodoos below on the Peekaboo Loopthe park provides a variety of options for a variety of abilities to enjoy the park up close at your own pace. Visit the "Hiking Trails" button on the front page of this app for more trail details.

image.title: Hikers on Queen's Garden
image.altText: Two hikers pass through a hole carved in limestone feature along a trail lined with trees and rocks
image.caption: The Queen's Garden provides an opportunity to descend among the hoodoos of the Bryce Amphitheater

title: Hike the Hoodoos
shortDescription: To encourage visitors to stay healthy while having fun, Bryce Canyon National Park has developed an activity called "Hike the Hoodoos!" Part hike, part scavenger hunt, visitors must hike at least 3 miles on specially-marked trails and find "Hike the Hoodoos" benchmark survey markers along the way. Visitors may either obtain rubbings of the benchmarks, or take pictures of themselves with the benchmarks, to prove they hiked the required distance.

image.title: Bristlecone Loop Hike the Hoodoos Gazebo
image.altText: An interpretive wayside display shows a peregrine falcon beside text near a wooden gazebo
image.caption: The Bristlecone Loop has one medallion along its 1.0 mile (1.6 km) trail.

title: Go Snowshoeing
shortDescription: Snowshoeing is allowed throughout the park on all trails. But be aware that though snowshoes make it possible to travel through deep powdery snow, snowshoeing is still a highly strenuous activity. Most snowshoers enjoy walks along the Rim Trail, Bristlecone Loop, Fairyland Road, and Paria Road.

image.title: Paria Snowshoe Hike
image.altText: A group of people in snowshoes stand on the rim of a limestone spire-lined canyon
image.caption: Ranger-led Snowshoe hikes provide you with snowshoes and a deeper understanding of the park.

title: Hike to Hemmed-in Hollow
shortDescription: The picturesque Hemmed-in Hollow Falls cascades nearly 210 feet over rugged Ozark bluffs, making it the highest waterfall between the Rockies and the Appalachians. This waterfall only flows after a considerable amount of rain, so please be mindful of recent precipitation before you attempt this difficult hike. The Hemmed-in Hollow Trail is an extremely steep and strenuous trail that will humble even the most experienced hiker.

image.title: The Hemmed- in Hollow Falls Bluff
image.altText: A large sandstone bluff line surrounded by small redbud trees.
image.caption: The Hemmed-in Hollow Falls bluff line surrounded by small redbud trees.

title: Paddling Gilbert to South Maumee
shortDescription: This reach is about 12 miles which makes it one of the less crowded sections of the river.
seasonDescription: The Buffalo River flows freely for 151 miles. Paddling is open year-round, depending on water levels.The river level varies from month to month, year to year, and section of the river depending upon rainfall. The western end of the Buffalo usually has enough water in the spring. More water makes this section attractive for visitors seeking a higher level of challenge with whitewater kayaking. The middle and eastern sections of the river are usually calmer and less challenging.In dry years, the floating season is short and can end before summer ends.

image.title: Gilbert river access
image.altText: blue river in foreground with many cars parked on tan gravel at center
image.caption: Parking is permitted on the Gilbert gravel bar. Park at your own risk.

title: Hike the Lost Valley Trail
shortDescription: The Lost Valley Trail is an easy to moderate hike through a box canyon sculpted by Clark Creek. At 2.4 miles round-trip, this trail features caves, waterfalls, a Native American bluff shelter, and breathtaking groves of American beech trees.

image.title: Eden Falls
image.altText: Eden Falls on the Lost Valley Trail
image.caption: Eden Falls on the Lost Valley Trail

title: Hike to Hideout Hollow
shortDescription: The Hideout Hollow Trail leads to a rock shelter that was once inhabited by a group of World War I draft dodgers called The Slacker Gang. The Slacker Gang was made up of 9 young men from the Cecil Cove area who refused to join the army and decided to go into hiding in the wilderness. The 9 young men remained in hiding for months before surrendering to the draft in 1918.

image.title: Hideout Hollow
image.altText: A view out into a forest from the back of a rock shelter
image.caption: Looking out into the forest from the back of a rock shelter. A hiker stands in front of us.

title: Hike to Big Bluff
shortDescription: The Centerpoint Trail is a strenuous hike that traverses the Ponca Wilderness, winding down an old wagon road descending nearly 1,300 ft. to the Buffalo River. The "Goat Trail" spurs off of Centerpoint and leads to iconic Big Bluff, which offers outstanding panoramic views of the Buffalo River and the rugged Ozark Mountains that surround it.

image.title: Big Bluff
image.altText: The expansive view of the Ponca Wilderness and Buffalo River from Big Bluff
image.caption: The expansive view of the Ponca Wilderness and Buffalo River from Big Bluff

title: Hike the Buffalo Point Campground Trails
shortDescription: The Buffalo Point Campground Trails give campers, day hikers, and leashed dogs a chance to stretch their legs between the campground and the historic cabin area at Buffalo Point. Hike through a mix of a pine and oak trees, a cedar glade, and past a sinkhole as you explore. Wildflowers dot the trail system throughout the spring and summer. Finally, the view from the Overlook Trail is one that you do not want to miss!

image.title: Buffalo Point Overlook Trail
image.altText: A trail meanders through a forest.
image.caption: A trail meanders through a forest.

title: Hike the Rush Mine Level Trail and Morning Star Interpretive Loop
shortDescription: This .25 mile to 1.5 mile trail offers beautiful views of Rush Valley and gives hikers an understanding of the historic, mining, landscape. In the 1880s, zinc ore was discovered in the hills and claims were staked out along Rush Valley and neighboring Clabber Creek. Eventually, a community of homes and businesses developed along Rush Creek and endured until the 1960s. Come and explore this unique history as you hike Rush Mountain.

image.title: Rush Historic Structures
image.altText: A weathered old house stands in the Rush Historic District.
image.caption: A weathered old house stands in the Rush Historic District.

title: Hike the Indian Rockhouse Trail
shortDescription: A hike on the Indian Rockhouse reveals geologic formations commonly found on a limestone landscape and gives hikers an opportunity to explore locations where ancient peoples sought shelter.

image.title: Indian Rockhouse
image.altText: A fifty foot bluff shelter frames the green forest as rays of sunlight shine into the bluff shelter.
image.caption: Sunlight streams into the Indian Rockhouse

title: Paddle Kyles Landing to Erbie
shortDescription: Downstream from the hustle and bustle of Kyles Landing, one can find solitude among this comparatively quiet, 5.7-mile stretch of river snaking through the Ponca Wilderness. Paddlers will cruise through adrenaline-inducing shoals, tranquil pools, and haystack waves on this section with fascinating sandstone formations adorning the banks.
seasonDescription: Private boaters can paddle this section year-round if conditions allow. However, rental boaters must adhere to the season established by the authorized concessionaire from whom they rent. See https://www.nps.gov/buff/canoe-rentals.htm for more information.

image.title: Paddleboarding
image.altText: Paddleboarding the Upper District of Buffalo National River
image.caption: A paddleboarder on the Buffalo River

title: Paddle Steel Creek to Kyles Landing
shortDescription: Hands-down the most beloved and popular section of the upper river, the 8-mile section from Steel Creek to Kyles Landing meanders through the heart of the Ponca Wilderness past towering bluffs, hidden side canyons, and relics of early settlement. Alternating between tumbling rapids and long, cerulean pools, paddlers will delight in the variety of pace and challenge.
seasonDescription: Private boaters can paddle this section year-round if conditions allow. However, rental boaters must adhere to the season established by the authorized concessionaire from whom they rent. See https://www.nps.gov/buff/canoe-rentals.htm for more information.

image.title: Big Bluff
image.altText: Canoeing beneath Big Bluff
image.caption: Canoeing beneath Big Bluff in the Ponca Wilderness of Buffalo National River

title: Hike the Cecil Cove Loop
shortDescription: This 7-mile loop winds through the wooded valley following Cecil Creek. The trail crosses Cecil Creek 5 times in the first 2 miles, so it may not be passable during rainy season due to high water. The Cecil Cove Loop passes old home sites, historic cemeteries, and provides beautiful scenic views during leaf-off. CAUTION: Starting in 2021 the Cecil Cove Trail experienced and continues to experience landslides. Proceed on the trail at your own risk and use extreme caution.
seasonDescription: After major rain events (primarily in springtime), creek crossings may be impassable and dangerous.

image.title: Cecil Cove Loop
image.altText: Thunder Canyon Falls, located in a canyon near the Cecil Cove Loop
image.caption: Thunder Canyon Falls, located in a canyon near the Cecil Cove Loop

title: Hike the Beaver Jim Villines Homestead Trail
shortDescription: This short interpretive loop begins at the Ponca Access of the Buffalo River near the intersection of Hwy. 43 and 74. Walk across the low-water bridge (when passable) and follow signs up the hill. This easy trail passes the old homestead and farm buildings of "Beaver" Jim Villines, an early fur trapper and trader in Boxley Valley.

image.title: Beaver Jim's Cabin
image.altText: Beaver Jim's Cabin in Starlight
image.caption: Beaver Jim's cabin under a starry sky

title: Hike the Buffalo River Trail - Woolum to Dillards Ferry
shortDescription: A long and difficult hike, the Buffalo River Trail between Woolum and Dillards Ferry stretches a majority of the middle district of Buffalo National River.
seasonDescription: While the trail is open year-round, rain and snow may make sections of this trail impassable. Please consider recent weather and coming weather before attempting this trail.

image.title: Map of the BRT, Wollum to Dillards Ferry
image.altText: A map indicating the length, elevation, and route of part of the Buffalo River Trail.
image.caption: Be sure to come prepared for this long hike, and follow "Leave no Trace" principles!

title: Hike the Buffalo River Trail - Boxley to Pruitt
shortDescription: The Buffalo River Trail (BRT) winds along the bluffs and ridgelines on the south side of the river, traversing the Ponca Wilderness past scenic overlooks, old home sites, and cascading creeks. This portion of the BRT is 37 miles long and is a popular thru-hiking destination for backpackers. Day hikers can access the BRT in several locations for shorter out-and-back or point-to-point hikes.

image.title: Buffalo River Trail at Steel Creek
image.altText: Buffalo River Trail at Steel Creek
image.caption: Hikers start down the Buffalo River Trail at Steel Creek

title: Paddle Buffalo National River with Your Pet
shortDescription: Paddling with your pet can be an enjoyable activity at Buffalo National River. Here are some trip suggestions along with helpful tips to make your time at the river a safe and pleasant experience. Share the river with your four-legged buddy!

image.altText: Dog floating on a kayak

title: Paddling Mt. Hersey to Woolum
shortDescription: This reach provides numerous bluffs, shoals and pools along the way.
seasonDescription: The Buffalo River flows freely for 151 miles. Paddling is open year-round, depending on water levels.The river level varies from month to month, year to year, and section of the river depending upon rainfall. The western end of the Buffalo usually has enough water in the spring. More water makes this section attractive for visitors seeking a higher level of challenge with whitewater kayaking. The middle and eastern sections of the river are usually calmer and less challenging.In dry years, the floating season is short and can end before summer ends.

image.title: Skull Bluff
image.altText: green canoes on river in front of grey cliff with large hole at river level
image.caption: Canoers explore Skull Bluff.

title: Paddling Carver to Mt. Hersey
shortDescription: Unassuming in its beauty and variety, the float from Carver to Mt. Hersey demonstrates the transition from upper to middle river landscapes.
seasonDescription: The Buffalo River flows freely for 151 miles. Paddling is open year-round, depending on water levels.The river level varies from month to month, year to year, and section of the river depending upon rainfall. The western end of the Buffalo usually has enough water in the spring. More water makes this section attractive for visitors seeking a higher level of challenge with whitewater kayaking. title: Paddling Rush Landing to the White River
shortDescription: This 30-mile paddling trip cuts through the Lower Wilderness Area to the mouth of Buffalo National River. This is a stretch of river that a majority of visitors never see. As you paddle through the Lower Wilderness you will be greeted by Woodcock Bluff, Sheep Jump Bluff, and Elephant Head Rock. You can also park your boat at the mouth of Big Creek and hike a 1/4 mile to the Cold Spring Schoolhouse, a historic Works Progress Administration structure, from the 1930s.
seasonDescription: Private boaters can paddle this section year-round if conditions allow. However, rental boaters must adhere to the season established by the authorized concessionaire from whom they rent. See https://www.nps.gov/buff/canoe-rentals.htm for more information.

If you are planning to hike the trail to visit the tidepools, please be aware that tidepool access varies with the tides. Best low tide viewing is when sea level drops below 0.7 feet (0.2 m) above sea level. The trail and tidepools are inacessible outside park hours of operation. Please make sure you plan tidepool visits during low tides that occur during normal hours. Learn more about visiting the tidepools found in Cabrillo's Rocky Intertidal Zone.

shortDescription: The Colorado and Green rivers have played a significant role in shaping the landscape of Canyonlands. Boating is a great way to see the park from the bottom up, and affords boaters a unique perspective.

image.title: Kayaker

image.caption: Kayaking sections of flatwater is a unique way to experience the park from the bottom up.

title: Canyonlands Junior Ranger Program
shortDescription: There are a few ways to become a junior ranger at Canyonlands. Free junior ranger booklets are available at park visitor centers, or you can download them from the park website. Filled with fun activities, these books reveal the wonders of Canyonlands to kids and parents alike. After completing certain exercises, you can earn a junior ranger badge and signed certificate.

image.caption: Earning your own badge is a a fun way to learn about the park.

title: Backcountry Camping in Canyonlands
shortDescription: What better way to connect with this wilderness of countless canyons than on foot? Canyonlands offers hundreds of miles of hiking trails with designated campsites for overnight backcountry travel.

image.title: Backcountry Camping

image.caption: Tents underneath the stars in Canyonlands

title: Experience the Shafer Trail
shortDescription: The Shafer Trail is a challenging, unpaved backcountry road for recreational users seeking the experience of a lifetime. High-clearance 4WD vehicles with a low range gear (4LO) are required. ATVs, OHVs, or UTVs are not permitted inside the park.

title: Auto Touring in Canyonlands
shortDescription: There are hundreds of miles of unpaved roads in Canyonlands, providing access to various campsites, trailheads, and viewpoints in the park's backcountry. Most roads require high-clearance, low range four-wheel-drive. Roads range in difficulty from intermediate to extremely technical. Research your route thoroughly before attempting these roads.

title: Rock Climbing at Canyonlands
shortDescription: The sandstone towers at the Island in the Sky attract the most rock climbers. We do not see many climbers in the rest of the park due to the poor rock quality and a lack of established routes.

title: Stargaze
shortDescription: Capitol Reef protects extremely dark night skies, and is a wonderful place to stargaze.
seasonDescription: Check the forecast and dress for the weather.

title: Bicycle Touring
shortDescription: Bicycling touring in Capitol Reef offers opportunities to explore paved and unpaved roads throughout the park. Explore colorful canyons, beautiful vistas of red rock country, and the verdant Fruita Historic District by bicycle.
seasonDescription: Check the weather before your visit. Roads can become impassable due to changing weather.

title: Scenic Drive Tour
shortDescription: Take Capitol Reef's Scenic Drive, and experience colorful cliffs and deep narrow canyons from the comfort of your vehicle.
seasonDescription:
Depending on the weather, the Scenic Drive, Grand Wash, and/or Capitol Gorge roads may be closed. Check the forecast before your visit, or call 435-425-3791, press 1 for more information, and 3 for the daily weather forecast. 

Flush toilets are available year-round at the visitor center, and seasonally in the picnic area and campground. Pit toilets are available at the parking areas in Grand Wash and Capitol Gorge.

In the Fruita Historic District, look for the Doc Inglesby and Chesnut picnic areas, as well as tables and a water fountain near the Gifford House. At the end of Capitol Gorge Road, off the Scenic Drive, there are covered picnic tables as well as a pit toilet.

title: Driving the Burr Trail
shortDescription: Drive the scenic Burr Trail from Glen Canyon's Bullfrog district, along the bottom of Capitol Reef, through Grand Staircase, to Boulder, UT. Distance: 67 miles (108 km) one-way Mix of paved and dirt roads, impassable when wet Four-wheel drive sometimes required. No RVs.
seasonDescription:
The weather in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area is usually typical for the high deserts. Summers are extremely hot with little, if any, shade. Winters are moderately cold with night time lows often below freezing. Spring weather is highly variable and unpredictable with extended periods of winds. Fall weather is usually nice and mild, a great time to beat the heat (and the crowds!).

Temperatures can range from 110° F (38°C) in June & July to 0° F (-16°C) in December & January. Precipitation is generally light (less than 6 inches [15.2cm] annually) though heavy rains and flash flooding is possible during the summer and fall "monsoons." Parts of the road may be impassable in inclement weather.

title: View the Night Sky at Capulin Volcano
shortDescription: View the night sky at a volcano! Capulin Volcano National Monument is a International Dark Sky Place, which means thousands of stars are visible in the night sky. On Saturday evenings during the summer, rangers conduct dark sky programs here.
seasonDescription:
Winter is very cold at night but usually clear unless there is a snowstorm. Bring lots of warm layers and be prepared for very cold weather. The Geminids Meteor Shower in December is very spectacular.

Spring is cold and usually clear and windy. Bring warm, windproof layers when viewing the night sky.

Summer and especially July and August have afternoon thunderstorms with clouds that obsure the night sky until early in the morning. The Milky Way is visible and the Perseids Meteor Shower in August is particularly amazing. Nights can still be cold so make sure to bring a jacket.

Fall is cold and usually clear most nights. Bring warm layers.

image.altText: Milky Way Stars over Capulin Volcano at night

title: Drive to the Top of Capulin Volcano
shortDescription: Drive to the top of an extinct cinder cone volcano on a historic road. Once at the top you can enjoy the views from the parking area or hike trails down into the crater of the volcano or around the rim of the crater.
seasonDescription:
Winter is cold with snowstorms and ice common. The road is closed when it's actively snowing or icy, though it is plowed to keep it open though the winter. Mornings often bring freezing fog, which coats the top of the volcano in rime ice. The trails remain open, though they are icy in spots so be aware of hazardous surfaces.

Spring brings variable temperatures and sometimes a late snowstorm. It is usually also very windy.

Summer is warm with temperatures in the 80s and 90s F (27-35 C). In July and August, afternoon thunderstorms that can bring heavy rain and hail are common. Whenever lightning is spotted within a 10 mile radius of the top of the volcano, both the top of the volcano and the road are closed for visitor safety as lightning often strikes the volcano. Heavy rain also sometimes causes cinder slides after which the road is closed to clear the cinders and mud off.

Fall brings cooling temperatures and variable weather.

image.altText: View of the Rim Trail to the left and the prairie and other volcanoes in the distance from the top

title: Explore the Visitor Center at Capulin Volcano
shortDescription: Learn more about volcanoes and Capulin's eruption by exploring the exhibits in the visitor center.
seasonDescription: The visitor center is open all year long, though it may be closed for inclement weather. Check the park website for current hours. It is also closed Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, and New Year's Day.

image.altText: Exhibits in the Visitor Center with a large volcanic bomb on the left and touch table on the right

title: Hike Trails at the Base of Capulin Volcano
shortDescription: The trails at the base of Capulin Volcano are less traveled and quieter than the ones on the top and offer a different view of the volcanic geology here.
seasonDescription:
Winter brings with it snow and ice as well as wind, so be prepared for cold weather and slippery areas on the trails. Occasionally the visitor center will close due to weather, and the restrooms and water at the picnic area are closed in the winter. However the trails are always open to hikers even when the visitor center is closed.

Spring is usually quite windy and occasionally there are snowstorms so be prepared for a variety of weather. Flowers usually start popping up along the trails in late May or early June.

Summer is usually mild, though occasionally temperatures will reach the high 90s F (36 C). The trails have little shade so be sure to wear sunscreen and bring water when hiking. July and August bring afternoon thunderstorms, so keep an eye on the weather and head back whenever there is lightning or thunder as lightning strikes the volcano quite often.

Fall brings cooler temperatures and sometimes snow or ice so be prepared for temperature changes. The gambel oak that covers the volcano changes colors from green to a dull orange around the end of October.

image.altText: View of a Solidified Lava Lake with Prairie Grass and Sunflowers on the Boca Trail

title: Become a Junior Ranger at Capulin Volcano

title: Hike the South Rim Trail
shortDescription: The South Rim Trail is the a moderate to hard trail, featuring several different scenic viewpoints.
seasonDescription: The South Rim Trail is best experienced during the summer. Cool temperatures at high elevation keep this trail and the park cooler than surrounding hiking opportunities. During the spring and fall, snow and ice are possible which can make the trail hazardous and muddy. During the winter, heavy snowfall covers the park - visitors are strongly encouraged to stay away from the rim of the amphitheater during the winter for their safety.

shortDescription: by the Island Ford Visitor Center to pick up your Junior Ranger Booklet and get to work on becoming the next park's Junior Ranger.

shortDescription: Escape the crowds with a short drive to Gold Branch in east Cobb County. Hike down to Bull Sluice Lake to wet a line or have a picnic in the woods. If you wish, take a nice long hike to really get away from the crowds.

title: Chattahoochee Cycling
shortDescription: What are you waiting for? Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area has bike trails to ride just outside the city. Some paved miles for people on their road bikes and some miles for the mountain bikers. Just remember to share the trails with pedestrians.

image.altText: Cyclist giving a thumbs up as he rides on trail with woods in the background.
image.caption: Isn't it a great day for a ride?

shortDescription: The Cochran Shoals Fitness Loop is a true multi-use trail. You'll find mothers pushing strollers, joggers avoiding the afternoon traffic, and cyclist in their cool p-jays.

image.title: Cochran Shoals Fitness Loop
image.altText: Snowy winter scene of solitary walker.
image.caption: I won't let a little snow stop me.

title: Trail to Natural Bridge
shortDescription: This trail is a great opportunity to avoid the crowds in March and to see wildlife. It crosses through a stunning variety of ecosystems before ending at a bridge overlook. The small water-carved bridge is located across the canyon. This hike is about the journey, not the bridge. Return the same way.

image.altText: Rock formations with a natural bridge featured.
image.caption: The bridge can be seen from a distance at the end of the trail.

title: Hike the Trails at Chiricahua
shortDescription: 17 miles of trails will take you into a wilderness of rocks. Chiricahua offers a range of day hiking options from easy to strenuous.
seasonDescription: Hiking the Chiricahua Mountains can be amazing any time of year. Summer temperatures can often reach the 80s and 90s. Summer monsoons can provide cooler temperatures than the rest of Arizona. Winters can leave ice or snow on the trails, but daytime highs are often pleasant. Come prepared for quick shifts in weather.

image.title: Hike the Trails
image.altText: a family hikes away from the camera with large rock formations towering over and scrubby trees
image.caption: Hiking trails travel right next to rock pinnacles.

title: Horseback Riding at Chiricahua
shortDescription: Come explore the "Wonderland of Rocks" on horseback!

image.title: Horseback Riding

image.caption: Horseback Riding

title: Birdwatching at Chiricahua

image.caption: Acorn woodpeckers are a colorful site.

title: Lower Rhyolite Canyon Trail
shortDescription: A good way to view the rocks without driving up the road, this mostly-level trail takes you to Rhyolite Canyon, a canyon lined with rock pinnacles. Walk 1.5 miles / 2.4 km until you reach the junction between Upper Rhyolite Canyon and Sarah Deming trails. Return the same way.

image.title: Lower Rhyolite Canyon
image.altText: Cactus in front of large canyon
image.caption: Lower Rhyolite Canyon

title: Sugarloaf Mountain Trail
shortDescription: This moderate trail to the top of Sugarloaf Mountain is 1.8 miles/2.8 kilometers roundtrip. Rising above the surrounding canyons, the summit of Sugarloaf Mountain at 7,310ft/2,228m is one of the highest points in the monument. The dark rock is dacite, evidence of a lava flow. Lightning activity is monitored from the Civilian Conservation Corps constructed fire lookout during the summer. Return the same way. Access is from the Sugarloaf parking lot.

image.title: View from Sugarloaf Mountain

title: Echo Canyon to Visitor Center

It goes downhill through spectacular rock formations in Echo Canyon. The last half of the hike is in shaded oak woodlands. Make sure you have transportation back to your vehicle or ride the seasonal hikers' shuttle at 9:00 am.

image.altText: Hillside full of rock formations
image.caption: Rhyolite Canyon

title: Echo Canyon Grottoes
shortDescription: Just 1/2 mile from the parking area, on the Echo Canyon Trail, visitors can be amazed by the tunnel-like rock formations. The Echo Canyon Grottoes are a great option for those who want to experience the rocks but have limited time or mobility.
seasonDescription: This trail is spectacular year-round. Summer may bring high temperatures and dangerous sun exposure OR monsoon rain and lightning. Winter may be icy for days after snow events.

seasonDescription: This trail is spectacular year-round. Summer may bring high temperatures and dangerous sun exposure OR monsoon rain and lightning. Winter may be icy for days after snow events.

Start the loop to the left and hike clockwise for the best views and easiest walking. Lots of rock steps make this a challenging loop, but it's worth the effort. There are three different ways to get to the loop, all of them being the same distance.

title: The Big Loop
shortDescription: For folks wanting to do everything, this 9.5 mile route consists of the Echo Canyon, Upper Rhyolite Canyon, Sarah Deming, Heart of Rocks, Big Balanced Rock, Inspiration Point, Mushroom Rock, and Ed Riggs trails. It features our balanced rocks. The trail begins from the Echo Canyon trailhead.

image.caption: View from The Big Loop trail

title: Bonita Creek Trail
shortDescription: Winding along Bonita Creek, usually dry, this trail connects the Bonita Creek and Faraway Ranch Picnic Areas. Look for wild animals, including migrating birds, deer, coatimundi, and javelina. This is an easy 1/2 mile trail.

image.title: Bonita Creek Trail
image.altText: Trees and desert plants, brown grass, and mountain in the background.
image.caption: View from Bonita Creek Trail

title: Winter Camping
shortDescription: Immerse yourself in the solitude of the "Silent City".

image.title: Winter Camping
image.altText: Two tents in the snow at a campsite in the City of Rocks.
image.caption: Immerse yourself in the solitude of the "Silent City".

title: Explore the Night Sky
shortDescription: A day in the park doesn't have to end when the sun goes down! A whole new world comes alive at night and is waiting to be explored. The dark sky over City of Rocks is an excellent place to experience the beauty of the night.

image.title: Balancing Boulder
image.altText: Silhouettes of 3 large pinnacles and a smaller balanced boulder under a purple and blue starry sky.

title: Become a City of Rocks Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Junior Rangers "Explore, Learn, and Protect" their national parks. Pick up a free booklet from the Visitor Center to learn about geology, nature, and history in City of Rocks National Reserve. Complete fun activities like scavenger hunts, fill-in-the-blanks, and word searches. Once you've finished the recommended number of activities, turn in the booklet, take the park oath, and earn your Junior Ranger Badge!

image.title: Exploring City of Rocks
image.altText: Kids play around a water filled depression on a granite slab formation.

title: Geologic & Historic Sites Driving Tour
shortDescription: A self-guided journey to discovering geologic wonders and historical sites in City of Rocks National Reserve. As you drive through the Reserve you will be able to view the featured rock formations and historic sites from your vehicle. Use your imagination as you observe the rocks to see animals, faces, and buildings and experience what it might have been like in this area in the past as you explore remnants of history.

image.title: Driving Through City of Rocks
image.altText: A vehicle driving on a dirt road with colorful fall foliage alongside.

title: Disc Golf at Castle Rocks
shortDescription: With the dramatic Castle Rocks landscape in the backdrop, this small three-hole disc golf course is fun for all ages and abilities. The lush grassy area of Castle Rocks Ranch has large shady trees that provide a welcome reprieve from summer heat. There are bathrooms, and picnic facilities in this area with more a short distance up the road at Stines Creek.

image.title: Disc Golf
image.altText: Two people watch a yellow disc flying toward the metal disc golf basket, castle rocks in the back.

title: Rock Climbing in City of Rocks and Castle Rocks
shortDescription: Popular since the 1970's, City of Rocks granite is internationally renowned among climbers. There are over 600 routes here, both traditional and sport. Climbs vary from 30-600 feet, rating from the relatively easy 5.6 to the extremely difficult 5.14.

image.title: Rock Climbing
image.altText: Two climbers ascend neighboring routes in a scenic granite ravine.

title: Hunting in City of Rocks and Castle Rocks
shortDescription: City of Rocks National Reserve was formed in part to preserve traditional uses of the land. It is one of few National Park System units that allows hunting. State and federal land around the Reserve, such as Castle Rocks State Park, Sawtooth National Forest, and BLM, are also open to hunting.

image.title: Hunting
image.altText: A man wearing camouflaged clothing with a bow and arrows on his back takes in a grand view.

title: Archery Course at Castle Rocks
shortDescription: This course at Castle Rocks State Park has more than 20 stations. Shot distance ranges from 20 yards to 60 yards depending on target size.

image.title: Archery
image.altText: A girl with a bow stands in front of a 3d foam target of a mountain goat.

title: Bike the Tea Kettle Trail
shortDescription: Tea Kettle Trail is a great mountain biking trail that runs between Bread Loaves and Elephant Rock. The trailhead can be accessed from the Bread Loaves group camping parking lot or the parking area next to Elephant Rock. From one end to the other, the trail is 3 miles. Mountain bikers can connect with other trails or ride on the road to create loops and longer rides.

image.title: Bikers in City of Rocks
image.altText: Two people ride bikes through juniper trees and sage brush.

title: Winter Photography
shortDescription: Capture spectacular winter views.

image.title: Winter Photography
image.altText: Photographers set up for a dramatic picture of storm clouds swirling around granite spires.

title: Winter Birding
shortDescription: Spot over 40 species during winter months.

image.title: Owl
image.altText: Owl in flight, snow in the backdrop.

title: Snowshoeing
shortDescription: Get out and explore the winter trails.

image.title: Snowshoeing
image.altText: Two people snowshoeing during a snow storm in Castle Rocks
image.caption: Get out and explore the winter trails.

title: Skiing
shortDescription: Tour the frosty granite spires.

image.title: Skiing
image.altText: Skis and poles sticking upright in the snow.
image.caption: Tour the frosty granite spires.

title: Ice Climbing
shortDescription: Explore epic rock and ice.

image.title: Ice Climbing
image.altText: A person climbing an ice formation hanging from the granite.
image.caption: Explore epic rock and ice.

title: Horseback Riding in City of Rocks
shortDescription: Horseback riding can be one of the best ways to experience much of the Reserve's backcountry.

image.title: Horseback Riding
image.altText: Horses and riders in a line traveling up a dusty narrow trail on a mountainside.

title: History of Pinnacle Pass Guided Hike
shortDescription: Join rangers on a short 1.10 mile guided hike to Pinnacle Pass. This feature of the California Trail is located on private land and only accessible to the public through this hike. The hike is easy to moderate, with a small hill leading up to the pass. Along the way you will see where the California Trail went south and met with the Salt Lake Alternate Trail, you will see emigrant signatures, and it is common to see snakes and fairy shrimp!

image.title: Pinnacle Pass
image.altText: Two rocky hills in the distance with a visible pass in between them. Spectacular cloudy sunset.

title: Hike the Geological Interpretive Trail
shortDescription: City of Rocks is well known for its geologic wonders. The Geological Interpretive Trail will guide you through many types of unique rock features and formations and explain the forces that created them. There are 12 interpretive stations along the 0.5 mile trail. The trail rises 160 feet in elevation, makes a loop, then retraces much of the same route back for a total of 1 mile.

image.title: Geologic Formations in City of Rocks
image.altText: Jagged granite pinnacles jutting up.

title: Hike Creekside Towers Trail
shortDescription: Creekside Towers is an out-and-back 1.2-mile trail. Nearby trails (such as Stairways or South Fork Circle Creek) could make for a longer, more adventurous loop. The gentle grade of 122 feet relative elevation is suitable for families with children or anyone looking for an easier hike. In spring and early summer enjoy the running creek and small cascading waterfall. Outstanding scenery, sculpted granite pinnacles, and a diversity of plants and animals await you.

image.title: Creekside Towers Creek
image.altText: A creek cascades wildly down a granite slab.

title: Fishing at the Castle Rocks Fish Pond
shortDescription: Besides fishing, the pond is also a great place to watch birds and wildlife. There is a walking path, benches to sit and enjoy the scenery, as well as a picnic table and fire ring.

image.title: Fishing at the Castle Rocks Pond
image.altText: A park ranger helps a young girl fishing on the bank of the pond.

title: Camping
shortDescription: Camping in City of Rocks, or nearby Smoky Mountain Campground is a great way to enjoy being out in nature. Relax beneath the cool shade of aspen, juniper, mountain mahogany, or pine. Spend the night surrounded by impressive granite formations and starry skies.

image.title: Camping in City of Rocks
image.altText: A small bumper pull camper parked with a spectacular view of distant granite formations.

title: Archeology of Castle Rocks Guided Hike
shortDescription: During this 1.10 mile ranger guided hike you will get to explore the archaeology of Castle Rocks State Park. The hike is easy to moderate with some elevation change. You will explore Native American pictographs, petroglyphs, and a rock shelter that was occupied for hundreds of years. Through this hike you will get a sense of what the landscape and everyday life was like thousands of years ago.

image.title: Shock and Awe Shelter
image.altText: View from inside a dark granite cave out to a bright sunny day, mahogany trees at the entrance.

title: Backcountry Camping in Indian Grove
shortDescription: Backcountry camping is available in the designated Indian Grove area within City of Rocks National Reserve. Permits are required for backcountry camping and must be approved prior to your arrival.

image.title: Indian Grove Area
image.altText: Grassy meadow with purple wild iris surrounded by lush pine trees.

title: Hike the City of Rocks Loop
shortDescription: This remote loop hike is a ranger favorite. The combination of pine trees, rock formations, and epic views offer a surprise at every turn of the trail.

image.title: View from North Fork Circle Creek Trail
image.altText: 2 prominent granite features jut up in the foreground with a rocky mountainous landscape behind.

title: Wayside Exhibits Loop at the Visitor Center
shortDescription: This short 0.23 mile loop trail behind the Visitor Center will introduce you to some of the resources that make City of Rocks special. You can see up close examples of the wagons emigrants used as they traveled along the California Trail.

image.title: Visitor Center Loop Trail
image.altText: A wayside exhibit sign next to a prairie schooner wagon replica, beautiful sunset clouds.

title: Birding in the City of Rocks Checklist Area
shortDescription: Few places in Idaho other than the City of Rocks Checklist Area offer such a high concentration of bird species, making this a top birding destination. The Checklist Area includes the National Reserve, Castle Rocks State Park, and the Almo and Upper Raft River valleys. These are some of the best locations in the Idaho for observing Pinyon Jay, Virginia's Warbler, Gray Flycatcher, Juniper Titmouse, Bushtit, Greater Sage-Grouse, Black-throated Gray Warbler, and Plumbeous Vireo.

image.title: Birding
image.altText: A Bullock's Oriele, yellow bird with black on its wings head and tail and white on wings.

title: Shop for Souvenirs at the Visitor Center
shortDescription: Stop in to chat with a Ranger or pick up maps, guide booklets, and other informative resources. We offer souvenirs such as books, mugs, apparel, postcards, stickers and more.

image.title: Visitor Center Store
image.altText: Retail area with books, maps, hats, and shirts lining the walls.

title: Snowmobiling
shortDescription: Take the road less traveled.

image.title: Snowmobiling
image.altText: Person riding a snowmobile in the City of Rocks.
image.caption: Take the road less traveled.

title: Accessible Visit to Colorado National Monument
shortDescription: Explore accessible ways to visit Colorado National Monument, from visitor center features to short trails to overlooks into the canyons.

image.title: Veterans Hike with Resiliency Ranger
image.altText: woman using wheelchair and service animal points to Serpents Trail sign with uniformed ranger behind
image.caption: Join a Resiliency Ranger program during the summer!

title: Short Hikes in the Monument
shortDescription: These out-and-back trails start from along scenic Rim Rock Drive in Colorado National Monument. All are less than two miles round-trip, perfect for short treks from the car to get better views of these outstanding canyons.
seasonDescription: Occasionally, winter snows or shoulder-season rainstorms will leave trails icy or muddy. Check weather conditions before your visit.

image.title: Short Hikes in the Monument
image.altText: two adults and two children stand on dirt path looking out towards wide open canyons
image.caption: Even a short hike can get you unparalleled views of the canyons.

title: Junior Ranger of the Monument
shortDescription: Become a Junior Ranger of Colorado National Monument by completing a booklet (pick up at Saddlehorn Visitor Center) to earn your badge.

image.title: Junior Ranger booklet from the Monument
image.altText: colorful booklet with illustrations of canyon sandstone towers
image.caption: Junior Ranger booklet from the Monument

title: Backpacking in the Monument
shortDescription: Backpacking or backcountry camping in the Monument is a great way to deepen your visit with the canyons. Monument, No Thoroughfare, and Ute Canyons, as well as Black Ridge and Monument Mesa, are excellent areas for overnights in the backcountry.

image.title: Sunset at Upper Ute Canyon
image.altText: sunset turns canyon walls a vibrant red-orange
image.caption: Sunset at Upper Ute Canyon

title: Start at Saddlehorn Visitor Center
shortDescription: Begin your visit to Colorado National Monument at the visitor center. Watch the orientation film, explore the exhibit hall, shop for souvenirs at the park store, talk with a ranger, earn your Junior Ranger badge, and get your National Parks Passport stamp.
seasonDescription: Hours change seasonally, so check the Operating Hours & Seasons for the most up to date information.

image.title: Saddlehorn Visitor Center
image.altText: low, flat brown building surrounded by trees and parking lot, backdrop of steep canyon walls
image.caption: Saddlehorn Visitor Center

title: Hiking from Saddlehorn Visitor Center
shortDescription: These hikes can be accessed from the visitor center. Several short hikes to incredible views begin here, as well as a longer trail perfect for a night in the backcountry. Come to the visitor center for an orientation film, Junior Ranger booklets, and more.
seasonDescription: In spring and summer, you will often find lots of wildflowers on these trails. In winter, some people choose to cross country ski on Black Ridge when there's enough snow.

image.title: Saddlehorn Visitor Center
image.altText: A low, mostly flat building with a flagpole and shrubs, standing before a desert canyon
image.caption: Saddlehorn Visitor Center

title: Hiking in Colorado National Monument
shortDescription: Colorado National Monument trails offer a hike for everyone from 0.25 mile to over 14 miles, from flat accessible surfaces to rugged canyons.
seasonDescription: Trails are open all year. During the winter, in shaded portions the trails can be icy. Cleated treads are recommended.

image.title: Ute Canyon Trail
image.altText: Dirt trail goes into desert canyon
image.caption: Discover beautiful canyons, interesting plants and perhaps even a glimpse of the bighorn sheep.

title: Road Biking on Rim Rock Drive
shortDescription: Road biking the 23-mile Rim Rock Drive offers cyclists a challenging ride with stunning views.

image.title: Cyclists on Rim Rock Drive
image.altText: five road cyclists surrounded by red slickrock and green shrubbery
image.caption: Cyclists on Rim Rock Drive

title: Travel on Rim Rock Drive
shortDescription: For panoramic views of Colorado National Monument's canyons and rock monoliths, a trip along Rim Rock Drive is a must.
seasonDescription: Rim Rock Drive is open year-round. During the winter, there may be short closures for snow removal from large storms. In the winter, icy spots can persist in shaded areas when most of the rest of the road is clear.

image.title: Rim Rock Drive
image.altText: Looking down at road as it curls into and out of red rock canyon.
image.caption: A look down at Rim Rock Drive from Fruita Canyon Overlook

title: Monument Canyon Loop Hike
shortDescription: This 5-mile loop can be extended for a deeper exploration into Monument Canyon. We recommend starting at the Lower Monument Canyon Trailhead to avoid the steep switchbacks below Rim Rock Drive.
seasonDescription: In spring and summer, you will often find lots of wildflowers on these trails. Some people choose to backpack and stay overnight in the canyons for excellent views of the night sky.

image.title: Lower Monument Canyon Trailhead
image.altText: gravel road leads to dirt parking lot, backdrop of sparsely vegetated canyon slops
image.caption: Lower Monument Canyon Trailhead

title: Hiking from Devils Kitchen Picnic Area
shortDescription: Many incredible hikes begin just inside the East Entrance to the Monument. Choose from short day hikes to longer, more difficult backcountry travel.
seasonDescription: In spring and summer, you will often find lots of wildflowers on these trails. In spring, you may find pools and waterfalls in No Thoroughfare Canyon.

image.title: Devils Kitchen Picnic Area
image.altText: Stone structure with open walls covering picnic tables, in an open area surrounded by canyon walls
image.caption: Devils Kitchen Picnic Area

title: Climbing in the Monument
shortDescription: The sandstone cliffs and spires of Colorado National Monument attract hundreds of climbers a year. Most routes in the park require "traditional" climbing techniques. The installation of new permanent hardware is prohibited.

image.title: Climber in Crack
image.altText: rock climber with red helmet perched in red sandstone crack
image.caption: Rock climber on Independence Monument

title: Shop for Monument Souvenirs
shortDescription: Shop for souvenirs at the Colorado National Monument Association (CNMA) park store, located in Saddlehorn Visitor Center. Preserve your memories of the Monument with keepsakes, apparel, stickers, books, and more. Proceeds from CNMA's retail operations, memberships, and donations support the Monument’s educational, interpretive, and scientific programs.
seasonDescription: Hours change seasonally, so check the Operating Hours & Seasons for the most up to date information.

image.title: CNMA store
image.altText: spacious store, wall-sized windows, various items for sale, hats, postcards, books, walking sticks
image.caption: CNMA store, located in Saddlehorn Visitor Center

title: Snowshoeing at Crater Lake
shortDescription: Snowshoeing is a popular activity during the long winter at Crater Lake National Park.

image.title: Snowshoeing at Crater Lake
image.altText: People snowshoeing with Crater Lake in the background.
image.caption: Visitors enjoy snowshoeing at Crater Lake.

title: Scenic Rim Drive
shortDescription: The historic Rim Drive includes 33-miles (53-km) of lake views, panoramic vistas, forests and meadows. The contours of the road were designed to compliment the natural landscape, and disappear from view as you look across the lake from any point.
seasonDescription: Snow can occur anytime of the year resulting in hazardous conditions and temporary road closures. Please drive with caution.

image.title: View of Rim Drive from Watchman Peak
image.altText: View of Rim Drive from Watchman Peak. Hillman Peak and Crater Lake in the background.
image.caption: View of Rim Drive from Watchman Peak

title: Biking at Crater Lake
shortDescription: Each year, increasing numbers of cyclists come to Crater Lake National Park to ride around the lake on the physically demanding, 33 mile (53 km) Rim Drive. Steep hills at high elevation may encourage even the most fit riders to pause at many of the road's thirty overlooks and pull-outs. The payoff however is spectacular scenery, viewed at a pace that few visitors choose to take enough time for.

image.title: Visitors Biking around Crater Lake
image.altText: Two visitors on bikes with Crater Lake in the background.
image.caption: Visitors biking around Crater Lake

title: Visit Craters in Winter
shortDescription: Tour a lava wonderland blanketed in snow. Winter visitors can enjoy skiing the groomed park road or venture into the park on snowshoes.

image.title: Craters in Winter
image.altText: A cross-country skier travels down the groomed park road in winter.
image.caption: When the Loop Road is closed, winter visitors tour the volcanic landscape on skis and snowshoes.

title: Hike Devils Orchard
shortDescription: Enjoy an easy, 0.5 mile walk through an open limber pine woodland.

image.title: Devils Orchard Nature Trail
image.altText: a paved trail in an open pine woodland covered with dark rocks and patches of tall grass
image.caption: Devils Orchard Nature Trail offers accessible views of an open, volcanic woodland.

title: Become a Craters Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Earn your Junior Ranger badge for Craters of the Moon while learning about the park by completing this fun activity book.

image.title: Crater of the Moon Junior Ranger
image.altText: a display featuring a junior ranger guidebook and several activities and junior ranger badges
image.caption: Explore, learn, and protect while becoming a Junior Ranger at Craters of the Moon!

title: Visit the Spatter Cones
shortDescription: Take a short walk to view some of the park's mini-volcanoes up close and personal.

image.title: Lone Hiker on Spatter Cones
image.altText: a person walking on a paved path up to a small volcanic cone
image.caption: The Spatter Cones are one of the shortest stops along the Loop Road.

title: Explore a Cave
shortDescription: Explore Craters' dynamic underground world of lava tubes.
seasonDescription: The caves are usually open late May through October. In the winter, the caves are closed and fill with hazardous snow and ice. This can cause a delayed reopening or early closure. Contact the visitor center or check current conditions before visiting the park.

image.title: Indian Tunnel
image.altText: A person walks down a set out stairs into the wide open entrance of a lava tube.
image.caption: Indian Tunnel is one of the easiest caves to access for most visitors.

title: Stargazing at Craters of the Moon
shortDescription: See the night sky like never before! The natural darkness of Craters of the Moon lends to superior stargazing opportunities.

image.title: Milky Way Over Craters
image.altText: a person standing on a rock silhouetted against the milky way
image.caption: The dark skies of Craters of the Moon showcase thousands of stars each night.

title: Backpack the Craters of the Moon Wilderness
shortDescription: Immerse yourself in the solitude of the Craters of the Moon Wilderness.

image.title: Backpacking Craters
image.altText: A hiker with a large backpack traverses a lava field.
image.caption: Backpacking is a unique way to experience the Craters of the Moon Wilderness.

title: Hike the North Crater Trail
shortDescription: This strenuous 3.5-mile trail drops into the mouth of North Crater.

image.title: North Crater Trail
image.altText: A hiker with a large backpack walks on a cinder trail toward a large volcanic cone.
image.caption: The North Crater Trail follows the rim of the crater and drops into its mouth.

title: Hike Broken Top Loop
shortDescription: Find a variety of unique volcanic features on this moderate-difficulty 1.8 mile loop.

image.title: Tree Molds Trailhead
image.altText: A narrow road winds through a volcanic landscape to a small parking area.
image.caption: The Tree Molds trailhead serves the Tree Molds Trail, Broken Top Loop, and the Wilderness Trail.

title: Hike Up Inferno Cone
shortDescription: Climb a short but very steep trail to the top of a volcanic cone for awe-inspiring views.

image.title: Inferno Cone
image.altText: Visitors start a steep climb up a bare cinder slope.
image.caption: The hike to the top of Inferno Cone is short but extremely steep.

title: Hike the Tree Molds Trail
shortDescription: This 2-mile trail winds through the Craters of the Moon Wilderness and features molds of ancient trees encased in lava.

image.title: Tree Molds
image.altText: dark rock featuring the impression of two fallen tree trunks
image.caption: Hikers can get up close to the impressions of fallen trees on the Tree Molds Trail.

title: Hike the Southend Loop
shortDescription: Take a 4.5 miles hike through the forest, over the marsh and along the beach. Take some time to explore the Dungeness historic district, wildlife and history is everywhere! This Is a great 3-4 hour day hike for first time visitors that provides a taste of the island’s diversity.

image.title: Beach Creek Marsh
image.altText: A view of the salt marsh through live oak trees
image.caption: The southend loop provides views of many different ecosystems on the island.

title: Plum Orchard Tour
shortDescription: Plum Orchard Mansion was built in 1898 by Lucy Carnegie for her son, George Lauder Carnegie, as a wedding present. This home reflects an opulent era in the island's history; one of recreation, relaxation, and time spent with family. This Visitors today can join a ranger for a 45-minutes tour of this 22,000 square foot home for a glimpse of such times.

image.title: Plum Orchard Piano
image.altText: Grand piano with chandelier above
image.caption: Step inside the Carnegie-era Plum Orchard mansion on a ranger-led tour offered three times daily.

title: Plan a Backpacking Trip
shortDescription: Backpacking on Cumberland Island can be a great experience when proper preparations are made. Failure to prepare can lead to a less than desirable and potentially dangerous experience.

image.title: Backpackers hiking on Cumberland Island
image.altText: A group of 5 back packers hiking along an open trail on Cumberland Island
image.caption: A properly planned backpacking trip can be a magical experience.

title: General Biking
shortDescription: Riding a bike can be a great way to get around the island. However, with no paved roads on the island it is important to understand the conditions on the island. Read on to find out if biking is right for your visit.

image.title: Biking on the Main Road
image.altText: Two bikers riding down the Main Road
image.caption: Biking can be a great way to get around the island, but make sure you know the conditions.

title: Bike to Plum Orchard
shortDescription: Take a 15-mile round trip bike ride up to the Plum Orchard mansion and take a tour of the Georgian-revival house. This is a strenuous 3-5 hour bike ride. Check with a ranger before starting out for current conditions.

image.title: Plum Orchard Mansion
image.altText: Large historic mansion and live oak trees with Spanish moss hanging down.
image.caption: Biking to Plum Orchard can be a rewarding experience, but know what to expect before you go.

title: Bring Your Own Bike
shortDescription: Bringing your own bike can provide more access to the island. Not all bikes are suited to be ridden on Cumberland Island. Read on to see if biking is a good choice for your visit.

image.title: Visitors bringing their own bikes
image.altText: Visitors pushing thier bikes onto the island
image.caption: Personal bikes can provide more access to remote parts of the island.

title: Ranger-Led "Footsteps" Tour
shortDescription: Walk with a ranger as you explore the Dungeness historic district and dive into the pivotal stories of its location. Tours are offered when the ferry arrives at the Dungeness dock (around 10:00 AM and 12:45 PM) on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, when staff is available. Ask if tours will be offered on the day of your visit. Tours last about an hour and cover roughly a mile in distance.

image.title: Ranger-Led "Footsteps" Tour
image.altText: Ruins of several story Dungeness mansion with window openings in tabby and brick.
image.caption: The "Footsteps" tour allows visitors to take a closer look at the island's storied history.

title: Kayak to the Island
shortDescription: Kayaking to Cumberland Island offers a different perspective and can be a rewarding experience. Advanced preparation is essential, however. This is only recommended for those with previous coastal kayaking experience.

image.title: Sea kayaking
image.altText: Front of kayak surrounded by water, overlooking salt marsh and vegetated island with clear sky above
image.caption: Plan ahead if paddling to Cumberland Island.

title: Lands and Legacies Tour
shortDescription: Take a van ride to the north end of the island. A guide will present the island's history.

image.title: First African Baptist Church
image.altText: A small wooden church painted white.
image.caption: The Lands and Legacies tour is a great way to explore the north end.

title: Become a Jr. Ranger
shortDescription: Join the National Park Service “family” by becoming a Junior Ranger. Complete the activity book, have a park ranger review it, and receive an official Junior Ranger badge for Cumberland Island. Pick up your booklet and badge from the Mainland Visitor Center and Sea Camp Ranger Station today.

image.title: Become a Junior Ranger
image.altText: Ranger hat with shark teeth
image.caption: Grab your activity booklet and become a Cumberland Island Junior Ranger today.

title: Swim at the Beach
shortDescription: With over 17 miles of undeveloped beach, no matter where you are on Cumberland Island you’re never too far from the beach. Swimming in the ocean can a great way to beat the heat on a hot coastal Georgia day.

image.title: In the Surf Cumberland Island
image.altText: Swimming in the surf
image.caption: Through the ages Cumberland's beach has been popular for recreation.

title: Hike to Little Greyfield
shortDescription: Take a secluded hike through the maritime forest and along the beach. This hike will take you through saw palmetto, wax myrtle and under the canopy of sprawling live oak trees. The trail will intersect with the Little Greyfield beach crossing about two miles in. Take this crossing through the dunes to a particularly isolated portion of the beach. Turn right and keep the ocean to your left to return to Sea Camp. You can also take this loop the opposite way.

image.altText: Trail head to the parallel trail

title: Birding on the Beach
