shortDescription: Birding on the beach can be successful in any season on Cumberland Island. There are many rear-round residents, and those around during breeding season, migrations, and winter alike. Be sure to pack your binoculars and head to the beach on your next visit to the island.

image.title: Willets on the Beach
image.altText: Willets on the Beach
image.caption: Viewing birds on the beach is promising in any season on Cumberland Island.

title: Shop at the Bookstore
shortDescription: Stop by the bookstore at Cumberland Island’s Visitor Center in Saint Marys, GA, open daily from 8:00 AM – 4:00 PM (closed Christmas Day). You will find books related to the island’s natural and cultural history, apparel, postcards, pins, patches, magnets, and more.

image.title: Visitor Center bookstore
image.altText: Visitor Center bookstore
image.caption: Stop by the bookstore at Cumberland Island's Visitor Center, open daily from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM.

title: Hike to Sea Camp Beach
shortDescription: With 17 miles of undeveloped beach, it is easy to find your own personal space on Cumberland’s beach. The wide-open space of the beach provides a striking contrast to the dense, tangled maritime forest. When you step out of the forest in the dunes, you feel like you are entering a whole new world. Whether you are looking for seashells, shorebirds or a tan, the beach on Cumberland will not disappoint.

image.title: Sea Camp beach
image.altText: Beach with dune and sea oat vegetation
image.caption: There are plenty of opportunities for exploration on Cumberland Island's miles of beach.

title: Photography
shortDescription: Cumberland is a magical place for photographers. Abundant wildlife, picturesque ruins, and lack of crowds make this a great place for taking photos.

image.title: Dungeness
image.altText: The burnt out ruins of a brick mansion
image.caption: There are endless photography subjects on the island.

title: Explore the Ice House Museum
shortDescription: Make a pitstop at the Ice House Museum to learn about the island’s history. Fill up your water bottle at the water bottle filling station and use the restrooms before heading on to Dungeness.

image.title: Ice House Museum
image.altText: A white building with pitched roof in an open field with a large live oak to the right.
image.caption: Stop by the Ice House to learn about the island's history

title: Hike the Nightingale Trail
shortDescription: The Nightingale Trail on the south end of the island is a great place to experience the interior of the maritime forest.

image.title: Nightingale Trailhead along the Main Roa
image.altText: Sign with text "Nightengale trail" with a path leading into the forest beyond.
image.caption: The maritime forest is a great place to find some solitude.

title: Hike the River Trail
shortDescription: The River Trail is 0.8 miles long and connects the Sea Camp and Dungeness docks. It takes you through the maritime forest and provides a few views of the intracoastal waterway.

image.title: River Trailhead at Seacamp
image.altText: Sign with text "river trail" with a path leading into the forest behind.
image.caption: The river trail connects the Sea Camp and Dungeness Docks.

title: Beachcombing
shortDescription: The ocean can bring many interesting things onto our beaches. Beachcombing is a popular activity on Cumberland Island. Shells are not found on the beach all the time, however. Read on to learn when is the best time to scour the beach for shells.
seasonDescription: Summer is the least preferred time to beachcomb.

image.title: Shells on the beach
image.altText: Several varieties of seashells line the beach
image.caption: Visitors may collect unoccupied shells and sharks teeth from the island.

title: Wildlife Viewing at Dungeness
shortDescription: Cumberland Island is a great place to view wildlife. Dungeness is a great place to look for the many common animals on the island and is an easy walk from the dock.

image.title: Armadillo
image.altText: A close up of an armadillo's face
image.caption: Dungeness is a great place to view wildlife including armadillos.

title: Birding at the Marsh Boardwalk
shortDescription: The extensive marshes around Cumberland Island provide great birding opportunities. One of the best places to get a view of the marsh is at the marsh boardwalk, just east of the Greene-Miller Cemetery. After you’ve gotten your history fix at the Dungeness ruins area, take the short walk to the marsh boardwalk, a birding hotspot.

image.title: Snowy egret flying through marsh
image.altText: Snowy egret flying through marsh
image.caption: Birds frequent the nutrient-rich salt marsh for the many food options it provides.

title: Hike to Dungeness
shortDescription: Take a hike to the southern most historical district to see the ruins of a Carnegie mansion, learn about what it took to upkeep the estate, check out wildlife and enjoy the view of the salt marsh. This short hike can be enjoyed in just 2 hours.

image.title: The Ruins of Dungeness
image.altText: Burnt out ruins of a brick and stone mansion. The blue sky can be seen through empty window frames.
image.caption: The Dungeness Ruins are a must-see on Cumberland Island

title: Birdwatching at Dungeness
shortDescription: Over 300 species of birds have been recorded on Cumberland Island. About 200 of these species are migratory, with the rest being year-round residents of the island. What birds you will find on the island will depend on what time of year you visit. The best birding is typically in the spring, when many birds stop over on Cumberland Island on their way north. Dungeness is a great area to view many different species.

image.title: Summer Tanager
image.altText: Bright red bird on a branch
image.caption: Summer tanagers can be spotted in the spring and summer.

title: Explore the Mainland Museum
shortDescription: Open from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM daily , the Mainland Museum for Cumberland Island National Seashore is a great starting place to learn more about the island’s diverse history. Exhibits explore the cultural and natural history of the island from prehistoric American Indians lives, through British occupation during the War of 1812, the Plantation Era, Gilded Age, and the island today.

image.title: War of 1812 Exhibit
image.altText: A museum display with manikins in uniforms, a historic painting and a large anchor on the wall.
image.caption: The British invasion of Cumberland Island is a forgotten aspect of the War of 1812.

title: Hike Curecanti Creek Trail
shortDescription: After descending from the high rim of the Upper Black Canyon of the Gunnison, the trail follows Curecanti Creek as it descends toward Morrow Point Reservoir.

image.title: Curecanti Creek hiking trail
image.altText: Curecanti Creek hiking trail
image.caption: Hikers pass by crystal cascades in the spruce and fir forest

title: Hike Pine Creek Trail
shortDescription: This trail follows Pine Creek as it cascades into the depths of the upper Black Canyon to Morrow Point Reservoir. It follows the old narrow gauge railroad bed along the reservoir.

image.title: Pine Creek Trail
image.altText: A footpath along a narrow canyon with water and trees
image.caption: The trail follows the upper Black Canyon to Morrow Point Reservoir.

title: Boat on Morrow Point Reservoir
shortDescription: For the more adventurous, Morrow Point Reservoir is a great location for canoeing or kayaking. The easiest access to launch hand-carried craft is via the Pine Creek Trail.

image.title: Morrow Point Reservoir
image.altText: A person standup paddleboarding on a reservoir between steep cliff walls
image.caption: Visitors can boat on hand-carried craft, such as kayaks or standup paddleboards

title: Boat on Crystal Reservoir
shortDescription: Crystal Reservoir provides backcountry flatwater boating opportunities. Hand-carried craft only. Access is from Mesa Creek Trail located at Cimarron.

image.title: Crystal Reservoir
image.altText: Tall canyon walls and rocky shoreline along a reservoir
image.caption: Crystal Reservoir

title: Hike Mesa Creek Trail
shortDescription: This trail crosses Crystal Reservoir via footbridge and meanders along the river's edge for views of the sheer canyon walls.

image.title: Mesa Creek Trail
image.altText: A footpath goes back and forth next to a narrow canyon and river
image.caption: A footbridge provides access to the north side of Crystal Reservoir.

title: Hike Neversink Trail
shortDescription: This short trail is located nearest to Gunnison along the Gunnison River and provides good birdwatching opportunities.

image.title: Neversink Trail
image.altText: A trail in autumn with yellow leaves and a path between trees
image.caption: Neversink Trail meanders under trees

title: Boat on Blue Mesa Reservoir
shortDescription: Blue Mesa Reservoir, the largest body of water in Colorado, has 96 miles of shoreline and provides opportunities for motorboating, paddleboarding, kayaking, canoeing, and more.

image.title: Blue Mesa Reservoir
image.altText: Multiple boats on a still water reservoir with mountains in the background
image.caption: Boats on Blue Mesa Reservoir

title: Hike Dillon Pinnacles
shortDescription: Ascending through sagebrush, ponderosa pine and riparian habitats, this 1.9-mile (3.2 km) trail offers spectacular views of Blue Mesa Reservoir, the distant San Juan Mountain peaks, and the eroded volcanic Dillon Pinnacles.

image.title: Dillon Pinnacles
image.altText: Tall rock spires in front of scrub land
image.caption: Dillon Pinnacles

title: Fishing at Curecanti
shortDescription: Fishing is allowed along the Gunnison River and all three reservoirs of Curecanti National Recreation Area. All Colorado State fishing regulations apply.

image.title: Gunnison River fishing
image.altText: A person casting a fishing rod next to a river
image.caption: Fishing at Beaver Creek

title: Drive East Portal Road
shortDescription: East Portal Road is a windy, steep scenic road down to the Gunnison River. East Portal is within Curecanti National Recreation Area, but only accessible from within Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park. Vehicles over 22 feet are prohibited on the East Portal Road.
seasonDescription: The road is closed in winter, typically from November to April.

image.title: East Portal Road
image.altText: A view of a steep canyon and greyish river
image.caption: Views of Black Canyon from the East Portal Road

title: Hike Hermits Rest Trail
shortDescription: Zigzagging through oak, pine, juniper, and fir, hikers descend more than 1750 ft (531 m) to a wooded camp and picnic sites on the shores of Morrow Point Reservoir.

image.title: Hermit's Rest Trail
image.altText: A trail with a view of mountains and overlooking a dam in the distance
image.caption: A view from Hermit's Rest Trail of Morrow Point Dam

title: Drive U.S. Highway 50
shortDescription: U.S. Highway 50 travels west from Gunnison and brings you into Curecanti National Recreation Area. The highway follows along the Gunnison River before reaching Blue Mesa Reservoir, continuing along its edge and crossing two bridges.
seasonDescription: The road is open year-round. Conditions can become icy or snow-covered during late fall through early spring, especially at higher elevations. Check Colorado Department of Transportation for current road conditions, construction, and closures.

image.title: Dillon Pinnacles
image.altText: Geologic formations on the side of a mesa in front of a body of water
image.caption: Dillon Pinnacles, one of the many scenic views along U.S. Highway 50

title: Drive CO Highway 92
shortDescription: Colorado (CO) Highway 92 crosses over Blue Mesa Dam and winds along the north rim of the Black Canyon, providing access to scenic overlooks and trailheads.
seasonDescription: The road is open year-round. Conditions can become icy or snow-covered during late fall through early spring, especially at higher elevations. Check Colorado Department of Transportation for current road conditions, construction, and closures.

image.title: Views from CO Highway 92
image.altText: A deep steep canyon with a narrow body of water running far below. Snow is dusted on the canyon rim
image.caption: View from Pioneer Point, one of the overlooks off CO Highway 92

title: Hike Crystal Creek Trail
shortDescription: Winding through abundant wildflowers, Gambel oak, aspens, conifers and a recovering burn area, Crystal Creek Trail is ideal for spring or fall hiking.
seasonDescription: This trail is popular during spring and fall.

image.title: View from Crystal Creek Trail
image.altText: A trail leading around a cliff edge with a view of mountains
image.caption: View from Crystal Creek Trail

title: Visit Cuyahoga Valley Farms and Markets
shortDescription: Agriculture has long been an important part of life in the Cuyahoga Valley. Today, there are eight farms that operate within the national park. Several have roadside stands or host events throughout the year. Learn more about these farms and about weekly farmers markets in and around the park.
seasonDescription: The farmers markets run throughout the year. In the summer, they take place at Howe Meadow. In the colder months, they move indoors.

image.title: Cuyahoga Valley Farmers Market
image.altText: A shopper reaches over table of vegetables to pay a smiling female vendor in embroidered shirt.
image.caption: Shopping for fresh produce at Cuyahoga Valley Farmers Market.

title: Go Mountain Biking in Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: The East Rim Trail system has stunning views, varied terrain, exciting obstacles, and an element of adventure for intermediate mountain bikers.
seasonDescription: Check the daily status on signs at the trailhead. Expect the trail system to be closed when conditions are wet or icy.

image.title: Mountain Biker at East Rim
image.altText: A mountain biker wearing a helmet banks around a curve at a 45-degree angle, on a wooded trail.
image.caption: The East Rim Trail system offers adventures for mountain bikers with intermediate skills.

title: Ride the Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad
shortDescription: All aboard the Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad! Learn more about this unique way to experience Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

image.title: Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad Engine
image.altText: Yellow, red, and black train engine approaches along tracks through a forest.
image.caption: Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad runs seasonal excursions through Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

title: Go Snowshoeing in the Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: Snowshoeing is a great way to explore and exercise in Cuyahoga Valley National Park when the conditions are right. We recommend waiting for there to be at least four inches of packed snow on the trail.

image.title: Snowshoeing in the Forest
image.altText: A group of people in winter hats snowshoes along a snow-covered trail in the forest.
image.caption: Snowshoeing can be a fun way to warm up in wintry weather.

title: Hike the Brandywine Gorge Loop
shortDescription: The Brandywine Gorge Loop circles a deep ravine carved by Brandywine Creek, and provides stunning views of Brandywine Falls along the way. Learn more about hiking this popular trail.

image.title: Brandywine Falls and Lower Boardwalk
image.altText: View down through bare trees at a deck overlooking a waterfall cascading into a gorge.
image.caption: The lower viewing platform at Brandywine Falls.

title: Become a Cuyahoga Valley Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Learn how kids ages 3 and older can become Junior Rangers of Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

image.title: Become a Cuyahoga Valley Junior Ranger
image.altText: A child wearing a ranger hat holds up their right hand, across a desk from a uniformed ranger.
image.caption: A Junior Ranger is sworn in at Canal Exploration Center.

title: Hike the Ledges Trail
shortDescription: The Ledges Trail circles a plateau of striking rock formations and provides stunning views along the way. Learn more about hiking this popular trail.

image.title: Ledges Stone Staircase
image.altText: Staircase of rough-hewn gray stones winds between two walls of green moss-covered rock, up to trees.
image.caption: This stone staircase is a popular feature along the Ledges Trail.

title: Visit Canal Exploration Center
shortDescription: Arrive by car, bike, or scenic railroad. Hands-on exhibits at this historic tavern and store bring the canal era to life. Lock demonstrations are offered seasonally. From here, you can stroll the Towpath Trail.
seasonDescription: Check the seasonal hours.

image.title: Visitors Inside Canal Exploration Ctr.
image.altText: Man holds a child over a touch table as four other adults look at exhibits; one uses a wheelchair.
image.caption: This electronic touch table is one of the popular interactive exhibits at Canal Exploration Center.

title: Find the Best Fall Colors in Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: Leaf peepers, grab your cameras! Here are our tips for where to find Cuyahoga Valley’s best fall colors throughout October.
seasonDescription: We are highlighting October, when we typically see the most dramatic fall colors in northeast Ohio.

image.title: Hale Farm and Village - Fall Colors
image.altText: Scenic view of red barn with grassy fields in foreground and hillside of colorful leaves behind.
image.caption: Fall colors at Hale Farm & Village in late October.

title: Stop by Boston Mill Visitor Center
shortDescription: Begin your adventure at Boston Mill Visitor Center. Pick up maps and shop for souvenirs. Staff and volunteers are available to help you plan a visit that fits your time and interests.
seasonDescription: Hours vary by season. Check our hours page to plan your visit.

image.title: Boston Mill VC Exterior and Sign
image.altText: Sign with stone base reads "Cuyahoga Valley national Park," a white two-story building behind it.
image.caption: Stop by Boston Mill Visitor Center to plan your park visit.

title: Go Fishing in the Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: Fishing is a great way to spend your day in Cuyahoga Valley National Park. Learn about the best places to fish and how to responsibly enjoy this pastime.

image.title: Fishing in the Cuyahoga Valley
image.altText: A boy sits on the edge of a dock fishing in a pond.
image.caption: Fish off an accessible dock at Kendall Lake or Horseshoe Pond.

title: Hike to Blue Hen Falls from Boston
shortDescription: Blue Hen Falls is a popular hike-in destination in the Boston area. Hikers can reach the waterfall via the Buckeye Trail from Boston Mill Visitor Center. Learn more about this popular hilly hike.
seasonDescription: The Buckeye Trail includes steep inclines, switchbacks, and stairs. Mud and ice can greatly impact trail quality during wet or wintry conditions.

image.title: Blue Hen Falls in autumn
image.altText: Water falls from a rim of gray rock, trees in the background; orange leaves dot the rocky hollow.
image.caption: Blue Hen Falls in autumn.

title: Short Towpath Trail Walks
shortDescription: These short walks along the Towpath Trail explore many highlights of the valley’s lowlands. They are recommended for people who have mobility disabilities, are visiting with children, or have limited time.
seasonDescription: While the Towpath Trail is open during the winter months, the park does not clear snow from the trail.

image.title: A couple strolls on the Towpath Trail.
image.altText: A woman walks beside a man on a flat trail, resting a hand on the back of his motorized wheelchair.
image.caption: A couple strolls the Towpath Trail near Beaver Marsh.

title: Find Spring Wildflowers in Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: Searching for wildflowers is a great way to connect with nature and stay active in spring. Discover what’s blooming along park trails.
seasonDescription: Late March to mid-May

image.title: Dutchman's breeches in bloom
image.altText: A dozen white blooms dangle off stems above lacy leaves. Each is V shaped with curled yellow points.
image.caption: Dutchman’s breeches is a delicate spring wildflower that prefers moist woodlands.

title: Go Birding in the Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: Birding is a popular activity at Cuyahoga Valley National Park. Thanks to the park’s wide variety of habitats, it is possible to observe more than 200 bird species throughout the year. Grab a field guide and a pair of binoculars and see what awaits your discovery.

image.title: Birding at the Beaver Marsh
image.altText: Uniformed ranger points upward, standing with several people on a wooden boardwalk, trees behind.
image.caption: A ranger leads a birding program at the Beaver Marsh.

title: Kid- and Autism-friendly Activities in the Everett Area
shortDescription: Three short walks in the Everett area offer sensory activities that appeal to children or individuals with autism. They include tactile and audio exhibits.

image.title: Family at Beaver Marsh on Towpath Trail
image.altText: Man and child with bike and helmet, stand in front of “Mammals and Birds” panel on wooden boardwalk.
image.caption: Chatting on the boardwalk at Beaver Marsh.

title: Let's Go Canalway Questing
shortDescription: Put your detective hat on! Quests are fun, self-guides hikes that help you explore the Ohio & Erie Canalway. Follow rhyming clues to hidden boxes. Sign the logbook and collect impressions of each hand-carved stamp.
seasonDescription: The questing season is April 15 to November 15. The Sense of Boston Quest is available all year.

image.title: Questing
image.altText: A girl bends over quest brochure as an adult’s hands stamp the back. They are on a wooden platform.
image.caption: Each quest box has a different ink stamp. Collect impressions of them all.

title: Plan Your Event at Cuyahoga Valley
shortDescription: Find out how you can host an event in the park.
seasonDescription: Hours vary by season and location.

image.title: Ledges Shelter Summer Event
image.altText: A crowd gathered around picnic tables under a rustic shelter made of sandstone and dark brown wood.
image.caption: Event at Ledges Shelter.

title: Explore Denali's Winter Trails
shortDescription: Whether on foot, skis or snowshoes, winter is a great time for you to explore Denali! Snow starts falling as early as September, although in some years the conditions aren't good for skiing until December, and it sticks around until April or May.
seasonDescription:
We consider "winter" to start by October, although in some years there isn't very much snow until November or even December. Once snow has arrived, it usually stays until April.

Trails are of course always hike-able, even when there is no snow.

image.altText: snowy forested landscape

title: Sightsee on a Denali Tour Bus
shortDescription: Summer sight-seeing in Denali is mainly done by bus, and there are several trips to choose from. Narrated tour bus trips are more expensive than non-narrated transit buses. From high up in a bus, it becomes possible to look over roadside brush, allowing you to enjoy the incredible scenery (and wildlife sightings, too!).
seasonDescription: The summer season in Denali is from May 20 to mid-September. There are short tours occasionally available a few weeks before and after summer; contact the tour bus company for details.

image.altText: a bus driving on a dirt road on the side of a mountain

title: Explore Mountain Vista & Savage River
shortDescription: While most of Denali’s sole road is restricted just to bus traffic, anybody can drive out to Mountain Vista and Savage River. Located about 15 miles inside the park, the area is scenic, featuring several trails (some short, one long) and a picnic area.
seasonDescription:
Vehicle access is limited in the fall, winter and spring. Depending on snow conditions, you may be able to drive here as early as April and as late as October. 

Access is more reliable in summer (May through September). 

The park is open in winter, but you would need to be ready to ski, hike or otherwise travel under your own power for about 10 miles from Park Headquarters to reach this area.

image.altText: a shallow river flowing between mountains

title: Hike a Short Trail From the Denali Visitor Center
shortDescription: At 6 million acres in size, Denali is incredibly vast, and hiking is possible almost anywhere in the park. However, there are only a handful of established trails in the park, and here you'll find a few suggestions for one or more short hikes from the Denali Visitor Center.
seasonDescription: These trails are accessible year-round. In fall, winter and spring, be careful as surfaces may be slippery or icy. Visitors coming outside of the summer season (i.e., mid-September to mid-May), please be aware that the Murie Science and Learning Center is the primary visitor facility; the Denali Visitor Center is only open in summer.

image.altText: a trail leading through a forest of spruce and aspen trees

title: Bike the Denali Park Road
shortDescription: Biking the Denali Park Road is a rewarding way to explore the park at a slower speed than vehicles allow. Experience a variety of terrain over the course of just a few hours as you pedal from forested areas up to expansive views of the tundra, then coast back downhill towards a river.
seasonDescription: Snow-free months in the spring, summer, and fall are the best months for accessing the park road with a typical bicycle. In winter, the road is snowy and closed to vehicles, but can be biked with a fat tire bike.

image.title: Biking in Denali
image.altText: a person riding a bicycle on a dirt road
image.caption: Many areas of the Denali Park Road are above tree-line, offering expansive views.

title: Berry Picking in Denali
shortDescription: Alaska is well known for it’s amazing and abundant berries in August and September—just ask any of the grizzly bears in Denali! A family friendly activity would be to strike off into the tundra and search for berries. Bring your bucket (or empty water bottle) to fill, or simply snack on the go.
seasonDescription:
Some lingonberries (lowbush cranberries) may be found in spring (April-June) in Denali, having overwintered from the previous year. These are tart and edible. Otherwise the berry season is late July until late September.

Blueberries are the earlier berry, and once they ripen to be blue all the way around (with no green coloration) they are edible. Lingonberries are best eaten after Denali has gotten at least one frost event—the berries will be crimson red. They can be eaten earlier (when still bright firetruck red) but will be even more tart.

image.title: Berry Picking Near Wonder Lake
image.altText: two women picking berries in a shrubby meadow, a huge snowy mountain visible in the distance
image.caption: Wonder Lake takes time to reach by bus, but is surrounded with blueberry bushes!

title: Discover the Boreal Forest: Identify Plants While Hiking in Denali
shortDescription: Denali is home to a beautiful variety of plant species, from tall Aspen trees to short Moss campion. With a diversity of habitat types that support water-loving to drought-tolerant plants, Denali is an excellent place to immerse yourself in the subarctic flora. The DenaliFlora App is the perfect companion for your botanical explorations.
seasonDescription: With only seven trees, identifying plants outside of summer is tricky (or impossible, when snow covers everything!). The main time to identify wildflowers and other plants is June through mid-July, when most plants are flowering, although identification is still possible before or after that roughly six-week window.

image.altText: woman looking at her smart phone and a plant on a trail

title: Sightsee on a Denali Transit Bus
shortDescription: Summer sight-seeing in Denali is mainly done by bus, and there are several trips to choose from. Transit bus trips are the cheapest and most flexible option, although they aren't narrated. From high up in a bus, it becomes possible to look over roadside brush, allowing you to enjoy the incredible scenery (and wildlife sightings, too!).
seasonDescription: The summer season in Denali is from May 20 to mid-September. The final day for shuttle bus trips each summer is the second Thursday after the Labor Day holiday.

image.altText: a green colored bus traveling a dirt road on a mountainside

title: Viewing Wildlife in Denali
shortDescription: Denali provides habitat for 39 species of mammals, 169 species of birds, 14 species of fish, and one species of amphibian The large animals that are often the most sought after can be surprisingly elusive. The so called “Big Five”—moose, caribou, Dall sheep, grizzly bears, and wolves, receive the most attention, but the is a great place to see a wide variety of wildlife. The longer you spend in the area, the better your chances to see wild animals!
seasonDescription: Buses only operate in summer (roughly mid-May to mid-September each year). Visiting before or after those dates is possible, though less of the park will be accessible by vehicle, which therefore reduces your chances to see wildlife a bit.

image.title: Caribou Sighting
image.altText: a bus parked on a gravel road near a caribou that is walking along the road
image.caption: Wildlife sightings are typically farther away, but on occasion an animal will wander down the road.

title: Hiking Off Trail in Denali
shortDescription: Denali National Park and Preserve has very few formal trails for a park of its size, but hiking off trail offers limitless opportunities for recreation and exploration. The terrain and bus system in Denali make hiking off trail less intimidating and more approachable than it may seem at first.

image.title: Off Trail Hiking
image.altText: A man hiking up a hillside in front of a vista of mountains and rivers
image.caption: Hiking off trail in Denali

title: Backpacking in Denali
shortDescription: A backpacking trip in Denali is unlike backpacking in most other national parks. Denali is about the size of Vermont, with only a handful of trails—most of which are near the entrance of the park for day-hiking, rather than overnight backpacking. This opportunity to set your own route and hike through a trail-less landscape amid wild animals and wilderness is rare in the 21st century.
seasonDescription: Summer is the most common time to backpack in Denali, although permits are available year-round.

image.title: Backpacking in Denali
image.altText: a man standing on a ridge top with a large backpack on
image.caption: Backpacking in Denali is unlike most other national parks.

title: Early Morning Hike to Horseshoe Lake
shortDescription: Horseshoe Lake is a lovely destination about 2 miles from the Denali Visitor Center. A trail loops around the entire lake, which is occasionally home to moose, beavers and a variety of bird-life. An early-morning visit to the lake is particularly pleasant, though any time of day is great to hike to the lake.

image.altText: people sitting on a forested lakeshore

title: Look for the Northern Lights (Aurora Borealis)
shortDescription: Aurora is like any weather phenomenon, where a forecast is issued each day. Unlike rain, though, aurora viewing can only occur when the far north is dark enough; and forecasts aren't nearly as precise as weather forecasts. Despite these challenges, any dark night in Alaska is a great time to look outside and hope for some signs of the Northern Lights!
seasonDescription:
A few unpredictable things are needed to see the aurora:

  • Dark enough
    Alaska is bright in the summer, with the sun up around-the-clock above the Arctic Circle and days nearly as long just below the Arctic. In Denali, it is too bright to see the aurora in June and July, and is too bright for most of May and August. 
  • Clear enough
    Even if the sky is dark, too many clouds will ruin your viewing opportunity. Clear skies are more common in the middle of winter, when the air is often very dry, but there can be plenty of clear nights in fall and spring, too.
  • Aurora-y enough
    The aurora happens year-round, and it can be forecast. Sometimes there is little or no auroral activity, and at other times it can be very active. Search "aurora forecast" with your favorite search engine to pick from among the many forecasting services on the internet.

image.altText: green auroral light in a dark sky, framed by trees

title: Walk on a Glacier in the Alaska Range
shortDescription: The rugged Alaska Range is home to Denali, the highest point in North America. For some visitors, a flight-seeing trip over or around "the Mountain" can be one of the most memorable parts of a visit to Alaska. Some companies are also authorized to land on a glacier in the park, letting passengers disembark for a short while.
seasonDescription: Private companies offer glacier landings and flight-seeing, not the National Park Service. Please contact individual companies for details on available dates.

image.altText: aerial view of mountains and a large glacier

title: Dog Mushing in Denali
shortDescription: Though Denali's dogs are not available for visitor sled rides, there are opportunities for visitors to arrange for day trips or multi-night trips through a privately owned sled dog kennel in the area.

image.altText: a team of dogs pulling a sled

title: Stargaze at Joyner Ridge
shortDescription: Joyner Ridge offers wide open spaces and little light pollution – the perfect combination for optimal stargazing. Set up your telescope, photograph the night sky with Devils Tower, or simply look up. There’s no wrong way to stargaze!
seasonDescription:
Spring: Early spring is a great time for catching last glimpses of winter constellations. 

Summer: Sunset is much later in the evening. The Milky Way will be overhead closer to midnight. 

Winter: Sunset is earlier, but the temperature is much colder. 

Fall: Early fall is a great time to see the Milky way overhead just after sunset.

image.title: Night Sky from Joyner Ridge
image.altText: a dark night sky filled with stars with Devils Tower and trees silhouetted below
image.caption: Joyner Ridge offers wide open views of the cosmos.

title: Hike Valley View Trail
shortDescription: Take a stroll through the prairie dog town with scenic views of the Belle Fourche River and Devils Tower. Valley View Trail is relatively level and short, perfect for kids or a quick leg stretch. Valley View Trail can also be used to connect the campground or picnic area to other parts of the park.
seasonDescription:
The trail is open year round, but is not maintained in winter.   

Summer: Very sunny and can get very hot.  

Winter: commonly has packed snow and ice. Snow also hides burrows and can make the trail treacherous.  

Spring and Fall: Suggested best time to hike.

image.title: Belle Fourche from Valley View Trail
image.altText: a blue river winds through prairie, with cottonwood trees and red cliffs in the background
image.caption: Valley View Trail is a nice stroll through the prairie dog town with picturesque views of the river.

title: Hike South Side Trail
shortDescription: South Side Trail offers an easy stroll through the prairie dog town or a convenient connector to other parts of the park. Catch the trail from the park amphitheater, Red Beds Trail, or prairie dog town pullouts. South Side Trail is a great way to reach the visitor center from the picnic area and campground, allowing you to skip the visitor center parking lot crowds.
seasonDescription:
The trail is open year round, but is not maintained in winter.  

Summer: Very sunny and can get very hot. 

Winter: commonly has packed snow and ice. Snow also hides burrows and can make the trail treacherous. 

Spring and Fall: Suggested best time to hike.

image.title: South Side Trail with visitors
image.altText: people walking along a dirt path through the prairie dog town, Devils Tower in the background
image.caption: South Side Trail is the perfect way to explore the prairie dog town.

title: Hike the Red Beds Loop Trail
shortDescription: Looking for a traditional hiking experience in the park? Check out this 2.8 mile loop around the Tower! Take in sights of the Tower from different angles and enjoy the beauty of the Belle Fourche River valley. As you climb up and down between the visitor center parking lot and the river valley, experience the geology of the park up close! Escape the crowds on the Tower Trail and take in sweeping vistas of the park and surrounding land.
seasonDescription:
The trail is open year round, but is not maintained in the winter.

Summer: Very sunny and can get very hot.

Winter: Commonly has packed snow and ice.

Spring and Fall: Suggested best time to hike.

image.title: Red Beds Trail in Late Summer
image.altText: Path winding through prairie grass, with cliff face, red rocks, and pine trees in background.
image.caption: A view of the Red Beds Trail in late summer.

title: Walk the Tower Trail Loop
shortDescription: Enjoy a walk around the base of one of the most unique geologic formations in the world! Learn about the natural and cultural history of Devils Tower National Monument, from theories about how it formed to the connections modern tribes maintain with the site today.
seasonDescription:
The trail is open year round, but is not maintained in the winter.

Summer: Very sunny and can get very hot.

Winter: Commonly has packed snow and ice.

Spring and Fall: Suggested best time to hike.

image.altText: A bench along a trail overlooking a valley.

title: Watch for Wildlife at Prairie Dog Town
shortDescription: Have you ever heard a prairie dog yip? Or seen a fox with its kits? There’s lots going on at the prairie dog town! Take some time to enjoy the wildlife in the park. Don’t forget to look up! The prairie dog town is a great place to spot turkey vultures, peregrine falcons, and other birds flying around the Tower. Use the pullouts along the Main Park Road near prairie dog town to observe this bustling environment.
seasonDescription:
Spring, summer, and fall: These are the best times of year to spot wildlife.

Winter: Most park animals will not be out due to cold temperatures.

image.title: Prairie Dog
image.altText: Prairie dog standing up outside of its burrow with the edges of the photo darkened.
image.caption: Check out the main attraction at prairie dog town!

title: Eat Lunch at the Devils Tower Picnic Area
shortDescription: After a long day of exploring, stop by the Devils Tower picnic area to enjoy your lunch! The Devils Tower picnic area provides visitors with a serene experience of the Tower. Located near the Bell Fourche Campground, take a walk under the cottonwood trees with your leashed pet or spend the afternoon enjoying the views.
seasonDescription:
Fall and winter: Check road conditions before visiting. Bathrooms and water are not available during these months. 

Spring and summer: Suggested best time to visit.

image.title: Devils Tower picnic area
image.altText: A large grassy field with picnic tables and trees throughout.
image.caption: Stop for lunch at the serene Devils Tower picnic area.

title: Hike Joyner Ridge Trail
shortDescription: Joyner Ridge provides the space and serenity to enjoy nature without the crowds. Visit a quieter part of Devils Tower by hiking the 1.5-mile (2.4 km) Joyner Ridge Trail. Take in scenic views of the Tower or visit at night to stargaze in the secluded northern part of the park. Experience this trail in spring to spot blooming wildflowers along the trail edge.
seasonDescription:
Summer and spring: Possibility for hot weather and many areas on the trail are not shaded. Bring plenty of water and sunscreen for your hike. 

Winter and fall: Trail is not maintained in the winter. It commonly has packed snow and ice from December through April.

image.title: The Tower from the Prairie
image.altText: A view of a tall grass prairie with a tree log in the foreground and Devils Tower in the back.
image.caption: See a stunning view of Devils Tower from the prairie at Joyner Ridge Trail.

title: Explore Wildflowers in Death Valley
shortDescription: Learn about the different flowers you might be able to see in Death Valley during spring months.
seasonDescription: Wildflowers only bloom in the spring months. Lower elevations see flowers mid February to Mid April, mid-level elevation see flowers early April to early may and higher elevations see them early May to mid July.

image.title: Wildflowers in Death Valley
image.altText: Notch-leaved Phacelia and Golden Evening Primrose bloom in a desert wash.
image.caption: Notch-leaved Phacelia and Golden Evening Primrose bloom in a desert wash.

title: Visit the Furnace Creek Visitor Center
shortDescription: Stop by the visitor center to speak with park rangers and pay park fees and purchase national park passes. View the exhibits about Death Valley's history and natural wonders. Watch the park film, which is 20 minutes in length and plays throughout the day. Shop at the bookstore - light snacks/sandwiches/water are available for purchase. Become a Junior Ranger! Complete the activities in the booklet and earn a badge.

image.title: Furnace Creek Visitor Center
image.altText: a one story block building and flag pole
image.caption: Take a picture next to the famous thermometer, see exhibits and park film, shop, or talk to rangers!

title: Bird Watching
shortDescription: Roadrunners and ravens and hummingbirds- oh my! With many resident and migratory species, bird watching opportunities abound in Death Valley.

image.title: Death Valley Hummingbird
image.altText: A green hummingbird with a purple and white throat drinks from a yellow flower.
image.caption: Hummingbirds take advantage of Death Valley blooms.

title: Harmony Borax Works Self Guided Walk
shortDescription: Harmony Borax Works was instrumental in drawing people to Death Valley in the late 1800s and in the subsequent popularity of the Furnace Creek area. The 1/4 mi (0.4 km) paved walking path at this site takes visitors back in time by exploring the ruins of the plant and associated townsite and an original twenty mule team wagon.
seasonDescription: The 1/4 mile walk is not recommended during extreme temperatures, especially after 10AM in the summer. Harmony Borax Works area can viewed from afar from the parking lot.

image.title: Harmony Borax Works Tour
image.altText: Two adults and a child look at a waist high sign next to a wooden and metal wagon in the desert.
image.caption: Learn about the famous Twenty Mule teams at Harmony Borax Works.

title: Tour Artists Drive
shortDescription: Enjoy a scenic drive through a geologic rainbow! Artists Drive is a one-way, nine mile (14.5 km) drive which passes through eroded, colorful desert hills. Artists Palette (a viewpoint) has the most colorful scenery along the road.

image.altText: A vehicle drives along a single lane road through colorful, eroded hills.

title: Drive Twenty Mule Team Canyon
shortDescription: A short scenic drive along an unpaved road through colorful badlands.

image.title: Twenty Mule Team Road
image.altText: A dirt road through bare brown and yellow striped hills.
image.caption: These badlands have been the setting for scenes from popular films including Star Wars Episode VI.

title: Experience Death Valley at Night
shortDescription: Death Valley is just as spectacular at night as it is during the day- learn about a few ways you can explore the park after dark.

image.title: Dark Sky Laser Pointers
image.altText: Seven people silhouetted pointing green lasers to the same spot in a dark night sky.
image.caption: Rangers offer special night sky programs during Death Valley's annual Dark Sky Festival.

title: Running in Death Valley
shortDescription: Go for a run in Death Valley! The park can be a very interesting and challenging place to test your road running or trail running abilities. Over 1,000 miles of paved and dirt roads, plus almost endless cross country opportunities await you. To enjoy the park safely, please run in the cooler months.
seasonDescription: Summer is extreme in Death Valley, the hottest place on earth, and we do not recommend running in the summer.

image.altText: A woman running along a dirt road in a diverse desert setting.

title: Day Hiking
shortDescription: Looking for somewhere to hike in Death Valley? The park has interpretive trails, hiking trails, and unofficial hiking routes, and is open to cross-country travel by foot in most places.
seasonDescription: Hiking is NOT advised in the lower elevations in the park during the summer months. Check out the trails that are higher in elevations for possible summer options. But be advised that temperatures at the Telescope Peak Trailhead can reach over 90 F in the summer.

image.title: Hiker at Dantes View
image.altText: A hiker stands on a rocky ridge looking away from the camera out on a vast white desert valley.
image.caption: The Dantes Ridge (Mt Perry) hike offers expansive views of Death Valley.

title: Visit Badwater Basin
shortDescription: Badwater Basin is the lowest elevation in North America at - 282 feet (- 86 m) below sea level. A visit to this otherworldly salt flat will provide you with a unique experience and a landscape that appears to stretch on forever. A short 1/4 mile (400 m) hike will you bring you to the polygon salt formations that Death Valley is famous for, or in the summer months, the view can be enjoyed from the parking area.
seasonDescription: Visiting in the summer means mostly staying in your vehicle and enjoying the view of the salt flat. We do not recommend being outside of your airconditioned vehicle for longer than 15 minutes during the extreme summer heat.

image.altText: An expansive salt flat with distant desert mountains and a pink sky sunset.

title: Hiking/Visiting with Pets
shortDescription: Due to the extreme weather, it is not usually a good idea to bring a pet to Death Valley if you want to do any exploring out of your vehicle. If you are traveling through the park with a pet, and want to know where they are allowed to go, this is where to find that info! Stick to the roads, developed areas, and campgrounds. Pets are not permitted in the Wilderness or out of the areas listed above.
seasonDescription: It is difficult to travel with a pet in Death Valley National Park if you plan to spend time away from your vehicle. Summer temperatures can be deadly, and pets should NEVER be left in a car, where temperature rises quickly.

image.altText: A man walks a dog on a leash down a dirt road in a desert setting.

title: Mountain Biking
shortDescription: Hundreds of miles of dirt roads are available for mountain biking exploration.

image.title: Mountain Biking
image.altText: A mountain biker rides down a dirt road toward the camera between yellow hills with few plants.
image.caption: Hundreds of miles of dirt roads with little traffic offer great opportunities for mountain biking.

title: Cycling
shortDescription: Whether you prefer flat and straight or mountainous and curvy, Death Valley has paved roads suitable for all levels of cycling enthusiasts.

image.title: Death Valley Cyclists
image.altText: Three cyclists ride on a paved road with desert plants on either side, and mountains in the distance
image.caption: Cyclists enjoying the views along one of the many paved roads in Death Valley.

title: Check Out Devils Golf Course
shortDescription: An immense area of rock salt eroded by wind and rain into jagged spires. So incredibly serrated that "only the devil could play golf on such rough links." Listen carefully and you'll hear sounds like tiny pops and pings. The sound is literally billions of tiny salt crystals bursting apart as they expand and contract in the heat.
seasonDescription:
Plan to visit in the cooler late fall, winter, and early spring months.

From mid-May to mid-September, this area can be extremely hot with temperatures reaching 120 F or higher.

image.title: Devils Golf Course
image.altText: Sharp, eroded salt formations stretch into the background.
image.caption: Jagged peaks of salt form the forbidding landscape here.

title: Hike the Cliff Trail
shortDescription: The Cliff Trial along the Raymondskill Ridge has gorgeous scenic views and just enough elevation gain to get the heart pumping.
seasonDescription: The Cliff Trail is great in all seasons. Snowshoeing and cross-country skiing are popular activities in the winter, while the trees are the stars of the show during spring and fall.

image.title: Hike the Cliff Trail
image.altText: A view from the Cliff Trail. The Raymonskill ridge hovering over the river and farmfields below.
image.caption: The Cliff Trail has amazing views of the Delaware River Valley in multiple spots along the trail.

title: Millbrook Village
shortDescription: Take a walk around Millbrook Village.

image.title: Millbrook Village
image.altText: A brown inn with a white fence on the left. A white two-story general store building on the right.
image.caption: The inn (left) and general store (right) are at the intersection of the old roads.

title: Easy Hike Along Hornbecks Creek
shortDescription: An easy, one-mile out and back hike along the Lower Hornbecks Creek will lead visitors to a small waterfall, but the waterfall is only part of the view!

image.title: Lower Hornbecks Creek Waterfall
image.altText: A small, tiered waterfall and pool with a small amount of snow around it.
image.caption: Lower Hornbecks Creek's waterfall in late winter.

title: Biking on the McDade Recreational Trail
shortDescription: Biking on the McDade Recreational Trail
seasonDescription: While the McDade Recreational Trail is open all year, the best seasons for biking are spring through fall.

image.title: Biking on the McDade Recreational Trail
image.altText: Three people bike onto the McDade Recreational Trail.
image.caption: Biking on the McDade Recreational Trail is a great family activity.

title: Snowshoe and Cross-country Ski on the McDade Trail
shortDescription: Snowshoeing and cross-country skiing on the McDade Recreational Trail.
seasonDescription: While the McDade Trail is open all year long, snowshoeing and cross-country skiing are only available in the winter while there is snow on the trail.

image.title: McDade Trail at Bushkill Access
image.altText: A snow-covered trail looking out at the sun shining on the Delaware River.
image.caption: The McDade Trail at Bushkill Access in winter.

title: Tour Old Mine Road
shortDescription: Take a tour of Old Mine Road.

image.title: Grist Mill at Millbrook
image.altText: A wooden grist mill three stories tall surrounded by fallen leaves.
image.caption: The grist mill at Millbrook is one of the historic structures in the village along Old Mine Rd.

title: Hike the Jones Hole Trail
shortDescription: 8.5 miles (13.6 km) round trip, out and back trail. Jones Hole Trail is a popular hike along a babbling brook near the northwest corner of Dinosaur National Monument. The creek offers good trout fishing. A Utah State fishing license is required. Backcountry camping requires a permit. Camping at Ely Creek requires advanced reservations. No pets allowed.

image.title: Hiker on the Jones Hole Trail
image.altText: A hiker walks on a trail through golden colored grass as tall cliffs rise on both sides.
image.caption: Hiker on the Jones Hole Trail as it approaches the Green River

title: Be a Dinosaur Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Junior Rangers help to "Explore, Learn, and Protect" our national parks. Anyone can be a Junior Ranger! Once you learn about the monument and the amazing resources found here, you will be able to share your knowledge with friends and family!

image.title: Dinosaur Junior Ranger
image.altText: An Allosaurus fossil skull with a junior ranger badge over the eye.
image.caption: Complete the junior ranger book to earn a badge 150 million years in the making.

title: Hike the Confluence Trail
shortDescription: 1.25 miles (2 km) round trip, out and back trail. Easy. The Confluence Trail provides a short and easy walk to the confluence of the Green and Yampa Rivers at Echo Park. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: The paved Harpers Corner Road, which provides access to the Echo Park Road and Echo Park Campground, is typically impassable in winter, due to snow and ice. The unpaved Echo Park Road, is impassable for all vehicles when wet, regardless of the time of year. Stop in at one of the Visitor Centers to inquire about road conditions before attempting the drive to Echo Park Campground. (Note: The Canyon Visitor Center in Dinosaur, CO is closed in winter).

image.title: Sunset Below the Confluence
image.altText: The Green River flows past trees under a blue sky along the Confluence Trail.
image.caption: This is the view downstream of the confluence of the Green and Yampa Rivers.

title: Hike to the Swelter Shelter Petroglyphs
shortDescription: 400 feet (122 m) out and back trail. Easy. This short hike to Swelter Shelter offers visitors an opportunity to view a variety of petroglyphs and pictographs very close to the road. Petroglyphs and pictographs are fragile, irreplaceable records of the past that many still hold sacred. Don't touch, trace, or take rubbings of them as it ruins the designs. This site is protected by federal law. Leashed pets are allowed.
seasonDescription: This path is short and may be covered with snow during the winter, but the road to this site is typically accessible year round.

image.title: Swelter Shelter in Snow
image.altText: A short stone wall covered in snow offers a place to view petroglyphs and pictographs.
image.caption: Swelter Shelter offers a place to see a variety of petroglyphs and pictographs.

title: Picnicking in Dinosaur
shortDescription: The Plug Hat Butte picnic area is located along Harpers Corner Road on the Colorado side of the monument.
seasonDescription: Snow may be present during the winter covering raod and trail surfaces.

image.title: Plug Hat Trail
image.altText: A paved trail moving between a snow covered pine and juniper forest.
image.caption: Plug Hat Butte is a peaceful location to relax in the monument.

title: Hike the Gates of Lodore Trail
shortDescription: 1 mile (1.6 km) round trip, out and back trail. Easy. The Gates of Lodore Trail is a short but scenic walk to a view of the Green River as it enters the Canyon of Lodore. A trail booklet is available at the Visitor Centers. No pets allowed.

image.title: Enjoying the View at Gates of Lodore
image.altText: Two women sit on a large rock as a green colored river flows into a canyon in the distance.
image.caption: Flat rocks at the end of the Gates of Lodore Trail provide a place to enjoy the scenery.

title: Hike the Harpers Corner Trail
shortDescription: 2 miles (3.2 km) round trip, out and back trail. Moderate difficulty. The Harpers Corner Trail runs along a narrow ridge to a spectacular viewpoint with views of the rivers far below. Along the way, hikers can gaze across the remote canyon country. A pamphlet for this trail is available at the Visitor Centers. The trail is typically inaccessible in winter. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: The Harpers Corner Road leading to this trail is typically impassable due to seasonal snow and ice. If you are visiting when snow is on the ground, contact the Information Desk at (435) 781-7700 to find out if the Harpers Corner Trail is open.

image.title: Harpers Corner View
image.altText: A person in a ball cap leans on a railing and looks towards large cliffs and mountains.
image.caption: A hiker enjoys the view of the Yampa River Canyon from the end of the Harpers Corner Trail.

title: Hike the Ruple Point Trail
shortDescription: 9.2 miles (14.8 km) round trip, out and back trail. Moderate to difficult. For most of its length, Ruple Point Trail crosses a rolling terrain filled with sagebrush and juniper. Near the end, a short descent rewards hikers with a breathtaking views of Split Mountain Canyon and the Green River below. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: The Harpers Corner Road, which leads to this trailhead, may be closed seasonally due to snow and ice.

image.title: View from Ruple Point
image.altText: Large walls of orange red rock rise as a river flows through a deep canyon.
image.caption: From the end of the Ruple Point Trail, hikers are rewarded with a view of Split Mountain Canyon.

title: Hike the Plug Hat Trail
shortDescription: 0.25 miles (0.4 km) round trip loop trail. Easy. The Plug Hat Trail offers scenic views of Dinosaur's rugged landscape from atop a sandstone butte. This trail is paved and wheelchair accessible. Leashed pets are allowed.
seasonDescription: The Harpers Corner Road leading to this trail may be seasonally impassible due to snow and ice.

image.title: Plug Hat Trail Bench
image.altText: A bench beside a paved path provides views of the canyons surrounding Plug Hat Trail.
image.caption: This paved trail offers accessible views of Dinosaur's rugged landscape.

title: Hike the Box Canyon Trail
shortDescription: 0.25 miles (0.4 km) round trip, out and back trail. Easy. The Box Canyon Trail is a relatively level and shady walk into a dead-end canyon. The trailhead is located on the north side of the parking area for the Josie Morris Cabin. This is typically a good hike for small children. Keep kids close, and watch for poison ivy. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: The last 2 miles (3.2) of the Cub Creek Road that leads to this trailhead are unpaved. This unpaved section may be closed to vehicles when wet with rain or snow. If the road to Josie Morris Cabin is closed to vehicles, the trailhead will be 2 miles (3.2 km) one-way from the end of the paved road, which lengthens the BoxCanyon hike to 4.25 miles (6.8 km) round-trip.

image.title: End of the Box Canyon Trail
image.altText: Large cliffs of white rock rise above green shrubs to a blue sky.
image.caption: The end of the Box Canyon Trail provides dramatic views of cliffs of Weber sandstone.

title: Hike the River Trail at Dinosaur National Monument
shortDescription: 3 miles (4.8 km) round trip, out and back trail. Moderate difficulty. The River Trail in Dinosaur National Monument connects the Split Mountain and Green River campgrounds. This trail climbs to a bench above the river and offers dramatic views of Spilt Mountain, the Green River, and Cub Creek Valley. In spring, the slopes may be briefly covered with an array of wildflowers. Leashed pets are allowed.

image.title: View from the River Trail
image.altText: A large river flows in late evening shadow as sun hits a large, rocky mountain in the distance.
image.caption: Hikers on the river trail get continual views of the Green River and Split Mountain.

title: Hike the Hog Canyon Trail
shortDescription: 1.5 miles (2.4 km) round trip, out and back trail. Easy. The Hog Canyon Trail is a pleasant hike into a box canyon near the Josie Morris Cabin. The trail is relatively flat and shaded, typically good for small children. Keep kids close, and watch for poison ivy. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: The last 2 miles (3.2) of the Cub Creek Road that leads to this trailhead are unpaved. This unpaved section may be closed to vehicles when wet with rain or snow. If the road to Josie Morris Cabin is closed to vehicles, the trailhead will be 2 miles (3.2 km) one-way from the end of the paved road, which lengthens the Hog Canyon hike to 5.5 miles (9 km) round-trip.

image.title: Hog Canyon Trail in Fall
image.altText: A narrow trail surrounded by brown grasses and vegetations leads to tall cliffs in the distance.
image.caption: The Hog Canyon Trail provides an easy hike in any season.

title: Hike Sound of Silence Trail
shortDescription: 3.2 miles (5.1 km) round trip loop. Moderate to difficult. The Sound of Silence Trail takes hikers through the geologic diversity of Dinosaur National Monument. Hikers encounter a variety of terrain, including an intermittent stream bed, upturned rock layers, desert badlands, and slickrock. A short rock scramble is required. There is no shade on this trail. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: Parts of this trail are slippery when wet. When snow is on the ground, this trail may require snowshoes. Additionally, there is a short rock scrambling section towards the end of the trail, which can be slippery and difficult to see when covered with snow or ice. Your safety depends on your own good judgement.

image.title: Hiker on the Sound of Silence Trail
image.altText: A tall man with a green backpack looks out at a valley of red colored rocks
image.caption: A hiker looks towards the area know as "the Racetrack"

title: Hike the Fossil Discovery Trail
shortDescription: 2.5 mile (4 km) round trip, out and back trail. Easy to moderate difficulty. The Fossil Discovery Trail gives visitors an opportunity to explore a variety of rock layers and see unexcavated fossils as they are often found by paleontologists. The most famous of these rock layers is the Morrison Formation, which contains dinosaur fossils. No pets allowed.

image.title: Saurpod Femur on Fossil Discovery Trail
image.altText: A closeup of a fossilized femur of a long-necked dinosaur on the Morrison spur of the trail.
image.caption: The Morrison Formation spur of this trail features many unexcavated dinosaur fossils.

title: Quarry Exhibit Hall
shortDescription: The Quarry Exhibit Hall allows visitors to view the wall of approximately 1,500 dinosaur bones in a refurbished, comfortable space.
seasonDescription: The shuttle to and from the Quarry Visitor Center to the Quarry Exhibit Hall runs seasonally through the summer every 15 minutes.

image.title: Quarry Exhibit Hall
image.altText: A shuttle bus parked in front of a large building with glass walls.
image.caption: The Quarry Exhibit Hall is the main attraction at the monument.

title: Hike the Bull Canyon Trail
shortDescription: 3 miles (4.8 km) round trip. Difficult. Bull Canyon is a steep, unmaintained trail in a remote section of the monument. It begins on the Yampa Bench Road and takes hikers into the Harding Hole area along the Yampa River. River users can use the trail to access other scenic overlooks. The campsites at Harding Hole are reserved for rivergoers during the high-use river season. Permits are required for overnight camping. No pets allowed.
seasonDescription: The unpaved Yampa Bench Road is typically impassable from winter to late spring, which prevents access to the trailhead located along the Yampa Bench Road. River rafters may find it easier to access the trail from the Harding Hole River Campsites when the Yampa Bench Road is impassable.

image.title: Bull Canyon
image.altText: Tall yellow colored cliffs rise on both sides of a narrow valley.
image.caption: Fall foliage mixes with the colorful cliffs along the Bull Canyon Trail.

title: Hike the Desert Voices Trail
shortDescription: 1.7 miles (2.7 km) round trip loop trail. Moderate difficulty. The Desert Voices Trail starts at Split Mountain. It wanders through valleys and over rocky outcrops, offering dramatic views of the surrounding landscape. No pets allowed.

image.title: Desert Voices Trail
image.altText: A trail on red colored soil leads through low shrubs with views of a rocky mountain in the distance.
image.caption: Hiking on the Desert Voices Trail provides dramatic views in any season.

title: Wildlife Viewing in Dinosaur
shortDescription: Many visitors to Dinosaur National Monument are often surprised by the variety of wildlife that lives here.

image.title: Rock Mountain Bighorn Sheep
image.altText: A mother bighorn sheep with her offspring on a rock outcrop.
image.caption: Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep frequent the canyons of the Green and Yampa rivers.

title: Drive the Echo Park Road
shortDescription: The 14 mile (23 km) unpaved Echo Park Road takes drivers into the heart of Dinosaur National Monument. This rugged road begins along the Harpers Corner Road, winds through scenic canyon country, and ends near the banks of the Green River at Echo Park. High-clearance vehicles with all-wheel-drive (AWD) are strongly recommended. RVs and trailers are not advised. The road is impassable when wet.
seasonDescription: Access depends on road conditions. The Echo Park Road is impassable when wet or snow covered.

image.title: Echo Park Road Dugway
image.altText: a red colored dirt road winds down a steep slope
image.caption: The Echo Park Road descends steeply from the Harpers Corner Road as it winds toward the Green River.

title: Drive the Island Park Road
shortDescription: The Island Park Road is an 18 mile (29 km) unpaved road that starts outside of Dinosaur National Monument and ends inside the park near the Ruple Ranch Site. The first 10 miles (16 km) are located outside of the park. The last 8 miles (13 km) reveal beautiful petroglyph panels at McKee Spring, a secluded campground at Rainbow Park, and stellar views of the Green River from Island Park. High-clearance vehicles are strongly recommended. The road is impassable when wet.
seasonDescription: Regardless of the season, this road is impassable when wet. The road is also typically impassable in winter.

image.title: Island Park Viewpoint
image.altText: The Green River twists through a landscape of canyons and yellowing trees at Island Park.
image.caption: Throughout the day, light and shadow may twist around canyons to illuminate Island Park's scenery.

title: Drive the Harpers Corner Road
shortDescription: Harpers Corner Scenic Drive is a 31 mile (50 km) paved road that offers wheelchair-accessible overlooks with spectacular views of Dinosaur's rivers and canyons. Along the way, visitors can enjoy picnic areas, as well as several paved paths and hiking trails. The road is accessible for most vehicles when clear of ice and snow. Harpers Corner Road is closed in winter, and reopens in spring when conditions allow.
seasonDescription: Harpers Corner Road is typically open from late spring through fall. Regardless of the season, inclement weather can render the road impassable. The road is typically closed in winter.

image.title: Harpers Corner Road Scenic Drive
image.altText: The paved Harpers Corner Road winds around yellow sandstone buttes dotted with desert shrubs.
image.caption: The Harpers Corner Road is winding and steep in some places.

title: Bicycling at Dinosaur
shortDescription: Bicycling is allowed on any road within Dinosaur National Monument, but is not allowed on any trails. Paved roads within the monument are narrow, and often have no shoulders. Bicyclists should take proper measures to stay safe, and bring plenty of water in summer.

image.title: Bicycling at Dinosaur
image.altText: A man stands with a bike along a dirt road
image.caption: Roads in Dinosaur provide an opportunity for biking.

title: Drive the Yampa Bench Road
shortDescription: The 18 mile (29 km) unpaved Yampa Bench Road offers visitors a look into the quieter side of Dinosaur. Running along a "bench" of land high above the Yampa River, visitors can experience incredible views and historic sites. High-clearance, four-wheel-drive (4WD) vehicles are strongly recommended for this rugged road. The road is impassable when wet.
seasonDescription: The Yampa Bench Road is impassable to all vehicles when wet with rain or snow. It may take several days to become passable after inclement weather. The road is generally impassable in winter.

image.title: Yampa River from Yampa Bench Road
image.altText: The Yampa River flows through Dinosaur's rugged sandstone canyons.
image.caption: The rugged Yampa Bench Road offers a getaway to the quieter side of Dinosaur's canyon country.

title: Drive the Tour of Tilted Rocks
shortDescription: This 10 mile (16) km paved tour along the Cub Creek Road in Utah provides a great introduction to Dinosaur National Monument. Take the Tour of Tilted Rocks to enjoy sweeping geology, historic homesteads, petroglyphs and pictographs, hiking trails, campgrounds, and scenic vistas! The road is usually accessible for passenger cars. Seasonal closures may affect the last 4 miles (6 km) of the road.
seasonDescription: The Cub Creek Road is typically open and accessible year-round. The unpaved section at the end of the drive is maintained and usually open, but may be impassable after severe rain or heavy snowfall.

image.title: Cub Creek Road View of Campground
image.altText: This view from the Cub Creek Road reveals Split Mountain rising above multicolored rock formations.
image.caption: Dinosaur's sweeping geology is showcased in many places along the Cub Creek Road.

title: View the Night Sky at Split Mountain

title: Birding at Flamingo
shortDescription: Flamingo offers ample birding opportunities along its many trail areas as well as around the visitor center and marina. The mix of mangrove and coastal prairie habitats host a bounty of wading birds, shorebirds and waterbirds throughout the year. Additionally, there is always the chance of seeing tropical marine life close to shore, including crocodiles and manatees.
seasonDescription:
Spring- Northward migration of songbirds and shorebirds peaks in April and May. Along the Guy Bradley Trail, resident Prairie Warblers forage alongside other warbler and vireo species stopping over on flights to breeding grounds in the northern United States. Sparrows may also be found in the coastal prairie scrub at the western end of the trail and around the Flamingo campground amphitheater. Additionally, look among foraging flocks of Brown-headed Cowbirds around the visitor parking areas for a Shiny Cowbird or two.

Summer- Although mosquitoes are most abundant during the summer and fall, this is the best time of year to look for hard-to-find resident birds, including Mangrove Cuckoo and Black-whiskered Vireo, which both breed in the mangrove habitats. Swallow-tailed Kites soar in large flocks hunting dragonflies over the open fields near the Flamingo entrance. White-crowned Pigeons may also be seen around the campground area.

Fall- The overlap of fall migration season and peak tropical weather season can result in massive fallouts of birds along the shores of Flamingo. Especially at high tide, look for beached seabirds and shorebirds, including Black Skimmer, Gull-billed Tern, Marbled Godwit, Wilson’s Plover, Black-bellied Plover, Willet, and various small sandpiper species near the campground amphitheater. An occasional Wilson’s Snipe may also be found in the coastal prairie scrub by the Flamingo tent camping area before the tent campsites are mowed for the winter.

Winter- The dry season brings higher wading bird activity and movement throughout the Flamingo area as birds follow the rise and fall of tides and inflow of freshwater for food. The coastal prairies around Flamingo and sometimes the mudflats in Florida Bay close by the camping area can host large mixed flocks of ibis, Roseate Spoonbills, Wood Storks, herons and egrets. Look closely and you may find a Great White Heron, a white subspecies of the Great Blue Heron that within the United States is only found in coastal South Florida and the Keys. Large numbers of American White Pelicans also spend the winter on Florida Bay.

image.caption: Shorebirds look for food along the shore near the Flamingo campground.

title: Birding Snake Bight Trail
shortDescription: Snake Bight Trail can be walked any time of year, but is easiest to walk in the winter when mosquitoes are not abundant. This trail offers the opportunity to see birds restricted to coastal habitats, including Reddish Egret. Other species of shorebirds such as Greater Yellowlegs, Black-necked Stilt, Black-bellied Plover and various other sandpipers can also be found. Shorebirds are most easily observed during high tide when water forces birds off mudflats farther out on Flori
seasonDescription:
Spring- Northward spring migration can bring many shorebirds, which are most easily identified in their breeding plumage at this time of year.

Summer- Although mosquitoes are most abundant during the summer and fall, this is the best time of year to look for hard-to-find resident birds, including Mangrove Cuckoo and Black-whiskered Vireo, which both breed in the mangrove habitats.

Fall- The overlap of fall migration season and peak tropical weather season can result in massive fallouts of shorebirds along Florida Bay.

Winter- Large, mixed flocks of herons, egrets, ibis, Wood Storks and Roseate Spoonbills can be seen in the mangroves along the trail, and American White Pelicans can be seen soaring overhead. At the end of the trail, look for shorebirds, Reddish Egrets, Bald Eagles and Ospreys, especially at high tide.

title: Birding Along the Anhinga Trail
shortDescription: The Anhinga Trail is a popular place to start your exploration at Everglades National Park, providing a ready sample of wetland wildlife including alligators, turtles, fish, plants, and birds, all along a short, three-quarter mile paved and boardwalk trail.
seasonDescription:
Spring- The height of the dry season brings both higher numbers of wading birds like herons and egrets, and migrating birds flying north to breed. Short-tailed Hawks, Swallow-tailed Kites and other birds of prey can be seen circling overhead, and the trees can host many colorful songbirds including warblers, vireos, and flycatchers.

Summer- As the water level rises, bird life becomes harder to see as animals spread out in search of food. Breeding birds that can be found in the park include Swallow-tailed Kite, Black-whiskered Vireo, White-crowned Pigeon and Mangrove Cuckoo. You will more likely hear these birds than see them, but listening first can often lead to good views of the bird in question.

Fall- The height of the wet season means minimal bird activity on the ground, but if you look to the sky, you may see many different birds of prey migrating south for the winter.

Winter- The dry season is the breeding season for most large birds in the park. On the Anhinga Trail, many of the namesake Anhingas build their nests in pond apples trees, readily visible from the trail. Other birds regularly seen here during the winter include Double-crested Cormorants, Great Blue, Tricolored and Green Herons, and the vividly colorful Purple Gallinule.

title: Walk the Anhinga Trail
shortDescription: The famous Anhinga Trail is a self-guided pavement and boardwalk trail winding through and over sawgrass marsh and freshwater slough. A paved path leads you along the water and to a looping boardwalk, providing views into the prairie and the clear waters of the slough. You may see alligators, fish, turtles, anhingas, and many other birds, especially during the winter, when the generally lower waters of the dry season concentrate aquatic wildlife in the slough.
seasonDescription:
The trail is open and popular year round. Wildlife is present at all times of the year, but is generally most abundant during the cooler and drier months of December-March. During these months, look for nesting birds, turtles and alligators.  

The summer months are quieter, as many of the animals prefer to stay in the shade and water, so consider visiting the trail in the early morning summer hours to catch a glimpse of what makes this trail so special.

title: Burma Trail

seasonDescription:
The backdune wilderness trail is hiked most comfortably in cold weather, as adult mosquitoes are not present. Ticks can be present year-round, though they are not as active in the winter. Tick checks should be performed after a hike.

Hiking the ocean beach adjacent to the wilderness area can be a more comfortable option in warmer months.

seasonDescription: Boaters may visit Fire Island year-round, but should be prepared for ice on the Great South Bay in the winters. While boaters may choose to dock at Sailors Haven and Watch Hill for day trips during winter months, water and power hookups are ony available during the spring, summer, and fall seasons.

title: Birding at Fire Island

seasonDescription: While birdwatching is best during migration seasons in the spring and fall, Fire Island sports a host of year-round resident bird species, as well as unusual winter visitors.

seasonDescription: The Scenic Drive usually opens sometime in May and closes in October after the first snow storm. Please contact the visitor center to see if the scenic drive is open.

seasonDescription: The Scenic Drive usually opens sometime in May and closes in October after the first snow storm. Please contact the visitor center to see if the scenic drive is open.

title: Beavers
shortDescription: The North American beaver is the second largest rodent in the world behind the Capybara of South America. Found throughout the U.S. and Canada, these semiaquatic ecosystem engineers constuct dams and lodges that affect the hydrology and ecology of their surroundings. As a keystone species, their presence in riparian habitats affects all neighboring animal and plant life.
seasonDescription: Although beavers are active year-round, they typically stay in their lodges during the winter unless retrieving stored food from under the water.

title: Wolverines
shortDescription: A mid-sized carnivore in the weasel family, the wolverine is active throughout the year in cold, snowy environments to which it is well-adapted. Wolverines are rarely seen and inhabit remote terrain. They are also known as one of the rarest and most elusive carnivores on the planet.

image.title: Wolverine
