image.caption: The primary threat to wolverines is habitat and range loss due to climate warming.

title: Mountain Goats
shortDescription: The mountain goat is one of the park's most inconic creatures. It is the only living member of its genus and is more closely related to caprines (the chamois of Europe and the gorals and serows of Asia) than to domesticated goats.

image.title: Photographing mountain goat
image.altText: A man takes a picture of a mountain goat standing on a rocky ledge.
image.caption: Visitors should be at least 75 feet (25 yards/23 meters) away when taking photos of mountain goats.

title: Listen to Glacier's Podcast
shortDescription: Rangers recommend Glacier's podcast, Headwaters: a podcast about how Glacier is connected to everything else!

image.title: Mountains at Sunset
image.altText: Blue mountains and a golden sunset with clouds
image.caption: View of Glacier's mountains at sunset.

title: Red Foxes
shortDescription: Red foxes are found throughout the northern hemisphere. In Glacier, they are adapted to a wide range of habitats, from open grasslands to dense forests. Most abundant in riparian areas and along the edges of forests, they are the smallest of the canids found in the park. Red foxes occur in several color phases, but they usually have reddish-yellow coats that are somewhat darker on the back and shoulders, black "socks" on their lower legs, and a white-tipped tail.

image.title: Red fox
image.altText: A red fox stands on forest ground.
image.caption: Red foxes often live on the forest edge, ensuring good places to den, hide, and scavenge or hunt.

title: Bighorn Sheep
shortDescription: Bighorn sheep live in a variety of habitats throughout the year. During the summer, they can be found in meadows, fellfields, and on mid-elevation slopes bordered by cliffs and ledges. In the winter, sheep frequent windswept and south-facing valleys and ridges where forage is blown free of snow. Bighorn sheep can often be seen in the parking lot of Logan Pass licking antifreeze from the pavement, which is the most easily accessible source of salt in their diet.

image.altText: a bighorn sheep pops its head up and over tall green grasses.

title: Gray Wolves
shortDescription: The subspecies of gray wolves (Canis lupus) found in Glacier is called the northern Rocky Mountain gray wolf (C. l. irremotus). There are three color variants: gray, white, and black. Wolves are secretive and elusive creatures, with sightings primarily being of lone wolves or pairs.
seasonDescription: Although still extremely rare, most sightings occur in the winter and spring.

image.title: Gray Wolf
image.altText: A wolf lays in the snow, with shoots of dead grass in the background. It has gray fur and gray eyes.
image.caption: You're more likely to hear than to see a wolf. They're typically heard in the North Fork area.

title: Elk
shortDescription: Glacier provides a summer range for a significant number of elk, while most winter at lower elevations outside the park. The subspecies occuring in Glacier is the Rocky Mountain elk (C. c. nelsoni). They feed on grasses, sedges, other herbs and shrubs, bark of aspen trees, conifer needles, burned bark, and aquatic plants.

image.title: Elk
image.altText: A group of about 9 elk stand and lay in snow up to their knees.
image.caption: A group of elk lay and stand amidst February snow.

title: Deer
shortDescription: Two types of deer are commonly seen thorughout Glacier: the northwestern white-tailed deer (O. v. ochrourus) and the Rocky Mountain mule deer (O. h. hemionus). Both will flee when in danger. Males grow antlers from April or May through August or September and then shed them in the spring.

image.title: Mule Deer
image.altText: A mule deer buck reaches back among grass and boulders.
image.caption: A mule deer buck reaches back among grass and boulders.

title: All about birding in Glacier National Park
shortDescription: Glacier provides a wonderful opportunity to birdwatch, with plenty of spaces for birders of all ages to sit, listen, and observe the sights and sounds of nature. With 279 documented species including raptors, songbirds, shorebirds, and waterfowl, the park’s variation in elevation and habitat types contribute to a high diversity of bird life.

image.title: Watching Golden Eagles on Mount Brown
image.altText: Three birders use binoculars to look for migrating raptors with a mountain in the background.
image.caption: Glacier is great for birding in the spring and summer but fall has its moments too!

title: White-Tailed Ptarmigan
shortDescription: The white-tailed ptarmigan is a medium to large chicken-like member of the grouse family. They are completely white in winter and barred grayish-brown in summer with white wings and tails and feathered feet. Breeding males will have a broad band of black markings across the chest and have red eye combs. Like chickens, they make clucking noises.

image.title: White-tailed ptarmigan
image.altText: A brown-speckled bird followed by two smaller chicks walks amongst rocks and vegetation.
image.caption: Ptarmigan are camouflaged to look like rocks in summer, then turn white in winter to match snow.

title: Mountain Bluebird
shortDescription: The mountain bluebird is a small bird with a round head and a straight, thin bill. Adult males are bright sky-blue, somewhat paler underneath. Adult females have duller blue wings and tails with gray breasts, crowns, throats, and backs. Their call sounds similar to a thin “tew” while their song is a warbled high “chur chur.”

image.title: Mountain Bluebird
image.altText: A sky-blue bird sits at the top of a coniferous tree against a gray sky.
image.caption: The mountain bluebird inspired the original Twitter icon.

title: Clark's Nutcracker
shortDescription: The Clark’s nutcracker has a pale- gray body, black wings with large white patches along the trailing edges, and a black tail with broad white stripes on either side. These birds typically travel in small flocks and call back and forth to communicate. They have a long, harsh, rising call that sounds similar to “shraaaaaaa.”

image.title: Clark's Nutcracker
image.altText: A small bird soars through the sky. It has a gray body with dark wings and white wingtips.
image.caption: Clark's nutcracker is distinctive in look and behavior. It's unlike any other corvid in Montana.

title: Harlequin Duck
shortDescription: One-quarter of Montana’s harlequin duck broods are born in Glacier National Park. These birds have a low reproductive rate and are very susceptible to habitat loss and degradation. Because of these characteristics, they are listed as a Species of Concern in the state of Montana.

image.title: Harlequin Duck
image.altText: An orange, gray, and white duck sits on a rock amidst rushing water.
image.caption: Harlequin ducks have been studied in the park since 1974.

title: Osprey
shortDescription: A large bird with a slim body, the osprey has long, narrow wings that have a sharp bend in flight resembling the letter “M.” Ospreys have dark-brown feathers on their back and are white underneath. They also have a notable dark mark at the “wrist” of their wing. An osprey’s call is high-pitched with a series of short, slightly wavering screeches that sound like “too-too-too-tee-tee-tee-tee-too-too.”

image.title: Osprey
image.altText: A bird with brown wings and a white breast and neck sits atop a bare branch with cobwebs.
image.caption: Ospreys are primarily near water sources with healthy fish populations.

title: Common Loon
shortDescription: One-fifth of Montana’s nesting loons are in Glacier National Park. Because of their limited range, small population, sensitivity to human disturbance, and loss of breeding habitats outside of the park, they are listed as a Species of Special Concern in Montana. Human disturbance along shores or getting too close to these birds can cause stress and may cause them to abandon their nests.

image.title: Common Loon
image.altText: Three black and white checkered birds glide on the water. One flaps its wings about to take flight.
image.caption: Loons need active conservation efforts because of their vulnerability.

title: Owls
shortDescription: There are four species of owls documented within Glacier, but their nocturnal nature may make it difficult to hear or see one of them while visiting.

image.title: Great Horned Owl
image.altText: An owl with feathers resembling eyebrows and yellow eyes stares down from a tree branch.
image.caption: The great horned owl has a deep stuttering call that sounds similar to "ho hoo hoo hoododo hooo ho."

title: Eagles
shortDescription: The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) and the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) can both be seen soaring over Glacier’s skies. As one of the most important golden eagle migration routes in North America, Glacier established a Hawk Watch International site in 2018 to monitor raptors during fall migration. Research has shown that human presence can disturb eagle nesting and foraging, so known nest areas in national parks are often closed to visitors.

image.title: Bald Eagles
image.altText: A large bird with a white head and brown body opens its beak towards another large brown bird.
image.caption: A bald eagle opens its beak as if talking to the other juvenile bald eagle.

title: Varied Thrush
shortDescription: These secretive birds rarely flaunt their flashy colors. Instead, they sing shyly from dense forests. Adult males have a light orange line over the eyes, blue-gray backs, and a burnt-orange throat and belly separated by a dark breast band but are heard much more often than seen. They have a distinctive song of a long, single whistle on one pitch; it can sometimes be mistaken for a human distress whistle.

image.title: Varied Thrush
image.altText: A black and bright orange bird lands atop a snow bank.
image.caption: Despite its bright coloring, the varied thrush is actually quite secretive and shy.

title: American Dipper
shortDescription: The American dipper is a stocky, round-bodied bird with grayish-brown feathers, a dark bill, and long, pale legs. The bird gets its name from bobbing up and down while standing, a funny but easily identifying trait. They sing a high-pitched song that is a series of whistled phrases, each repeated two to four times with a buzzy call that sounds similar to “dzeet.”

image.title: American Dipper
image.altText: A round gray-blue bird sits on a pale brown rock in the water.
image.caption: The American dipper has a white eyelid which shows when it's blinking.

title: Fire-Adapted Woodpeckers
shortDescription: Glacier is the perfect home for several fire-adapted woodpeckers. These are birds that depend on regular wildfire to create their habitat. Listen for “thunks” or knocking sounds of woodpeckers as they excavate tree cavities in search of a meal.

image.title: An American three-toed woodpecker
image.altText: A bird with a white and black striped breast and black top feathers hangs onto a tree trunk.
image.caption: American three-toed woodpeckers are often seen in recently burned areas.

title: American Martens
shortDescription: Martes americana The American marten, also called a pine marten, is part of the weasel family. Pine martens have short limbs and a long, bushy tail. They are light to dark brown or black with a throat patch that is an irregular shape and size, with ranges in color from buff to bright orange.

image.title: American marten
image.altText: An animal with short limbs and a bushy tail sits on a snow-covered tree branch.
image.caption: The American marten

title: Weasels
shortDescription: Glacier National Park has many members of the weasel family that call the park home. Two of those animals are the short-tailed weasel or ermine (Mustela erminea) and the long-tailed weasel (Mustela frenata).

image.title: Short-tailed weasel
image.altText: A small weasel with light brown fur on top and white fur below on the ground of the forest.
image.caption: A short-tailed weasel with its summer coat.
image.credit: NPS photo by Jacob W. Frank.

title: Pikas
shortDescription: The American pika, a member of the order Lagomopha, is not a rodent, but related to rabbits and hares. Piles of drying vegetation, called haystacks, and a distinctive high-pitched call are the most recognizable indicators of active pika habitat. Pikas are sensitive to temperatures above 77.9°F (25.5°C); therefore, they are most active during cooler parts of the day.
seasonDescription: Pikas are active year-round. They will be difficult to spot in the winter as they travel through tunnels in talus fields under snow. When there's not snow on the ground, they can be seen darting agilely around on rocks.

image.altText: A pika eats a leaf

title: Northern River Otters
shortDescription: The northern river otter is the most aquatic member of the weasel family. They can swim underwater up to 6 miles per hour (9.6 kph) for two to three minutes at a time. They aren't as agile or fast on land unless they find snow or ice, where they can move rapidly by alternating hops and slides reaching speads of 15 miles per hour (24 kph)

image.title: Northern river otter
image.altText: A sleek brown creature sticks its black nose into the air beside a pond with green lily pads.
image.caption: A northern river otter.

title: Mountain Lions
shortDescription: The mountain lion (Puma concolor), also known as the cougar, is one of the two largest cat species in North America and is a top predator native to Glacier. The subspecies in Glacier is the North American cougar (P.c. couguar).

image.title: Mountain lion
image.altText: A large mountain lion with brown eyes and tan fur is seen in the branches of a coniferous tree.
image.caption: A mountain lion seen from the branches of a coniferous tree.

title: Moose
shortDescription: Four subspecies of moose (Alces alces) exist in North America. The subspecies in Glacier is the Shiras moose (A. a. shirasi) and is found in forested areas and willow flats from southeastern British Columbia to northern Colorado. Moose are better adapted to survival in deep snow than other ungulates in the park, and are usually solitary or in small family groups.

image.title: Moose
image.altText: A dark brown moose with light brown velveted antlers stands in a field with yellow flowers.
image.caption: A bull moose walks through a field of yellow wildflowers.

title: Marmots
shortDescription: Marmots are one of the largest rodents in Glacier. Early settlers called them "whistle pigs" due to their vocalizations of loud whistles and "screams," which stem out of fear or excitement. They are typically active in the morning, late afternoon, and evening.

image.altText: A yellow-bellied marmot stands on top of a rock.

title: Coyotes
shortDescription: Coyotes (Canis latrans) are intelligent and highliy adaptable animals. The subspecies in Glacier is the mountain coyote (C. l. lestes). Often mistaken for a wolf, the coyote is about one third of the wolf's size, with a slighter build. Its coat ranges from tan to buff and sometimes gray, with some orange on its tail and ears.

image.title: Coyote in the snow
image.altText: A coyote sits in a snow-filled landscape while looking back towards the camera.
image.caption: Coyotes can be found thriving in urban areas as well as in remote wilderness.

title: Columbian Ground Squirrels
shortDescription: The Columbian ground squirrel has a well-developed colonial social structure. When they sense danger, they will make a shrill chirp as an alarm call. They are vulnerable to predators such as long-tailed weasels, hawks, coyotes, and grizzly bears.

image.title: Columbian ground squirrel
image.altText: A light brown furred rodent stands on its hind legs on a rock overlooking grasses.
image.caption: A Columbian ground squirrel overlooks a grassy meadow.
image.credit: NPS photo by Jacob W. Frank.

title: Canada Lynx
shortDescription: Canada lynx are similar to bobcats in appearance, but differ in several distinct ways. Lynx are grayer in color, with less distinctive spotting, and have much larger paws and longer ear tufts. The tail tip of a lynx is entirely black, while the tail tip of a bobcat has a white underside. In 2000, the US Fish and Wildlife Service listed the Canada lynx as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.

image.title: Canada lynx
image.altText: A large gray cat sits in the snow staring at the camera.
image.caption: A Canada lynx sits in the snow.

title: Bobcats
shortDescription: The bobcat has many color variations such as red-brown fur with indistinct markings or light buff with dark spotting. They are similar to the Canada lynx, but have shorter ear tufts and a short tail with several black rings that do not fully circle it and no black tip. Their tracks are about 2 inches (5 cm) from top to bottom.

image.title: Bobcat
image.altText: A patterned, orange-furred cat steps on a snow-covered log alongside icy water.
image.caption: A bobcat next to a river.

title: Bears
shortDescription: Glacier is home to two species of bears: grizzly bears (Ursus arctos horribilis) and black bears (Ursus americanus). Both species come in a range of colors from black to brown, reddish, or blond.

image.title: Black Bear
image.altText: A black bear sitting on boulders surrounded by small, yellow wildflowers and green vegetation
image.caption: A fed bear is a dead bear. It's up to YOU to save a bear's life.

title: Bats
shortDescription: Bats are part of the mammalian order Chiroptera, which is ancient Greek for "hand wing." There are over 1,200 species of bats worldwide, with 9 species that call Glacier National Park home. All of Glacier's bat species are insectivores (insect-eaters).
seasonDescription: Bat activity has been documented every month of the year in Glacier, but it is unlikely that you will see one during the winter. Some species do not hibernate but migrate long distances to areas where temperature and insect populations remain high enough for continued activity.

image.title: Hoary Bat
image.altText: A bat with light and dark brown fur is held in someone's hands.
image.caption: A hoary bat

title: All about wildlife watching safety
shortDescription: View wildlife across Glacier National Park's vast landscapes. The diversity of habitat types creates opportunities for a wide range of animals. Find more information on everything from the large and majestic elk of the prairies, to the small stonefly of glacier-fed streams on Glacier National Park's website.

image.title: Watching Golden Eagles on Mount Brown
image.altText: Three birders use binoculars to look for migrating raptors with a mountain in the background.
image.caption: Glacier is great for birding in the spring and summer but fall has its moments too!

title: Drive Going-to-the-Sun Road
shortDescription: A drive across this engineering marvel has been a quintessential part of any trip to Glacier since the 1930s.
seasonDescription: Though portions of Going-to-the-Sun Road remain open year round, seasonal conditions (snow!) mean a drive across the whole road is only possible during summer months. Check Glacier’s Road Status page before your trip.

image.altText: Car drives uphill over triple arched stone bridge

title: Attend One of Glacier's Evening Programs
shortDescription: Evening programs are a chance for rangers to help visitors find amazing meaning in specific park resources.
seasonDescription: June-September

image.altText: Tribal member addresses crowd seating on benches

title: Visit One of Glacier's Historic Lodges
shortDescription: Step inside one of the historic lodges and pretend you are a traveler on the Great Northern Railway in the 1910s.
seasonDescription: Lake McDonald Lodge is generally open May-September. Many Glacier Hotel is generally open June-September.

image.altText: A hand holds historic photo aligned with actual historic hotel building

title: Check out a Mission 66 Visitor Center
shortDescription: These visitor centers are worth a stop for the information and exhibits provided, as well as their historic architecture.
seasonDescription: St. Mary Visitor Center is open late May to early October. Logan Pass Visitor Center opens when Going-to-the-Sun Road plowing is complete and closes late September.

image.altText: Flagpoles in front of modern building with exaggerated roofline

title: Take a Half-Day Hike in Glacier
shortDescription: Glacier is a hiker’s paradise. Spend part of your day on one of these 3-5 hour hikes.
seasonDescription: Trails are covered in snow throughout the winter, causing hiking to take a seasonal backseat to activities like snowshoeing and cross-country skiing. Check Glacier’s Trail Status webpage or at a ranger station to stay updated as trails are cleared of snow and debris in spring.

image.altText: Rocky trail along creek in dense mossy forest

title: Take a Full Day Hike in Glacier
shortDescription: Glacier is a hiker’s paradise. Spend your whole day in nature on one of these popular trails.
seasonDescription: Trails are covered in snow throughout the winter, causing hiking to take a seasonal backseat to activities like snowshoeing and cross-country skiing. Check Glacier’s Trail Status webpage or at a ranger station to stay updated on trails' changing conditions.

image.altText: Group of three hikes subalpine trail toward large mountain

title: Experience the Huna Tribal House
shortDescription: Take a walk on the Łingít trail to see the first permanent clan house in Glacier Bay since Łingít villages were destroyed by an advancing glacier over 250 years ago.

image.altText: a large building with traditional alaska native carvings on the front at sunset

title: Kayak the Beardslees
shortDescription: If you’re visiting Glacier Bay on a budget, one of the more accessible wilderness areas of the park is the Beardslee Islands. Kayak through these peaceful, wild waters and look for wildlife along the shoreline for a true Glacier Bay adventure.

image.altText: an aerial image of the beardslee islands on a clear day

title: Hike the Trails at Bartlett Cove
shortDescription: Bartlett Cove has the only developed trails in the park. The forests and shorelines offer great hiking opportunities through a beautiful setting and a chance to see all manner of wildlife. Spend some time, stretch your legs, and discover the wonders of the park!

image.altText: a wooden boardwalk in a dense, mossy rainforest

title: Camp at Bartlett Cove
shortDescription: The Bartlett Cove Campground is steps away from incredible views of the Fairweather Mountains and the bay. Spend a night in this enchanting rainforest campground and listen to whales from where you sleep.

image.altText: a blue tent at a wooded campsite

title: Explore Gustavus
shortDescription: The town of Gustavus is considered the gateway to Glacier Bay. This charming Alaskan community offers plenty for travelers to explore as they make their way to the park.

image.altText: houses along a grassy riverbank

title: Stop by the Glacier Bay Visitor Center
shortDescription: Stop by the Glacier Bay Visitor Center to watch a program, join a ranger on a walk, or just explore the exhibits yourself. There's plenty to learn for visitors of all ages.
seasonDescription: The Glacier Bay Lodge is open daily from Memorial Day through Labor Day. Check hours on the park's Basic Information page.

image.altText: a large building in a forested area on a beach

title: Scramble down Cathedral Wash Trail
shortDescription: Follow Cathedral Wash trail as it climbs down to meet the Colorado River on its sandy bank. The 3 miles (4.8 km) round-trip challenging hike descend into the rocky wash, traveling through the Kaibab Limestone and Toroweap Formations of the Grand Canyon Group. Some rock scrambling required.
seasonDescription: During summer months temperatures can be extreme, reaching over 100 ° F (38°C) by early afternoon. Do not hike during the warmest parts of the day. Bring plenty of water. Be aware of flash floods.

image.title: Cathedral Wash
image.altText: Two hikers descend steep lawyers of reddish brown rock on the wash trail.
image.caption: Hikers descend the steep trail at Cathedral Wash.

title: From Your Boat To The Bridge
shortDescription: There is one designated trail within the boundaries of Rainbow Bridge National Monument. It runs the length of the monument, from the boat dock on one side, to the border with the Navajo Nation on the other. We ask that you stay on this trail when you visit Rainbow Bridge for your safety and out of respect for the local Native American tribes that hold this place special to them.
seasonDescription: While Rainbow Bridge National Monument is open all year, it is most heavily visited in the summer months. Despite the lack of shade and 100+ degree temps, visiting Rainbow Bridge in the summer is easiest because boat travel is easiest then.

image.title: On the trail from the dock to the bridge
image.altText: Paved trail in sandstone canyon
image.caption: Once you disembark, take the path through the canyon to the observation areas for Rainbow Bridge

title: Driving the Burr Trail
shortDescription: Drive the scenic Burr Trail from Glen Canyon's Bullfrog district, along the bottom of Capitol Reef, through Grand Staircase, to Boulder, UT. Distance: 67 miles (108 km) one-way Mix of paved and dirt roads, impassable when wet Four-wheel drive sometimes required. No RVs.
seasonDescription:
The weather in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area is usually typical for the high deserts. Summers are extremely hot with little, if any, shade. Winters are moderately cold with night time lows often below freezing. Spring weather is highly variable and unpredictable with extended periods of winds. Fall weather is usually nice and mild, a great time to beat the heat (and the crowds!).

Temperatures can range from 110° F (38°C) in June & July to 0° F (-16°C) in December & January. Precipitation is generally light (less than 6 inches [15.2cm] annually) though heavy rains and flash flooding is possible during the summer and fall "monsoons." Parts of the road may be impassable in inclement weather.

image.title: Burr Trail
image.altText: Dirt road that curves around a large rock. Road sign indicating steep incline ahead.
image.caption: The winding switchbacks and steep inclines of the Burr trail are not for every vehicle.

title: Swimming in Lake Powell
shortDescription: Swimming is a popular activity at Lake Powell, especially in the summer when water temperatures can surpass 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Please be aware that there are no life guards or officially designated swim beaches at Lake Powell or on the Colorado River. Water Quality conditions can change at your favorite swim areas.
seasonDescription: Swimming in Lake Powell is best enjoyed mid-summer to early fall. As temperatures drop in the winter and early spring, the risk of hypothermia increases. Be aware of your surroundings and your swimming capabilities.

image.title: Swimming in Lake Powell
image.altText: Four people swim backwards away from a houseboat railing
image.caption: A dip in the Lake after a hot day of boating hits the spot

title: Day Trip or Backpack Hike to Coyote Gulch
shortDescription: Open year-round but most popular in Spring and Fall, Coyote Gulch is a tributary of the Escalante River with several entry points for day hiking or backpacking in the Escalante Canyons of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area and Grand Staircase National Monument. This is a wilderness area, prepare to pack out everything you bring in.
seasonDescription: Hikes along Coyote Gulch are more popular in the spring and fall, as it is too cold in the winter and too hot in the summer to truly enjoy the hike. But the area is open year-round. Check weather conditions and water availability before you go.

image.title: Canyon and Butte, Coyote Gulch
image.altText: Sandstone canyon and butte with autumn trees.
image.caption: Buttes line the way along Coyote Gulch

title: Off Road Vehicles in Glen Canyon
shortDescription: Off-road vehicle use is allowed in the park only on National Park Service-designated ORV routes and areas, delineated by ORV route maps. Some Shoreline Access Areas indicated on the maps may not be available seasonally, due to changes in lake level. Note: There are 388 miles of Designated Roads of which 304 miles are unpaved.

image.title: ORV in Glen Canyon
image.altText: A jeep on a dirt road in a sandstone canyon
image.caption: Know where you can go for ORV driving in Glen Canyon

title: Driving to Alstrom Point
shortDescription: Drive the semi-improved roads to Alstrom Point, in the southwest region of Glen Canyon National recreation Area along the border with Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument near Big Water, UT. Distance: 46 miles round-trip, about 4 hours if you do not stop to look at the scenery Mix of paved and dirt roads, impassable when wet Four-wheel drive recommended for the final five miles and required at the last parts of the road. No RVs.
seasonDescription:
The weather on the drive to Alstrom Point is usually typical for the high deserts. Summers are extremely hot with no shade. Winters are moderately cold with night time lows often below freezing. Spring weather is highly variable and unpredictable with extended periods of winds and possible snowmelt flash floods. Fall weather is usually nice and mild, a great time to beat the heat (and the crowds!).

Temperatures can range from 110° F (38°C) in June & July to 0° F (-16°C) in December & January. Precipitation is generally light (less than 6 inches [15.2cm] annually) though heavy rains and flash flooding is possible during the summer and fall "monsoons." Parts of the road may be impassable in inclement weather.

image.title: View of Gunsight Butte from Romana Mesa
image.altText: Sandstone cliffs, buttes, and mesas. Just a bit of a lake in the distance.
image.caption: The view of Gunsight Butte from Romana Mesa on the way to Alstrom Point

title: Contemplate Your Place in the Landscape At The Big Map
shortDescription: The Glen Canyon and Surrounding Area Relief Map sits in a place of honor at the Powell Museum & Archives next to Glen Canyon Conservancy's Flagship office. Use it to help plan your Glen Canyon adventure, or pretend you are in space looking down at the landscape. Whoa.

image.title: The Big Map
image.altText: Relief map depicting desert landscape with a man-made lake. Metal railings
image.caption: Visit the Big Map when you visit the Powell Museum.

title: Driving the Hole in the Rock Road
shortDescription: The Hole-in-the-Rock road is an historic pioneer trail turned path to adventure. This 62 mile (100 km) one-way section runs from Escalante, UT to the western edge of Lake Powell. This road is rough, impassable in inclement weather, and 4WD only for the last 7 miles. Along the way are quite a few trailheads for the Coyote Gulch and other Escalante River trails in Glen Canyon.
seasonDescription:
The weather in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area is usually typical for the high deserts. Summers are extremely hot with little, if any, shade. Winters are moderately cold with night time lows often below freezing. Spring weather is highly variable and unpredictable with extended periods of winds. Fall weather is usually nice and mild, a great time to beat the heat.

Temperatures can range from 110° F (38°C) in June & July to 0° F (-16°C) in December & January. Precipitation is generally light (less than 6 inches [15.2cm] annually) though heavy rains and flash flooding is possible during the summer and fall "monsoons." The road will not be passable in inclement weather.

image.title: The Hole-in-the-Rock Road
image.altText: A dirt road with large sandstone boulder
image.caption: Check the weather report before heading out on this road

title: Lonely Dell Ranch Historic Site
shortDescription: Hidden between the shade of trees near the muddy Paria River sits Lonely Dell Ranch. This historic site was once home to those who operated the river crossing at Lees Ferry. Life was challenging on the homestead, but the families who chose to live on this secluded outpost left behind a story of hard work and perseverance.
seasonDescription:
During summer months temperatures can be extreme, reaching over 100 ° F (38°C) by early afternoon. Do not hike during the warmest parts of the day. Bring plenty of water, Take breaks in the shade near the main ranch house. 

Be flash flood aware if you continue hiking up the Paria River Trail.

image.title: Lonely Dell Ranch
image.altText: Rustic log cabin sits in the shade of tall trees surrounding by red rock canyon walls.

title: Lake Powell Shoreline Primitive Camping
shortDescription: "Backcountry" Shoreline camping on Lake Powell can range from toughing out the desert winter from your kayak to "roughing it" in a multimillion dollar houseboat and any level of camping/glamping in between. Enjoy the beaches of Lake Powell the way that best suits you.
seasonDescription:
The weather in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area is usually typical for the high deserts. Summers are extremely hot with little, if any, shade. Winters are moderately cold with night time lows often below freezing. Spring weather is highly variable and unpredictable with extended periods of winds. Fall weather is usually nice and mild, a great time to beat the heat (and the crowds!).

Temperatures can range from 110° F (38°C) in June & July to 0° F (-16°C) in December & January. Precipitation is generally light (less than 6 inches [15.2cm] annually) though heavy rains and flash flooding is possible during the summer and fall "monsoons."

We recommend lightweight, light colored clothing for summer, including a hat. Layers of clothing are best for other times of the year.

title: Hike the Bolinas Ridge Trail
shortDescription: Admire redwood forests and expansive views of the Olema Valley on this dog-friendly, multi-use trail. This up-to-11-mile-long trail begins at either at the Bolinas Ridge Trailhead along Sir Francis Drake Boulevard or at the trail's southern end at the Fairfax-Bolinas Road's junction with the West Ridgecrest Rd. Allow about 5 minutes to drive from Bear Valley to the trail's northern trailhead. Allow about 30 minutes to drive from Bear Valley to the trail's southern trailhead.
seasonDescription:
Winter

The heaviest rainfall occurs in the winter months. Come prepared for rain and drizzle to possibly last for several days. In between winter rains, it is often sunny, calm, and cool.

Spring

Most spring days are windy. Expect cool temperatures in March. By late May and early June, temperatures can be quite pleasant.

Summer

Although there is very little rain during summer months, there is often dense fog, which tends to burn off by mid-day. Afternoons are often sunny and warm to hot with a light breeze.

Fall

Point Reyes experiences some of the clearest days in late September, October, and early November. The occasional storm will start rolling through in late October, bringing clouds, wind, and rain. The strongest winds occur in November and December during occasional southerly gales.

title: Splash in Medano Creek
shortDescription: Medano Creek is a popular seasonal stream enjoyed by all ages.
seasonDescription:
Medano Creek Month-by-Month in an Average Year

April is the second snowiest month of the year at Great Sand Dunes, but there are also some sunny days with highs in the 60s. Spring is the windy season throughout the southwestern United States, especially afternoons, though mornings are usually calm. The creek begins to trickle down as the snow on the Sangre de Cristo Mountains melts. By late April the creek may be a few inches deep. Cottonwood trees and willows along the creek are not yet leafed out.

Late May is near the peak of Medano Creek's annual flow. While it is still springtime and winds may arise, especially in the afternoon, May temperatures are generally moderate, with highs in the 60s-70s F. However, snow is still possible at this elevation in May! Trees and bushes along the creek leaf out. There may be some "no-see-ums" (tiny biting gnats), but mosquitoes are rarely out in May. Late May and early June are the best opportunity to experience "surge flow", where waves up to about 20 inches (50 cm) high flow down across the sand. In wet years with good peak runoff, children can float down the waves on flat inflatable toys. Water comes out of the mountains cold, but warms up significantly when the sun shines on it for a few hours as it spreads across the sand. Because of the creek's popularity, late May and early June weekends are extremely crowded, with long lines of traffic, overflowing parking lots, a crowded beach, and full campgrounds. If possible, plan your visit on a weekday this time of year.

June brings warmer temperatures for water play and generally pleasant conditions the first week of June. But as the creek becomes much lower and warmer around the second week of June, mosquitoes emerge in large numbers. Move away from vegetation, to the far side of the creek to avoid the worst of the mosquitoes: they don't like open sand, but prefer to be near shady bushes and trees. By late June, the water level will be fairly low, only 1 or 2 inches (1-5cm). Because of the creek's popularity, late May and early June weekends are extremely crowded, with long lines of traffic, overflowing parking lots, a crowded beach, and full campgrounds. If possible, plan your visit on a weekday this time of year.

In July, unless there are significant ongoing rains, the creek will begin to retreat back toward the mountains, drying up at the main visitor area near the Dunes Parking Lot. It will continue to gently flow (1/2" - 1" deep) along the eastern edge of the dunefield, near the Castle Creek picnic area. Castle Creek is accessible by high clearance 4WD vehicle on the Medano Pass Primitive Road. Visitors without 4WD may also access the creek in late summer by hiking approximately 2 miles (3.5 km) up the creekbed from the Dunes Parking Lot, or approximately 0.7 miles (1km) from the Point of No Return parking area. Mosquitoes usually disappear after the water retreats. July is the warmest month at the park, with average highs in the low 80s F.

In August and September, the creek will likely be completely gone from the main visitor area near the Dunes Parking Lot. It may continue to gently flow (1/2 to 1 inch or 1-2cm deep) along the eastern edge of the dunefield, near the Castle Creek Picnic Area. Castle Creek is accessible by high clearance 4WD vehicle on the Medano Pass Primitive Road. Visitors without 4WD may also access the creek late summer by hiking approximately 2 miles (3.5 km) up the creekbed from the Dunes Parking Lot, or 0.7 miles (1km) from the Point of No Return parking area. Mosquitoes typically disappear along with the creek.

title: Explore the Dunes
shortDescription: Explore the tallest dunes in North America! The centerpiece of Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve is the 30-square-mile (78-square-km) dunefield, featuring the tallest dunes in North America. Because there are no trails, you can venture out anywhere you'd like to discover unusual insects, plants, wildlife tracks, ripples, and sand grains of every color.
seasonDescription: Spring can sometimes bring high winds, mainly in the afternoon. Temperatures can vary widely: highs may reach into the 60s F, or only into the 30s F with snow and an even colder windchill. In summer, daytime high temperatures average 75-80 degrees F. However, sand surface temperatures can soar to 150 degrees F on sunny summer afternoons. Fall is generally mild, with highs in the 50s - 70s F, with chilly nights in the 20s - 30s F. Be prepared, though, for the occasional cold fall storm, bringing icy rain or even snow. Cold temperatures are the norm in winter, although sunshine is generally abundant, and the dry air doesn't feel nearly as cold as more humid eastern winters. Average highs are in the teens-30s F, with lows averaging minus 15 F to minus 5 F in the coldest part of winter. Snow may fall and blizzards occasionally occur, so bring warm, layered clothing and sturdy footwear.

image.title: Girl on Dunes
image.altText: Girl with backpack standing on dunes at sunset
image.caption: Explore any part of the dunefield!

title: Sandboarding and Sand Sledding
shortDescription: Sandboarding and sand sledding are the most popular activities on the dunes. Read the information on this page to have a positive, fun, and safe experience.
seasonDescription: Sandboarding and sand sledding can occur any time of year, but in winter months, some retailers will not rent the sleds due to potential damage from frozen sand. When snow falls on the dunes, consider bringing snow equipment instead.

image.title: Two Girls Sand Sledding
image.altText: Two girls speed down a dune on a specially designed sand sled.
image.caption: Two girls speed down a dune on a specially designed sand sled.

title: Experience the Night
shortDescription: Half the park is after dark! Night at Great Sand Dunes can include dunes exploration under a bright full moon, viewing thousands of stars on a clear moonless night, listening for owls along the foothills, or observing migrating amphibians on a wet night.
seasonDescription: Experiencing the night is available year round, but be prepared for frigid conditions in winter months. The Milky Way is highest and most visible in the sky in late summer and early fall. Any moonlight will make the Milky Way difficult to see, so time your visit for a moonless evening.

image.title: Milky Way over Medano Creek
image.altText: The Milky Way over a shallow stream flowing across sand at night
image.caption: The Milky Way is visible on moonless nights in summer and fall.

title: Hike Montville Nature Trail or Mosca Pass Trail
shortDescription: Just above the dunefield are montane woodlands of pinon and ponderosa pine, subalpine aspen and conifer forests, alpine lakes and rugged mountains over 13,000 feet (4,000 m) in elevation. The easiest access to forest in the national park is on the Montville Nature Trail and Mosca Pass Trail.
seasonDescription: Montville Trail is generally accessible year round, but there may be small snowdrifts in winter months. Mosca Pass Trail is generally not accessible for hiking in winter and early spring due to deep snow; snowshoes or backcountry skis may be needed on the upper parts of the trail from November through April.

image.title: Montville Nature Trail
image.altText: Two girls hiking on a forested trail
image.caption: Montville Trail and Mosca Pass Trail feature aspen and conifer forests along a small creek.

title: Hike Medano Lake and Mount Herard
shortDescription: Take your 4WD vehicle around the dunes and up to Medano Pass, hike to a small alpine lake, then continue to the summit of 13,297 ft (4,053 m) Mount Herard for an aerial perspective on the entire dunefield! This is a physically demanding but incredibly rewarding way to experience many of Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve's ecoystems, from desert dunes to alpine tundra. Watch the high-energy 40-second video to get a glimpse of this unique experience!
seasonDescription: Medano Pass Primitive Road access is seasonal, and depends on snowpack and creek levels. On average, the pass opens around late May, and closes by November. There are typically snowdrifts on the trail and tundra through at least mid-June, and often into July.

image.title: Dunes from Mount Herard
image.altText: Alpine tundra in foreground, part of the dunefield at right, and snow-capped Blanca Peak
image.caption: The incredible 360 degree views from the summit of Mount Herard include the dunefield and more.

title: Hike Sand Creek Lakes
shortDescription: Sand Creek Lakes are part of the alpine watershed of Great Sand Dunes National Preserve. A longer drive and hike is required to reach these lakes, but the mountain scenery is worth the effort. Check with a ranger for conditions before travel. Snow may block these trails from November into June.
seasonDescription: The area is open year round, but unless you have snowshoes and avalanche gear, plan to access the lakes only in summer or fall. In an average snow year, there are still some snowdrifts on the trail through June. Mid-summer is the prettiest time of year to visit the lakes, when flowers are blooming, grass is green, and snowfields still lace the mountains.

image.title: Lower Sand Creek Lake
image.altText: An alpine lake with conifer trees at the side, and rocky summit with snow
image.caption: Sand Creek Lakes are a completely different environment from the dunes!

title: 4WD Medano Pass Primitive Road
shortDescription: Drive a a 4WD around the eastern edge of the dunes then over a forested mountain pass. Be prepared for soft sand, creek crossings, and rocky terrain.
seasonDescription: The rpass typically opens by late May, and stays open through part of November. Check current conditions on the park website.

image.title: Jeep on Medano Pass Primitive Road
image.altText: A white Jeep crosses a creek surrounded by gold aspen trees
image.caption: A Jeep crosses a creek in fall on the Medano Pass Primitive Road

title: Hike to Abrams Falls
shortDescription: Walk 5 miles (8 km) roundtrip through rhododendron, hemlock, and pine-oak forest to a 25-foot (7.6-m) waterfall and scenic pool. Swimming in the pool is not recommended due to slippery rocks and a dangerous undertow.

image.title: Abrams Falls
image.altText: Waterfall flows over rocks and pours into greenish colored pool with rocks and shrubs around it.
image.caption: Hike 5 miles (8 km) roundtrip from the Abrams Falls Trailhead in Cades Cove.

title: Hike the Gatlinburg Trail
shortDescription: Enjoy a riverside stroll approximately 4 miles (6.4 km) roundtrip through a cove hardwood forest along one of the only dog- and bike-friendly trails in the park. This trail includes sections of sidewalks and roadsides as well as graded dirt path.

image.title: Gatlinburg Trail
image.altText: A bridge over a river surrounded by green trees. A road past the bridge in the distance.
image.caption: Hike 4 miles (6.4 km) roundtrip from the Sugarlands Visitor Center to River Road in Gatlinburg.

title: Hike to Chimney Tops Overlook
shortDescription: Hike 3.5 miles (5.6 km) roundtrip on this popular but challenging trail to enjoy views of surrounding mountains and the Chimney Tops pinnacles. This trail is steep and rocky at times, and includes bridges, stairs, and some lingering signs of 2016 wildfires.

image.title: Chimney Tops Trail View
image.altText: An Appalachian mountain view on a sunny day. Trees and other vegetation in the foreground.
image.caption: Hike 3.5 miles (5.6 km) roundtrip from Chimney Tops Trailhead on Newfound Gap Road.

title: Hike to Mount Le Conte on Bullhead Trail
shortDescription: One of five routes to Mount Le Conte, the Bullhead Trail offers consistent views. The strenuous hike is 13.6 miles (21.9 km) roundtrip. Near the beginning, visitors will see rocky cliffs and climb the Bullhead, a heath-covered bald that may resemble a bull's head from a distance.

image.title: Mount Le Conte on Bullhead Trail
image.altText: Sweeping mountain views below a pink and purple sky. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 13.6 miles (21.9 km) roundtrip from the Old Sugarlands Trailhead on Cherokee Orchard Road.

title: Hike Smokemont Nature Trail
shortDescription: Hike 0.62-mile (1 km) roundtrip on Smokemont Nature Trail which provides a peaceful escape and views of the surrounding peaks.

image.title: Hike Smokemont Nature Trail
image.altText: A footlog bridge over a stream in the forest.
image.caption: Hike Smokemont Nature Trail

title: Hike Bradley Fork Trail
shortDescription: The Bradley Fork Trail offers a scenic and diverse outdoor experience, featuring picturesque creeks, seasonal wildflowers, fishing access, horseback riding opportunities, and backcountry camping.

image.title: Hike the Bradley Fork Trail
image.altText: A small cascading waterfall on rocks in a stream.
image.caption: Hike 7.3 miles along Bradley Fork Trail from Smokemont Campground to Hughes Ridge Trail.

title: Hike to Chasteen Creek Cascade
shortDescription: Hike 3.6 miles (5.8 km) roundtrip through hardwood forest following the path of mountain streams to a peaceful cascade. This trail is wide, well-graded, and regularly used by both hikers and horse riders.

image.title: Chasteen Creek Cascades
image.altText: A cascading waterfall surrounded by greenery and rocks. A hiker icon in the corner.
image.caption: Hike 3.6 miles (5.8 km) roundtrip from the Bradley Fork Trailhead in Smokemont Campground.

title: Hike Kephart Prong Trail to Historic CCC Camp
shortDescription: Follow the flow of mountain streams 4 miles (6.4 km) roundtrip through hardwood forest and across several log footbridges to the remains of a CCC camp and the Kephart Shelter.

image.title: Kephart Prong Trail
image.altText: Stairs and a log bridge with handrails cross a stream near trees and rocks. A hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 4 miles (6.4 km) roundtrip from a paved pull-off 5 miles north of Smokemont Campground.

title: Hike West Prong Trail
shortDescription: Hike 5.4 miles (8.7 km) roundtrip on West Prong Trail

image.title: Things to do- West Prong
image.altText: A half log footbridge over top of a stream in the forest.
image.caption: Hike 5.4 miles (8.7 km) roundtrip on West Prong Trail.

title: Hike to Twentymile Cascade
shortDescription: Hike 1.2 miles (1.9 km) roundtrip along a wide gravel roadbed that follows a mountain stream to a cascade surrounded by moss-covered rocks and mixed hardwood forest.

image.title: Twentymile Cascades
image.altText: A stout waterfall cascading into a pool near a large boulder. A fallen tree in right frame.
image.caption: Hike 1.2 miles (1.9 km) roundtrip from the Twentymile Trailhead

title: Hike to Ramsey Cascades
shortDescription: Hike 8 miles (12.9 km) roundtrip on this popular but relatively challenging trail through cove hardwood forest to see the tallest waterfall in the park. The trail begins on an old roadbed but becomes narrower and rockier crossing multiple footlog bridges and streams as it ascends.

image.title: Ramsey Cascades
image.altText: A cascading waterfall framed by large rocks and green vegetation.
image.caption: Hike 8 miles (12.9 km) roundtrip from Ramsey Cascades Trailhead on Ramsey Prong Road in Greenbrier.

title: Hike to Mount Le Conte on Trillium Gap Trail
shortDescription: One of five routes to Mount Le Conte, Trillium Gap Trail to Mount Le Conte is 13 miles (20.9 km) roundtrip and rewards hikers with mountain views, diverse forest, and a waterfall. Near the summit, the best views are at Cliff Top and Myrtle Point, both marked with signs.

image.title: Mount Le Conte on Trillium Gap Trail
image.altText: A sweeping mountain vista below a pink and light purple sky. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 13 miles (20.9 km) roundtrip from Trillium Gap Trailhead near Gatlinburg.

title: Hike to Grotto Falls
shortDescription: Hike 2.6 miles (4.2 km) roundtrip on Trillium Gap Trail as it crosses multiple streams and sections of old-growth forest to reach a unique waterfall you can walk behind. This trail is well-traveled but prone to muddy and slippery conditions.

image.title: Grotto Falls
image.altText: A waterfall surrounded by rocks, moss, and plants. Trail leads behind it. A hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 2.6 miles (4.2 km) roundtrip from the Trillium Gap Trailhead.

title: Hike the Oconaluftee River Trail
shortDescription: Enjoy a riverside stroll approximately 3 miles (4.8 km) roundtrip on one of the only pet- and bike-friendly trails in the park. This popular trail is relatively flat, wide, and graveled and follows the Oconaluftee River through elk habitat and hardwood forest.

image.title: Oconaluftee River Trail
image.altText: A wide, curving river lined by green trees. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike ~3 miles (4.8 km) roundtrip from the Oconaluftee Visitor Center to Cherokee.

title: Hike the Finley Cane, Bote Mountain, Lead Cove Loop
shortDescription: Hike 6.9 miles (11.1 km) on this looped route that links three shorter trail sections, offering a chance to experience the biodiversity of Bote Mountain at various elevations.

image.title: Finley Cane to Bote Mtn to Lead Cove
image.altText: A vast mountain view. Hiker icon in lower right corner.
image.caption: Hike the 6.9-mile loop from Finley Cane to Bote Mountain, to Lead Cove.

title: Walk Sugarlands Valley Nature Trail
shortDescription: Wander through a cove hardwood forest with streamside views, rock walls, and historic stone chimneys on this half-mile (0.8 km) loop along a paved, flat trail. The trailhead is adjacent to a small parking area with several accessible spaces along Newfound Gap Rd (US 441) near Sugarlands Visitor Center.

image.title: Sugarlands Valley Nature Trail
image.altText: A wooden bridge on a paved trail in the woods.
image.caption: Walk half a mile (0.8 km) roundtrip from the Sugarlands Valley Nature Trailhead on US 441.

title: Hike to Laurel Falls
shortDescription: Hike 2.6 miles (4.2 km) roundtrip through a mixed hardwood forest to an 80-foot (24-m) waterfall. Enjoy a few views of the mountain landscape before arriving at the waterfall. PLEASE NOTE: Laurel Falls Trail is expected to close starting in mid-December for 18 months.

image.title: Laurel Falls Trail
image.altText: A two-tiered waterfall framed by greenery. Hiker icon in lower right corner.
image.caption: Hike 2.6 miles (4.2 km) roundtrip from the Laurel Falls Trailhead on Little River Road.

title: Hike Little River Trail
shortDescription: Once a railroad bed, the Little River Trail now offers a peaceful hike through the Elkmont area of Great Smoky Mountains National Park. As you follow the river’s gentle flow, you’ll pass remnants of the old Elkmont community—stone chimneys and foundations quietly tucked into the forest.

image.title: Hike Little River Trail
image.altText: A rocky river in the forest with a hiker icon at the bottom of the page.
image.caption: Hike a portion or the entire length of Little River Trail.

title: Drive Foothills Parkway (Chilhowee to Walland)
shortDescription: Drive 16.6 miles (26.7 km) one-way on Foothills Parkway from Chilhowee to Walland.

image.title: Foothil parkway w 129 to Walland
image.altText: A road through the woods with a sign for Lookrock tower on the right
image.caption: Drive Foothills Parkway from Chilhowee to Walland.

title: Drive Foothills Parkway (Walland to Wears Valley)
shortDescription: Drive 14.75 miles (23.74 km) one-way on Foothills Parkway from Walland to Wears Valley.

image.title: Drive Foothills Parkway W
image.altText: A roadway bridge with mountain views, the lower corner has a car icon.
image.caption: Drive from Walland to Wears Valley on the Foothills Parkway.

title: Drive Foothills Parkway (Cosby to I-40)
shortDescription: Drive 5.6 miles (9.01 km) one-way on Foothills Parkway from Cosby to I-40.

image.title: Drive foothill parkway east
image.altText: A road with a scenic mountain view and large pull-off.
image.caption: Drive Foothills Parkway between I-40 and Cosby

title: Hike to the Little Greenbrier School and Walker Homesite
shortDescription: Hike 3.4 miles (5.5 km) roundtrip from Metcalf Bottoms Picnic Area through hardwood forest to see remnants of stonework, the historic one-room Little Greenbrier School, and the preserved homesite of the Walker family. This trail includes sections of well-packed dirt path and wide gravel roadbed.

image.title: Little Greenbrier School
image.altText: A dark brown, wooden schoolhouse gravel path in front of it. Hiker icon in photo corner.
image.caption: Hike 3.4 miles (5.5 km) roundtrip from the Metcalf Bottoms Picnic Area.

title: Walk Cable Mill Area Trails
shortDescription: Visit the Cable Mill area for a glimpse into a traditional Appalachian farming community.

image.title: Cable Mill Area
image.altText: A mill house with a ramp leading to the entrance tucked in a lush forest.
image.caption: Explore the historic Cable Mill area.

title: Hike to Charlies Bunion
shortDescription: Hike a popular section of the Appalachian Trail for 8 miles (12.9 km) roundtrip through spruce-fir forest to enjoy panoramic views and a unique rocky outcrop surrounded by exposed cliffs.

image.title: Charlies Bunion
image.altText: A narrow trail with sweeping views to the left on a partly cloudy day. A hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 8 miles (12.9 km) roundtrip on the Appalachian Trail section starting at Newfound Gap Overlook.

title: Hike Cooper Road Trail
shortDescription: Hike 10.9 miles (17.5 km) one-way on Cooper Road Trail.

image.title: Cooper Road Trail
image.altText: A water crossing along a trail in the forest, in the bottom right corner is a hiker icon.
image.caption: Hike 10.9 miles (17.5 km) one-way on Cooper Road Trail.

title: Hike Cove Hardwood Trail
shortDescription: Hike 0.75 miles (1.2 km) roundtrip on Cove Hardwood Trail to explore a forest of giants and wind through a lush mountainside.

image.title: Cove Hardwood_things to do
image.altText: A trail with wooden steps wandering through the woods, in the lower corner is a hiker icon.
image.caption: Hike the 0.75 miles (1.2 km) roundtrip Cove Hardwood Trail loop

title: Hike to Mount Le Conte on the Appalachian Trail and Boulevard Trail
shortDescription: The longest of the five routes to Mount Le Conte, this strenuous hike—16.2 miles (26.1 km) roundtrip—offers a variety of views and includes part of the Appalachian Trail. Charlies Bunion, a rocky outcrop, is a short but rewarding detour.

image.title: Mount LeConte on AT and Boulevard
image.altText: Sweeping mountain views under a pink and purple sky. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 16.2 miles (26.1 km) roundtrip from Appalachian Trailhead at Newfound Gap Overlook.

title: Walk to John Oliver Cabin
shortDescription: Explore the scenery of Cades Cove and the historic John Oliver Cabin and homesite with a short path—0.3 miles (0.5 km) roundtrip—suitable for wheelchairs and strollers. The trail gives way to level, packed gravel once it reaches the complex of log structures.

image.title: John Oliver Cabin
image.altText: A wooden cabin with a covered porch on either side near a fence and trees. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Walk 0.3 miles (0.5 km) roundtrip from the parking area for the John Oliver Cabin in Cades Cove.

title: Hike to Steve Woody House
shortDescription: Walk 2 miles (3.2 km) roundtrip through a hardwood forest on a wide, well-graded path following a mountain stream to reach the historic Steve Woody Place, which was once the center of a sprawling homestead with several outbuildings.

image.title: Steve Woody House
image.altText: A white historic home in a grassy field with forest behind it. A wooden sign labels the home.
image.caption: Hike 2 miles (3.2 km) roundtrip from Rough Fork Trailhead at the end of Cataloochee Road.

title: Hike to Mount Le Conte on Rainbow Falls Trail
shortDescription: Hike 13 miles (21 km) roundtrip on one of five routes to Mount Le Conte that includes a waterfall, rocky ascents, and forest views. Lush forests line the trail and hikers will intersect the Bullhead Trail, Alum Cave Trail, and Trillium Gap Trail before reaching the summit.

image.title: Mount Le Conte on Rainbow Falls Trail
image.altText: Sweeping mountain views under a pink and purple sky. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 13 miles (20.9 km) roundtrip from the trailhead on Cherokee Orchard Road.

title: Hike to Look Rock Tower
shortDescription: Walk along a short, paved trail 0.8 miles (1.3 km) through the forest to an observation tower with panoramic views of the Smokies and Blount County, Tennessee. This trail includes some mild to moderate inclines.

image.title: Look Rock Tower View
image.altText: View of rolling mountains with fall colors, a partly cloudy sky and gold trees in the foreground
image.caption: Hike 0.8 miles (1.3 km) roundtrip from the Look Rock Tower Trailhead on Foothills Parkway West.

title: Hike to Andrews Bald
shortDescription: Hike 3.6 miles (5.8 km) roundtrip descending through high-elevation, spruce-fir forest to a popular grassy bald known for its flowering azaleas in summer and views of the surrounding mountains. The return hike to the trailhead involves a relatively strenuous climb.

image.title: Andrews Bald
image.altText: Sweeping mountain views. Shrubs and short trees in a grassy field in the foreground plus hiker icon.
image.caption: Hike 3.6 miles (5.8 km) roundtrip from the Forney Ridge Trailhead near the Kuwohi parking area.

title: Hike the Little River, Cucumber Gap, Jakes Creek Loop
shortDescription: Hike 5.4 miles (8.7 km) on a pleasant and shady loop connecting three trails with streamside views, historic structures, and prolific spring wildflower displays. Trail conditions vary from paved road and graveled path to narrower and rockier sections with minor stream crossings.

image.title: Little River Trail
image.altText: A rocky river lined by green trees and shrubs. A hiker icon in the lower right corner of photo.
image.caption: Hike 5.4 miles (8.7 km) roundtrip beginning in the Elkmont historic area.

title: Hike Deep Creek Trail to Indian Creek Falls
shortDescription: Hike 1.6 miles (2.6 km) roundtrip along Deep Creek, which features views of two waterfalls, Tom Branch Falls and Indian Creek Falls.

image.title: Deep Creek Trail to Indian Creek Falls
image.altText: A bridge over a stream in the forest. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 1.6 miles (2.6 km) roundtrip on the Deep Creek Trail to see Indian Creek Falls

title: Drive Lakeview Drive
shortDescription: Drive 11.4 miles (18.3 km) roundtrip on Lakeview Drive.

image.title: Drive Lakeview Drive
image.altText: A road winds through dense trees.
image.caption: Drive Lakeview Drive.

title: Hike to Alum Cave Bluffs
shortDescription: Hike 4.6 miles (7.4 km) roundtrip to see the Alum Cave Bluffs and stroll through Arch Rock on this popular hike on Alum Cave Trail. The trail crosses two mountain streams via footbridges before it climbs through sections of old-growth forest.

image.title: Alum Cave_things to do
image.altText: A cave like overhang over a trail with a mountain view.
image.caption: Hike Alum Cave Trail.

title: Hike to Lynn Camp Prong Cascades
shortDescription: Go on a woodland stroll following an old railroad bed along a mountain stream, 1.4 miles (2.3 km) roundtrip, to a dramatic cascade. The trail is mostly wide and flat and gently ascends through rhododendron and some cliff-like rock outcroppings.

image.title: Lynn Camp Prong Cascades
image.altText: A short, cascading waterfall framed by boulders and orange, fallen leaves. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 1.4 miles (2.3 km) roundtrip from the Middle Prong Trailhead near Tremont.

title: Hike the Deep Creek Waterfalls Loop
shortDescription: See three waterfalls on a loop around the Deep Creek area. Hike 2.4 miles (3.9 km) on several short trail segments to reach Juney Whank Falls, Indian Creek Falls, and Tom Branch Falls.

image.title: Juney Whank Falls in Deep Creek
image.altText: A waterfall closely hugging the rocks surrounded by moss, shrubs, and trees.

title: Hike to Rainbow Falls

image.title: Rainbow Falls
image.altText: A thin waterfall on a rocky cliff surrounded by trees. Hiker icon in corner.
image.caption: Hike 5.6 miles (9 km) roundtrip from Rainbow Falls Trailhead on Cherokee Orchard Road.

title: Hike Porters Creek Trail

title: Hike Goldmine Loop via Tunnel Bypass Trail

title: Hike to Hen Wallow Falls
shortDescription: Hike 4.3 miles (6.9 km) roundtrip through a hardwood forest with hemlock and rhododendron to a popular 90-foot (27-m) waterfall. This trail includes some steep sections and switchbacks.

As you ski or snowshoe on the road you will wind through forest and marsh habitats, covered in deep snow and ice. Be aware that not all is frozen underfoot, thin ice can be dangerous—use caution.

title: Visit the historic Frijole Ranch
shortDescription: Frijole Ranch is a delightful oasis on the edge of the dry, lower slopes of the Guadalupe escarpment which truly captures the rugged sprit of the American West. Today the Frijole Ranch History Museum occupies the old ranch headquarters and displays the human history of the Guadalupes. The grounds are open from dusk to dawn, with picnic tables at the parking area and under the large shade trees in the courtyard. Bring your binoculars; this is an excellent location for birding!

This is an extremely rewarding trail, offering both the variety of McKittrick Canyon and the grandeur of the high ridges that surround it.

shortDescription: The journey to the top of McKittrick Ridge is "the toughest hike in Texas." This arduous hike is best enjoyed as an overnight hike allowing for rest, recovery, and fabulous night skies at the McKittrick Ridge Wilderness Campground. An overnight Wilderness Use Permit is required for camping.
