title: Guadalupe Ridge Trail (GRT)
shortDescription: This trail covers 100 miles (161 km) through Carlsbad Caverns National Park, Lincoln National Forest, Bureau of Land Management, and Guadalupe Mountains National Park. Over 20 miles (32 km) of this trail is within Carlsbad Caverns National Park.
seasonDescription: Environmental conditions (weather and heat) dictate narrow periods when the GRT can be safely completed, generally in the spring and fall. From November to April be prepared for high winds throughout the route.

image.title: Guadalupe Ridge Trail
image.altText: Photo of the desert landscape along the Guadalupe Ridge Trail.
image.caption: View of the desert landscape along the Guadalupe Ridge Trail.

title: Pinery Trail
shortDescription: The Pinery Trail offers visitors an opportunity to take a quick walk on a paved trail. The trail also features ruins of the Old Butterfield Stagecoach Route Pinery Station built in 1858.

image.title: Visitors on the Pinery Trail
image.altText: Two people walk a paved path through a bright desert landscape
image.caption: Visitors on the Pinery Trail.

title: Bringing Horses
shortDescription: Camping is authorized for overnight horse users only at the visitor horse corrals, with a permit. The visitor horse corrals and campsites at Frijole Horse Corral Campground and Dog Canyon Campground can be reserved in advance of the visit.

image.title: Dog Canyon Horse Corral
image.altText: Horse corrals and camping trailers with desert hills rising behind.
image.caption: Horse corrals and camping trailers at Dog Canyon.

title: Dealing with Human Waste
shortDescription: Nothing can spoil a trip in the Guadalupe Mountains Wilderness as quickly as the discovery of human waste or toilet paper at a prime camping spot or along the trail. Always use the restroom before hiking. If you are on the trail for the day or an extended trip, be prepared to pack out human waste, toilet paper, diapers, and hygiene products. Human waste disposal bags are highly recommended to transport solid waste.

image.title: Toilet paper along a trail
image.altText: White toilet paper lays along a desert mountain landscape
image.caption: Toilet paper doesn't belong in the desert.

title: Tejas Thru Hike
shortDescription: The Tejas Trail is the primary north/south through trail within the park, connecting the Pine Springs Trailhead with the Dog Canyon Trailhead at the park's northern boundary. This major artery can be used to connect to numerous other trails to make a variety of loops. The central portion of the trail from Pine Top until the McKittrick Canyon Trail junction is forested, passing through the Bowl and numerous drainages.

image.title: Tejas Trail scene
image.altText: A trail cuts through a desert mountain landscape.
image.caption: The Tejas Trail below the Pine Top Campsites.

title: Hike to Fall Colors
shortDescription: Bright fall colors of deciduous trees are not common in the southwest, but elevation and environment combine in the Guadalupe Mountains for a seasonally striking display usually from mid-October to Mid-November. A series of short and long hikes of varying degrees of difficulty will bring you to glimpse of this annual splendor.
seasonDescription: Fall colors depend greatly on precipitation and weather patterns and the peak period can vary from year to year. Generally, the best time of the year for viewing fall colors is the last week of October and the first week of November. Be aware that weekends during the fall colors season can be full to capacity throughout the park; plan for a weekday visit if possible.

image.title: Fall colors in McKittrick
image.altText: A woman carrying a backpack walks along a trail surrounded by vibrant fall foliage.
image.caption: Hiking through fall colors in McKittrick Canyon

title: Campground Connector Trail
shortDescription: This short trail connects the visitor center to the campground and the trailhead area at Pine Springs.

image.title: Connector trail
image.altText: A trail is marked by two orange cones
image.caption: The connector trail begins at the visitor center parking lot.

title: Overnight on McKittrick Ridge
shortDescription: The journey to the top of McKittrick Ridge is "the toughest hike in Texas." This arduous hike is best enjoyed as an overnight hike allowing for rest, recovery, and fabulous night skies at the McKittrick Ridge Wilderness Campground. An overnight Wilderness Use Permit is required for camping.

image.title: McKittrick Ridge
image.altText: A mountainous ridge with trees and rocks looms in the distance
image.caption: McKittrick Ridge

title: Pine Springs to McKittrick Canyon
shortDescription: The Tejas Trail is the primary north/south through trail within the park, connecting the Pine Springs Trailhead with the Dog Canyon Trailhead at the park's northern boundary. The central portion of the trail from Pine Top until the McKittrick Canyon Trail junction is forested, passing through the Bowl and numerous drainages. As the trail descends from McKittrick Ridge, visitors are provided with a panoramic experience of the canyon.

image.title: McKittrick Ridge
image.altText: A mountainous ridge with trees and rocks looms in the distance
image.caption: McKittrick Ridge

title: Guadalupe Peak
shortDescription: Climb to the "Top of Texas" with a hike up Guadalupe Peak. Guadalupe Peak is a rewarding, although very strenuous, 8.4 mile round trip hike with a 3,000 foot elevation gain. It will take from six to eight hours to complete the hike. The peak provides fantastic views from the highest point in the state of Texas (8,751 feet / 2,667 meters). It also introduces hikers to several of the park’s ecosystems including the high desert and the high elevation forests.
seasonDescription: Guadalupe Peak is the most popular trail in the park. If hiking on a weekend, expect trailhead parking to fill early in the day. Overflow parking for the trailhead is located at the Pine Springs Visitor Center.

image.title: A Guadalupe Peak sunset
image.altText: A hiker stands on a peak with lower mountains in the background at sunset
image.caption: A Guadalupe Peak sunset

title: Hiking with a Group
shortDescription: In order to protect sensitive ecosystems and limit the impacts on the natural landscape, day-use hiking groups may not be larger than twenty persons on any trails in the park. This page provides suggestions on how to split your group up in order to preserve Wilderness character, and limit adverse impacts on park resources.

image.title: Hikers on the Guadalupe Peak Trail
image.altText: A group of hikers relax along a trail high up on a mountain
image.caption: Hikers take a break on the Guadalupe Peak Trail

title: Manzanita Spring
shortDescription: The Manzanita Spring Trail is a 0.5 mile (0.8 km) out and back trail that begins adjacent the Frijole Ranch. Manzanita Spring is a wide pool that provides excellent bird watching opportunities.

image.title: Manzanita Spring
image.altText: A pool of water surrounded by vegetation and blue sky
image.caption: Manzanita Spring

title: Indian Meadow Nature Trail
shortDescription: The Indian Meadow Nature Trail is an easy 0.6 mile loop that begins across the road from the ranger station and next to the group campsite, offering good views of the landscape. At a leisurely pace it takes 30-45 minutes. The trail is rated easy as it remains almost level after crossing an arroyo.

image.title: Indian Meadow Nature Trail
image.altText: A gravel trail cuts through a grassy meadow with a tall desert mountain cliff rising behind.
image.caption: The Indian Meadow Nature Trail circles a meadow at Dog Canyon.

title: Hunter Peak
shortDescription: The hike to Hunter Peak is a challenging day hike done as a loop up the Bear Canyon Trail and down the Tejas Trail that provides solitude, stunning views, and opportunities for side trails into the Bowl area.
seasonDescription: While the steep Bear Canyon Trail (2,000 foot elevation gain in 1.8 miles) can be intimidating, during the fall colors season (mid-October to mid-November), the canyon is likley to be vibrant with changing color.

image.title: Hunter Peak at sunset
image.altText: A desert mountain peak is lit by the setting sun as it rises above the landscape around it.
image.caption: Hunter Peak at sunset

title: Smith Spring Trail Loop
shortDescription: Begin this hike at the trailhead sign. Look for birds, mule deer, and elk as you walk this loop trail to the shady oasis of Smith Spring. Take a break here and enjoy the gurgling sounds of the tiny waterfall before continuing around to sunny Manzanita Spring. Scars from wildland fires of 1990 and 1993 are evident along the trail. The trail is rated moderate, with a round-trip distance of 2.3 miles. Allow one to two hours.

image.title: Smith Spring
image.altText: Water cascades down rocks in a forested setting.
image.caption: Smith Spring

title: Marcus Overlook
shortDescription: Hiking the Bush Mountain Trail from Dog Canyon out to the Marcus Overlook and back makes an excellent and usually solitary day hike in the Guadalupe Mountains. From the Marcus Overlook, there are commanding views south into the Guadalupe Mountains and westward.
seasonDescription: Even with the higher elevations on the northern part of the park, summer temperatures may make this hike unsafe or at the very least unpleasant. Expect high winds (in excess of 30MPH from November through March). This route on the northern portion of the Bush Mountain Trail has little to no shade.

image.title: Looking west from the Marcus Overlook
image.altText: From a high point, a desert grasslands stretches into the distance with ridges in the background.
image.caption: Looking west from the Marcus Overlook

title: Pratt Cabin
shortDescription: Enjoy the shortest distance into the heart of the canyon by hiking to Pratt Cabin and return (a distance of 4.8 miles). Along this walk you will cross the stream once before arriving at the historic structure. Enjoy a snack or lunch at the picnic tables near or at Pratt Cabin, or sit for a spell on the porch. Volunteers staff Pratt Cabin on occasion; take a look inside the stone structure.

image.title: Volunteer speaks to a visitor seated on
image.altText: Volunteer speaks to a visitor seated on the porch of a stone cabin
image.caption: On fall weekends volunteers staff the Pratt cabin to answer visitor questions.

title: Lost Peak Saddle
shortDescription: Hiking the Tejas Trail from Dog Canyon out to the Lost Peak Saddle and back makes an excellent day hike in the Guadalupe Mountains.
seasonDescription: Even with the higher elevations on the northern part of the park, summer temperatures may make this hike unsafe or at the very least unpleasant. Expect high winds (in excess of 30MPH from November through March).

image.title: The Summit of Lost Peak
image.altText: A desert mountain ends abruptly with a grey cliff
image.caption: The Summit of Lost Peak

title: Foothills Loop
shortDescription: This moderate loop route uses the Frijole Trail and the Foothills Trail to make a loop below the eastern escarpment of the Guadalupe Mountains.
seasonDescription: While this is generally a year-round route in good weather, the Foothills Loop will be open and exposed to high temperatures from late summer through early Fall.

image.title: Foothills Loop view
image.altText: A desert mountain landscape with buildings and a prominent point in the background.
image.caption: View towards Frijole Ranch from the Foothills Loop.

title: The Grotto and Hunter Line Shack
shortDescription: Stretch out your day hike into McKittrick Canyon by hiking to the Grotto. Elevation gain doubles as you travel further up canyon, but is still mild at less then 600 feet gained from the trailhead. Exposed cave features and stone picnic tables near the Hunter Line Shack make for a fabulous lunch destination.
seasonDescription: McKittrick Canyon is beautiful all year but is especially well known for fall colors in late October.

image.title: Stone picnic tables at the Grotto.
image.altText: Stone tables and benches are located near a cliff with rock overhangs and alcoves.
image.caption: Stone picnic tables at the Grotto.

title: Permian Reef Trail
shortDescription: The Permian Reef Trail climbs the north side of McKittrick Canyon to the top of Wilderness Ridge, providing sweeping views into South McKittrick Canyon. Among the least used trails in the park, this long climb is rewarded with solitude and dramatic landscape views.
seasonDescription: The slopes above the canyon face south so receive full sun all day, hence the hike is best avoided during hot periods in summer.

image.title: The Permian Reef Trail
image.altText: A stone trail winds up a steep desert slope.
image.caption: The Permian Reef Trail features a dramatic climb up the north side of McKittrick Canyon.

title: Devil's Hall
shortDescription: The strenuous route to Devil's Hall departs from the Pine Springs Trailhead and is 4.2 miles round-trip. After the first mile the trail enters a rocky wash which leads hikers to an impressive natural rock staircase that connects to a "hallway" formed by steep canyon walls. Rock surfaces in the wash can be slippery when dry and visitors should exercise caution on this hike.
seasonDescription: While this is generally a year-round route in good weather, Devil's Hall can be a good hike for fall colors from mid-October to mid-November.

image.title: Devil's Hall
image.altText: Groups of people in the sunlight at the end of a narrow tall canyon.
image.caption: At Devil's Hall

title: El Capitan Viewpoint
shortDescription: On the climb up Guadalupe Pass on U.S. Highway 62/180 just a few miles west of the Pine Springs area, this roadside pull-off provides an unparalleled view to the summit of El Capitan.

image.title: El Capitan Viewpoint
image.altText: A roadside picnic shelter stands below a prominent mountain peak.
image.caption: El Capitan Viewpoint

title: McKittrick Canyon Nature Trail
shortDescription: This fascinating, short trail passes an intermittent seep that lies hidden in junipers, then wanders up a southwest slope along an arroyo. Here, plants and animals tolerate true desert conditions. At the top of the trail you can look down at the mouth of McKittrick Canyon and read about Permian Reef geology.

image.title: Hiking the nature trail
image.altText: A uniformed park ranger and visitors hike up a desert trail
image.caption: The McKittrick Canyon Nature Trail is a short trail with dramatic views.

title: Salt Basin Dunes Trail
shortDescription: The white gypsum sands of the Salt Basin Dunes rise 100 feet from the desert floor and provide a brilliant contrast to the dark, towering cliffs of the Guadalupe Mountains. From the trailhead, follow the trail to the gypsum sand dune field with excellent views of the western escarpment of the Guadalupe Mountains. There is no shade along the trail, so carry plenty of water and avoid hiking in the midday heat.
seasonDescription: Visitation to the Salt Basin Dunes can be problematic during the summer months when temperatures can exceed 100°F. Summer storms may produce heavy rains that can make the access road impassable for days or weeks at a time.

image.title: Hiking on the Salt Basin Dunes
image.altText: Two people stand on white sand dunes in front of a desert mountain range
image.caption: Hiking on the Salt Basin Dunes

title: What Time Is It?
shortDescription: Guadalupe Mountains National Park is in the Mountain Time Zone. Visitors relying on electronic devices may be misled, as cell signal service for the park comes from towers located in the Central Time Zone. We strongly suggest that you set your phone or other device to Mountain time during your visit.

image.title: You are in Mountain Time
image.altText: A sign reads "Entering Mountain Time Zone" with Guadalupe Mountains in the Background
image.caption: Visiting along the time zone boundary requires some planning

title: Drive to Dog Canyon
shortDescription: Dog Canyon, the park's remote north district, is only seven miles as the crow files, but a full two hour drive [one-way] from Pine Springs through a panoramic Chihuahuan Desert and mountain landscape.

image.title: The approach to Dog Canyon
image.altText: View from a road of a long canyon wall in the desert landscape.
image.caption: Approaching Dog Canyon from the north.

title: Drive to the Five Points Vista
shortDescription: Located line of sight to Dog Canyon, the Five Points Vista is a scenic overlook near the end of the Guadalupe Rim Road in the Lincoln National Forest's Guadalupe Ranger District. This viewpoint offers spectacular views of the 'Rim' and the Guadalupe Mountains.

image.title: Five Points Vista
image.altText: A roadside pull-off with a Forest Service sign
image.caption: Five Points Vista

title: Highway 54 To The Guadalupes
shortDescription: From the south, Texas State Highway 54 leads directly to the Guadalupes from Van Horn, Texas. Running between the Delaware Mountains to the east and Sierra Diablo on the west, the highway provides a dramatic approach to the Guadalupe Mountains, and on a clear day, you can see the mountains ahead of you for forty miles.
seasonDescription: Conditions on Guadalupe Pass can vary due to seasonal weather conditions and high winds. Use caution.

image.title: El Capitan as seen from the highway.
image.altText: A tall promontory point rises above a desert landscape
image.caption: El Capitan as seen from the highway.

title: Leave No Trace
shortDescription: Each of us plays a vital role in protecting our national parks. As we spend time outdoors, in the natural world and in wilderness, it’s important to be conscious of the effects our actions may have on plants, animals, other people, and even entire ecosystems. Following the Leave No Trace Seven Principles, summarized below, can help us minimize those impacts.
seasonDescription: Leave No Trace principles can be followed in any visit to ensure that the you leave the park better than you found it.

image.title: Leave No Trace Cards
image.altText: A hand holds two waterproof cards with text in front of a green background
image.caption: Leave No Trace Cards

title: Highway 62/180 to the Guadalupes
shortDescription: Every visitor to Guadalupe Mountains National Park travels U.S Highway 62/180. Connecting El Paso, Texas to Carlsbad, New Mexico, the highway provides breath-taking views of the park from the north, south, and west. The highway enters the park for five miles and a series of access roads provide access to park features.
seasonDescription: Conditions on Guadalupe Pass can vary due to seasonal weather conditions and high winds. Use caution.

image.title: The view along Highway 62/180
image.altText: Desert mountians rise past a paved highway.
image.caption: Approaching Pine Springs on Highway 62/180

title: Can I Take My Dog?
shortDescription: Opportunities for pets are limited. Leashed pets may walk on the short Pine Springs Campground connector trail or along the Pinery Trail from the visitor center to the Butterfield Stage Station.

image.title: Pinery Trail Sign
image.altText: A signpost contains information about a trail
image.caption: The Pinery is one of two trails that pets are allowed on in the Guadalupe Mountains.

title: Drive to the Salt Basin Dunes
shortDescription: The white gypsum sands of the Salt Basin Dunes rise 100 feet from the desert floor and provide a brilliant contrast to the dark, towering cliffs of the Guadalupe Mountains. This is a lesser used area of the park; a drive to the dunes provides excellent views of El Capitan and the western escarpment of the Guadalupe Mountains.
seasonDescription: Visitation to the Salt Basin Dunes can be problematic during the summer months when temperatures can exceed 100°F. Summer storms may produce heavy rains that can make the access road impassable for days or weeks at a time.

image.title: Western escarpment
image.altText: A desrt mountain range looms over a low desert foreground with sand dunes in the distance
image.caption: The western escarpment rises dramatically over the Salt Basin Dunes

title: Search and Rescue Policy
shortDescription: Search and rescue actions are conducted on a discretionary basis. The level and necessity of the response is determined through evaluation of the situation by field personnel. Rescuer safety is always our first priority. This park expects visitors to exhibit a high degree of self-reliance and responsibility for their own safety in line with the difficulty of their chosen activities. There is little to no cell reception in most areas of the park.

image.title: Devil's Hall Carryout
image.altText: A group of uniformed staff carry a wheeled litter down a rocky trail in a desert mountain terrain
image.caption: Rangers and firefighters carry a wheeled litter down the Guadalupe Peak Trail

title: Virtual Summit Log
shortDescription: When you reach a summit or other destination in the park, take a group photo or selfie in areas of the park and post to social media and include the hashtag #GuadalupeMountains #guadalupepeak #hunterpeak #lostpeak or others hashtags using your device and social media service.

image.title: Group on Hunter Peak Summit
image.altText: Three people stand on the summit of a mountain peak
image.caption: Modern technology allows visitors to record their hike while leaving no trace of their visit.

title: Shop at the Park Store
shortDescription: The park store is operated by Western National Parks Association, an official non-profit partner of the National Park Service dedicated to supporting the educational mission of Guadalupe Mountains National Park. The park store has a wide range of books, maps, travel guides, and other items available for retail sale. These products complement the interpretive themes you experience when visiting the park. The park store is located in the Pine Springs Visitor Center.

image.title: Park Store
image.altText: A retail space with books and other items for purchase shown on shelves and racks
image.caption: The park store is inside the visitor center

title: Celebrate the Fire Horse
shortDescription: Stop by the Thousand Springs Visitor Center for scheduled Year of the Horse events and lectures.

image.title: 2026: Year of the Fire Horse
image.altText: Illustration of a red horse surrounded by flowers.
image.caption: Celebrate the Year of the Horse at Hagerman Fossil Beds.

title: Birding in the Hagerman Valley
shortDescription: The Hagerman Valley is one of the most popular birding destinations in southern Idaho.

image.title: Birding in the Hagerman Valley
image.altText: Two ducks take off from a pond surrounded by thick vegetation.
image.caption: The Hagerman Valley is a hotspot for birding in southern Idaho.

title: Enjoy a Picnic
shortDescription: Pack up a meal to enjoy with friends or family at a covered picnic shelter along the park road.
seasonDescription: The park road and scenic overlooks are open year-round. During winter, snow and ice may be present on roads, trails, and sidewalks.

image.title: Picnic area at the Snake River Overlook
image.altText: A picnic table under a shelter overlooks the Snake River.
image.caption: Take in scenic views over lunch at the Snake River Overlook.

title: Hike the Emigrant Trail
shortDescription: The Emigrant Trail roughly parallels visible remnants of the Oregon Trail, capturing some of the experience of mid-1800s emigrants moving West.

image.title: Hike the Emigrant Trail
image.altText: Panoramic view of a trail cutting through scrub-covered hills, descending into a valley.
image.caption: The Emigrant Trail parallels visible remnants of the Oregon Trail.

title: Become a Hagerman Fossil Beds Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Visitors of all ages and abilities can become a Hagerman Fossil Beds Junior Ranger.

image.title: Become a Junior Ranger
image.altText: Junior ranger booklets, badges, and a ranger hat are scattered across a table.
image.caption: Pick up a booklet at the visitor center to start earning your junior ranger badge!

title: See Fossils on Display
shortDescription: See fossils on display and learn about Hagerman's contributions to the science of paleontology.

image.title: Fossil Exhibits
image.altText: A fossil horse in a large room of posters and display cases.
image.caption: The Thousand Springs Visitor Center is the only place to see fossils in the monument.

title: Take a Scenic Drive
shortDescription: Take in stunning views of the Snake River, the fossil beds, and the Hagerman Valley along five miles of park road. Stop at the Snake River and Oregon Trail Overlooks for scenic viewpoints and educational exhibits.
seasonDescription: The park road and scenic overlooks are open year-round. During winter, snow and ice may be present on roads, trails, and sidewalks.

image.title: scenic views from the park road
image.altText: View overlooking the Snake River, with the steep bluffs of the fossil beds lining the other side.
image.caption: Take in scenic views of the river and the fossil beds from the Snake River Overlook.

title: Become a Haleakalā Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Complete activities featuring the plants, animals, and history of Haleakalā to earn your Junior Ranger badge!

image.title: Junior Ranger Booklet
image.altText: A colorful cover shows native plants and animals and says "Junior Ranger Activity Book."
image.caption: Junior Ranger activities are a great way to learn about Haleakalā and the National Park Service.

title: Moderate Hike into Haleakalā's Crater
shortDescription: Enter the park's Wilderness on the Keoneheʻeheʻe (Sliding Sands) Trail and take a moderate out-and-back hike partway down the windswept cinder slope. This is among the most popular hikes in the park thanks to its unbeatable crater views.
seasonDescription: Temperatures generally start off cool in the morning and warm up in the afternoon all year. Winter is the rainy season in Hawaii, and there may be an increased chance for fog or storms in the afternoon, no matter the season.

image.title: Start of Keoneheʻeheʻe Trail
image.altText: A trail leads down into a colorful volcanic valley.
image.caption: Gain a new perspective for the crater on the Keoneheʻeheʻe Trail.

title: Enjoy the Sunrise
shortDescription: Start your day at the top of Haleakalā. With an advance sunrise reservation, visitors can await the dawn from any of four lookouts leading to the summit.
seasonDescription: Sunrise reservations are available year round. No matter the season, plan for cold, windy weather at the summit. Temperatures can often approach or even dip below freezing. Weather is unpredictable, and storms can quickly blow in and obscure views of the crater and the sunrise.

image.altText: A dawn sky colors clouds yellow and pink, silhouetting an overlook shelter.

title: Strenuous Hike Across the Crater Floor
shortDescription: Experienced hikers can "thru" hike the crater from Keoneheʻeheʻe (Sliding Sands) Trailhead, across the crater floor, and out to Halemauʻu Trailhead. This hike is extremely strenuous and should only be undertaken by individuals who are equipped for a wilderness environment.
seasonDescription: Temperatures generally start off cool in the morning and warm up in the afternoon all year. Winter is the rainy season in Hawaiʻi, and there may be an increased chance for fog or storms in the afternoon, no matter the season. Always come prepared with both sun and rain protection, along with extra layers and emergency shelter.

image.title: Hiker at Puʻu Halāliʻi
image.altText: A hiker walks a trail between two red and yellow cinder cones.
image.caption: Have an otherworldly adventure in the park's Wilderness Area

title: Short Hike to Leleiwi Overlook
shortDescription: Take a short .3 mile (.5 km) roundtrip walk out to Leleiwi Overlook. Pass native plants on your way to a spectacular view of the crater and the Koʻolau Gap.

image.title: Leleiwi Overlook
image.altText: A path with a railing leads to an overlook next to a deep volcanic valley
image.caption: On a clear day, Leleiwi offers excellent crater views.

title: Shopping
shortDescription: The HPPA operates three bookstores at Haleakalā National Park and they are located at Park Headquarters, Haleakalā Visitor Center, and Kīpahulu Visitor Center. The HPPA also maintains an online bookstore.

image.title: HQVC Bookstore
image.altText: A bookstore with shelves of books, bottles, and plush animals
image.caption: The HPPA bookstore located at Headquarters Visitor Center

title: Moderate Hike to the Crater Edge
shortDescription: Meander through native shrubland to glimpse rare forest birds and a variety of plants found only in Hawaiʻi.
seasonDescription: Temperatures generally start off cool in the morning and warm up in the afternoon all year. Winter is the rainy season in Hawaiʻi, and there may be an increased chance for fog or storms in the afternoon, no matter the season.

image.title: Scenic Overlook from Halemauʻu Trail
image.altText: a rocky trail follows a ridgeline surrounded by shrubs.
image.caption: Even a short hike can reveal new sites and sounds of the park's wilderness.

title: Moderate Hike up to the Bamboo Forest
shortDescription: Listen to the sounds of the bamboo forest as the towering stalks creak, clack, and clang along the Pīpīwai Trail! Pick up the trail to the left of the Kīpahulu Visitor Center. The hike is 1 mile (1.6 km) round trip with an average hiking time of 1 hour. Be prepared for a hot hike and carry water, a snack, and sun protection!

image.title: Pīpīwai Trail with Bamboo NPS
image.altText: A canopy of bamboo rises from the left and right blocking out the blue sky above.

title: Short Hike to Makahiku Falls
shortDescription: Golden light. Verdant forests. White waters. View Makahiku Falls from the Pīpīwai Trail in the Kīpahulu District of Haleakalā National Park.

image.title: Makahiku Falls
image.altText: White waters fall over a cliff surrounded by verdant trees.

title: Park Bookstore
shortDescription: Hawaiʻi Pacific Parks Association operates the official park bookstores at the Welcome Center and the Kahuku Unit.

image.title: Hawaiʻi Pacific Parks Association Store
image.altText: A bookshelf lined with books about Hawaii
image.caption: HPPA store in Kīlauea Visitor Center

title: Hōlei Sea Arch

image.altText: A viewpoint of dramatic sea cliffs with a wayside exhibit in the foreground

image.altText: Pit crater with stone wall in the foreground

shortDescription: Traverse the rugged Kaʻū Desert and see footprints left by Native Hawaiians long ago.

title: Puʻuloa Petroglyphs Trail
shortDescription: Hike across a lava field to the largest group of petroglyphs in Hawaiʻi.

shortDescription: Take a strenuous hike to a pit crater filled with an array of native Hawaiian species.

shortDescription: A loop hike through a unique area of biological diversity with rare plants, birds, and old-growth trees.

image.altText: Rays of sunlight through trees

shortDescription: Hike down to the floor of Kaluapele (Kīlauea caldera), with possible longer connections to Byron Ledge, Kīlauea Iki, and Nāhuku.

shortDescription: Catch views of Kīlauea caldera, feel the breath of the volcano at Steaming Bluff (Wahinekapu), and walk through lush rainforest.

title: Backcountry Camp at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park
shortDescription: Looking for solitude or adventure? The vast backcountry on Kīlauea and Mauna Loa provides ample opportunities.

title: See Crater Rim Drive and Chain of Craters Road
shortDescription: Drive the two primary roads in the park for a scenic adventure through a dynamic geological and cultural landscape

image.caption: Chain of Craters Road

title: Goat Rock Trail
shortDescription: The Goat Rock trail offers stunning views of the Ouachita Mountains and the recharge zone for the thermal springs. Limited parking is available at the overlook on North Mountain. The trailhead starts south of the parking area.

image.title: Goat Rock Viewpoint
image.altText: A black metal rail surrounds an outcropping overlooking rolling, forested hills.
image.caption: The Goat Rock viewpoint

title: Become a Hot Springs Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Kids visiting Hot Springs National Park may earn a Junior Ranger badge by completing a number of activities as they explore the park. The Junior Ranger booklet is available at the Fordyce Bathhouse Visitor Center.

image.title: Magnifying lens
image.altText: Two children in long sleeved shirts and hats hold up a magnifying lens
image.caption: Junior Ranger Day, 2019

title: Camp at the Gulpha Gorge Campground
shortDescription: BASIC INFORMATION Camping at Gulpha Gorge Campground costs $34 per night for all sites. All sites have full hookups: 30 and 50 amp electric, water and sewer connections. Sites are not pull-through. Each campsite has a picnic table, pedestal grill, and water.

image.title: Camping at Gulpha Gorge Campground
image.altText: RV parked at campsite in the woods.
image.caption: RV at Gulpha Gorge Campground.

title: Oak Trail
shortDescription: The northeastern end of Oak Trail is mostly flat. The trail is fairly steep for a short distance between West Mountain Trail and West Mountain Drive.

image.title: Oak Trail
image.altText: A mossy stone wall lines a paved dirt pathway through the woods.
image.caption: The Oak Trail where it meets the Canyon Trail.

title: An Overview: Hot Springs and North Mountain Trails
shortDescription: The Hot Springs and North Mountain trails are popular since they are easy to reach and provide scenic views. You can get to these trails via Stephen’s Balustrade (grand staircase) behind the Fordyce Bathhouse, Hot Springs Mountain Drive, and the Gulpha Gorge Campground. See the Hot Springs and North Mountain trail map for more information.
seasonDescription: Trails are accessible and enjoyable all year long.

image.title: Hot Springs Mountain Trail
image.altText: Gravel hiking trail surrounded by a dense forrest.
image.caption: Hot Springs Mountain Trail

title: Honeysuckle Trail
shortDescription: Honeysuckle Trail connects Peak Trail with Hot Springs Mountain Trail.

image.title: Honeysuckle Shelter
image.altText: A stone shelter built in a 1930s style sits alongside a gravel trail.
image.caption: Shelter at the intersection of the Honeysuckle and Floral Trail.

title: Short Cut Trail
shortDescription: Short Cut Trail connects Oertel Trail with Hot Springs Mountain Trail near the picnic area atop Hot Springs Mountain.

image.title: Short Cut Trail
image.altText: A picnic area with many tables sit beneath the shade of the trees.
image.caption: View from the Short Cut trailhead

title: West Mountain Trail
shortDescription: Both sections of West Mountain Trail have gradual change in elevation. Note: West Mountain Trail can be made into a loop by using Mountain Top Trail (elevation change: 400 feet in this section).

image.title: West Mountain Trail
image.altText: A stone shelter sits on a hillside overlooking a rolling landscape.
image.caption: Shelter near the West Mountain Trail.

title: Whittington Trail
shortDescription: The flat, gravel trail is popular with joggers and walkers. Whittington Trail loops around Whittington Park.

image.title: Whittington Park
image.altText: A white foot bridge crosses over a small creek amidst a vibrant open park with tall trees.
image.caption: Whittington Park

title: Mountain Top Trail
shortDescription: Mountaintop trail can be linked with Canyon Trail and West Mountain trail to complete a loop around West Mountain. If hiking southward, the trail is strenuous, as it gains elevation quickly. If hiking northward, there is a steady rise in elevation until you cross Sunset Trail; the trail descends steeply to the trailhead at Whittington Park.

image.title: Mountain Top Trail
image.altText: A rocky trail curves through the trees on a hillside.
image.caption: A view of a trail on West Mountain.

title: Canyon Trail
shortDescription: The West Mountain trails can be reached from downtown via Canyon Trail. The trailhead is behind the Mountain Valley Water building. The section between West Mountain Drive and West Mountain Trail is very steep.

image.title: Canyon Trail
image.altText: A ranger in uniform walks up the curved trail through the forest.
image.caption: A ranger walks up the Canyon Trail.

title: Pullman Trail
shortDescription: The Pullman Trail is the only trail in the park that allows bicycles. This moderate trail passes an archeological site and connects with the city's Northwoods Trails.

image.title: Pullman Trailhead Sign
image.altText: Three trail head signs line the front of a trailhead that leads into the forest.
image.caption: Pullman trailhead signage

title: Upper Dogwood Trail
shortDescription: Upper Dogwood trail has short rises and long stretches of flat trail. It can be combined with the Lower Dogwood Trail or the Goat Rock Trail to create a longer hike.

image.title: North Mountain Overlook
image.altText: Rolling hills and forested hillsides extend towards the horizon.
image.caption: View from the North Mountain overlook.

title: Lower Dogwood Trail
shortDescription: Lower Dogwood Trail climbs North Mountain. Near the top, boulders mark the westernmost tip of the trail. From there, the trail drops downhill.

image.title: Hiking along a Trail
image.altText: Two people hike along a rocky trail.
image.caption: Hiking around North Mountain

title: Arlington Trail
shortDescription: Ask for directions to the trailhead from staff at the Arlington Hotel lobby. Arlington Trail will connect with Lower Dogwood Trail.

image.title: Arlington Lawn
image.altText: A lush, green lawn lays before a tall, wide, tan hotel building.
image.caption: Arlington Lawn

title: Floral Trail
shortDescription: Floral Trail connects Lower Dogwood Trail and Honeysuckle Trail. From either trailhead you will descend into a valley and climb the other side.

image.title: Floral Trail
image.altText: A packed gravel path leads through a forested hillside.
image.caption: A view of a trail on Hot Springs Mountain.

title: Gulpha Gorge Trail
shortDescription: Gulpha Gorge Trail connects the Gulpha Gorge Campground to many of the park's trails. The trail going west from the campground is steep.

image.title: Gulpha Trail
image.altText: A stone pathway crossed a flowing river with tall trees in the background.
image.caption: Gulpha Gorge trail crosses Gulpha Creek before heading up the mountain.

title: Tufa Terrace Trail
shortDescription: This paved trail can be reached from the Grand Promenade or Arlington Lawn. The lower portion of the Tufa Terrace Trail is near the Hot Water Cascade.

image.title: Tufa Terrace Trail
image.altText: A railed, thin pathway leads through bright green trees and brush.
image.caption: Lower Tufa Terrace Trail

title: Grand Avenue Trail
shortDescription: Grand Avenue Trail connects Oertel Trail with Grand Avenue. A local motel lies just south of the trailhead.

image.title: Looking Up
image.altText: A young man stands in the middle of a packed gravel trail looking up to the lush green trees.
image.caption: Looking up on the trail

title: Fountain Trail
shortDescription: This short trail begins on Fountain Street below the entrance to Hot Springs Mountain Drive. Use it to reach Honeysuckle Trail by crossing the road.

image.title: Fountain Trail
image.altText: A gravel path leads through an a hillside forest.
image.caption: A view from Hot Springs Mountain.

title: Reserve Trail
shortDescription: Reserve Trail connects Oertel Trail with Spring Street and Reserve Street at a "Y" intersection.

image.title: Reserve Trail
image.altText: A shaded, highly vegetated piece of the forest with knobby, thin trees.
image.caption: A glimpse of the forests in Hot Springs.

title: Hot Springs Mountain Trail
shortDescription: Hot Springs Mountain Trail is an easy stroll around the top of the mountain with several scenic overlooks.

image.title: Pagoda on Hot Springs Mountain
image.altText: A white pagoda with a red roof sits on the edge of a hillside.
image.caption: Hot Springs Mountain pagoda

title: An Overview: West Mountain Trails
shortDescription: The West Mountain trails are less traveled, providing greater opportunities for wildlife sightings. You can get to these trails via Whittington Park and the Canyon Trailhead. See the West Mountain trail map for more information.
seasonDescription: Trails are accessible and enjoyable all year long.

image.title: Hiking Trail on West Mountain
image.altText: Dirt hiking trail surrounded by dense forrest.
image.caption: People hiking on West Mountain.

title: Sunset Trail
shortDescription: Sunset Trail is the longest trail in Hot Springs National Park, covering approximately 10 miles one-way. Crossing all types of terrain, the trail makes its way through the most remote areas of the park. This trail is divided into three sections: West Mountain (2.8 miles), Sugarloaf Mountain (2.6 miles), and Stonebridge Road (3.8 miles). Sunset Trail can be combined with Hot Springs and North Mountain trails and West Mountain trails to complete a strenuous 15 mile loop hike.
seasonDescription: The trail is accessible and enjoyable all year long.

image.title: Sunset Trail
image.altText: Hiking trail through a dense forest with the sun setting through the trees.
image.caption: Sunset Trail

title: Oertel Trail
shortDescription: From downtown, ascend the Stephen's Balustrade (grand staircase) behind the Fordyce Visitor Center to the Grand Promenade and climb the next two sets of steps until you reach the gravel road. Take the road right until you reach an iron gate; the trailhead begins here. Oertel Trail ranges from moderate to very steep grade.

image.title: Oertel Trail
image.altText: Gravel paths converge on the grass.
image.caption: The path to the Oertel Trail

title: Peak Trail
shortDescription: Peak Trail leads to the Hot Springs Mountain Tower. The Trail is 0.6 mi (1.0 km) long with an elevation gain of 644 - 1044 ft (196-318 m). It has a 12.6% grade. The trailhead is located near the center of the Grand Promenade. Peak Trail is paved then turns to gravel and connects to many other hiking trails around Hot Springs Mountain.
seasonDescription: The Peak Trail is accessible and enjoyable all year long.

image.title: Peak Trail to Mountain Tower
image.altText: Dense wooded area with a tall mountain observation tower at the peak of the mountain.
image.caption: Peak Trail to Mountain Tower

title: Grand Promenade National Recreation Trail
shortDescription: This National Recreation Trail is the entry point for many of the Hot Springs and North Mountain trails from downtown.

image.title: The Grand Promenade Afternoon Walk
image.altText: A man walks with his dog down a red brick path surrounded by bright green trees.
image.caption: The Grand Promenade

title: Bicycle Riding
shortDescription: Biking through national parks is a great way to see beautiful scenery and discover new places. Cyclists are allowed and welcome to ride on any of the paved roads in the park. The roads up to North Mountain and West Mountain maintain a progressive incline with moderate traffic, so please use caution and plan accordingly. *Bicycles are not allowed on the Grand Promenade or on the sidewalk in front of Bathhouse Row.

image.title: Biking West Mountain
image.altText: A lone bicycle rider wearing a blue jersey rides up an open mountain road.
image.caption: Biking in the Park

title: Photography in the Park
shortDescription: Photography is an important part of national park history. Photographers took pictures to show why special places needed protection. People were able to see how beautiful and unique park landscapes were even if they could not visit them in person. Today, professional and amateur photographers alike travel from around the world to capture scenic and historic vistas.

image.title: Gulpha Creek
image.altText: Water flows through a rocky creek bed, surrounded by lush greenery.
image.caption: Gulpha Creek at the Gulpha Gorge Campground

title: Birdwatching in the Park
shortDescription: Birds are everywhere. They soar overhead, flit through branches, walk on the ground, and swim in the water. From the tiny calliope hummingbird to the gigantic California condor, a great diversity of birds finds a home in the national parks. Even more species pass through during migration. Casual observers and hardcore birders alike can experience the joy of birds and birding in a national park.

image.altText: Bird with red head searches for food in tree

title: The Bathhouse Row Emporium
shortDescription: Visit the America’s National Parks™ Store at Hot Springs National Park to shop a curated selection of quality educational products and books that will help extend the park experience. Explore products in person or at the America’s National Parks™ Online Store. Your purchases in the park and online directly support educational programs at this park.

image.title: Bathhouse Row Emporium
image.altText: Large rounded windows behind display cases of souvenirs
image.caption: Bathhouse Row Emporium in the Lamar Bathhouse

title: Visit Display Springs
shortDescription: Touch the Thermal Springs
seasonDescription: The display spring is available for viewing all year long.

image.title: Display Spring
image.altText: A hot spring with a rock foundation around it.
image.caption: Display Springs behind the Maurice Bathhouse.

title: Visit the Hot Water Cascade
shortDescription: Located at Arlington Lawn, this is the largest visible spring in the Park. Hot water emanates from the hill side near the Grand Promenade and flows under the path, down a steep cliff into two pools.

title: Ride to the Top of Hot Springs Mountain Tower
shortDescription: 216 feet above Hot Springs Mountain and 1,256 feet above Sea level is the breathtaking panoramic view of the park and its surrounding countryside. Originally being made of wood in 1877, the tower was rebuilt with steel and an elevator in 1982 with both open and enclosed observation decks.
seasonDescription: Seasonal hours of operation.

image.title: Hot Springs Mountain Tower
image.altText: Observation tower overlooking mountain.
image.caption: Hot Springs Mountain Tower

title: Drink the Water
shortDescription: Thousands of visitors highly endorse the good quality of the hot springs water and fill bottles to take home.
seasonDescription: Thermal and Cold Spring fountains are open and flowing all year long, unless noted otherwise.

image.title: Thermal Spring Jug Station
image.altText: Person filling up glass water jugs.
image.caption: Thermal Spring Jug Station

title: Soak in the Springs
shortDescription: Even though there are no soaking opportunities outdoors, Bathhouse Row does have 2 available facilities that offer visitors the chance to fully submerge and relax in the thermal water. The thermal springs are piped directly into both of these bathhouses, offering users a true and authentic experience of the water.

image.title: Buckstaff Bathhouse
image.altText: Three story building that reads Buckstaff Baths.
image.caption: Buckstaff Bathhouse, 2020.

title: 1966 Hiking Challenge
shortDescription: The 1966 Hiking Challenge is comprised of 19 hikes that cover 66 miles of trail in the park, celebrating the park’s founding in 1966. We will offer 19 weekly ranger led hikes every Saturday at 8:00 am starting on May 11 and culminating at the Outdoor Adventure Festival on September 14.

title: One Hour Excursions
shortDescription: Whether you have an hour, a half day, or a full day, the beaches, dunes, and trails of the Indiana Dunes offer relaxation, inspiration, and fun adventures.

image.altText: Marram grass grows along side a sandy trail

title: Half Day Adventures
shortDescription: Whether you have an hour, a half day, or a full day, the beaches, dunes, and trails of Indiana Dunes offer relaxation, inspiration, and fun adventures. This list highlights some of the must-see sights in the park. This is perfect for people planning a day trip.

image.altText: Trees with brightly colored leaves line the trail at Chellberg Farm.

title: Full Day Expeditions
shortDescription: Whether you have an hour, a half day, or a full day, the beaches, dunes, and trails of Indiana Dunes offer relaxation, inspiration, and fun adventures. This list highlights some of the must-see sights in the park. This is perfect for people planning a day full of activities and possibly an overnight.

image.altText: Surfer rides the waves at Portage Lakefront and Riverwalk at the Indiana Dunes National Park.

title: Paddling Lake Michigan and Waterways at Indiana Dunes
shortDescription: Kayaking is increasingly popular on Lake Michigan since the inception of the Lake Michigan Water Trail and in area waterways like the Little Calumet River and Burns Waterway. Try a new challenge by kayaking or canoeing the Little Calumet River Water Trail: East Branch.

image.title: Paddling the Waterways
image.altText: Paddling at Indiana Dunes
image.caption: Paddling the many Lake Michigan waterways

title: Swimming at Indiana Dunes West Beach
shortDescription: Fifteen miles of sandy beach along the southern shore of Lake Michigan offer a wide variety of recreational activities. Whether it's enjoying a summer sunset stroll or marveling at the arctic beauty of Lake Michigan's shelf ice, you can enjoy the beach in all seasons.

image.altText: Person surfing the waves around sunset at Portage Lakefront and Riverwalk.

title: Horseback Riding at Indiana Dunes
shortDescription: Enjoy an equestrian ride through ancient dune formations on the Glenwood Dunes Trails system. These trails are the only horseback trails and you must bring your own horse. The trail is host to almost 15 miles of interconnected loops. Be sure to bring a map as there are 13 junctions interconnecting the loops.
seasonDescription: Horseback riding is prohibited in the winter to allow for the cross-country skiers.

image.title: Horseback Riding at Glenwood Dunes Trail
image.altText: Horseback Riding at Glenwood Dunes Trail
image.caption: Horseback Riding at Glenwood Dunes Trail

title: Become an Indiana Dunes Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Indiana Dunes National Park has a lot to explore, both in the park and online. Check out this page for fun things to do to explore the park virtually. Become a Junior Ranger Today!

image.altText: Ranger talks to child while holding a Junior Ranger booklet

title: Explore Biological Diversity in the Park
shortDescription: The park is comprised of over 15,000 acres of dunes, oak savannas, swamps, bogs, marshes, prairies, rivers, and forests. It contains 15 miles of Lake Michigan shoreline spanning the distance from Gary to Michigan City. Lake Michigan is part of the largest complex of freshwater lakes in the world. The national park's beaches are the park's most significant recreational resource.

image.altText: Great Blue Heron flies in for a landing at the Great Marsh with the setting sun in the background.

title: Hiking Indiana Dunes
shortDescription: Indiana Dunes is home to one of the most biologically diverse habitats in the nation. Hiking is a great way to explore these fascinating landscape. Traverse over 50 miles of trails that lead you through shorelines, dunes, wetlands, prairies, river systems, oak savannahs, cultural sites and more.

image.title: Hiking the Dunes
image.altText: Hiking the Dunes
image.caption: 14 trails in one of the most diverse habitats. Trek over 50 miles of beautiful scenery!

title: Birding at Indiana Dunes National Park
shortDescription: Located at the southern tip of Lake Michigan, the national park is an important feeding and resting area for migrating birds. Lake Michigan influences the migration patterns of bird species. During the fall migration, southbound birds follow the north-south shoreline and are funneled into the Indiana Dunes. The large expanse of open water and miles of shoreline also attract large numbers of wintering birds.

image.title: Bird Watching at the Great Marsh
image.altText: Bird Watching at the Great Marsh
image.caption: Visitors taking photos and spotting birds in the Great Marsh with a ranger.

title: Become an Isle Royale Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Become an Isle Royale Junior Ranger and learn about the isolated island, the unique plants and animals found in the park, the island’s cultural history, and Leave No Trace principles.

image.title: Isle Royale Junior Ranger Booklet
image.altText: Children sit around a table working on Junior Ranger booklets while a Park Ranger stands nearby.
image.caption: Becoming a Junior Ranger is a great way to learn about Isle Royale National Park.

title: Attend a Rock Harbor Ranger Program
shortDescription: Attend a Rock Harbor ranger program at Isle Royale National Park. Learn about the isolated island, it's cultural history, and the critters who call the island home. Topics include moose, wolves, geology, shipwrecks, island biogeography, wilderness, and more. Ranger programs also include guided hikes and tours.

image.title: Rock Harbor Ranger Program
image.altText: Park Ranger answers visitor questions on Isle Royale trail.
image.caption: Guided hikes and ranger programs are intimate ways to learn about the island.

title: Explore Raspberry Island

title: Guided Cave Tours
shortDescription: Ranger-guided tours are required to enter Jewel Cave, and the various tours are offered at scheduled times, which vary by season. With four different tour options, there is something for all skill levels and interests.
seasonDescription:
Due to COVID-19, all advanced reservations for the Scenic Tours are suspended until further notice. No cave tours are available at this time.

Tours are offered year-round; however, tour availability changes seasonally. Please contact the Visitor Center for the most up to date schedule.

image.title: Ranger leading a cave tour.
image.altText: Ranger leading people down stairs during cave tour.
image.caption: Park Ranger leads a group of visitors down stairs during a cave tour at Jewel Cave.

title: Jewel Cave Ranger Programs
shortDescription: A variety of talks, demonstrations and guided nature hikes are offered on the surface. Program topics include cave exploration, wildlife, fire ecology, Jasper Fire, wildflowers and plants of the area, and other subjects. Programs are regularly scheduled from mid-June through mid-August, and may be offered throughout the rest of the year. Contact the Visitor Center for current program schedule. There are no fees for these programs.

image.altText: Ranger with antlers in front of crowd.

title: Hiking Trails
shortDescription: There are many opportunities for exploring on the surface at Jewel Cave National Monument. The 1,279 acre park is located in a Ponderosa pine forest, easily seen along the short Roof Trail. The Jasper Fire of August 24, 2000, has changed the scenery of the Monument but it is an opportunity to see first hand the forest recovery process along the Canyons Trail.
seasonDescription: Weather can vary greatly in the Black Hills. Check the weather before heading out on the trails and be prepared for storms to pop up quickly at times.

image.altText: Wooden sign to Historic Area .5 miles and Visitor Center .4 miles

title: Wildflower Viewing
shortDescription: There are 393 documented plant species at Jewel Cave National Monument. Wildflowers are commonly seen in bloom near the Visitor Center, at the Historic Area, and along all surface trails. Enjoy the flowers - look at them, smell them, compare them, sketch them, photograph them - but please do not pick or otherwise disturb them!

image.altText: Yellow flower in front of a field of pink flowers

title: Historic Area
shortDescription: The Historic Area has a picnic area, the Historic Cabin built in 1935 by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), and the Historic Entrance to Jewel Cave. While there is no access to the cave except on a guided tours, visitors are encouraged to complete the .25 mile (.4 km) walk down to see the Historic Entrance used by the Michaud brothers and park rangers to enter the cave since 1900.
seasonDescription: The parking area is only open in the summer months (June to September), but visitors are welcome to park at the Visitor Center and hike to the Historic Area from the main parking lot.

title: Wildlife Viewing
shortDescription: Jewel Cave National Monument sits in a zone between Eastern and Western wildlife species. Due to this, there is a huge variety of wildlife to be seen at Jewel Cave. Take a hike along one of the trails or explore the Historic Area for the best chance of seeing some of the amazing wildlife that calls the Black Hills home.

title: Visit the Brick Mural
shortDescription: The Tucker Theater mural at Gateway Arch National Park honors those who made the Arch possible. Created by artist Jay Tschetter, it features a 13-foot steel Arch model, construction scenes, and national landmarks. Made from 2,500 sculpted bricks, it was dedicated in 1998. The mural includes figures like Eero Saarinen, Luther Ely Smith, and others who played key roles in the Arch’s creation and legacy.

shortDescription: The Museum at the Gateway Arch covers 200 years of history about the westward expansion of the United States with an emphasis on St. Louis’ important role during that era.

And, it is well within reach.

title: Thomas Condon Overlook Trail
shortDescription: This 0.25 mi (0.4 km) long trail starts at the far end of the Thomas Condon Visitor Center parking lot and ends at an overlook of the river valley.

title: Trail of Fossils
shortDescription: The Trail of Fossils is 0.25 mi (0.4 km) long and is the best trail in the monument to see real fossils. Look for leaf imprints and pieces of wood within the boulders that have fallen from the cliffs. No collecting is allowed and please stay on trail.

image.title: Trail of Fossils leaf
image.altText: A leaf fossil in a rock
image.caption: Leaf Fossil Along Trail of Fossils

title: Story in Stone Trail
shortDescription: The mostly level Story in Stone Trail loops through dramatic pillars of blue-green claystone rocks that make up the Turtle Cove formation of John Day Fossil Beds. Before the trail intersection, the walkway is paved for 900 ft (275 m). Please stay on trail, no collecting permitted, and keep your pets leashed.

image.title: Story in Stone Trail

image.caption: Story in Stone

title: Sheep Rock Overlook Trail

image.altText: A pointed mountain with a river flowing in front through green fields

title: River Trail
shortDescription: Starting at the Cant Ranch parking lot, this 0.6 mi (1 km) long trail passes through historic fields and alongside a historic fruit orchard on its way to the John Day River. Fruit may be collected from the orchard when in season, but please do not climb the trees since the branches are old and brittle.

title: Painted Cove Trail
shortDescription: The Painted Cove Trail is 0.25 mi (0.4 km) roundtrip. The Painted Cove is an amazing color palette of vibrant rocks. A portion of this trail features a level boardwalk to cross over sensitive soils. Please stay on the designated trail.

image.title: Painted Cove Trail

title: Red Scar Knoll Trail

image.title: Red Scar Knoll

title: Painted Hills Overlook Trail

title: Leaf Hill Trail

Exhibits and fossil replicas along the trail tell the story of the fossil landscape.  Dog owners please note: There are over a dozen metal bridges on this trail. All have rough footplates that many dogs refused to cross. You may need to carry your dogs across the bridges. No collecting is allowed and off-trail hiking is strictly prohibited. Please stay on

It starts both at the Blue Basin parking lot and also connects along the Island in Time Trail. No collecting is permitted and off-trail hiking is strictly prohibited. Please stay on trail.

title: Hike Skull Rock
shortDescription: A relatively flat, 1.7-mile loop trail. Hike through the large, granite boulder fields around the Jumbo Rocks area, including one near Park Boulevard that closely resembles a Skull.
seasonDescription: The park is dangerously hot in the summer. If hiking in the summer, get to the trailhead before 10 am and always let a safety buddy know where you are going and when you plan on leaving the park. There is no cell service and no running water on the Skull Rock Trail. Always check the weather before heading into the park, and consider delaying your hike if the weather conditions are too extreme.

title: Hike Panorama Loop Trail

seasonDescription: The summer heat can be deadly. This trail is not recommended during the summer. If hiking during high heat, get to the trailhead before 9 am and always let a safety buddy know where you are going and when you plan on leaving the park. Cell service is unreliable and cannot be garaunteed. There is also no running water. Always check the weather before heading into the park, and consider delaying your hike if the weather conditions are too extreme.

title: Paddle the East Branch of the Penobscot River (From Lunksoos Boat Launch to Big Seboeis)
shortDescription: Enjoy paddling the East Branch of the Penobscot River in Katahdin Woods and Waters!
seasonDescription:
The flow of East Branch of the Penobscot River varies substantially throughout the year. For up to date information about water levels in the river please visit: East Branch Penobscot River at Grindstone, Maine - USGS Water Data for the Nation. Flow rates from the Matagamon Dam can be found from a USGS real-time streamgage.

  • At levels less than 250 CFS paddling is not recommended. 
  • 550-950 CFS is excellent flow rate for paddling.  
  • At Levels above 3000 CFS, paddling is dangerous. Be aware that there may be rapids with large, breaking diagonal waves where there is normally none.
  • Paddling upriver may not be possible at CFS levels above 3000 CFS.

title: Remote Base Camping
shortDescription: A camping trip into Lake Clark's trail-less wilderness can be a spectacular and rewarding experience. Thorough preparation and careful trip planning will help ensure you have a safe and meaningful trip. Here you will experience undeveloped wilderness, self-reliance, and solitude to an extent seldom found elsewhere.
seasonDescription:
Lake Clark National Park and Preserve has two distinct climate areas: the coast and the interior. The coast is often foggy and wet, with an average annual rainfall of 40 to 80 inches. The interior averages only 17 to 26 inches. The same weather systems that bring precipitation to the coast also bring milder winters; the interior often suffers temperatures as low as -40 degrees Fahrenheit.

Visitors to Lake Clark National Park and Preserve might bask in warm, gentle sunshine, be pummeled by fierce storms, or get soaked by rain. Weather conditions can change rapidly, and the mountainous terrain channels fierce winds. Gusts in the 30-50 mph range are not uncommon.

Frost and snow can occur any time, but are most common from September to early June. Lake Clark typically begins freezing in November and melts in April. Ice conditions dictate whether planes on floats or skis can land.

In general, visitors should be prepared to experience a number of different weather conditions during their stay in Lake Clark. Sturdy rain gear and waterproof footwear are a must, and smart travelers make sure to layer clothing.

title: Explore How Salmon Are Sustaining Southwest Alaska Communities

Lake Clark protects clean cold water within these spawning grounds. The NPS works alongside subsistence users, councils, and the State of Alaska to steward these special waters which help sustain the economy and the culture of Alaska. title: Black Canyon National Water Trail
shortDescription: In 2014, the Secretary of Interior designated this portion of the Colorado River as a National Water Trail, making it the first in the Southwest and the first to flow through a desert. Paddlers and boaters alike come to the Black Canyon to enjoy serenity and the awe-inspiring geologic formations.
seasonDescription:
Visitors can paddle or boat year-round. Fall and winter allow for cooler temperatures, but days where you can experience high winds, often making it hard to paddle. Late spring and summer bring hot temperatures, but allow you to cool off. Be aware that monsoon season bring torrential rains and can cause flash flooding.Always be prepared for changing conditions and weather.

Plan accordingly.
