title: Hike to Bumpass Hell
shortDescription: Hike the three-mile, round-trip trail to the largest hydrothermal area in the park.
seasonDescription: The trail to reach Bumpass Hell is at a high elevation and receives significant snowpack. The Bumpass Hell Trail is closed throughout spring and often into early summer due to severe snow/ice hazards. On average, it opens by Fourth of July weekend, however actual opening dates vary with each year's snowpack.

image.title: Bumpass Hell Trail
image.altText: Four young kids hiking on a trail backed by a large volcanic peak and rocky, tree-lined slopes.
image.caption: Bumpass Hell Trail is popular with hikers of all ages.

title: Sledding & Snowplay in the Southwest Area
shortDescription: The steep slopes behind the Kohm Yah-mah-nee Visitor Center are a popular destination for sledders. Lassen's deep snowfall also provides ample opportunity for snowplay. Snowman building contest, anyone?
seasonDescription: The Southwest Area usually has enough snow for snowplay between December and April. Current snow depths can be found on the current conditions webpage.

image.title: Sledding in the Southwest Area
image.altText: A landscape photo of a snow-covered hill with people playing and a building in the background.
image.caption: The steep slopes behind the visitor center are popular for sledding.

title: Snowshoe a Winter Route
shortDescription: Enjoy Lassen’s winter wonderland by snowshoe! Meander along the park highway route (snow-covered Hwy 89), circuit an icy lake, visit boiling hydrothermal features, or, for intrepid explorers, summit a snowy peak.
seasonDescription: Whenever the park has enough snow, typically December through April.

image.title: Snowshoe a Winter Route
image.altText: three people snowshoeing on a wide snow-covered route in a wooded mountain area
image.caption: When roads and trails are hidden under snow, you can still explore the park on snowshoes.

title: Ski & Snowboard at Lassen
shortDescription: Enjoy Lassen’s winter wonderland by ski or snowboard! Cross-country ski along one of the park’s numerous winter routes or, for experienced explorers, backcountry ski and snowboard one of Lassen’s mountain slopes.
seasonDescription: Whenever the park has enough snow, typically December through April.

image.title: Skiing & Snowboarding at Lassen
image.altText: a lone skier on a steep mountain slope
image.caption: Enjoy Lassen's 30 feet of annual snowfall on skis or snowboard.

title: Sledding & Snowplay in the Manzanita Lake Area
shortDescription: Sled a wintery slope, build a snowman, or otherwise enjoy Lassen's winter wonderland at the Manzanita Lake area. Got snow?
seasonDescription: The Manzanita Lake Area usually has enough snow for snowplay between December and April. Current snow depths can be found on the current conditions webpage.

image.title: Sledding & Snowplay in the ML Area
image.altText: a family preparing to sled down a snowy hill
image.caption: Manzanita Lake offers gentle hills good for young children just learning to sled.

title: Drive Lassen Volcanic National Park Highway
shortDescription: The 30-mile park highway connects the northwest (Manzanita Lake) and southwest entrances of the park. This scenic route passes through dense forest, winds around alpine lakes and meadow, crests at 8,512 feet near Lassen Peak Trailhead, and descends steep volcanic slopes into the southwest area. Designated turnouts and parking areas provide opportunities to enjoy the highway highlights.
seasonDescription: The park highway closes to through traffic at one mile from both the Northwest Entrance and Southwest Entrance in the winter and early spring seasons (approximately December through May) due to snow. Vehicles can access the Kohm Yah-mah-nee Visitor Center from the Southwest Entrance and the Loomis Plaza from the Northwest Entrance when the highway is closed for the winter/spring snow season.

image.title: Driving the Park Highway
image.altText: A black vehicle drives on a mountain road toward a large volcanic peak with large patches of snow.
image.caption: Drive the 30-mile-long, scenic highway through Lassen Volcanic National Park.

title: Fish Manzanita Lake
shortDescription: Manzanita Lake is one of the most popular fishing spots in the park and it is easily accessible. This lake holds a fair number of rainbow and brown trout and is rated as a blue-ribbon fly fishery by the state of California Department of Fish and Game.
seasonDescription: Manzanzanita Lake is frozen or snow-covered in the winter season, approximately November through May.

image.title: Fishing Manzanita Lake
image.altText: A man holds a fly fishing on a blue lake backed by conifer trees and volcanic peaks.
image.caption: Manzanita Lake is the most popular fishing lake in the park.

title: Visit Sulphur Works
shortDescription: This steamy spot is accessible via a short walk along Lassen Volcanic National Park Highway. Sulphur Works is the easiest to access of the park's seven hydrothermal areas.
seasonDescription: Sulphur Works is accessible by vehicle only in the summer and fall seasons. The park highway is closed to through traffic due to snow approximately November through April. Sulphur Works can be accessed in winter and spring via oversnow travel. Learn more about visiting Sulphur Works in the winter.

image.title: Sulphur Works
image.altText: A road lined by wooden guardrails curves through a hydrothermal area of barren, steaming ground.
image.caption: Lassen Volcanic National Park Highway cuts through Sulphur Works hydrothermal area.

title: Hike to Kings Creek Falls
shortDescription: The Kings Creek Falls trail leads to a large roaring waterfall draped in ferns and other green plants which thrive off the mist generated by the falls.
seasonDescription: The Kings Creek Trailhead is located at high elevation (7,300 feet). The park highway must be open to through traffic to reach the trailhead. The park highway closes to through traffic in the winter and early spring seasons (approximately December through May) due to snow. Snow can linger on the Kings Creek Trail well into June or July. Hikers may benefit from snowshoes, snow/ice traction devices, and/or trekking poles when snow is present.

image.title: Kings Creek Falls Overlook
image.altText: A fenced overlook above a 30-foot-high waterfall.
image.caption: Kings Creek Falls overlook provides a safe view of the 30-foot-high waterfall.

title: Fish Butte Lake
shortDescription: Fly fishing, Fishing Butte Lake
seasonDescription: The day use area is accessible in the summer months, approximately June through October.

image.title: Fish Butte Lake
image.altText: Two women fishing from a row boat on a lake backed by a lava flow and a volcanic peak.
image.caption: Two women fishing in Butte Lake in 1941.
image.credit: NPS History Collection / George A. Grant

title: Hike Lassen Peak
shortDescription: Hiking Lassen Peak
seasonDescription: Lassen Peak is covered with many feet of snow in the winter. There is also avalanche danger. It takes special equipment and training to ascend the mountain in winter.

image.title: Lassen Peak Trail
image.altText: A family hikes up a rocky a trail above a bright blue alpine lake and distance volcanic peaks.
image.caption: Lassen Peak Trail features continuous, panoramic views.

title: Hike Reflection Lake Loop
shortDescription: A short and relatively flat walk offers views of Lassen Peak and Chaos Crags volcanoes, often seen reflecting in the water. The trailhead is across the road from the Loomis Museum.
seasonDescription: Reflection Lake Trailhead is located at 5,890 feet in elevation. Snow can linger on the Reflection Lake Trail well into April. The trail is best enjoyed without snow; typically May through October.

image.title: Lassen Peak from Reflection Lake Trail
image.altText: Lassen Peak and Reflection Lake as seen from the Reflection Lake Trail
image.caption: Reflection Lake Trail Rewards with Views of Lassen Peak

title: Walk Devastated Area Interpretive Trail
shortDescription: Trailside signs on this wheelchair-accessible, 0.2-mile loop provide an introduction to the 1915-1916 Lassen Peak eruption and the resulting Devastated Area.
seasonDescription: The Devastated Area Trailhead is located at high elevation (6,400 feet). The park highway must be open to the Devastated Area to access the trailhead by vehicle. The park highway closes to through traffic in the winter and early spring seasons (approximately December through May) due to snow. This 10-mile section of highway is the first to be cleared of snow in the spring and may open to vehicles in late spring. Snow can linger on the Devastated Area Trail well into June.

image.title: Devastated Area Trail
image.altText: A girl and a woman stand next to a boulder and interpretive sign on a walkway.
image.caption: Trailside signs describe the 1915-1916 Lassen Peak eruption that created the Devastated Area.

title: Walk Lily Pond Interpretive Trail
shortDescription: A half-mile, self-led, interpretive loop explores the rich diversity of plant and animal life in the Manzanita Lake Area.
seasonDescription: Lily Pond Interpretive Trailhead is located at 5,890 feet in elevation. Snow can linger on the Lily Pond Interpretive Trail well into April. The trail is best enjoyed without snow; typically May through October.

image.title: Lily Pond
image.altText: A pond covered in green plants lined by grass and surrounded by conifers.
image.caption: Lily Pond along the Lily Pond Interpretive Trail

title: Walk Manzanita Lake Trail
shortDescription: Manzanita Lake Trail is an easy, mostly flat walk suitable for families with young children. It is not stroller-friendly. The walk offers scenic views of Lassen Peak and Chaos Crags volcanoes and birding and wildlife watching opportunities. The trail is popular for sunset viewing.
seasonDescription: The Manzanita Lake Trailhead is located at high elevation (5900 feet). The trail can be accessed year-round. Snow can be present on the Manzanita Lake Trail through April. Hikers may benefit from snowshoes, snow/ice traction devices, and/or trekking poles when snow is present.

image.title: Manzanita Lake Trail
image.altText: A looks out on a brush-lined lake backed by volcanic peaks.
image.caption: Manzanita Lake Loop affords spectacular views of Chaos Crags and Lassen Peak.

title: Visit Sulphur Works in Winter
shortDescription: Enjoy the sights and sounds of Sulphur Works hydrothermal area via a two-mile, round-trip over-snow route in the Southwest Area.

image.title: Snowshoer at Sulphur Works
image.altText: A woman on showshoes takes a photo of a large mudpot in a mountain landscape.
image.caption: Enjoy the sights, sounds, and scents of Sulphur Works.

title: Cave Tours
shortDescription: Join a ranger as you discover the complex history and intricate geology of the worlds longest cave system.
seasonDescription: Tour schedule varies by seasons. Check the current cave tour schedule of tour offerings for the dates of your visit to the park.

image.title: Broadway
image.altText: A large cave passage with a paved trail on the right side.
image.caption: Follow in the footsteps of visitors from over two hundred years of history.

title: Become a Mammoth Cave Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Do you want to explore, learn about, and protect Mammoth Cave? If so, become a Mammoth Cave Junior Ranger! The Junior Ranger activity book is appropriate for all ages and is a great way to get more in-depth knowledge about the world’s longest cave and to learn about the natural wonders of the park.

image.title: Junior Ranger Badge
image.altText: A plastic junior ranger badge sitting on a ranger hat
image.caption: You can earn your very own Mammoth Cave Junior Ranger badge.

title: Explore Wildflowers at Cedar Sink
shortDescription: Stunning rock faces, cave springs, and geological panoramas, you will experience a wide array of seasonal wildflowers and biodiversity.
seasonDescription:
There are many striking wildflowers to see throughout the warmer parts of spring, summer, and fall.  

As wildflowers bloom and give way to other wildflower species, visitors are consistently rewarded by frequent visits to cedar sink throughout the year and even throughout single seasons.

image.altText: White flowers

title: Viewing Park Wildlife
shortDescription: Mammoth Cave is home to a wide variety of plant and animal life ranging from rare exotic cave species to more common woodland creatures. While viewing wildlife can be a highlight of any park visit, it is important to remember that animals in the park are wild. Precautions must be taken to keep not only you, but the wildlife safe.

image.title: Cave Salamander
image.altText: A orange salamander with black spots.
image.caption: Cave salamanders can often be found just inside the cave entrance.

title: Attend a Ranger-led Program
shortDescription: Attending a ranger-led program in the park is a great way to discover new things and learn more about the Mammoth Cave National Park.

image.title: Transportation Talk
image.altText: A ranger talks to two park visitors near a historic train
image.caption: Attend a Transportation Talk to learn about the history of the Mammoth Cave Railroad.

title: Houchin Ferry to Brownsville
shortDescription: This short trip travels along the Green River from Houchin Ferry inside Mammoth Cave National Park to the former site of Lock and Dam #6 or the Brownsville boat ramp.

image.title: Green River at Houchin Ferry
image.altText: A river with tall trees on each bank
image.caption: Paddling along the Green River is great way to spend a quiet day in the park.

title: Nolin River Dam to Houchin Ferry
shortDescription: This trip starts at the Tailwater Recreation Area below the Nolin River Dam north of the park.

image.title: Nolin River Dam
image.altText: A view of a river valley from the top of a dam
image.caption: The Nolin River seen from the top of the Nolin River Dam.

title: Green River Ferry to Houchin Ferry
shortDescription: This longer section of the Green River is less traveled then the popular Dennison Ferry to Green River Ferry trip.

image.title: Launching a kayak
image.altText: Two people carrying a red kayak down to the river
image.caption: Canoes and kayaks can be rented from one of the area outfitters.

title: Dennison Ferry to Green River Ferry
shortDescription: This popular river trip takes paddlers from the Dennison Ferry Day Use Area to the Green River Ferry.

image.title: Child in a kayak
image.altText: A child paddling a kayak along a river
image.caption: A day on the river can be fun for the entire family.

title: River Safety and Regulations
shortDescription: Safety is your responsibility. Follow these tips for a safe and enjoyable river trip.

image.title: Canoes and PFD
image.altText: Two canoes sitting on a rack with a PDF hanging.
image.caption: Life jackets are always required to be worn when on the rivers in the park.

title: Planning Your River Trip
shortDescription: Over 30 miles of the Green and Nolin Rivers trace through the Mammoth Cave National Park and offer a wealth of recreational opportunities.

image.title: Canoes and Kayaks
image.altText: Canoes and kayaks sitting on the bank of a river.
image.caption: At low water levels, gravel bars make a great place for a lunch break during a paddle trip.

title: Explore the park on Horseback
shortDescription: Mammoth Cave National Park is an exceptional destination for anyone who loves to see the world from the back of a horse.

image.title: Two horseback riders
image.altText: Two people on horseback cross a small stream
image.caption: Exploring the parks north side trails by horseback is popular year-round.

title: See the Stars
shortDescription: Since prehistoric times, humans have looked up at the night sky and pondered the wonders of the universe. People have used the stars and planets to navigate, keep track of time, and to connect with other cultures. Regardless of your reason, Mammoth Cave National Park provides an ideal place for stargazing.

image.title: Night Sky
image.altText: A dark night sky full of stars with a tree in the foreground lit up with a red glow.
image.caption: Half the park is after dark!

title: Ride the Big Hollow Trail
shortDescription: Explore the north side of the park on your mountain bike on the only mountain bike trail in the park.

image.title: Mountain Bike
image.altText: A young woman riding down a narrow trail on a mountain bike.
image.caption: The Big Hollow Trail is the only bike trail on the parks north side.

title: Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike and Hike Trail
shortDescription: Originally opened in 1886 the Mammoth Cave Railroad brought early tourists to Mammoth Cave and other neighboring caves in the area. Today, a portion of the path of the former Mammoth Cave Railroad has been converted into a 9-mile hike and bike trail.

image.title: Hike and Bike
image.altText: A young man rides a bike alone on a gravel trail.
image.caption: Retrace the path of the Mammoth Cave Railroad on the hike and bike trail.

title: Road Biking
shortDescription: For visitors wishing to travel to Mammoth Cave National Park on two wheels instead of four, the park roadways offer miles of scenic and forested landscape to enjoy on the ride.

image.title: Road bike
image.altText: Two people with bikes resting on a bench.
image.caption: The visitor center area offers many areas to rest after a long bike ride.

title: Take a Ridge-top Walk to Sunset Point
shortDescription: Visitors to Mammoth Cave National Park Marvel over the Green River Valley while visiting the popular overlook, Sunset Point.
seasonDescription: Many visitors enjoy visiting Sunset Point during peak foliage times in the spring and fall.

image.altText: A winter view above a river valley

title: Visit Mesa Verde's Historic Administrative District
shortDescription: Take a walk amid the early park structures that comprise the Historic Administrative District of Mesa Verde National Park. Established in 1987 the historic district comprises structures with architectural designs based in strong indigenous cultural traditions and blend into their environment. The Pueblo Revival style buildings have a unique place in the development of architecture in this country.

image.title: Mesa Verde's Historic District
image.altText: Rock and timber building surrounded by yucca, brush, and trees.
image.caption: The Chapin Mesa Archeological Museum is part of the historic district.

title: Explore the Mesa Top Loop Road
shortDescription: The 6-mile (10 km) Mesa Top Loop takes you through 700 years of Ancestral Pueblo history. From remains of early pithouses and masonry villages to multi-storied cliff dwellings, the archeological sites along this loop show how early Pueblo architecture evolved. Archeology and Pueblo oral histories shed light on what life may have been like for people who lived, worked, and raised families here for generations.
seasonDescription: The Mesa Top Loop is open year-round. The road may temporarily close during winter snowstorms until the road and trails can be cleared.

image.altText: Four images that include housing styles from stone-masonry villages to wood and mud roofed shelters

title: Visit the Mississippi River Visitor Center
shortDescription: The Mississippi River Visitor Center provides fun activities for people of all ages as well as highlighting the fascinating human history of the Mississippi River. This a great place to start your exploration of this important river!

image.title: Mississippi River Visitor Center
image.altText: Lobby area with maps and desk.
image.caption: Lobby Area of the Mississippi River Visitor Center

title: Earn a Junior Ranger Badge
shortDescription: Becoming a Junior Ranger means learning more about the history, resources, and communities within the 72 mile stretch of the Mississippi National River and Recreation Area. Junior Rangers help our park rangers by learning about the park and sharing what they’ve learned with others, exploring the park, and by helping to protect its resources.

image.altText: Kids raising their hands to earn a junior ranger badge.

title: Enjoy a Coffee with a Ranger!
shortDescription: Start every Friday right with Coffee With a Ranger! Each week brings a different subject, and park ranger, exploring the wonderful world of birds, beers, mushrooms, geology and more within the park!

image.title: Coffee With a Ranger
image.altText: A collage of different park rangers talking.
image.caption: Coffee With a Ranger

title: Go on a Day Hike at Coldwater Spring
shortDescription: Enjoy a nice day hike and many opportunities for wildlife viewing, photography, and reflection at Coldwater Spring! Trails surround a restored prairie oak savannah and wetlands in this culturally and historically significant gem that is open year-round.

image.title: Coldwater Spring Prairie
image.altText: Planted prairie grasses on a summer day.
image.caption: Trail view of the prairie at Coldwater Spring

title: Kayak in the park with Paddle Share
shortDescription: Paddle the park with Paddle Share, self-serve kayak sharing system in the Twin Cities metro area that lets you rent a boat and paddle to a destination downriver!

image.title: Mississippi River Paddle Share
image.altText: Two persons in a kayak on the river.
image.caption: Kayaking the Mississippi River

title: Hunting in the MNRR
shortDescription: Hunting & trapping is permitted in Bow Creek and Goat Island Recreation Areas in accordance with site-specific regulations.

image.title: Turkey in the MNRR
image.altText: Two turkey in Ponca State Park
image.caption: Turkeys in the Missouri National Recreational River

title: Wildlife Watching in the MNRR
shortDescription: Missouri National Recreational River is a great place to go to observe mammals in their native and wild habitat. Wild animals are an important and vital part of our natural ecosystem. We humans can learn a great deal by carefully observing animals.

image.title: Two ground squirrels and a grey squirrel
image.altText: Two ground squirrels and a grey squirrel by a cottonwood tree in Riverside Park
image.caption: Two ground squirrels and a grey squirrel by a cottonwood tree in Riverside Park

shortDescription: stargaze

image.altText: Milky Way Galaxy and Stars
image.caption: Milky Way Galaxy

title: Fishing in the MNRR
shortDescription: Fishing is a main recreational activity in the Missouri National Recreational River.

image.title: Chief Standing Bear Bridge aerial image
image.altText: Aerial image of Chief Standing Bear Bridge near Niobrara State Park with sandbars and side channels.
image.caption: Missouri River has various fishing opportunities along the 39-Mile and 59-Mile stretches.

title: Backcountry Camping in the MNRR
shortDescription: Missouri National Recreational River offers primitive, Leave-No-Trace camping available at Bow Creek, Green Island, and Goat Island Recreation Areas.

image.title: Backcountry Camping
image.altText: a tent in a prairie overlooking the forest
image.caption: Experienced hikers may enjoy pitching a tent in the backcountry.

title: Paddle the MNRR
shortDescription: Paddle the two free-flowing sections of the Missouri, North America's longest river, a vestige of the untamed American West.

image.title: Kayaking and Canoeing on the River
image.altText: River ranger kayaking on the river near the Meridian Bridge on the Missouri River.
image.caption: MNRR ranger kayaking on the river.

title: Boating in the Missouri NRR
shortDescription: Whether you are fishing or enjoying the scenery and wildlife, boating is a great way to experience the river.

image.title: Boating on the Missouri
image.altText: Motor boat on the Missouri making waves with various sail boats behind it.
image.caption: Boating on the Missouri

title: Biking in the MNRR
shortDescription: Various partners have different biking paths.

image.title: Cyclist along riverfront at Missouri HW
image.altText: Cyclist biking dirt path along riverfront. Leafy trees and wetlands habitat in distance.
image.caption: Cyclist along riverfront at Missouri headwaters

title: Become a MNRR Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Do you care about exploring, learning about, and protecting the Missouri River? If yes, become a Junior Ranger! There are many ways to earn a Junior Ranger badge at Missouri National Recreational River, and this fun activity book is a great place to start. This booklet includes activities like crosswords, drawings, matching activities, maps, and more to help you learn about the Missouri River.

image.title: NPS Junior Rangers
image.altText: Four junior rangers with the vests and badges.
image.caption: National Park Service Junior Rangers

title: Watch "River of Change"
shortDescription: This 18-minute film tells the story of Missouri National Recreational River. Learn about the park's wildlife as well as the history of the river, explorers, and people who lived along the river.

image.title: River of Change
image.altText: River of Change title card with various individuals in kayaks on the Missouri River.
image.caption: River of Change

title: Tour the Mobile Ranger Station
shortDescription: The Mobile Ranger Station travels to schools, special events and programs and is often set up in various sites along the MNRR. If you're interested in its schedule contact Park Ranger Dugan Smith at 605-665-0209 Ext 28 or visit our park calendar on our webpage or the NPS app to see where it is headed next!

image.title: Mobile Ranger Station
image.altText: Mobile Ranger Station with image of Missouri River on it.
image.caption: Mobile Ranger Station

title: Walk the Historic Meridian Bridge
shortDescription: The bridge allows you to cross from South Dakota to Nebraska while offering splendid views of the Missouri National Recreational River. The bridge also connects to the City of Yankton Forest Tract with hiking trails that lead to the river. Parking is available near the intersection of Walnut and Second Street in Yankton, SD. Average visit time: 30 minutes.

image.altText: Yankton Double Decker Meridian Bridge over Missouri River. Snow on the ground and covering the bench

title: Explore the Middle Missouri with Lewis and Clark
shortDescription: Explore the Missouri River through the perspective of Lewis and Clark with these notable places within the MNRR.

image.altText: Overlooking the Missouri River containing sandbars and trees along the banks. The river bends right.

title: Visit Mulberry Bend Overlook
shortDescription: Great view of the river and sandbars from the overlooks. A paved trail takes visitors from the parking lot to several interpretive wayside exhibits that define the natural and cultural history of the river. Continue your journey by exploring a bur oak forest on the Nature Trail. Average visit time: 30 minutes. Nature Trail may take 60 minutes.

image.altText: Mulberry Bend Overlook MNRR entrance sign made on top of stone entrance stand

title: Hike the Kelso Dunes
shortDescription: Hike the Kelso Dunes
seasonDescription: Summer temperatures may be as high as 120 Degrees F. Hikers have suffered severe heat illness injuries who attempt to hike in midday summer sun. Summer hikers should consider hiking at night or complete their hike before 9 am. The distance to the highest point on the dune is further than it appears. Use caution!

image.title: Enjoy the Kelso Dunes
image.altText: Ripples and vegetation in the sand during evening light
image.caption: Mornings or early evenings are a great time to enjoy the textures

title: Hike the Rings Loop
shortDescription: The Rings Loop Trail is a popular 1.5 mile hike that takes you past beautiful scenery and ancient petroglyphs, and up a series of metal rings. This is a moderately difficult hike, and generally flat until the rings climb.
seasonDescription: Hole in the Wall sits at about 4400 feet, keeping it a little cooler than other lower areas in the Preserve. Summer days can still be too hot, so plan accordingly. Snow is possible in winter.

image.altText: Banshee Canyon, along the Rings Loop Trail

title: Visit Kelso Depot
shortDescription: Kelso Depot Visitor Center and Museum contains a wealth of information on the human and natural history of the area. Come learn about the plants, animals, and people who have called this area home at some point in history. Rangers are available to answer questions and distribute maps. There is an auditorium featuring a 20 minute film, which is a good introduction to Mojave National Preserve.
seasonDescription: Kelso Depot is Currently CLOSED as of January 2022 due to mechanical failure and repair of heating and airconditional system. Please visit Visitor Centers page for current hours and status

image.altText: Train tracks run by outside the Kelso Depot

title: Visit a Lava Tube
shortDescription: Come explore underground in a lava tube! Around 27,000 years ago, lava flowed across the surface here. As the red-hot liquid lava stream flowed, its top cooled in the air, blackening and solidifying like a freezing creek in wintertime. The liquid lava beneath continued to flow under the solid surface, which left behind this hollow tube: frozen in time.
seasonDescription: The lava tube is accessible all year, though the road can become more difficult after rain.

image.altText: A beam of light shines into the lava tube

title: Teutonia Peak trail
shortDescription: The Teutonia Peak Hike is a great way to examine the aftermath of the Dome Fire up close. The hike is three miles round-trip and takes between 2 and 3 hours for most people.
seasonDescription: This area is very hot in the summer, so plan accordingly. If you are visiting in the summer do this hike in the early morning or evening.

image.title: Patchiness along Teutonia Peak Trail
image.altText: A sandy trail. On the left, charred Joshua trees & blackened ground. On the right, live green brush
image.caption: Patches of unburned woodland along the trail show a natural "before and after" of the Dome Fire.

title: Wander Through the Joshua Trees
shortDescription: The densest concentration of Joshua trees lies along Cima Road. Although about 1/3 of the Preserve's Joshua Trees were burned during the August 2020 Dome Fire, many healthy individuals remain on Cima Road. This makes it a a wonderful spot to observe Joshua trees, icons of the Mojave Desert! Explore by car or foot. We recommend walking the Teutonia Peak trail if you want to get close to Joshua trees impacted by that fire. This area is hot during the summer, so plan ahead.
seasonDescription: The Joshua trees are beautiful all year, but if you come in late winter - early spring you may catch them in bloom.

image.altText: Joshua trees

title: Hike Desert Sand Dunes
shortDescription: Take a day hike on the Kelso Dunes! Enjoy an approximately three mile round-trip trail to the top of cream-colored dunes, formed over millennia by wind and sand. If you're lucky, you might even hear the dunes sing. This hike can be strenuous and hot. Bring water and sunscreen.
seasonDescription: Summer temperatures frequently become dangerously hot for this hike, and there is no shade. Fall - spring provide perfect days for visiting the dunes.

image.altText: Sand dunes under a cloudy blue sky

title: Behold the Granite Mountains
shortDescription: A paved pullout about seven miles north of Highway 40 on Kelbaker Road allows visitors to park their cars and enjoy the view of the Granite Mountains. There is parking for five vehicles at a time. This is a great location to catch a sunset or to have a leisurely tailgate picnic.

image.title: Granite Mountains, view from viewpoint
image.altText: The granite mountains look like tan boulders piled on top of each other. Green bushes in foreground.
image.caption: The beautiful Granite Mountains look different every time of day and every season.

title: Day Hiking at Mount Rainier National Park
shortDescription: Looking for easy and enjoyable trails that the whole family can experience together? Consider the following trails in the Longmire, Paradise, Ohanapecosh, Sunrise, and Carbon River/Mowich areas of Mount Rainier National Park. These day hikes range from short strolls to longer trails through the wilderness.
seasonDescription: Many park roads close to vehicles during the winter, limiting the ability to reach trails.

image.title: Sunrise from Sourdough Ridge Trail
image.altText: A road curves through subalpine meadows underneath a glaciated peak wrapped in clouds.
image.caption: Sourdough Ridge Trail has spectacular views of the Sunrise area and Mount Rainier.

title: Wilderness Camping at Mount Rainier National Park
shortDescription: With 97% of the park designated wilderness, backpacking and wilderness camping is one of the best ways to experience Mount Rainier National Park.
seasonDescription: For wilderness camping, summer is defined as May 15 to September 30 and when snow depth is less than two feet outside these dates. Winter is defined as when snow depth is greater than two feet (5 feet at Paradise) between the period of October 1 to May 14.

image.title: Backpacking at Sunrise
image.altText: A backpacker on a rocky trail pauses to overlook a forested valley and mountain ridges.
image.caption: A backpacker hikes along a trail in the Sunrise Area on route to a wilderness camping site.

title: Hike to Silver Falls
shortDescription: Enjoy a moderate, family-friendly loop hike through the forest to a beautiful waterfall along the Ohanapecosh River.
seasonDescription: This trail is typically hikeable from May to October. The Ohanapecosh area is not accessible by vehicle during the winter months.

image.title: Silver Falls
image.altText: A cascading waterfall flows over steep rocks
image.caption: Silver Falls, Mount Rainier National Park

title: Hike to Spray Falls
shortDescription: Enjoy a short hike from Mowich Lake to a large cascading waterfall fed by a glacier.
seasonDescription: The Mowich Lake area is generally open mid-July to mid-October, accessible via SR 165. The Mowich Lake Road is unpaved after the first three miles and may be rough.

image.title: Spray Falls
image.altText: Veil-like waterfall cascades over large cliff with small boulders in foreground
image.caption: Spray Falls

title: Hike Rampart Ridge
shortDescription: This loop trail explores the forest around Longmire, with glimpses of Mount Rainier and the Nisqually River Valley.
seasonDescription: While Longmire is open year-round, snow can make this trail hazardous in winter. Winter hikers and snowshoers must have experience with navigation.

image.title: Rampart Ridge Trail
image.altText: View of Mount Rainier from Rampart Ridge Trail
image.caption: View of Mount Rainier from Rampart Ridge Trail

title: Climbing Mount Rainier
shortDescription: Mount Rainier, the most heavily glaciated peak in the contiguous United States, offers an exciting challenge to the mountaineer. Climbers must be in excellent physical condition and well prepared. Learn more about the requirements for climbing Mount Rainier.
seasonDescription: Climbing season is typically in the spring to early summer. Check the route briefs for details on seasons for specific routes.

image.title: Climbers on Mount Rainier
image.altText: A string of climbers, darkly silhouetted against a white, glacier-covered slope, follow a boot track
image.caption: Climbers cross a glacier on Mount Rainier.

title: Camping at Mount Rainier
shortDescription: Enjoy an extended, relaxing visit to Mount Rainier in one of the park's campgrounds.
seasonDescription: The campground season generally runs from late May to early October depending on snow conditions. Check the Operating Hours of the campgrounds in between seasons to confirm open status.

image.title: Ohanapecosh Campground
image.altText: Two tents in campground surrounded by forest
image.caption: Ohanapecosh Campground

title: Cloudy Day Activities at Mount Rainier
shortDescription: Everyone loves beautiful days when Mount Rainier is visible and the skies are blue! However, sometimes the weather does not cooperate. There is still so much to appreciate on days when the clouds roll in. Enjoy this list of park ranger favorites for days when the mountain isn’t out!
seasonDescription: Certain areas are closed seasonally, while others are open year-round. Please refer to the activity descriptions or check with a park ranger for the availability of each activity at the time of your visit.

image.title: Clouds Surrounding Mount Rainier
image.altText: Clouds partly cover a glaciated mountain that rises above a meadow and forest.
image.caption: Mount Rainier emerges from the clouds, viewed from the Skyline Trail.

title: Explore Longmire in Winter
shortDescription: Make a day of it by visiting in Longmire in winter. Hike or snowshoe through the forest with views of Mount Rainier and bubbling mineral springs. Explore the Longmire Historic District and warm up with a hot meal in the National Park Inn.
seasonDescription: Longmire is open year-round, but conditions can change rapidly in winter. Be prepared for snow and ice on trails. Wear warm clothing and shoes, and bring the winter 10 essentials if planning to recreate.

image.title: Winter Recreation in Longmire
image.altText: Several people walk along a snowy road in front of a view of a snow-covered mountain and forest.
image.caption: Enjoy a walk around Longmire with views of Mount Rainier.

title: A Day In Longmire
shortDescription: Plan a day in Longmire, whether you are looking for mountain views, historic architecture, or hiking trails for all abilities.

image.title: Longmire Administration Building in Fall
image.altText: A wood and stone historic building framed by conifer trees and vine maples with red foliage.
image.caption: Explore the historic structures of Longmire year-round.

title: Visit the Valor Memorial at Longmire
shortDescription: Visit the Valor Memorial at Longmire to honor the Mount Rainier National Park Rangers who made the ultimate sacrifice.
seasonDescription: Longmire is open year-round; however, the path and viewing area at the Valor Memorial may be covered in snow during the winter.

image.title: Valor Memorial at Longmire
image.altText: Three park rangers stand next to a stone memorial made of seven basalt columns
image.caption: Park rangers visit the Valor Memorial in Longmire

title: Spring Recreation
shortDescription: Spring comes slowly to the mountain. While wildflowers bloom along city streets, the snow at Paradise may be higher than your head! Planning your spring trip to the mountain in advance is key to a safe and enjoyable visit.

image.title: Glacier Vista in Paradise Meadows
image.altText: Three hikers crossing a large patch of snow with Mount Rainier in the background.
image.caption: As late as early July hikers may have to navigate snow and ice at higher elevations.

title: Road Trip Around the Mountain
shortDescription: Even if you never step foot outside your vehicle, a drive through Mount Rainier National Park can be a rewarding experience. This road trip experience follows the historic design of the park from Nisqually Entrance to Paradise and then connects to the east side and Sunrise.
seasonDescription: Most park roads are only open during the summer, typically from late June to October. The road from Nisqually Entrance to Longmire/Paradise is open year-round.

image.title: Stevens Canyon Road
image.altText: A road curves through a forested valley next to a lake and under a mountain range.
image.caption: Stevens Canyon Road is one of the scenic routes through Mount Rainier National Park.

title: Kid-Friendly Hikes at Mount Rainier
shortDescription: Looking for kid friendly hikes to do while visiting Mount Rainier? This list should help you find the right hike for your group depending on where you are in the park.
seasonDescription: Some of the trails listed are in areas that receive large amounts of snow that lingers into July. Check in at a visitor center to learn what trails are snow free and more accessible.

image.title: Sunrise Meadows
image.altText: Subalpine meadow and trail with Mount Rainier in the background.
image.caption: The meadow along the Silver Forest Trail at Sunrise Mount Rainier

title: Mount Rainier: Off the Beaten Path
shortDescription: Mount Rainier National Park is substantial in size, but congestion still occurs during peak season and during times of nice weather. Escaping the crowds completely can be a challenge, but there are ways to still plan a rewarding visit. This guide provides alternatives to popular locations like Paradise and Sunrise. However, the secret is out! Even relatively less popular areas can still be busy.
seasonDescription: Except for Longmire, most areas are closed for the winter season. Note the general season for each area and check hours of operation before heading out.

image.title: Glacier Basin Trail
image.altText: A view from a trail of a glaciated mountain peak rising above a forested valley.
image.caption: Mount Rainier and Little Tahoma from the Glacier Basin Trail in the White River area.

title: Bicycling at Mount Rainier National Park
shortDescription: Bicycling at Mount Rainier National Park is both scenic and challenging. Bicycles are allowed on park roads but they are not permitted on any hiking trails.
seasonDescription:
Many park roads close for the winter. Closed roads may be open to non-motorized vehicles like bicycles. Always check signs on closed road gates before proceeding.

During snow plowing operations or when otherwise posted, park roads are closed to all use, including hiking, skiing, snowmobiles, and bicycling.

image.title: Bicyclists on Stevens Canyon Road
image.altText: Two bicyclists descend a steeply curving road bordered by snow banks.
image.caption: Bicyclists on Stevens Canyon Road in the spring. Always check gate signs before proceeding.

title: Try en plein air painting at Mount Rainier National Park
shortDescription: With just a little planning you can create art anywhere. Take time to really experience your favorite viewpoint by painting a picture in the park.
seasonDescription: Painting is possible year round, but winter conditions are potentially adverse and challenging.

image.title: A visitor paints in the park
image.altText: A female figure viewed from behind stands at an easel painting a picture of the tall mountains in fr
image.caption: A visitor paints the Cowlitz range from an overlook in Mount Rainier National Park.

title: Full Moon Hikes at Mount Rainier
shortDescription: Trail options and safety tips when hiking under a full moon at Longmire, Paradise, and Box Canyon at Mount Rainier National Park.
seasonDescription: Night access to Paradise is restricted during the winter, and open from spring to fall. Stevens Canyon also has limited access in winter, and is only open during the summer. Longmire is accessible all year, but can still be snowy in the winter.

image.title: Starry Sky above the Tatoosh Range
image.altText: A starry night sky above a ridge of rocky mountain peaks.
image.caption: The starry night sky above the Tatoosh Range viewed looking south from Inspiration Point.

title: Stargazing in Paradise & Stevens Canyon
shortDescription: Learn how to safely star gaze in the Paradise and Stevens Canyon Road areas of Mount Rainier National Park.
seasonDescription: The Paradise area is closed overnight during the winter. Typically, Paradise is open over night from May-November. Stevens Canyon Road is open during the summer only, typically from late May to October.

image.title: Cassiopeia & Mount Rainier
image.altText: A starry sky stretches above a large volcanic peak.
image.caption: Cassiopeia constellation above Mount Rainier viewed from Inspiration Point.

title: Paddle Sports at Mowich Lake
shortDescription: Paddle sports offer a unique opportunity to get out on the water and experience wilderness lakes that are scattered across Mount Rainier National Park. Mowich Lake is the largest lake in the park and is one of the easiest to access, though still challenging.
seasonDescription: While lakes are open year-round, access can be limited during the winter and most lakes freeze and are snow covered well into spring. Mowich Lake Road closes for the winter.

image.title: Paddle sports at Mowich

image.caption: A folding kayak and an inflatable kayak on the bank of Mowich Lake.

title: Enjoy a Winter Wonderland at Paradise
shortDescription: Winter brings into focus a frosty view of the mountain. An abundance of snow creates a winter recreation paradise, but also brings the challenges of icy, snowy roads. The road to Paradise is plowed, when possible, to allow access. Spend hours at Paradise or add a stop in Longmire to make a full day of winter fun.
seasonDescription: Paradise is open year-round when road conditions allow. Be prepared for snow and ice on trails, as well as the road. Wear warm clothing and shoes, and bring the winter 10 essentials if planning to recreate.

image.title: Sunset at Paradise
image.altText: Pink-orange sunset light illuminates a set of tracks along a snowy path and large wood building.
image.caption: There are many opportunities to explore Paradise in winter including snowshoeing and winter camping.

title: Explore Waterfalls from Longmire to Paradise
shortDescription: This tour is a great opportunity to see four of Mount Rainier's stunning waterfalls between Longmire and Paradise without taking on any long or strenuous trails.
seasonDescription: Many of the trails and viewpoints are snow covered in spring and winter.

image.title: Narada Falls
image.altText: A waterfall cascades off a cliff with a rainbow arching through the mist of the waterfall.
image.caption: Narada Falls with a rainbow. This waterfall is located on the road between Longmire and Paradise.

title: Hike to Shriner Peak Fire Lookout
shortDescription: Embark on a strenuous hike up to a historic fire lookout with adjacent backcountry camping sites and enjoy views of Mount Rainier and the surrounding valley.
seasonDescription: The road to access Shriner Peak Trailhead, SR 123, closes in the winter from the north via SR 410 at Chinook Pass to the south at the junction of SR 123 and Stevens Canyon Road.

image.altText: View of Mount Rainier from Shriner Peak Fire Lookout
image.caption: View of Mount Rainier from Shriner Peak Fire Lookout, June 24, 2023.

title: Hike to Gobblers Knob Fire Lookout
shortDescription: Hike to the historic Gobblers Knob Fire Lookout perched on a rocky outcrop above Lake George.
seasonDescription: Westside Road to the Dry Creek Trailhead is open to vehicles during the summer season only, typically May-November. During the winter, snowshoers and cross-country skiers can still use the closed road.

image.title: Gobblers Knob Fire Lookout
image.altText: View of glaciated mountain from wooden fire lookout
image.caption: View of Mount Rainier from Gobblers Knob Fire Lookout

title: Hike to Bench and Snow Lakes
shortDescription: Enjoy a short hike to picturesque Bench and Snow Lakes with views of Mount Rainier and the Tatoosh Range.
seasonDescription: The trailhead is located along Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes. Stevens Canyon Road is open to vehicles during the summer season only, typically June-September. While the trailhead is outside of the construction closure area, be sure to check the Stevens Canyon Road Rehabilitation Project page before you plan to travel on Stevens Canyon Road as sections may be closed on the weekdays during the summer.

title: Beginner's Guide to Snowshoeing
shortDescription: Mount Rainier National Park is a great place for beginner and experienced snowshoers to explore the winter landscape.
seasonDescription: Generally, the best months for snowshoeing in the park are December through March.

title: Hike to Burroughs Mountain
shortDescription: Hike the Burroughs Mountain Trail for outstanding mountain views and to visit the most accessible tundra in the Cascade Range.
seasonDescription: The Sunrise Road usually opens in late June or early July and closes in late September to early October. Due to its high elevation, the Burroughs Mountain trail can remain snow-covered after the road to Sunrise opens. Check trail conditions before hiking early in the summer season.

image.title: Burroughs Mountain Trail

title: Hike Emmons Moraine Trail
shortDescription: Enjoy a short hike from the White River Campground through the forest to a view of the Emmons Glacier and a beautiful turquoise lake colored by glacial silt.
seasonDescription: The White River area is typically open late June to late September depending on weather and road conditions.

title: Explore Tipsoo Lake
shortDescription: Interested in exploring Tipsoo Lake but don't know what to do? This list should help you find the right activity.
seasonDescription: Snow may still linger in early summer, impacting what activities at Tipsoo Lake can be done.

image.title: Tipsoo Lake

title: Hike Nisqually Vista Trail
shortDescription: The easy Nisqually Vista trail offers stunning year-round views of Mount Rainier, the Nisqually Glacier, and the Tatoosh mountain range as well as seasonal delights, such as summer wildflowers and fall foliage.
seasonDescription: Easy day hike in Summer and Fall. Marked snowshoe route in Winter to early Spring.

title: Visit the 10th Mountain Division Memorial
shortDescription: Take a short walk up the Skyline Trail to visit the 10th Mountain Division Memorial which honors the U.S. Army Troops who trained at Paradise during World War II.
seasonDescription: Paradise is open year-round but the memorial is covered by the snow in the winter.

title: Star Gazing at Sunrise
shortDescription: Come explore the parks after dark! Star gazing is a great way to end a long day of hiking and exploring the park. The Sunrise area is a perfect spot for star gazing. There are several ways to view the stars at sunrise from staying in the parking lot to hiking on trails. There is something for everyone.
seasonDescription: The Sunrise Road is open during the summer season only.

image.caption: View the night sky around Mount Rainier from Sunrise.

title: Longmire Historic District Walking Tour
shortDescription: At Mount Rainier, designers selected massive logs and glacial boulders as the building materials best suited for integrating new structures with their natural settings. This style of architecture, known as "National Park Service Rustic", can be seen throughout the Longmire District on this walking tour.

image.title: Longmire Administration Building

title: Hike and Bike Westside Road in Mount Rainier
shortDescription: Hike or bike Westside Road through a dynamic landscape that is evidence of outburst floods that closed this portion of road to public vehicle traffic. Hike the trails that lead off this road lead to meadows, views of glaciers, and historic patrol cabins.

shortDescription: Go on an adventure and try to identify the three most commonly abundant trees that surround the entire Ohanapecosh area.

title: Complete a Mount Rainier Junior Ranger Booklet
shortDescription: Complete a Junior Ranger booklet and collect a Mount Rainier Junior Ranger badge. Learn more about the plants and animals of the park and how Mount Rainier was formed.
seasonDescription: Junior Ranger booklets can be picked up from the Longmire Museum year-round. The Jackson Visitor Center at Paradise is open daily during the summer and on weekends during the winter. The Sunrise and Ohanapecosh Visitor Centers are only open during the summer season. Many of the activities and observations in the book can be done year-round.

title: A Half-Day in Paradise
shortDescription: With just 4 hours, visitors can enjoy glacier views, blooming wildflowers, and rich cultural history at the most popular subalpine meadow in the park!
seasonDescription: Paradise is open year-round but the activities described here are available during the summer season. Myrtle Falls and Nisqually Vista Trails are typically accessible mid-July to late September. Check with a ranger for up-to-date conditions.

title: Family-Friendly Paradise Activities
shortDescription: Whether you’re pushing a stroller or traveling with grandparents, Paradise offers activities the whole family can enjoy together.
seasonDescription: While Paradise remains open throughout the winter, there is often deep snow and limited services well into spring. These activites are best suited for snow-free conditions from June to October.

shortDescription: Enjoy all that the Ohanapecosh area has to offer with these four activities.

shortDescription: Photographers of all skill levels can enjoy photographing the Mount Rainier wildflowers. Follow these simple tips and tricks to optimize your photoshoot in the park.
seasonDescription: Exact flowering dates vary by year. Follow the park on social media, check the Discover Wildflowers webpage during the summer, or call a ranger station to learn what is currently blooming and where to find it.

title: A Day In Sunrise
shortDescription: If you are looking for great views of Mount Rainier, stunning wildflower meadows, interesting history, or a chance to see wildlife, look no further than Sunrise! Use this guide to help plan your day in Sunrise and explore all this part of Mount Rainier National Park has to offer.
seasonDescription: The Sunrise Road is open during the summer season only, typically from July through September.

shortDescription: If you are wondering exactly what you could do at Cougar Rock Campground aside from sleep, then we've got you covered. Here are some activities that you can do while staying at Cougar Rock Campground.

image.altText: Mount Rainier with a few clouds in the sky. Below the mountain are tall evergreen trees and a river.
image.caption: Mount Rainier viewed from a log bridge over the Nisqually River near Cougar Rock Campground.

shortDescription: Mount Rainier is famous for its wildflowers, but blooming season is short and varies with elevation. Discover the best times to visit to view wildflowers.

title: A Day In Paradise
shortDescription: The Paradise area of Mount Rainier National Park has it all—history, hiking, wildflowers, and wildlife viewing opportunities, and more! Use this guide to help you decide what to do on your day in Paradise.

image.title: Paradise at Mount Rainier
image.altText: Buildings and a road tucked against a mountain slope surrounded by green meadows.
image.caption: Paradise has it all - mountain views, wildflower meadows, history, and more!

title: Fishing at Mount Rainier National Park
shortDescription: Mount Rainier is not known for fishing, but many lakes were historically stocked with non-native fish. Anglers can play an important role in protecting native fish populations by following fishing regulations and reducing numbers of non-native fish.
seasonDescription:
• Lakes are open year-round excluding lakes closed to fishing
  • Streams and rivers in the Nisqually, Cowlitz, Puyallup, and Ohanapecosh watersheds are open from the first Saturday in June until October 31st
  • Streams and rivers in the White, Carbon, Mowich, West Fork, and Huckleberry watersheds are open from the first Saturday in June until Labor Day. The fishing season closes earlier in the year in watersheds with species listed under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) to protect them while they are spawning.

title: Stargazing Events in Southeast Utah
shortDescription: Rangers occasionally lead stargazing programs and events at parks throughout southeast Utah. Learn about what to expect and check out a schedule of stargazing events at Arches and Canyonlands national parks and Hovenweep and Natural Bridges national monuments. Even when formal programs are not offered, people are welcome to enjoy the parks after dark on their own.

image.altText: people illuminated in red gather around a telescope pointed at a starry sky

title: Hike to Sipapu Bridge
shortDescription: Sipapu Bridge’s tremendous span inspires and awes the imagination. Hike to the second largest natural bridge in the United States and, along the way, explore the geology of this fascinating region. You will fully appreciate this incredible natural feature with an adventurous canyon hike.
seasonDescription:
Spring and Fall: Suggested visiting time is spring and fall.

Summer: Summer temperatures often reach 100°F (38°C).

Winter: In the winter, the hike to Sipapu Bridge can be treacherous.
The trail may be muddy, icy, and slick. This north-facing trail is in the shade for much of the day. Snow and ice will remain on the trail longer than elsewhere in the park. A long set of metal stairs and numerous ladders can become frost-covered and slippery. This trail should only be attempted by well-prepared, experienced hikers in the winter. If snow and/or ice are present, snow cleats, crampons, and/or hiking poles are highly recommended. Always check conditions before hiking in winter.

image.altText: Sipapu natural stone bridge view from side

title: Walk to the Owachomo Bridge Viewpoint
shortDescription: This viewpoint provides sweeping vistas of the smallest, and perhaps oldest, bridge in the park. This trail is good for any time of day or season. As the final stop along the loop road, Owachomo Bridge is the perfect conclusion to your visit at Natural Bridges National Monument.
seasonDescription: All seasons – Suggested visiting time is spring and fall. Summer temperatures often reach 100°F (38°C), and the trail provides no shade. Winter snow and ice may make the paved walkway slippery. If snow and/or ice are present, snow cleats, crampons, and/or poles are recommended.

image.altText: view of Owachomo Bridge from viewpoint

title: Hike to the Horse Collar Ruin Overlook
shortDescription: Get a birds-eye view of Horse Collar Ruin from this mesa-top overlook. A short hike over slickrock provides the chance to ponder what life may have been like 700 years ago. From the overlook, see the remarkably-preserved ancestral Puebloan structures and the surrounding canyon country.
seasonDescription: All seasons – The Horse Collar Ruin Overlook Trail is open year-round, but roads may close in winter due to extreme weather conditions. Summer months get very hot, with temperatures in the 100s. Suggested visiting time is spring and fall.

image.altText: circular stone structures tucked into an alcove in the cliff-side

title: Hike to Kachina Bridge
shortDescription: Named for the petroglyphs on its side, hiking to the base of Kachina Bridge is taking a trip back in time. Gain new perspectives as you stand beneath the widest, and probably youngest, natural bridge in the park.
seasonDescription:
Spring and Fall: Suggested visiting time is spring and fall.

Summer: Summer temperatures often reach 100°F (38°C).

Winter: In winter months, this trail may be muddy, icy, and slick. The short ladder may become frost-covered and slippery, and the steep switchbacks can be difficult to traverse after snowfall. If snow and/or ice are present, snow cleats, crampons, and/or hiking poles are highly recommended. Always check conditions before hiking in winter.

image.altText: view of Kachina natural bridge from below

title: Walk to the Kachina Bridge Viewpoint
shortDescription: This trail provides aerial views of Kachina Bridge and the surrounding landscape. Desert plants abound along this winding, paved trail. Conveniently located halfway along the scenic loop drive, this paved trail is a hub for other, more rugged trails.
seasonDescription: Suggested visiting time is spring and fall. Summer temperatures often reach 100°F (38°C), and the trail provides no shade. Winter snow and ice may make the viewpoint inaccessible. If snow and/or ice are present, snow cleats, crampons, and/or poles are recommended.

image.altText: Kachina Bridge from viewpoint

title: Hike to Owachomo Bridge
shortDescription: Owachomo Bridge is the most accessible and most photographed natural bridge in the park. It's also likely the oldest natural bridge in the park. See this ancient wonder up close with a half-mile round-trip hike.
seasonDescription:
Spring and Fall: Suggested visiting time is spring and fall.

Summer: Summer temperatures often reach 100°F (38°C).

Winter: If snow and/or ice is present, snow cleats, crampons, and/or hiking poles are highly recommended. Because it is in the sun for much of the day, this trail usually clears of ice and snow fairly quickly during sunny days. Always check conditions before hiking in winter.

image.altText: Owachomo Bridge view from base

title: Walk to the Sipapu Bridge Viewpoint
shortDescription: The Sipapu Bridge Viewpoint is your first introduction to the natural bridges – and what a great place to start! This viewpoint provides scenic views of the second largest natural bridge in the United States and the largest in the park. The viewpoint is just a few minutes drive from the visitor center.
seasonDescription: All seasons – Suggested visiting time is spring and fall. Summer temperatures often reach 100°F (38°C), and the trail provides no shade. Winter snow and ice may make the viewpoint inaccessible. If snow and/or ice are present, snow cleats, crampons, and/or poles are recommended.

image.altText: Sipapu Bridge and surrounding landscape

title: Trail Run Grandview Rim Trail
shortDescription: Trail run that is 3.1 miles. This is an out and back route that is on different compositions. It is mostly a dirt path with varying degrees of hardness. In fall, when leaves are falling, be aware that the leaves can block view of any dips in the trail terrain.
seasonDescription: This trail is open year round. During the summer there is a heavy canopy of Rhododendrons to keep the air cool. Druing the Fall, there can be a large amount of leaf litter that can make running this route a bit hazardous due to divets and dips not being apparent due to the leaves obscuring the view. The winter is great, but can be prone to snow.

image.title: View from the Main Overlook at Grandview
image.altText: Colored photo looking down into the gorge at a bend in the New River
image.caption: The view from the main overlook at grandview

title: Hunting in the Park
shortDescription: Hunting is permitted in any areas designated as National Preserve. Knowing your location and rules for that area are the hunter's responsibility. There are areas where hunting is prohibited in New River Gorge National Park and Preserve, including safety zones near public areas and the 800 acre section of the park at Grandview (these are all the areas designated as New River Gorge National Park, Camp Brookside, the Arrowhead Trail Area, the Park Loop Trail Area, and Burnwood.
seasonDescription: The season for this activity is regulated by general hunting regulations of the West Virginia Department of Natural Resources.

image.title: Hunting in New River
image.altText: Two men walking in the woods wearing blaze orange hunting vests.
image.caption: Two hunters walking in New River Gorge

title: Trail run at Endless Wall
shortDescription: Endless Wall Trail is and excellent place for a trail run but due to the volume of other hikers, this trail runner would recommend that this be an early morning location. The trail is easy to moderate for elevation change and if you make a loop and run on the road to connect the two parking areas, the loop will be approximately 3.0 miles in all. There are a few must sees and that is a detour off the main trail and follow the sign for Diamond Point. The view is amazing.
seasonDescription: The Endless Wall trail provides amazing viewing overlooks into the New River Gorge and is quite lovely all year round.

image.title: Views from Endless Wall Trail
image.altText: Views of the rock face from Endless Wall Trail
image.caption: Breathtaking views of Endless Wall

title: Trail Run or hike the Little Laurel Trail
shortDescription: The 4.0 mile roundtrip trail run or hike is strenuous. The terrain is crushed rock for most of the trail, but there are a few areas that the terrain can be a bit uneven. If you start at the trailhead in the Grandview location, it will be downhill for 2.0 miles and then uphill for 2.0 miles. There will be just over 1000 foot change in elevation for this trail.
seasonDescription: The Little Laurel Trail is delightful all year round. Whether you are hoping to get in some views of the river (in the winter when the tree canopy isn't blocking your view), or to feel that cool temperature change in the heat of the summer, this trail is a favorite for many trail runners, hikers, and mountain bikers all year round.

image.title: Little Laurel Trailhead
image.altText: View of the beginning of the Little Laurel Trail from the Grandview location. The trail is wooded.
image.caption: Little Laurel Trailhead

title: Castle Rock Hike
shortDescription: Amazing hike that brings you right next to the layers of rocks that make-up the gorge. The trail is uneven and requires some scrambling over some of the rock obstacles. The steps are made up of rocks and can be super slippery when wet. This trail is not recommended if there is ice or snow due to potential slipping hazards.
seasonDescription: The Castle Rock Trail is beautiful year round. Take caution when rocks are wet or when there is snow or ice.

image.title: Amazing Castle Rock
image.altText: Combination of rocks that include Sandstone, shale, conglomerate, and coal.
image.caption: Amazing Rocks of Castle Rock Trail

title: Bicycling at New River Gorge
shortDescription: New River Gorge National River offers over fifty miles of mountain bike trails, varying from easy to difficult in terrain and distance.

image.title: Bicycling
image.altText: mother and child riding bikes on a trail
image.caption: Biking is fun for all ages

title: Stroll on the Sandstone Boardwalk
shortDescription: Stroll along the Sandstone Falls Boardwalk.
seasonDescription: The Sandstone Falls Boardwalk is open year-round and offers fantastic views of the New River.

image.title: Sandstone Falls Boardwalk
image.altText: View of the Sandstone Falls with the mountains in the background and the river surging.

title: Sandstone Falls Overlook
shortDescription: Wildlife Observation Nature Observation
seasonDescription: This overlook is accessible all year round.

image.caption: Aerial View of the Sandstone Falls from the Overlook

title: Brooks Overlook
shortDescription: Brooks Overlook is a favorite viewing spot for visitors and locals. There is a pair of Bald eagles that reside, year round, on Brooks Island and catching a glimpse of them is sure to spark delight.
seasonDescription: The views from the Brooks Overlook down to the Brooks Island below is enchanting all year long.

image.title: Brooks Overlook
image.altText: The island below is called Brooks Island. There is a pair of Bald eagles who have a nest on it.
image.caption: Can you see the nest?

title: Grandview Main Overlook
shortDescription: The Grandview Main Overlook is located about two football fields in distance from the parking area near the Grandview Visitor Center. There is a kiosk that is a triangular shaped structure with maps and information and the walking path to the Overlook begins at this location.
seasonDescription: The Grandview Main Overlook is a favorite destination for many. Photographers love the sunrise photo opportunities. Wildlife enthusiasts love to birdwatch. Many stargazers are also drawn to this location. The view is delightful year round.

image.title: Main Overlook at Grandview at sunrise
image.altText: Main Overlook at Grandview at sunrise
image.caption: Sunrise to Inspire

title: View the Overlooks at the Canyon Rim Visitor Center
shortDescription: Canyon Rim Visitor Center overlooks for the New River Gorge Bridge and the New River Gorge

image.altText: View of the deep gorge filled with clouds. A river is seen at the bottom peeking from the clouds
image.caption: View of the New River from the Gorge Overlook at the Canyon Rim Visitor Center

shortDescription: Hike the Grandview Rim Trail
