title: Climbing at New River Gorge
shortDescription: With over 1,400 established climbing routes, New River Gorge National Park and Preserve has become one of the most popular climbing locations in the country.

image.title: Climbing at New River Gorge
image.altText: rock climber maneuvering around a small overhang
image.caption: The hard sandstone cliffs of the lower gorge challenge climbers.

title: Fishing at New River Gorge
shortDescription: New River Gorge National Park and Preserve offers many outstanding opportunities for fishing in teh New River and its tributaries.

image.title: Fishing
image.altText: girl wearing life jacket and fishing in a river
image.caption: The New River and its tributaries offer outstanding opportunities for fishing.

title: Whitewater Boating
shortDescription: Whitewater rafting and kayaking is one of the more popular activities at New River Gorge. Boaters can go with an outfitter or on your own if you have the proper experience. The New River is characterised by big, powerful rapids and a boulder strewn river gorge.

image.title: Whitewater Boating
image.altText: close up of rafters in whitewater
image.caption: The New River offers exceptional whitewater boating opportunities.

title: Scenic Drive on Fayette Station Road
shortDescription: The scenic Fayette Station Road provides outstanding views of the gorge and the river while passing under the New River Gorge Bridge three times as it winds up and down the steep sides of the gorge.
seasonDescription: The road is open throughout the year, but winter can see ice and snow, making conditions dangerous. Check weather forecast before driving Fayette Station Road in winter.

image.altText: road passing under a bridge

title: Bike the Cowboy Trail
shortDescription: The Cowboy Trail is a hiking and biking trail created from the historic bed of the railroad track that passed through Valentine, NE, and the Sandhills. Many hikers and bikers covet the views of the Niobrara National Scenic River from the 148 foot historic bridge, not far from Valentine.
seasonDescription: The Cowboy Trail can be enjoyed in all seasons for a variety of activities such as hiking or walking, biking, equestrian, dog sledding, snowshoeing, and cross country skiing.

image.title: Cowboy Trail Historic Bridge
image.altText: A metal bridge with wood walkway extends across a green landscape with a river below.
image.caption: The Cowboy Trail's 0.25 mile long, 148 foot high, historic bridge crosses the Niobrara River.

title: Float the Niobrara River
shortDescription: Experience the beauty of the Niobrara National Scenic River up close and personal by floating the gentle waters through six ecosystems, past waterfalls, and under historic bridges. A gem in the Sandhills of the Great Plains.

image.title: Tube Flotilla on the Niobrara River
image.altText: a collection of 7 tubes on the river, with 13 people floating on them; they are tied together.
image.caption: Groups come to float the Niobrara where it is easy to stay together for a gently ride.

title: Shoot Winter Photography at Fort Falls
shortDescription: See the Niobrara River in the light of a winter lens. Photographers can find winter scenery, natural phenomena's, wildlife, canyons, waterfalls, and the perfect angles for those golden hour photos in many places along the Niobrara River, but Fort Falls is one of our favorites.
seasonDescription: For Winter Photography, we recommend bundling up! Wear a heavy coat, hat, gloves, boots, and thick pants. Temperatures can be as cold as -20 F, but are usually around 20 F for most of the winter; being near water makes it feel even colder out because of the humidity. Snow is normal, so boots with traction are highly recommended to keep visitors from slipping on walkways and stairs to and from the Fort Falls.

image.title: Crooked Creek
image.altText: A small creek flows through a snowy landscape.
image.caption: Leading lines bring depth to Nature Photography in Winter.

title: Hike to Fort Falls
shortDescription: This scenic 1.0 mile hike highlights the 45-foot-tall Fort Falls and the shores of the Niobrara National Scenic River on the Fort Niobrara National Wildlife Refuge. With free parking, this hike can be shortened to few the Fort Falls and the River's Banks in less than 0.25 miles.
seasonDescription: This trail can be accessed year round, but hiking in the winter on the metal walkways and stairs is hazardous. Crampons may be helpful for grip.

image.title: Fort Falls, 45 Feet Tall.
image.altText: A waterfall curves down the side of a dark canyon wall before forming a wide shallow pool below.
image.caption: The Fort Falls in summer.

title: Fishing the Noatak
shortDescription: Fishing in the Noatak National Preserve is a dream trip for many enthusiasts.

image.title: Fishing the Noatak Preserve
image.altText: Man standing with fishing pole on tundra, water in the background
image.caption: Fishing the Noatak National Preserve should be on the bucket list of fishing fanatics

title: Visit the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center
shortDescription: Trying to figure out where to go and what to do in Northwest Alaska? The Northwest Arctic Heritage Center is a great place to meet rangers and acquire information on Cape Krusenstern National Monument, Kobuk Valley National Park, and Noatak National Preserve.

image.altText: A sample of exhibits at the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center including Dall Sheep and caribou.

title: Float the Noatak
shortDescription: A float trip by canoe on the Noatak River

image.altText: Two grizzly bears sitting on a gravel bar along the Noatak River with mountains in the background.

title: Day Hiking in North Cascades
shortDescription: Hike the North Cascades to experience some of the finest mountain country in North America.
seasonDescription: The park's winters are wet, and snowfall is heavy. Access is often limited during these winter months by impassable or closed roads, so be sure to check current conditions.

image.title: Hiking in the North Cascades
image.altText: Two hikers walk along a trail with mountains in the distance.
image.caption: Hiking in the North Cascades

title: Plan a Backcountry Trip
shortDescription: Backcountry camping in the North Cascades can be an exciting adventure for prepared hikers.
seasonDescription: Low elevation trails are most visited between April and October, with the driest weather from mid-June to September. Visitation to the highcountry (above 5,000 feet/ 1524 m) is greatest after the snows melt, generally from July through early October. The best snow mountaineering conditions are often June and July. The park is open year round, but heavy winter precipitation limits road access and increases backcountry hazards between November and March.

image.title: Backpacking
image.altText: Three backpackers hike through a meadow with mountains in the distance.
image.caption: Backpacking in North Cascades

title: Fishing in the North Cascades
shortDescription: Fishing is popular in many lakes and rivers of the North Cascades.

image.title: Fishing from Colonial Creek
image.altText: Two men sit fishing in chairs on a wooden pier
image.caption: Fishing on Diablo Lake from Colonial Creek Campground

title: Paddling in the North Cascades
shortDescription: Kayaking, canoeing, and paddleboarding are popular on the lakes of the North Cascades.

image.title: Canoes at Colonial Creek
image.altText: Two silver canoes loaded with camping gear sit on the shore of a lake.
image.caption: Canoes at Colonial Creek Campground

title: Motorboating in the North Cascades
shortDescription: Motorboating is a popular activity on Gorge, Diablo, and Ross lakes, and Lake Chelan.

image.title: Boat Dock at Stehekin
image.altText: Motorboats are docked on a large lake with mountains in the background
image.caption: The main dock in Stehekin, on Lake Chelan.

title: Rafting in the North Cascades
shortDescription: The Skagit and Stehekin rivers attract many whitewater enthusiasts for rafting and kayaking, especially during the summer months.
seasonDescription: Spring runoff can make for dangerous high water in some areas. Always check the weather forecast before boating.

image.title: Rafting the Skagit River
image.altText: A group paddle a raft on a wide river.
image.caption: Rafting on the Skagit River

title: Tuafanua Trail
shortDescription: Moderate = 2.2mi/3.54km total; 219ft/67m elevation gain; 2-3 hours. The trail leads you via ladders, steps, and ropes to a rocky beach, where you can enjoy the sound of the waves and take in the Western view of Pola Island.

image.title: Tuafanua Trail
image.altText: Outdoors; landscape view of sandy beach foreground, blue waters, and steep cliffs in background.
image.caption: Enjoy the stunning view of Pola Island from a different angle.

title: Mount Alava Trail
shortDescription: Difficult = 7mi/11.27km total; 1,607ft/490m elevation gain; 4-5 hours. Trail can be steep, slippery, and rocky in places. Stunning panoramic views from the summit. Lush rainforest environment, great for bird and fruit bat watching.

image.title: Mount Alava Trail
image.altText: Outdoors; person holding binoculars looking out through greenery at blue waters in the distance.
image.caption: Well worth a strenuous hike for a stunning view.

title: Lower Sauma Ridge Trail
shortDescription: Easy = 0.4mi/0.64km total; 232ft/7m elevation gain; 30-45 minutes. A gentle climb to an archaeological site featuring ancient grinding stones, this trail combines history with incredible views of the northeast coastline and the Vai’ava Strait.

image.title: Lower Sa'uma Trail
image.altText: A row of men seen from behind hiking a narrow trail downward on low stone steps surrounded by trees.
image.caption: Hikers on Lower Sa'uma Trail.

title: Pola Island Trail
shortDescription: Easy = 0.1mi/0.16km total; 30ft/9m elevation gain; 15-30 minutes. This short, easy trail leads you to the untouched shores of the South Pacific; delivering big rewards with views of the rugged coastline and Pola Island, a sanctuary for nesting seabirds.

image.title: Pola Island Trail
image.altText: Outdoors; group of young adults facing an adult standing next to sign, trail and forest behind.
image.caption: Enjoy one of the easiest strolls on the island.

title: Upper Sauma Ridge Trail
shortDescription: Strenuous = 3.2mi/5.15km total; 1,489ft/454m elevation gain; 3-4 hours. Hike a challenging trail through a dense rainforest, surrounded by native trees and birds. Enjoy one of the island’s most beautiful views of Vatia village and Pola Island at the summit.

image.title: Upper Sauma View
image.altText: Outdoors; view of water below, mountains behind, framed with lush greenery.
image.caption: The hike is worth it when you get views like this.

title: Fruit Bat Watching
shortDescription: Fruit bats are the only native mammals found in American Samoa. The two species of fruit bat and one insect-eating bat species are harmless to people. They have a wingspan close to three feet. As fruit eaters, fruit bats are excellent and vital pollinators. Plants rely on the fruit bat to spread its seeds through droppings. A colony of fruit bats ensures that the tropical rainforest remains healthy and full of new trees.

image.title: Fruit bats flying over a tree.
image.altText: A fruit bat flies over a tree with other fruit bats in its branches, against a blue sky.
image.caption: A fruit bat flies over a tree with other fruit bats in its branches.

title: Snorkeling
shortDescription: Each island of American Samoa supports a coral reef ecosystem in its coastal waters. These coral reefs support a variety of marine life typical of tropical Indo-Pacific waters. To date, over 950 species of fish and over 250 species of coral have been documented.

image.title: Snorkeling in Vatia Village.
image.altText: A snorkeler floats near the top of the image at the water's surface, with coral in the foreground.
image.caption: A snorkeler floats over coral.

title: Take a boat ride to Aunu'u
shortDescription: About one mile southeast of Tutuila’s eastern tip is the volcanic island of ‘Aunu’u, the smallest inhabited island. It can be reached by boat and explored by foot. 'Aunu'u Island is an excellent exposure of a relatively young flow of basalt inter-bedded with layers of tuff. The site also illustrates erosion by wave action and is covered with dense tropical vegetation.

image.title: Take a boat ride to Aunu'u.
image.altText: A red and silver boat with a blue canopy sits in shallow waters between a beach and a lush island.
image.caption: Take a boat ride to Aunu'u and see the island.

title: Birdwatching on Lower Sauma Trail
shortDescription: Over 35 species of native birds fly in American Samoa’s skies. Each has its own story and place in our culture.

image.title: Birdwatch on the Lower Sauma trail.
image.altText: A yellow bird with red markings on its head, upper wing, and chest sits on a leafy green branch.
image.caption: Checkout a variety of birds on the Lower Sauma trail.

title: Walk the Moments in Time Trail
shortDescription: Take a peaceful stroll at Barnes Point on Lake Crescent on the Moments in Time Trail.

image.title: Moments in Time Trail
image.altText: A trail leads through an old growth forest surrounded by ferns.
image.caption: Take an easy stroll through an old-growth forest on the Moments in Time Trail.

title: Hurricane Ridge Shuttle
shortDescription: Skip the stress and help the environment by taking a Clallam Transit bus to Hurricane Ridge! This summer season bus transports park visitors directly from downtown Port Angeles, Washington, to one of Olympic National Park's most scenic destinations.
seasonDescription: The Clallam Transit bus to Hurricane Ridge is only available in the summer season.

image.title: Hurricane Ridge
image.altText: A view of Hurricane Ridge with the Olympic Mountains in the distance.
image.caption: View the Olympic Mountains and surrounding subalpine ecosystems at Hurricane Ridge.

title: Watch for Salmon at Salmon Cascades
shortDescription: In the late summer and early fall, salmon can be seen leaping from Salmon Cascades on the Sol Duc River! Get a glimpse on a viewing platform located above the cascades.

image.title: Salmon Cascades
image.altText: A salmon jumping up a waterfall.
image.caption: Watch for salmon leaping up the Sol Duc River at Salmon Cascades.

title: Observe Animals at Olympic National Park
shortDescription: In the park, we humans are privileged to be visitors to wild animals' home. We can treat their home with respect and care.

image.title: Deer buck sunset Hurricane Hill
image.altText: A deer with antlers in velvet grazes on a mountain hillside, backlit by sunset.
image.caption: A Columbia Blacktail Deer grazes on Hurricane Hill at sunset.

title: Take a Short Hike Near the Visitor Center
shortDescription: Near the Olympic National Park Visitor Center, two short loop hikes take visitors through peaceful, green lowland forests.

image.title: Peabody Creek Trailhead
image.altText: A trailhead with a sign that reads "Peabody Creek Trail."
image.caption: The Peabody Creek Trail begins at the Olympic National Park Visitor Center parking lot.

title: See Madison Falls
shortDescription: Madison Falls is a stunning 60-foot waterfall near the Elwha River. It's also one of the most accessible destinations at the park, making it a great stop for families and visitors of all abilities.

image.title: Madison Falls
image.altText: A waterfall rushes over mossy rocks to a pond below.
image.caption: Madison Falls is at the end of one of the park's most accessible trails.

title: Backpack in Olympic National Park
shortDescription: While this app is a great tool for "front country" visits (places you can get to with a car, bike, or short hike), it's not meant to guide you through the back country. For that we have the Wilderness Information Center - WIC for short. The WIC rangers can talk through routes, gear, and trail conditions with you, and set you up with a permit.

image.title: Dosewallips 01
image.altText: A rushing river tumbles over boulders.
image.caption: The Dosewallips River

title: Go to the Beach
shortDescription: A trip to the Olympic Coast is sure to be memorable! Olympic National Park contains several beach areas along the coast, each with something to offer. Learn more about popular beaches and start planning your trip!
seasonDescription: Olympic National Park's beaches are at their best in the summer, but a trip in the fall, winter and spring can be exciting, too! If you visit in winter, be prepared for stormy weather and unpredictable waves.

image.title: Rialto Beach
image.altText: A person walks along a rocky beach.
image.caption: Experience the majestic Pacific Coast at beaches like Rialto Beach, pictured here.

title: Take a Pet-Friendly Hike
shortDescription: Pets: they’re our faithful friends and loyal companions. But at Olympic National Park, they aren’t allowed everywhere! You can still have a great time at Olympic with pets, but be sure to read carefully and follow the rules so you know what to do and where to go.

image.title: BARK Ranger at Olympic National Park
image.altText: A black and white dog poses with a ranger hat.
image.caption: Bringing pets to Olympic National Park can be lots of fun - just be sure to follow the BARK rules!

title: Play in the Snow in the Olympic Mountains
shortDescription: Hurricane Ridge provides opportunities for snowshoeing, cross-country and downhill skiing, snowboarding, tubing and more. Hurricane Ridge's winter season is generally mid-December through the end of March.

image.title: Skiers at Hurricane Ridge
image.altText: Skiers on a rope tow on a snowy slope.
image.caption: Winter fun at Hurricane Ridge.

title: Tidepooling on the Olympic Coast
shortDescription: There are special places that allow you to see sea creatures up close without leaving the beach! Tidepools are home to fascinating creatures like sea stars, anemones, barnacles, nudibranchs, crabs, and more.
seasonDescription: Summer generally has the lowest low tides, exposing more of the tidepools.

image.title: Ruby Beach tidepools
image.altText: A rocky beach shore
image.caption: Tidepools at Ruby Beach

title: Hike the Historic Old County Road!
shortDescription: Enjoy scenic views along an 8-mile one-way hike as you explore a historic wagon road through the Sonoran Desert!

image.title: Old Country Road
image.altText: A dirt road meanders past organ pipe and saguaro cacti towards a small mountain.
image.caption: Enjoy the quiet wilderness as you hike a historic wagon road.

title: Hike the Estes Canyon/Bull Pasture Loop
shortDescription: The moderate Estes Canyon trail provides ample wildlife and wildflower viewing opportunities while a steep, strenuous climb up the Bull Pasture spur trail will reward visitors with spectacular views of the Sonoran Desert.
seasonDescription: While the Estes Canyon/Bull Pasture can be experienced all year round, please be aware that summer and fall temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit. Please plan your activities accordingly and practice desert safety.

image.title: Hiking Bull Pasture
image.altText: Female visitor hikes on desert trail, surrounded by
image.caption: The 800 foot climb to Bull Pasture rewards visitors with some of the best views in the monument.

title: Hike the Senita Basin Loop
shortDescription: Easy loop trail located in a low elevation area on the south side of the Puerto Blanco Mountains. This lush basin is one of the few places you can see all three of the park’s columnar cacti coexisting: saguaro, organ pipes, and the senita cacti. The most impressive groves of senita cacti are along the road into Senita Basin and near the trailhead.
seasonDescription: While the Senita Basin Loop trail can be experienced all year round, please be aware that summer and fall temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit. Please plan your activities accordingly and practice desert safety.

image.title: Senita Cacti
image.altText: Large senita cacti growing in Senita Basin, part of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.
image.caption: Some of the best examples of senita cacti are located along the road leading into Senita Basin.

title: Drive the Ajo Mountain Loop
shortDescription: The Ajo Mountain Drive is a 21-mile (34 km) graded, one-way dirt road that gives visitors an excellent overview of the landscape and flora or Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. The drive takes approximately 2 hours, and has been designed so that a passenger car, driven with caution, may be taken over it safely. Trailers, buses and RVs over 25 ft (8 m) are prohibited on the drive. Several hikes and backcountry camping can be accessed from this drive.
seasonDescription: While Ajo Mountain Drive can be experienced all year round, please be aware that in the summer temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit and plan your activities accordingly.

image.title: Boulder Canyon along Ajo Mountain Drive
image.altText: A rocky canyon filled with boulders and bright green Sonoran desert vegetation
image.caption: This scenic loop takes you up into the surprisingly lush, green canyons of the Ajo Mountains.

title: Hike to Lost Cabin
shortDescription: Looking for a lengthier hike that showcases Organ Pipe’s mining history? This 8 mile (12.9 kilometers) round-trip hike includes the Victoria Mine site and an old stone mining house known as Lost Cabin.
seasonDescription: While Lost Cabin trail can be experienced all year round, please be aware that summer and fall temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit. Please plan your activities accordingly and practice desert safety.

image.title: Lost Cabin
image.altText: The corner of a historic, dilapidated stone building, constructed of local granite.
image.caption: Lost Cabin, like most of the structures in the park, was constructed using stone found locally.

title: Hike to Victoria Mine
shortDescription: Experience Organ Pipe’s mining history by hiking to Victoria Mine, one of the oldest prospecting sites in southwest Arizona and the heart of gold and silver mining in the Organ Pipe area.
seasonDescription: While this trail can be experienced all year round, please be aware that summer and fall temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit. Please plan your activities accordingly and practice desert safety.

image.title: Victoria Mine Store
image.altText: Historic one-room building made with stone walls and no roof, located in a desert.
image.caption: Miners could find food and other essentials at the Victoria Mine store.

title: Unearth Dripping Springs Mine
shortDescription: Stumble upon an old copper mine while exploring along the trail in the Puerto Blanco Mountains!

image.title: Dripping Springs Mine
image.altText: The landscape around the mine features a tall saguaro forest and large purplish mountains.
image.caption: Enjoy beautiful mountain scenery as you wind your way to Dripping Springs Mine.

title: Hike Alamo Canyon
shortDescription: The Alamo Canyon Trail follows an old road to a historic ranch house and corral, and provides ample wildlife and wildflower viewing opportunities.

image.title: Alamo Canyon
image.altText: Desert trail leading towards red colored canyon. Saguaros grow next to the trail.
image.caption: The Alamo Canyon trail leads to a historic ranch once run by Birdie and Bill Miller.

title: Hike Arch Canyon
shortDescription: One of the most photographed sites along the Ajo Mountain Drive are the double arches carved into the mountains. Walking the easy, relatively flat Arch Canyon trail provides wonderful opportunities to see wildflowers and gaze upon the rhyolite arches.

image.title: Double Arches and Moonrise
image.altText: Two natural arches, stacked on top of each other, with the moon peeking out from behind.
image.caption: Moonrise over the double arches

title: Walk Your Pet along Palo Verde Trail
shortDescription: Easy, pet-friendly trail that connect the Kris Eggle Visitor Center to Twin Peak Campground. Provides beautiful views of the Ajo Mountains.
seasonDescription: While Palo Verde Trail can be experienced all year round, please be aware that summer and fall temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit. Please plan your activities accordingly and practice desert safety.

image.title: Palo Verde Trail Sign
image.altText: Brown trailhead sign reading "Palo Verde Trail, Campground 1.3 miles" with pet-friendly icon.
image.caption: Palo Verde trail is one of three pet-friendly trails in the monument.

title: Watch the Sunset from Desert View Trail
shortDescription: Searching for that quintessential desert sunset? The Desert View trail has your back! This short, 1.2 mile (1.9 km) can be reached from Twin Peaks Campground and loops around striking stands of organ pipe cacti. The Desert View trail offers great views for sunrise or sunset.
seasonDescription: While Desert View trail can be experienced all year round, please be aware that summer and fall temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit. Please plan your activities accordingly and practice desert safety.

image.title: Desert View at Sunset
image.altText: Hiker with backpack and camera stares out at mountains in the distance on a desert trail at sunset.
image.caption: A small hill along the trail provides colorful sunset views of the monument and Mexico.

title: See Endangered Pupfish Along the Visitor Center Nature Trail
shortDescription: Next to the Kris Eggle Visitor Center is a 1/10th of a mile paved nature trail that loops by a small pond and showcases native Sonoran Desert plant life. The trail begins by the back door of the visitor center and loops back around to the parking lot.

image.title: Visitors at Visitor Center Pond

title: Birding at Organ Pipe
shortDescription: Organ Pipe sits along a primary migratory flyway, creating an oasis for bird enthusiasts of all levels. In addition to hosting an exciting array of migratory birds during fall and spring, we also have 36 species of resident birds that can be found year round at Organ Pipe.
seasonDescription: While birding can be enjoyed year round at Organ Pipe, fall and spring are the best time to see migrating birds like warblers, orioles and the occasional waterfowl.

title: Drive the North Puerto Blanco Loop
shortDescription: For those looking for a longer, more rugged scenic drive through Organ Pipe, Puerto Blanco Drive is a great way to experience some of the park’s volcanic geology, mining history, and natural springs. The 41 mile Puerto Blanco Loop is broken into two parts: North Puerto Blanco Drive and South Puerto Blanco Drive.

image.title: Entrance to North Puerto Blanco Drive
image.altText: Dirt road leading into the desert. At the entrance is a gate and sign about border activity.
image.caption: Beyond Pinkley Peak, North Puerto Blanco Drive is a high clearance vehicle road.

title: Drive South Puerto Blanco Road
shortDescription: South Puerto Blanco Drive is a two-way, graded dirt road that follows the southern boundary of the park and provides access to Senita Basin and Quitobaquito Springs. Great examples of organ pipe, senita, and saguaro cacti are visible along this route. This road can be washboarded – reduce your speed and allow extra time. These roads are doable in a normal passenger car. Trailers, buses, and motorhomes over 25 feet (8 meters) are prohibited on the drive.
seasonDescription: While South Puerto Blanco Drive can be experienced all year round, please be aware that in the summer temperatures can reach upwards of 110 degrees Fahrenheit and plan your activities accordingly.

title: Round Spring Guided Cave Tour
shortDescription: Discover the amazing world beneath your feet! Round Spring Cave is considered the most spectacular cave within Ozark National Scenic Riverways. Large, varied formations fill over a mile of the passage, which has been well-preserved over the years. There is no better way to learn about Ozark caves than through a tour!
seasonDescription: Round Spring Cave Tours are currently suspended for the 2025 season. The bridge to the cave was destroyed by a flood. A replacement is scheduled for installation in July. The cave will remain closed until further notice.

title: Fly Fishing Clinics
shortDescription: Join a local fly-fishing legend and learn the art of this gentle sport in a free workshop! Clinics are currently offered for youth and parents. All skills levels are welcome; call (573) 858-3297 for details and reservations. Park Ranger Mark Van Patten will lead the course. Demonstrations cover various fly rod casting methods, proper catch and release techniques, and strategies for fly presentation. Other lessons will discuss equipment, flies, and entomology.

title: Hike the Chimney Rock Trail

seasonDescription:
Winter

The heaviest rainfall occurs in the winter months. Come prepared for rain and drizzle to possibly last for several days. In between winter rains, it is often sunny, calm, and cool.

Spring

Most spring days are windy and Chimney Rock frequently experiences strong breezes. Expect cool temperatures in March. By late May and early June, temperatures can be quite pleasant, even warm.

Summer

Although there is very little rain during summer months, there is often dense fog throughout the day in July, August and September with temperatures often 20 degrees cooler than at Bear Valley.

Fall

The coastal areas of Point Reyes experience some of the clearest days in late September, October and early November. The occasional storm will start rolling through in late October, bringing clouds, wind, and rain. The strongest winds occur in November and December during occasional southerly gales.

title: Hike to Secret Beach and Skylight Cave
shortDescription: Skylight Cave is a sea cave with a collapsed ceiling at the north end of Secret Beach, which is located within the Phillip Burton Wilderness along the eastern shore of Drakes Bay. Even though Skylight Cave is only 2.5 miles (3.8 km) from the closest parking lot at Limantour Beach, it is usually only safe to visit at tides that measure -1 (negative one) foot or lower. The best thing you can do to guarantee a safe, fun visit to Secret Beach and Skylight Cave is to be prepared!
seasonDescription:

Fall

Duxbury Reef near Agate Beach County Park in Bolinas, outside of park boundaries, is another good place to tidepool.

title: Tule Elk Viewing At Point Reyes National Seashore
shortDescription: Locations and suggestions for spotting the herds of tule elk that call Point Reyes home.
seasonDescription:
While tule elk are active year-round, August through October is an exciting time of year in Point Reyes, as it is the rut season for the tule elk (otherwise known as mating or breeding season)! Visitors will likely hear bull elk bugling and may even get to see a couple of bull elk sparring with each other. Take extra caution when visiting during this time and be aware of your surroundings. Do not come between two bull elk, or between a bull and a group of cows (female elk). Please be extra mindful of cows with calves at any time of the year.

seasonDescription: While Rainbow Bridge National Monument is open all year, it is most heavily visited in the summer months. Despite the lack of shade and 100+ degree temps, visiting Rainbow Bridge in the summer is easiest because boat travel is easiest then.

title: Enjoy a Scenic Drive on Old Fall River Road
shortDescription: Built between 1913 and 1920, a drive up Old Fall River Road is an incredible 9.4-mile scenic drive. At Alpine Visitor Center, use Trail Ridge Road to return to the east side of RMNP.
seasonDescription: Old Fall River Road is a seasonal road that is open typically from early July through early to mid-October. During the winter, the road is closed to vehicles. Weather can change quickly in the Rocky Mountains. Temporary closures can go into effect at any time.

title: Enjoy a Scenic Drive on Trail Ridge Road
shortDescription: Enjoy a scenic drive across Trail Ridge Road in Rocky Mountain National Park. Trail Ridge Road is 48-miles one-way and connects the towns of Grand Lake and Estes Park during the summer season.
seasonDescription:
Trail Ridge Road is the highest continuous paved road in the United States, climbs to 12,183 feet and connects the towns of Estes Park and Grand Lake.

Because weather conditions may change rapidly at higher elevations, park visitors should be prepared to adjust travel plans accordingly at any time. For updates, call the park’s Trail Ridge Road recorded status phone line at 970-586-1222. Park staff will update the recorded line when/if the road status changes.

image.caption: Mishe Mokwa Trail

title: Solstice Canyon Trail
shortDescription: Travel through a beautiful, shaded riparian environment on the Solstice Canyon Trail alongside a year-round creek.

image.title: Sunset View from Solstice Canyon
image.altText: Pink sunset over the ocean from a view within Solstice Canyon.
image.caption: Pink sunset over the ocean from a view within Solstice Canyon.

title: Satwiwa Loop Trail
shortDescription: This area was set aside for the preservation and celebration of Native American cultures.

image.title: Boney Mountain
image.altText: Boney Mountain at sunset with rock and cactus in foreground.
image.caption: Boney Mountain at sunset with rock and cactus in foreground.

title: Viewing the William Henry Jackson Collection
shortDescription: A selection of the Scotts Bluff National Monument collection of the works of William Henry Jackson is displayed in the monument visitor center.

image.altText: A sketch of a wagon train moving through a narrow, rugged pass.

title: Drive the Scotts Bluff Summit Road
shortDescription: A 1.6 mile drive from the Scotts Bluff Visitor Center Parking Lot to the summit of Scotts Bluff. This drive features scenic views and interesting geology. Vehicles longer than 25 feet (7.6 meters) and/or higher than 11 feet 7 inches (3.53 meters) are prohibited. All trailers are prohibited.
seasonDescription: The Summit Road is open year-round. However, it may close due to rockfall or adverse weather conditions.

image.altText: A car approaches a tunnel on a steep, winding road.

title: Scotts Bluff Ranger Programs
shortDescription: Learn more about Scotts Bluff National Monument by attending a ranger-guided program!
seasonDescription: The primary season for ranger programming is the summer. Programs may be offered periodically at other times of the year. See the monument calendar for a listing of upcoming programs and events.

image.title: Costumed Interpretation at the Wagon
image.altText: Two rangers, dressed as emigrants on the Oregon Trail, talk with a visitor next to a covered wagon.
image.caption: Join a park ranger to learn more about the natural and cultural history of Scotts Bluff!

title: Backcountry Hiking South Bluff
shortDescription: Backcountry hiking on South Bluff is difficult and should only be attempted by experienced hikers. Please check in with the ranger at the visitor center.
seasonDescription: South Bluff may be hiked at any time of the year. However, spring and fall tend to offer the most comfortable hiking conditions.

image.title: Sentinel Rock on South Bluff
image.altText: A sandstone bluff is dusted with snow.
image.caption: South Bluff is a wonderful place for experienced hikers to explore.

title: Stamp Your Passport Book
shortDescription: Stamp your "Passport to Your National Parks" book in the Scotts Bluff National Monument Visitor Center!
seasonDescription: Visitor Center hours vary by season.

image.title: Scotts Bluff Passport Stamps
image.altText: Five rubber stampers rest on a black shelf labeled "Passport Cancellation Station."
image.caption: There are five passport stamp cancellations available at Scotts Bluff National Monument.

title: Become a Scotts Bluff Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Earn your Scotts Bluff National Monument Junior Ranger badge!

image.title: Junior Rangers take the Pledge
image.altText: Five junior rangers raise their right hands and take the Junior Ranger Pledge with a NPS Ranger.
image.caption: The Scotts Bluff Junior Ranger program is fun for all ages!

title: Hiking Scotts Bluff National Monument
shortDescription: There are nearly four miles of hiking trails at Scotts Bluff National Monument. There is a trail for every ability.
seasonDescription: Ice and snow can make hiking trails in winter treacherous, particularly north-facing portions of the Saddle Rock Trail.

image.altText: Two hikers walk towards an interesting rock formation.

title: Scotts Bluff Cell Phone Audio Tour
shortDescription: The Scotts Bluff National Monument Cell Phone Audio Tour is a great way to learn more about the natural and cultural history of this famous landmark on the Oregon and California Trails.
seasonDescription: The Cell Phone Audio Tour can be accessed at any time. If you plan on hiking the monument trails to the stops on the tour, please be aware that weather conditions or rock fall may close portions of the trail or render them difficult to traverse.

image.title: Cell Phone Tour
image.altText: A woman stands on a paved trail with a cellular phone to her ear and a view of sandstone bluffs.
image.caption: The Scotts Bluff cell phone tour is a fun way to learn more about the history of this landmark.

title: Enjoy a Picnic at Scotts Bluff
shortDescription: Enjoy a picnic at Scotts Bluff National Monument

image.title: Picnic at the Shelter
image.altText: Two ladies enjoy a picnic at a picnic shelter.
image.caption: Enjoy eating outdoors at the Scotts Bluff picnic area.

title: Bicycling at Scotts Bluff National Monument
shortDescription: Bicycling can be a great way to experience Scotts Bluff National Monument. There are two locations in the monument where bicycling is permitted: the Prairie View Trail, and the Summit Road when it is closed to vehicular traffic.
seasonDescription: Bicycling is permitted in Scotts Bluff National Monument year-round. However, temperatures and wind conditions are most favorable for cycling in late spring through early fall.

image.title: Scott's Bluff
image.altText: A pair of bicyclists are seen riding towards a distinctive sandstone rock formation.
image.caption: Scotts Bluff National Monument

title: Saddle Rock Trail Geology Hiking Tour
shortDescription: This 1.6 mile hike on the Saddle Rock Trail features 435 feet of elevation change. Participants will have an opportunity to observe and learn about some unique geological features and the processes that created the landscape of Scotts Bluff National Monument.
seasonDescription: The Saddle Rock Trail is open year-round. However, snow and ice may make sections of the trail slippery and dangerous.

image.title: Inspecting Knobby Concretions
image.altText: A park ranger takes a close look at concretions of limestone embedded in sandstone.
image.caption: Learn more about the geological processes that shaped Scotts Bluff.

title: Paradise Creek
shortDescription: Explore Paradise Canyon in the Foothills of Sequoia National Park. This gentle trail parallels Paradise Creek, taking you past waterfalls and pools.
seasonDescription: The Foothills area can get hot in the summer and air quality can be poor. If you're hiking during the summer, we recommend that you hike early in the morning or late in the day.

title: Wolverton Winter Trail
shortDescription: This short trail connects the Old Lodgepole Road with the Wolverton Parking area. This steep hillside route requires considerable control for downhill travel when skiing away from Wolverton.

image.title: Wolverton Winter Trail
image.altText: A group of visitors walking down a snowy trail.
image.caption: This steep hillside route requires considerable control for downhill travel.

title: Visit the Foothills Visitor Center
shortDescription: This visitor center is one mile past the Ash Mountain entrance station along the Generals Highway. Stop here for information, maps, books, gifts, and restrooms. Browse exhibits about the ecology and human history of the foothills, and join a free ranger-led program.

image.title: Foothills Visitor Center
image.altText: Foothills Visitor Center
image.caption: The Foothills Visitor Center is open most days of the year.

title: Explore Hidden Sequoias at Muir Grove
shortDescription: Take a hike to a sequoia grove that is tucked away from the road. Muir Grove provides a quiet experience among these giant trees. If you find other sequoia groves to be a bit crowded, take a walk to experience Muir Grove.
seasonDescription: The campground is open late June through early September. If you wish to hike to Muir Grove outside of these dates, you may park your car outside the gate. Please don't block the gate.

title: See the General Sherman Tree in Snow
shortDescription: Enjoy an up-close experience walking around the big trees, including the largest tree on Earth.

image.title: General Sherman in Snow
image.altText: A person is dwarfed under an immense sequoia tree. The ground and tree branches are covered in snow.
image.caption: Visit the world's largest tree in the peaceful quiet of winter.

title: Visit the Kings Canyon Visitor Center
shortDescription: At the Kings Canyon Visitor Center, learn about three regions in Kings Canyon National Park: giant sequoia groves, Kings Canyon, and the High Sierra. Watch a 15-minute movie (English/Spanish). A park store sells books, maps, and educational materials.

image.title: Kings Canyon Visitor Center
image.altText: A museum display at Kings Canyon Visitor Center
image.caption: Learn about the sequoia groves at the Kings Canyon Visitor Center.

title: Monarch Lake
shortDescription: Upper and Lower Monarch Lakes are gorgeous alpine lakes that lie at the base of Sawtooth Peak. You can hike this 10-mile route as a day hike or an as an overnight backpacking trip, but be aware that camping is only allowed several miles into your route. There is an elevation gain of 2,867 feet.

image.title: Monarch Lake
image.altText: A woman fishing in an alpine lake surrounded by granite walls.
image.caption: Monarch Lake is an alpine lake in the High Sierras.

title: Eagle and Mosquito Lakes
shortDescription: Both Eagle and Mosquito lakes offer beautiful views of Mineral Kings alpine landscape. Eagle and Mosquito Lakes trails share the same route for the first 2 miles. The trail for both is 10 miles out and back with over 3,000 feet of elevation change.

image.title: Mosquito Lake
image.altText: A large lake surrounded by forest covered granite walls.
image.caption: Mosquito Lake

title: Cold Springs Nature Trail
shortDescription: The Cold Springs Nature Trail is a great option for visitors looking for an easier trail and staying at the Cold Springs Campground. Many of the hikes in the Mineral King area are long and steep. This route is a gentle hike 3 mile (4.8 km) hike with a 500-foot elevation gain and offers a taste of the Mineral King area.

image.title: Cold Springs Nature Trail
image.altText: A sign reading "Cold Springs Campground" nestled between yellow plants.
image.caption: You can find the Nature Trail in Cold Springs Campground.

title: Roaring River Falls
shortDescription: This is a short, paved walk to a cool waterfall (literally and figuratively!) On a hot day, it’s a great place to stop because the powerful falling water creates its own wind! Watch the mist swirl through the treetops as you take a moment to relax and cool off.

image.title: Roaring River Falls
image.altText: A large waterfall pumps water out into a pool.
image.caption: Roaring River Falls is only 0.5 miles from the parking lot.

title: Road's End
shortDescription: Road's End is the last stop in the Cedar Grove area, at the literal end of Highway 180. This area is the jumping off point for many high Sierra hiking trails, but also is an access point for easy trails in the valley.

image.title: Road's End
image.altText: A ranger station next to a trail leading into a forest.
image.caption: Get a wilderness permit at the Road's End Ranger Station.

title: Mist Falls
shortDescription: An 8-mile round-trip walk to this spectacular cascade makes a great all-day walk. The first miles are relatively flat and open; in the last mile the wooded trail gains 600' in elevation. Be careful once there: Mist and spray make the surrounding rocks slippery and treacherous. Too often people have slipped and fallen in here.

image.title: Mist Falls
image.altText: A cascading waterfall with massive granite mountains in the background.
image.caption: Mist Falls

title: Zumwalt Meadow
shortDescription: Zumwalt Meadow is one of the park's most iconic, scenic meadows. Explore a 1 - 3 mile trail that begins near the Kings River, crosses a riparian corridor, and then climbs gently along a rocky hillside.

image.title: Zumwalt Meadow
image.altText: A large meadow underneath towering granite walls.
image.caption: View wildlife in this large meadow.

title: Big Stump
shortDescription: The first resting spot after the park entrance station on Highway 180, this picnic area makes this a perfect stop to get your bearings after the drive from the San Joaquin Valley. From here, you will find the trailhead for the Big Stump Trail, which leads to the Mark Twain Stump via a 2-mile (3.2-km) hike.

image.title: Big Stump
image.altText: A stump of a large sequoia tree with a ladder attached to it.
image.caption: The McKinley Tree

title: Panoramic Point
shortDescription: Look outward from Panoramic Point across hundreds of miles of Kings Canyon National Park and neighboring national forest lands

image.title: Panoramic Point
image.altText: A view of a vast mountain landscape.
image.caption: View features like Hume Lake, Spanish Mountain, and the Obelisk in the distance.

title: General Grant Tree
shortDescription: The General Grant Trail is an easy, 0.5 mile loop through the Grant Grove of sequoias. The General Grant Tree is not one of the oldest, but it has the advantage of growing in a spot with bright sunlight and plenty of water, so it grew larger quickly. It holds two additional titles: the Nation's Christmas Tree (not the National Christmas Tree, which gets decorated in Washington, D.C.) and the country's only living national shrine.

image.title: General Grant Tree
image.altText: A large tree reaching up into a cloudy sky.
image.caption: The General Grant Tree is the world's second largest tree by volume.

title: Moro Rock
shortDescription: A stone and concrete stairway leads to the top of Moro Rock, a granite dome that towers over the Generals Highway. From the top, enjoy sweeping views of the hills below and the wilderness to the east.
seasonDescription: The stairway is closed when it is snowy or icy.

image.altText: People stand along the narrow ridge of Moro Rock, surrounded by railing. Photo Paul Johnson

title: Crystal Cave
shortDescription: A tour through Crystal Cave will give you an inside look at the complex world that lies beneath our feet. Spend time with a guide and learn about the unique geologic features and animal creatures found within the cave.

image.altText: A paved trail passes through Crystal Cave. Photo by Alison Taggart-Barone

title: Crescent Meadow
shortDescription: The Crescent Meadow Trail is an ideal place for photography and a relaxing walk. Follow the flat, 1.5-mile (2.4-km) loop trail around Crescent Meadow, where bright green vegetation contrasts with the red bark of giant sequoias.
seasonDescription:
This road generally opens for the season by the Wednesday before Memorial Day in late May and closes when it becomes impassable due to snow.

Vehicle traffic to Crescent Meadow not permitted in on weekends or on holidays-access to this area is via shuttle only.

image.altText: Crescent Meadow by Alison Taggart-Barone

title: Tunnel Log
shortDescription: Since 1935, people have been driving through Tunnel Log. You too can join in on the novelty of driving through a fallen Sequoia.
seasonDescription: This road generally opens by the Wednesday before Memorial Day in late May and closes when it becomes impassable due to snow.

image.altText: A truck drives through Tunnel Log, while a group of people pose for a photo above.

title: The General Sherman Tree
shortDescription: The General Sherman Tree is a must-see while visiting the Giant Forest. It is the largest tree in the world by volume.
seasonDescription: This trail is not always free of snow in winter. Travel with caution in winter months and check current park conditions webpage, as trekking poles and shoe cleats may be advised.

image.title: General Sherman Tree
image.altText: Visitors stand in front of a massive sequoia tree.
image.caption: View the world's largest tree by volume.

title: Sequoia Historic Entrance Sign
shortDescription: Stop by this historic entrance sign to take pictures and learn about its unique significance to Sequoia National Park.

image.title: Sequoia Historic Entrance Station
image.altText: A painted sign of an indigenous person with the words Sequoia National Park.
image.caption: Take a picture and learn about the history of this sign.

title: Clover Creek Winter Trail
shortDescription: This one-way trail is currently marked to the Twin Lakes hiking trail junction. Return to Wuksachi on the same trail.

image.title: Clover Creek
image.altText: A snowy landscape of a road going over a creek.
image.caption: After a few switchbacks, the trail crosses the Clover Creek Bridge.

title: Panther Winter Trail
shortDescription: Taking its name from Panther Gap (8,600 feet), the Panther Trail is part of a difficult loop for experienced skiers. Steep grades and dense forests guard the great views from Panther Gap.

image.title: Panther Winter Trail
image.altText: A skier walks down a trail among a snowy landscape.
image.caption: Overnight camping is allowed in the vicinity of Panther Gap, wilderness permits are required.

title: Trail of the Sequoias Winter Trail
shortDescription: A challenging alternative to the Crescent Trail, the Trail of the Sequoias explores the eastern edge of the Giant Forest. This trail is not for novice skiers.

image.title: Trail of the Sequoias Winter Trail
image.altText: A visitor on a trail poses among a snow covered landscape.
image.caption: This route includes several deep pitches through thick forest.

title: Crescent Winter Trail
shortDescription: The trail connects the General Sherman Tree with the end of Crescent Meadow Road (see Crescent Meadow Road Trail). The trail passes through the heart of the Giant Forest. The skiing is mostly easy, but has several short grades that require turning through the thick forest.

image.title: Crescent Winter Trail
image.altText: A skier skis down a trail past a large sequoia tree.
image.caption: This trail passes through the heart of the Giant Forest.

title: Old Lodgepole Road Winter Trail
shortDescription: This old road connects the Lodgepole Visitor Center with the General Sherman Tree. The skiing is easy, except for a steep grade as the trail approaches the General Sherman Tree.

image.title: Old Lodgepole Road
image.altText: A group of visitors with snowshoes walk down a trail.
image.caption: Trails can either be used for cross country skiing or snowshoeing.

title: Bear Hill Winter Trail
shortDescription: The trail follows the old Bear Hill Road and travels under the shade of giant sequoias and mixed conifers. Bear Hill Road is wide and easy to follow with a moderate grade.

image.title: Bear Hill Winter Trail
image.altText: A sign reading "Bear Hill" pointing to a snowy trail.
image.caption: Bear Hill is a wide and easy to follow moderate trail.

title: Pear Lake Winter Trail
shortDescription: The Pear Lake Trail is the most challenging of the marked ski trails in Sequoia National Park. The trail climbs steeply through dense fir forest, then ends at the Pear Lake Winter Hut.

image.title: Pear Lake Winter Trail
image.altText: A group of cross country skiers ski up a vast snowy landscape.
image.caption: The Pear Lake Trail is the most challenging of the marked ski trails in Sequoia National Park.

title: Alta Winter Trail
shortDescription: The Alta Trail descends nearly 1,000 feet from Wolverton to Giant Forest and connects with several other trails. This is a difficult ski with steep terrain and many trees.

image.title: Snowshoeing Alta Trail
image.altText: A skier skis down a trail with a snowy landscape in the background.
image.caption: Route markers may be difficult to track on some trails. Carry a map with you to be safe!

title: Crescent Meadow Road Winter Trail
shortDescription: The most popular of the Giant Forest’s ski trails, Crescent Meadow Road begins at the west end of the Giant Forest Museum Plaza. The entire route is an unplowed road with gentle to moderate grades and lots of giant sequoias.

image.title: Moro Rock on Crescent Meadow Road
image.altText: Snowy conditions on a large granite dome.
image.caption: The trail to the top of Moro Rock is not safe in winter and should not be ascended if there is ice.

title: Sunset Rock Winter Trail
shortDescription: This easy trail leads through a mixed-conifer forest of red firs, Jeffrey pines, sugar pines, and incense cedars to a large granite dome. Once there, take a seat on the dome and enjoy the sweeping views of a deep canyon that was carved by the Kaweah River. If you're there for sunset, sit back and enjoy the colorful show! When finished, return on the same trail back to the Giant Forest Museum.

image.title: Sunset Rock Winter Trail
image.altText: A woman stands on a granite dome watching the sunset.
image.caption: Snow or no, Sunset Rock is a great place to see the sunset in winter.

title: Grant Grove Loop Winter Trail
shortDescription: Visit one of the world's largest living trees. President Coolidge proclaimed the General Grant tree the Nation's Christmas tree in 1926, making it the perfect place to visit for the winter.

image.title: General Grant Tree Winter Loop Trail
image.altText: A snow covered giant sequoia tree trunk with a half buried sign in front of it labeled General Grant
image.caption: We highly recommend bringing traction devices to put on your footwear before you go on this hike.

title: Panoramic Point and Park Ridge Winter Trail
shortDescription: One of the most popular winter trails in this area begins at the village and follows the unplowed road to the top of Park Ridge. Panoramic Point offers spectacular views of the snow-covered mountains in Kings Canyon.

image.title: Panoramic Point Trail
image.altText: A snow covered trail going uphill, surrounded by pine trees.
image.caption: Panoramic Point is often very snowy and has a strong uphill climb.

title: North Grove Loop Winter Trail
shortDescription: The North Grove Loop travels through a magnificent grove of giant sequoias. Skiers will find it easier to follow this loop trail counterclockwise to avoid some of the sharper downhill curves in the road.

image.title: North Grove
image.altText: A snowshoer looking up at a sequoia on the North Grove Loop.
image.caption: Snowshoeing is a popular activity in the winter.

title: Big Trees Trail Wildlife
shortDescription: Park wildlife are often seen along the Big Trees Trail, an easy and accessible path that starts at Giant Forest Museum and takes you around a meadow lined with mature sequoias.
seasonDescription: Trail is not always clear of snow in winter season.

image.title: Giant Forest Deer
image.altText: A young deer stands between two giant sequoia trunks.
image.caption: A young deer in the Giant Forest.

title: Learn about Giant Sequoias
shortDescription: Before you investigate the area, stop here at the Giant Forest Museum to learn about giant sequoias and area history.

image.altText: Giant Forest Museum

title: Snowshoe with a Ranger
shortDescription: Our popular ranger-guided snowshoe walks are a great way to explore snowy trails. Snowshoe programs are usually offered from December through March, as long as there is at least 8 inches of snow on the ground.
seasonDescription: Snowshoe programs are usually offered December through March, as weather permits. Check the online calendar or at a visitor center for an up to date schedule.

image.altText: A ranger leads a tour through the snow

title: Take a Short Hike to Buena Vista Peak
shortDescription: Would you like to hike, but don’t have a lot of time? Head to Buena Vista Peak, which is only a 1-mile hike to a spectacular viewpoint. You’ll be rewarded with views of Redwood Canyon and the Kings Canyon high country.
seasonDescription: The Buena Vista trail can be hiked throughout the year, but we recommend hiking this trail in the summer or fall. Icy conditions and deep snow can be present in winter and early spring.

title: Hike to a Bird's Eye View
shortDescription: Take a short hike to little-known viewpoint, called Eagle View. This vista is just as spectacular as Moro Rock, but with fewer people. Enjoy the bird's-eye view of the Sequoia Kings Wilderness and the High Sierra.

image.altText: Eagle View

title: Discover Tokopah Valley and Falls
shortDescription: The Tokopah Falls Trail is great place to see the “classic” Sierra Nevada landscape. Sheer granite cliffs, a dense conifer forest, and a rushing river create a peaceful mountain scene.

image.altText: A person sits on rounded rocks at the base of Tokopah Falls.

title: Discover Sheep Creek Cascade
shortDescription: Visit Cedar Grove, in the heart of Kings Canyon. Once there, take a hike through a forested ravine to a shady glen and a small cascading waterfall called Sheep Creek Cascade. You’ll also see views of the Monarch Divide.
seasonDescription: The road into Cedar Grove is open from late April - mid November.

title: Bike the River Road
shortDescription: Explore this little-known dirt road in Kings Canyon National Park: the River Road in Cedar Grove. The traffic on the road is light, so it is good for biking, walking, running, or walking your dog. And it's a great place to escape the busier spots in the park.
seasonDescription: The road into Cedar Grove is open from late April - mid November.

title: Crescent Meadow Wildlife
shortDescription: Keep your eyes and ears open for wildlife as you hike along the Crescent Meadow in trail Sequoia's Giant Forest.

image.title: Nursing Bear
image.altText: A brown colored black bear nurses her cub in green grass.
image.caption: A black bear nurses her cub.

title: Tokopah Falls Wildlife
shortDescription: Keep your eyes and ears open for wildlife as you hike along the Tokopah Falls trail.

image.altText: A yellow-bellied marmot stands on top of a rock.

title: Visit the Lodgepole Visitor Center
shortDescription: With brand new museum exhibits, a Park Store, and a wilderness information counter, the Lodgepole Visitor Center is the place to be.
seasonDescription: Potential closures due to snowfall and road conditions.

image.title: Lodgepole Visitor Center
image.altText: Lodgepole Visitor Center
image.caption: With new exhibits, Lodgepole Visitor Center is a must-see!

title: Hike the Wuksachi Trail
shortDescription: Head out on the Wuksachi Trail to Lodgepole for a walk through fir forests, meadows, and creeks. Venture into the wilderness by connecting to the Twin Lakes Trail for Cahoon Meadow, or continue to Lodgepole, where you can catch the Purple Route 2 shuttle back to Wuksachi Lodge (summer only).
seasonDescription: The free Sequoia Shuttle system operates during the summer only. In the winter, be prepared for snow conditions.

image.altText: Trees with green and yellow leaves stand behind a field of yellow grass

title: Hike Among the Giants
shortDescription: There is no better way to explore the Giant Forest than by going out on the trails. Try a stroll on the Congress Trail, a 2-mile (3.2-km) loop that starts from the General Sherman Tree and takes you into the heart of a sequoia grove.
seasonDescription: During winter, trail may be covered in snow and more suitable for snowshoeing. Check the our current conditions webpage for updated information.

image.altText: A hiker travels along a park trail. Image by Tuan Nguyen.

title: Explore the Winter Forest by Foot
shortDescription: There is no better way to see the snow covered Giant Forest than to get out on the trails and walk around. Whether you rent snowshoes or bring your own, snowshoeing around a sequoia grove is a fun experience for people who are well-prepared.

image.altText: A hiker heads through snow toward sequoia trees

title: Discover the Lodgepole-Sherman Tree Trail
shortDescription: Explore the Giant Forest on your way to the General Sherman Tree. Take the 2.8 mile Lodgepole-Sherman Tree Trail from the Lodgepole Campground, then catch the Green Route 1 shuttle back to the parking lot.
seasonDescription: The Lodgepole-Sherman Tree Trail and the General Sherman Tree are accessible year-round. However, the Sequoia Shuttles operate only during the summer.

image.altText: The Sherman Tree, a giant sequoia tree

title: Enjoy a 360-Degree View at Little Baldy Dome
shortDescription: Hike on a lesser-known trail in Sequoia National Park. The Little Baldy trail takes you through a mixed-conifer forest to the top of a granite dome. Once there, you can take in a 360-degree panoramic view.
seasonDescription: The Little Baldy Trail can be hiked throughout the year, but we recommend hiking this trail in the summer or fall. Icy conditions and deep snow can be present in winter and early spring.

title: View Sunset from Sunset Rock
shortDescription: Are you looking for the perfect spot for sunset? Head to Sunset Rock in the Giant Forest. This less trafficked trail is a great option for escaping the crowds and enjoying the colorful sunset.
seasonDescription: The Sunset Rock Trail can be hiked throughout the year, but we recommend hiking this trail in the summer or fall. Icy conditions and deep snow can be present in winter and early spring.

title: Explore Sub-Alpine Landscapes at Mineral King
shortDescription: In Sequoia National Park visit Mineral King, a beautiful valley at 7,500 feet. This area can be used as a basecamp for day hikes to lakes and alpine wonderlands.
seasonDescription: The Mineral King Road is open from late May through the last Wednesday of October, weather permitting.

title: Play in the Snow at Wolverton
shortDescription: Sitting at 7,250 feet (2,160 m) above sea level, snow transforms Wolverton Meadow into a winter wonderland. This is a great place for people of all ages and abilities to play in the snow.

image.altText: Families play in the snow on a hill with scattered trees

title: Ski Through the Sequoias
shortDescription: For skiers with more experience, the Trail of the Sequoias is a great opportunity to find some solitude among the big trees.

image.altText: A snow covered trail leads into a sequoia grove

title: Discover a Winter Meadow
shortDescription: With easy access from Giant Forest Museum, this trail goes along the Moro Rock – Crescent Meadow Road. This gentle sloping trail will take you by dozens of sequoia trees, including the famous Tunnel Log. At the end of the trail, enjoy the serenity of Crescent Meadow.

image.altText: A snow covered meadow surrounded by tall trees

title: Winter Driving and Snow Chains in Sequoia National Park
shortDescription: In winter, you must be prepared for snowy or icy mountain roads and cold temperatures. Tire chains can be required on any park road at any time from fall through late spring.

image.altText: A man smiles at the camera as he finishes installing tire chains

title: Learn the Inside Story at a Ranger Program
shortDescription: Discover the parks with an expert! Learn more at an all ages ranger program.

image.altText: a ranger and a family examine mortar holes

title: Become a Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Become a Junior Ranger!

image.altText: A ranger swears in a child as a Junior Ranger

title: Picnic Among the Giants
shortDescription: Gather around a picnic at these spots from Giant Forest to Grant Grove.

image.altText: A long picnic table sits under trees next to a campfire ring with grill

title: Old Rag Circuit
shortDescription: PARK BOUNDARY | Visitors must obtain an Old Rag day-use ticket in advance of this hike. Pets are not allowed. Old Rag is a popular, very strenuous hike with sweeping views and several scrambles across large rocks. This route starts from the Old Rag parking area on the boundary of the Park.

image.title: Old Rag Mountain
image.altText: A man extends his hand on top of a rock to a woman below.

title: Stony Man
shortDescription: MILE 41.7 | Pets are not allowed on this hike. This enjoyable hike brings you to an outstanding view of the Shenandoah Valley, Massanutten Mountain, and beyond.

image.title: Stony Man Summit
image.altText: A woman with a baby on her back takes a picture with her phone on top of a mountain summit.
image.caption: NPS | M. O'Neill

title: Whiteoak Falls (Lower)
shortDescription: PARK BOUNDARY | An easier hike to the base of the lower falls in Whiteoak Canyon. Note that a Park entrance fee is still required.

image.title: Whiteoak Canyon Falls
image.altText: A creek runs through a green forest.

title: Turk Mountain
shortDescription: MILE 94.1 | A hike to the 2,981’ summit of Turk Mountain, located in the Shenandoah Wilderness, that provides a wonderful view to the west.

image.title: Turk Mountain
image.altText: A mountain peak in the distance.

title: Riprap - Wildcat Ridge
shortDescription: MILE 90 or 92.1 | This loop can be hiked from Riprap Parking or Wildcat Ridge Parking. It takes you through the forests of the Shenandoah Wilderness and over several stream crossings, while offering beautiful views of the hollows and valley to the west and north.

image.title: Riprap (Chimney Rocks)

title: Visit Glen Haven Historic Village
shortDescription: Glen Haven is the best-preserved cord wood station on the eastern shore of Lake Michigan, and perhaps in the entire Great Lakes. It was a company town, eventually diversifying into farming, canning of fruit, and tourism. Today, the history of Glen Haven is still preserved within several buildings that you can visit during your trip to Sleeping Bear Dunes. In the summer, these buildings are open to visit and staffed with knowledgeable and friendly volunteers.
seasonDescription: The exterior buildings and exhibits are available year-round. The interior museum spaces are only open in the summer.

image.title: Glen Haven
image.altText: Shelves filled with historic items and an old coffee grinder on counter.
image.caption: Visit the General Store

title: Explore Pierce Stocking Scenic Drive

Wind through cool forests of sugar maple and beech trees. Take a moment along the way to enjoy a picnic, take a walk, or just linger in the sunshine.
seasonDescription:
The Pierce Stocking Scenic Drive is closed to vehicles for the annual winter and spring closure. 

The drive is open for hiking and walk-in recreation during the vehicle closure. The road includes steep inclines that may become hazardous due to wet leaves, wind, and rain, which can create slippery and unsafe conditions. Visitors are advised to use caution.

title: Nature Trails
shortDescription: Three nature trails (shorter in length) allow visitors to experience the tallgrass prairie first-hand, while remaining in closer proximity to visitor services. These trails are dog friendly, but please help all visitors enjoy them by keeping dogs on a visible 6' maximum leash and picking up after your pet. Enjoy your hike by following these important safety rules. Permits are not required to hike the trails. All trails open 24 hours; no camping.
seasonDescription: Trails are open 24/7 365 days a year except during times of prescribed fire.

image.title: Southwind Nature Trail
image.altText: Mowed and gravel path make up the Southwind Nature Trail.
image.caption: The viewshed on the Southwind Nature Trail.

title: Take a Self-Guiding Tour of the Ranch
shortDescription: Stephen F. Jones named his ranch the Spring Hill Farm and Stock Ranch for the springs found on the hill west of the house. The house was built on a hillside with a two-story exposure on the upper side and a three story on the lower level. The three-level limestone barn measures 60 feet by 110 feet and is built into the hillside. It originally was roofed with 5,000 pounds of tin and sported a very large double-header windmill. Other outbuildings make up the ranch complex.

image.title: Visit the historic buildings
image.altText: Aerial photo showing the historic ranch buildings.
image.caption: Explore the historic ranch buildings and learn about ranching in the Flint Hills.

title: Try Catch and Release Fishing

title: Explore Tallgrass Visitor Center
shortDescription: Park rangers attend the visitor center with a range of exhibits. Geology, ecology, history, and culture all shaped today's Tallgrass Prairie. A modest gift shop provides souvenirs and the park stamp for collecting memories. Junior Ranger books, event posts, trail maps, and brochures constantly draw visitors.
seasonDescription: Tallgrass Prairie Visitor Center regularly closes for 3 holidays: Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Year's Day.

image.title: Visitor Center
image.altText: Wall exhibits dsplay several ecology topics
image.caption: Visitor Center displays geology, ecology, and cultural effects on the tallgrass prairie.

title: Take 12 to West Branch
shortDescription: Up for a full day hike? Set out for marker 27 on the north end of the preserve. This 12 mile rounder provides a grand view of the landscape, bison, and who knows what else. Learn more about backcountry hiking.
seasonDescription:
The prairie has a unique beauty during each season. 
Bison in Windmill Pasture may be more dangerous during calving season in spring and the rutting season in fall.

image.title: Prairie Fire Loop
image.altText: A mown trail cuts through waste high grasssloping down to a line of trees.
image.caption: Prairie Fire Loop reaches deep into the heart of the prairie.

title: Bison viewing on the Scenic Overlook Trail
shortDescription: Walk along the gravel trail into the unplowed Flint Hills. Here an array of prairie wildlife make their home. The trail winds uphill through Windmill Pasture where a bison herd grazes. It continues to a hilltop on the far side. Several trail options allow extended backcountry hikes or alternate routes when bison block the path. The visitor center to the overlook is just over 3 miles (5 km) one-way.
seasonDescription: The trails are open to public hiking all year round. Caution entering the pasture with bison. Maintain 100 yards distance from bison for safety reasons. Bison may be more aggressive during rutting season in the fall and calving season in the early summer.

image.title: Scenic Overlook Trail
image.altText: Bison graze in an open prairie stretching to the horizon.
image.caption: Bison viewing draw many hikers up this popular trail.

title: Break on the Bottomland Trail
shortDescription: The Bottomland Trail offers many amenities and a short walk through the prairie. It's an ideal stop for passing through with a tight schedule. The fine gravel trail loops through a small meadow by the river.
seasonDescription:
Winter walks are tranquil. Animal tracks are fun after fresh snow.
Spring brings fresh green sprouts and more animal sightings.
Summer explodes in color and pollen. The scene changes every few weeks from April through October.
Fall brings the full height of plant growth to bear. "Tall in the Fall" accurately describes the vegetation reaching four to seven feet.

seasonDescription: The Monument is open year-round. In spring-summer, wildflower blooms may be visible generally from March-May. In summer, temperatures usually exceed 100° F (38° C) by noon. In winter, average low temperatures range from 38-57° F (3-14° C).

title: Hike the Bouchoux Trail to Jensen's Ledges
shortDescription: A difficult uphill hike leads to a dazzling waterfall and an amazing panoramic view of the Upper Delaware River Valley at the summit of Jensen's Ledges. Along the way, bluestone piles hint at the history of bluestone quarrying. This trail is managed by the New York State Department of Enviornmental Conservation.
seasonDescription:
The Bouchoux Trail is open year-round. Please exercise caution and situational awareness with weather conditions while hiking. Be mindful the trail can get very muddy after heavy rain and quite slippery in wet, snowy, and icy conditions.

Please be especially careful when hiking during hunting season. Wear bright or flourescent orange or pink.

During all seasons, there is always a risk of ticks. Please check for ticks on yourself and any pets after hiking. 

Hikers may get more extensive views of the valley at the ledges during winter to early spring, before foliage grows in.

title: Primitive Camping at Buckhorn Natural Area
shortDescription: Camp right on the Delaware River at Buckhorn Natural Area. This is a free primitive camping area, although a permit is required. There are no facilities at this campsite and this campsite can only be reached by boat. However, it is an excellent camping spot for river users interested in multi-day paddling-camping trips along the Upper Delaware.
seasonDescription:
This camping area is open year-round. However, due to weather conditions and that it is only accessible by boat, we strongly recommend campers utilize these campsites between late spring and early fall, when air and water temperatures are warmer. 

A water temperature between 70°F and 80°F is recommended for swimming, paddling, tubing, and other river activities. Please be aware hypothermia is possible, even during the summer, while on the river. Always bring extra layers with you.

title: Float from Damascus to Skinners Falls
shortDescription: Float this short stretch of river from Damascus River Access to Skinners Falls River Access. This stretch is approximately 3 river miles and takes on average 1.5 hours to float. This stretch of river has no rapids, only riffles and thus should be a relatively peaceful float.
seasonDescription:
Although the Upper Delaware River is open year-round to recreate, summer is generally the best time of year to float due to warmer air and water temperatures. 

At water temperatures of 70°F and below, there is an increased risk of cold water shock, which affects one’s ability to respond and recover after capsizing or falling into the water. Inner tube users are also more likely to get wet compared to boaters. 

The ideal water temperature for water activities is between 70°F - 80°F. Summer water temperatures range from 50°F - 90s (°F), with spring and fall being cooler. Winter water temperatures can fall below freezing by December. Please check the river temperatures before setting off on your trip and ensure you have the appropriate equipment to have a safe trip.

As a result, life jackets must be worn between November 1 and April 30 when boating, canoeing, and kayaking. This is mandated in both Pennsylvania and New York boating law.

title: Winter Eagle Watching at the Lackawaxen River Access
shortDescription: Although many eagles call the Upper Delaware River region home during all months of the year, winter is a particularly good time to go bald eagle-watching in the park. Wintering bald eagles visit, increasing the population of eagles in the area. Furthermore, during weekends in January and February, volunteer docents are available at the Lackawaxen River Access to answer questions and promote good “Eagle Etiquette.”
seasonDescription: The height of eagle-watching season is in the winter, when wintering bald eagles come to this area for the winter from Canada and northern New York State. However, there is a population of eagles that call the Upper Delaware River area home year-round, thus eagles can be spotted in the area during any time of year. During weekends in January and February, there are volunteer docents available to answer questions. Eagle programming is cancelled during inclement weather. Please be mindful of changing weather and road conditions.

title: Hike the D&H Towpath Trail
shortDescription: Enjoy this easy 0.8 mile walking trail that takes you along the Delaware River and remains of the historic Delaware and Hudson (D&H) Canal. This trailhead is adjacent to the historic Roebling Aqueduct, Roebling Aqueduct Tollhouse, and within a few minutes' drive of the Zane Grey Museum, all managed by the National Park Service.
seasonDescription: The Towpath Trail is open year-round, though the most popular times of the year to hike are late spring through fall. During high-water and flooding events, the Towpath Trail can be damaged and temporarily closed. Please exercise caution and situational awareness with weather and river conditions while hiking. During all seasons, there is always a risk of ticks. Please check for ticks on yourself and any pets after hiking.

The park is owned and managed by Sullivan County Parks and Recreation.

Please note this trail is closed from December 1st - March 31st. This trail is located on land owned and managed by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.
seasonDescription:
This trail is only open between April 1st to November 30th. This closure is enforced for the protection of wildlife during critical winter months.

seasonDescription: The Damascus Trail is open year-round. Please exercise caution and situational awareness with weather conditions while hiking. During all seasons, there is always a risk of ticks. Please check for ticks on yourself and any pets after hiking.
