image.altText: dirt/grass trail surrounding by towering hemlock trees
image.caption: Enjoy both serene forest and lush wetlands along the Damascus Forest Trail.

title: Hike the Cabin District Interpretive Trail
shortDescription: The Cabin District Interpretive Trail is a gentle, 0.6-mile round-trip route through the historic ranch headquarters for Baca Land & Cattle Company. It takes 30-60 minutes to complete. Leashed pets are welcome.

image.title: Commissary
image.altText: A historic log building overlooking a montane grassland.
image.caption: The historic commissary along the Cabin District Trail.

title: Hike the Cerro Abrigo Loop
shortDescription: This 7.2-mile (11.6 km) loop gently ascends a lava dome and then contours around it, offering great views of the eastern half of the caldera. This hike takes 3-4 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The backcountry is closed to vehicular traffic from November 15 to May 14.

image.title: Fall Colors from Abrigo
image.altText: A vast, mountainous view with colorful trees in the foreground.
image.caption: Fall colors and views from Cerro Abrigo.

title: Hike the San Antonio Mountain Trail
shortDescription: The San Antonio Mountain Trail is a strenuous, 11-mile round-trip hike that climbs to the summit of San Antonio Mountain. It takes 5-6 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The backcountry is closed to vehicular traffic from November 15 - May 14.

image.title: View from San Antonio Mountain
image.altText: Fall colors mixed in with evergreens in a mountainous view
image.caption: Fall colors viewed from San Antonio Mountain

title: Horseback Riding in Valles Caldera
shortDescription: With Valles Caldera's rich ranching history, horses have been part of this landscape for over 100 years. Learn about how to participate in this legacy and ride your horse at Valles Caldera National Preserve today.

image.title: Horseback Riding Jaramillo
image.altText: Two people ride horses along a gravel road through a montane grassland.
image.caption: Riding the Caldera Road through Valle Jaramillo.

title: Hunting in Valles Caldera
shortDescription: Valles Caldera National Preserve is one of New Mexico's premier elk hunting locations. Between 2,500 and 3,000 elk occupy the preserve for breeding, calving and foraging.
seasonDescription:
The elk hunt runs from September thru December.
The turkey hunt runs from April thru December.

image.title: Les Glassing
image.altText: A man wearing camouflage uses binoculars to look across a forested landscape.
image.caption: A hunter glassing before his hunt.

title: Take a Self-Guided Tour of the Cabin District
shortDescription: This self-guided audio tour walks through a day in the life of a seasonal worker at the Baca Ranch in the 20th century.

image.title: Commissary
image.altText: The back of a historic wooden building overlooking a montane grassland
image.caption: The historic commissary in Valles Caldera's Cabin District.

title: Bike the Valle Grande Loop
shortDescription: This bike route loops around Valle Grande, providing spectacular views along the entire route.
seasonDescription: The route is available all year-round, depending on weather conditions. Only part of the trail is maintained, so the stretch along Cerro del Medio may be wet, muddy, or snow-covered depending on the season.

image.title: Biking near Cerro del Medio
image.altText: Two people sitting on their bicycles along a rough dirt trail with mountains in the background.
image.caption: Along the trail near Cerro del Medio

title: Take a Scenic Drive through Valle Grande
shortDescription: The Valles Caldera Entrance Road is a scenic, four-mile-long gravel road through the heart of Valle Grande. This drive offers outstanding wildlife viewing opportunities, volcanic vistas, and several places to get out and explore on foot.
seasonDescription: This driving route is available all year round unless winter weather temporarily closes the road.

image.title: Valle Grande East
image.altText: A sweeping montane grassland with forested hills in the background.
image.caption: East Valle Grande from an overlook on NM-4.

title: Hike the Valle Grande Exploration Trail
shortDescription: The Valle Grande Exploration Trail (formerly known as the Pond Trail) is a gentle, 0.8-mile round-trip hike to a pond in the heart of Valle Grande. It takes approximately 1 hour to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: This is one of the few trails that is accessible year-round.

image.title: Valle Grande Pond
image.altText: A large pond in the middle of a montane grassland with forested mountains in the background.
image.caption: The Valle Grande Exploration Trail terminates at a pond on La Jara Creek.

title: Hike the South Valle Grande Trail
shortDescription: The South Valle Grande Trail is a 2-mile round-trip hike that descends to the edge of Valle Grande, offering excellent wildlife viewing opportunities. The hike takes 1-2 hours. Leashed pets are permitted.
seasonDescription: This is one of the few trails that is accessible year-round at Valles Caldera National Preserve.

image.title: Valle Grande Trail
image.altText: A large boulder in a vast, grassy valley surrounded by forested hills.
image.caption: Views from the South Valle Grande Trail.

title: Hike the South Mountain Trail
shortDescription: The South Mountain Trail is an 8.2-mile round-trip hike that climbs to the summit of South Mountain. The hike takes 4-5 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.

image.title: South Mountain Summit
image.altText: Looking down from a montane meadow across miles and miles of mountains.
image.caption: A montane meadow awaits you at the summit of South Mountain.

title: Hike the Rabbit Ridge Trail
shortDescription: The Rabbit Ridge Trail is a 2.4-mile round-trip hike that climbs to the south rim of Valles Caldera. It takes 1-2 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: This is one of the few hiking trails that is accessible year-round at Valles Caldera National Preserve.

image.title: Rabbit Ridge Trail
image.altText: A view into a large valley with distant mountains.
image.caption: A view into Valle Grande from the Rabbit Ridge Trail.

title: Hike the Rabbit Mountain Loop
shortDescription: The Rabbit Mountain Loop (2.9 miles, 4.7 km round-trip), formerly known as the Coyote Call Trail, contours along the southern rim of the caldera, offering great views of Valle Grande and Redondo Peak. The loop takes 1-2 hours. Leashed pets are permitted.
seasonDescription: This is one of the few hiking trails that is accessible year-round at Valles Caldera National Preserve.

image.title: Rabbit Mountain Loop
image.altText: A view from a mountain into a large, grassy valley near sunset.
image.caption: Valle Grande from the Rabbit Mountain Loop.

title: Hike the Jemez River Trail
shortDescription: The Jemez River Trail (formerly Hidden Valley Trail) is a 3.4-mile round-trip hike into a picturesque canyon along the East Fork Jemez River. The hike takes 1-2 hours. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: Use extra caution on this trail in the winter. The trail follows the stream very closely in places, so snowy conditions can cover up the stream, causing hikers to step into the water by accident.

image.title: Hidden Valley with Snow
image.altText: A snow-covered landscape with a small stream meandering through rock spires and evergreen trees.
image.caption: The East Fork of the Jemez River meanders through a snowy canyon.

title: Hike the Cerro La Jara Loop
shortDescription: The Cerro La Jara Loop is a gentle, 1.4-mile hike around Valles Caldera's smallest and youngest volcanic dome. The hike takes approximately 1 hour. Leashed pets are permitted.
seasonDescription: This is one of the few hiking trails that is accessible year-round at Valles Caldera National Preserve.

image.title: Hiking La Jara Trail
image.altText: Two leashed dogs walk side-by-side in front of us on a narrow trail in a large grassland valley
image.caption: Roxy and Zuma, two leashed dogs, walk side-by-side on the Cerro La Jara Loop.

title: Hike to History Grove
shortDescription: Located about 0.8 miles (1.3 km) beyond the Volcano Discovery Center, History Grove is one of the last remaining pockets of old-growth forest in Valles Caldera National Preserve.

image.title: Road to History Grove
image.altText: A gravel road winds through a montane grassland toward a stand of old-growth forest.
image.caption: A gravel road winds along northern Valle Grande toward History Grove.

title: Fish the East Fork in Hidden Valley
shortDescription: Hike the Jemez River Trail to Hidden Valley, where the Rio Grande chub, Rio Grande sucker, and longnose dace are the dominant fish species.
seasonDescription: Ice-off usually occurs in April. On high snowpack years, the East Fork floods outside its banks and may be inaccessible and/or in poor condition for fishing until May.

image.title: Rio Grande Chub Hidden Valley
image.altText: A small fish being held in a hand within a narrow valley next to a mountain stream.
image.caption: A Rio Grande chub caught in the East Fork Jemez River in Hidden Valley.

title: Hike the Cerro Del Medio Loop
shortDescription: This 13.8-mile (22.2 km) loop circles Cerro Del Medio, Valles Caldera's oldest lava dome. The hike takes 7-8 hours. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The backcountry is closed to vehicular traffic from November 15 - May 14.

image.title: Cerro Del Medio scenery
image.altText: A forested lava dome with scattered boulders
image.caption: Views along the Cerro Del Medio Loop

title: Stargaze in Valles Caldera
shortDescription: As an International Dark Sky Park, Valles Caldera National Preserve offers outstanding opportunities for night sky viewing along NM State Route 4 and through regularly scheduled programs.

image.title: Aurora over Valle Grande
image.altText: Neon ribbons of pink, purple, and green lights, the aurora borealis, loom over a valley at night.
image.caption: The aurora borealis made a surprise appearance during "After Hours in the Caldera" 2024.

title: Take the Self-Guided Hemish Connections Audio Tour
shortDescription: Since the 1100s CE, Valles Caldera has been at the center of Hemish (Pueblo of Jemez) religion, culture, and history. During this self-guided tour, you will hear tribal leaders discuss these special connections to the landscape.
seasonDescription: Front-country stops on this auto tour are accessible year-round, but backcountry stops are only accessible by vehicle from May 15 - November 15 each year.

image.title: Pueblo of Jemez Leaders
image.altText: A group of park rangers and Pueblo of Jemez leaders stand together in an old growth forest.
image.caption: Park rangers and Hemish leaders stand together in History Grove.

title: Take a Self-Guided Geology Tour of Sulphur Springs
shortDescription: This self-guided geology tour in the National Park Service smartphone app leads hikers to Sulphur Springs, a unique geothermal area at Valles Caldera National Preserve.
seasonDescription: Sulphur Springs is open to visitation year-round, but Forest Road 105 can become impassable in winter weather. Please call the park for current road conditions before attempting to drive to the trailhead in the winter.

image.title: Sulphur Springs
image.altText: A green pond in a geothermal landscape of bleached gravel.
image.caption: Sulphur Springs is an active geothermal area at Valles Caldera National Preserve.

title: Take a Self-Guided Geology Hike Around Cerro La Jara
shortDescription: This self-guided geology tour in the National Park Service smartphone app leads hikers around Cerro La Jara, which is Valles Caldera's youngest and smallest lava dome.
seasonDescription: The Cerro La Jara Loop is accessible year-round.

image.title: La Jara Fog
image.altText: Fog settles into a montane grassland surrounding a forested lava dome.
image.caption: Cerro La Jara cloaked in fog.

title: Take a Self-Guided Auto Tour of Valles Caldera
shortDescription: This self-guided driving tour leads visitors through Valles Caldera National Preserve while recommending various stops at photo locations, geologic features, and historic structures.
seasonDescription: Front-country stops are accessible year-round, but backcountry tour stops are only accessible by vehicle from May 15 - November 15 and with a daily backcountry vehicle pass.

image.title: Valle Grande
image.altText: A sweeping, montane grassland dotted with forested lava domes.
image.caption: View of Valle Grande from the main park entrance.

title: Bike the Alamo Canyon to Valle Seco Lasso
shortDescription: The Alamo Canyon to Valle Seco Lasso is a 13.5-mile bike route through the western portion of Valles Caldera National Preserve. This ride features 1,800 feet of elevation gain and a speedy final descent through the park's densest concentration of geothermal features.

image.title: Alamo Canyon Pano
image.altText: A vivid blue pond surrounded by lush grasses and evergreen trees.
image.caption: One of the geothermal ponds in Alamo Canyon.

title: Bike the Redondo Foothills Loop
shortDescription: The Redondo Foothills Loop is a moderately strenuous, 9.5-mile bike route beginning in the Cabin District. This ride features flowy descents, 771 feet of climbing, and great views of Valle Grande.

image.title: Two Cyclists
image.altText: Two cyclists ride along a flat, gravel road through a montane grassland.
image.caption: Two cyclists ride the backcountry road portion of the Redondo Foothills Loop.

title: Fish in Valle San Antonio
shortDescription: San Antonio Creek is famous throughout New Mexico for wild brown trout and beautiful scenery. Reserve your backcountry vehicle pass to fish this stream seasonally from May 15 - November 15.
seasonDescription: The backcountry vehicle route that leads to San Antonio Creek is closed from November 15 - May 15 each year.

image.title: San Antonio Creek
image.altText: A narrow stream meanders through a lush montane meadow.
image.caption: San Antonio Creek flowing through Valle San Antonio.

title: Fish San Antonio Creek
shortDescription: San Antonio Creek is famous throughout New Mexico for wild brown trout and beautiful scenery. Reserve your backcountry vehicle pass to fish this stream seasonally from May 15 - November 15.
seasonDescription: The backcountry vehicle route that leads to San Antonio Creek is closed from November 15 - May 15 each year.

image.title: Near the T
image.altText: A distant angler flyfishes a narrow stream meandering through a montane grassland.
image.caption: Fishing San Antonio Creek near the "T" on the backcountry route.

title: Fish the Headwaters of San Antonio Creek
shortDescription: San Antonio Creek is famous throughout New Mexico for wild brown trout and beautiful scenery. Reserve your backcountry vehicle pass and drive to Valle Toledo to fish this stream's headwaters!
seasonDescription: The backcountry vehicle route that leads to San Antonio's headwaters is closed from November 15 - May 15 each year.

image.title: Fishing San Antonio
image.altText: A boy wearing a cowboy hat flyfishes a narrow stream in a montane grassland.
image.caption: Flyfishing on Upper San Antonio Creek.

title: Hike the Garita Trail
shortDescription: The Garita Trail is a 7.6-mile round-trip hike to the northern rim of Valles Caldera. It takes 3-4 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: Valles Caldera's backcountry is closed to vehicular traffic from November 15 - May 14.

image.title: La Garita
image.altText: A sweeping view from a high alpine meadow overlooking Valles Caldera.
image.caption: The view from La Garita summit looking into Valles Caldera.

title: Hike the Sulphur & Alamo Canyon Loop
shortDescription: The Sulphur & Alamo Canyon Loop is a strenuous, 12.2-mile trail through Valles Caldera's geothermal areas. It takes approximately 6 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.

image.title: Alamo Canyon Pond
image.altText: A bright blue geothermal pond surrounded by green grass, wildflowers, and conifer trees.
image.caption: Alamo Canyon features several geothermal ponds.

title: Hike the Cerro Seco Loop
shortDescription: The Cerro Seco Loop is a strenuous, 11.2-mile round-trip hike that circles a lava dome with fantastic views of the caldera's north rim. It takes 5-6 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The backcountry is closed to vehicular traffic from November 15 - May 14.

image.title: Cerro Seco Loop
image.altText: A view of Redondo Peak from the Cerro Seco Loop.
image.caption: A view of Redondo Peak from the Cerro Seco Loop.

title: Hike the Northwest Rim Trail
shortDescription: At 18.6 miles round-trip, the Northwest Rim Trail is ideal for trail runners. At an average hiking pace, it takes 9-10 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The backcountry is closed to vehicular access from November 15 - May 14.

image.title: NW Rim Trail
image.altText: Looking across a mountain meadow to a grove of conifer trees and a distant mountain.
image.caption: Spectacular views along the Northwest Rim Trail.

title: Hike the Indios Creek Trail
shortDescription: The Indios Creek Trail is a 7.8-mile round-trip hike that follows a creek to the northern boundary of the park. It takes about 4 hours to complete. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The backcountry is closed to vehicular traffic from November 15 - May 14.

image.title: Indios Creek Trail
image.altText: A two-track road traverses a large, golden valley surrounded by forested mountains.
image.caption: Indios Creek Trail skirts the edge of a beautiful montane grassland.

title: Hike to Sulphur Springs
shortDescription: Sulphur Springs—a site bubbling with geothermal activity—is accessed via a 1-mile (1.6-km) round-trip hike on the Sulphur Creek Trail. This hike takes approximately 30-60 minutes. Pets are not permitted.
seasonDescription: The last mile of Sulphur Creek Road/FR 105 gets very rough in the winter and is often impassable by vehicle.

image.title: Sulphur Springs_Irene Owsley
image.altText: A hilly, geothermal landscape of bleached rock and soil largely devoid of vegetation.
image.caption: Sulphur Springs

title: Fish the East Fork Headwaters
shortDescription: Hike or bike the Rincon Trail to the East Fork headwaters, where wild rainbow trout and browns predominate.
seasonDescription: Ice-off usually occurs in April. On high snowpack years, the East Fork floods outside its banks and may be inaccessible and/or in poor condition for fishing until May.

image.title: East Fork Headwaters
image.altText: A large pool in a stream flowing through a lush montane grassland.
image.caption: A pool in the headwaters of the East Fork Jemez River.

title: Fish the East Fork Jemez River
shortDescription: A picturesque and meandering stream, wild rainbow trout and browns can be found in the headwaters of the East Fork of the Jemez River. Rio Grande suckers and Rio Grande chubs predominate elsewhere.
seasonDescription: Ice-off usually occurs in April. On high snowpack years, the East Fork floods outside its banks and may be inaccessible and/or in poor condition for fishing until May.

image.title: Tenkara
image.altText: An angler fishes a narrow stream in a foggy montane grassland.
image.caption: Fishing the East Fork Jemez River

title: Horseback Riding from the Welcome Station
shortDescription: Enjoy the beauty of Valle Grande as you trek down the entrance road on your own horse.
seasonDescription: Due to the additional wear and tear that horse trailers can have on the gravel roads, there is a seasonal restriction of when equestrian permits are valid.

image.title: Horseback riding in Sulphur Canyon
image.altText: Two people riding on their horses along a dirt trail.
image.caption: Horseback riding in Valles Caldera

title: Fish the Upper Jaramillo Creek
shortDescription: The upper stretch of Jaramillo Creek offers a challenge for anglers with the reward of catching some truly large brown trout. The creek meanders through the lush Valle Jaramillo, which creates pools and overhanging banks for trout to hide in.

image.title: Fishing Jaramillo Creek
image.altText: A man flyfishing on a narrow stream through a montane meadow full of purple wildflowers.
image.caption: Jaramillo Creek is famous for gigantic brown trout.

title: Ski the Cerro La Jara Loop
shortDescription: This 1.5-mile (2.4 km) ski loop circles Cerro La Jara, the smallest volcanic dome in the park, which formed about 500,000 years ago when lava oozed up and onto the caldera floor.
seasonDescription: Accessible in the winter when there is snow. Being in Valle Grande, the snow level can be variable as winds will blow the snow around.

image.title: Family exploring in the snow
image.altText: Family walking on a snow-covered grassland and pulling a sled.
image.caption: Family exploring in the snow

title: Fish the Middle Jaramillo Creek
shortDescription: Jaramillo Creek is the middle of the three fishable streams in Valles Caldera. The middle section of the creek runs from Cerro Pinon upstream to the Cerro Abrigo Trailhead.
seasonDescription: Access by vehicle is available May 15-November 15. All other times, you will need to hike, bike, or ski to Jaramillo Creek.

image.title: Fish the Middle Jaramillo Creek
image.altText: An angler casting a fly-fishing line toward a stream meandering through a grassland.
image.caption: Angler fishing the Jaramillo Creek

title: Wildlife Viewing in the Caldera
shortDescription: Valles Caldera provides excellent habitat for a wide variety of animals, and there are plenty of opportunities for viewing wildlife like elk, bears, prairie dogs, coyotes, and birds.

image.title: Mule Deer
image.altText: A male mule deer with large antlers looking through a thick forest.
image.caption: Mule deer are abundant all across the caldera.

title: Valles Caldera Junior Ranger Program
shortDescription: Valles Caldera National Preserve currently offers two versions of its Junior Ranger program: an experiential activity booklet designed for in-park completion, and an online program for kids who are unable to visit the park in-person.

image.title: Junior Ranger Mitch
image.altText: A boy wearing a Junior Ranger hat and vest filled with badges stands at Valles Caldera's sign.
image.caption: Junior Ranger Mitch at the Valles Caldera entrance sign.

title: Valles Caldera Junior Angler Program
shortDescription: Get reeled into fishing with the Junior Ranger Let’s Go Fishing! Booklet.

image.title: Jr Angler Program
image.altText: A drawn picture of a Ranger with a child fishing by a mountain river.
image.caption: Explore and see what it takes to be a Jr Angler!

title: Snowshoeing in Valles Caldera
shortDescription: Winter is a spectacular time to visit Valles Caldera National Preserve. The park has miles of groomed and ungroomed trails for the adventurous snowshoer.
seasonDescription:
Snow volume varies from year to year, so check our Current Conditions webpage for the most up-to-date information. The ski and snowshoe season usually lasts from mid-December to mid-March. The trails are open all year to hiking, biking, and horseback riding.

Vehicle access during the winter season is limited to the Cabin District.

image.title: Snowshoeing in Valle Grande
image.altText: A woman in a green coat smiles as she snowshoes toward us.
image.caption: Snowshoes are available for rent at the Entrance Station.

title: Hiking in Valles Caldera
shortDescription: Hiking routes within Valles Caldera range from flat strolls through montane grasslands to steep climbs on forested lava domes. As this land was a private ranch for over 150 years, the majority of hiking routes follow old logging and ranching roads. Since Valles Caldera is a relatively new National Park Service site, trails are not well-marked, and most trailheads do not yet have signs. For this reason, it is important for hikers to carry a detailed park map and GPS.

image.title: Family at La Jara Pond
image.altText: A family with young children stands beside a pond overlooking a vast grassland.
image.caption: Valles Caldera offers a broad range of trail distances and difficulties.

title: Cross-Country Skiing in Valles Caldera
shortDescription: Winter is a spectacular time to visit Valles Caldera National Preserve. The park has miles of groomed trails for the adventurous skier.
seasonDescription:
Snow volume varies from year to year, so please check our Current Conditions webpage for up-to-date information. The ski and snowshoe season usually lasts from mid-December to mid-March. The trails are open all year to hiking, biking, and horseback riding.

Vehicle access during the winter season is limited to the Valle Grande area. The best places to park for access to groomed ski trails are the Entrance Station and the Ranger Station.

image.title: XC Ski Tour
image.altText: Two people on cross-country skis glide down a snowy, groomed path.
image.caption: Cross-country skiers on a ranger-guided tour.

title: Reef Bay Trail
shortDescription: Reef Bay Trail is a strenuous hike that will take you past some of the oldest and tallest trees on the island. Danish sugar plantation ruins, stone walls from cattle grazing, and ancient rock carvings left behind by the pre-Colombian Taino can be found along the trail. During rainy season the waterfall can be spectacular.

image.altText: Petroglyphs of Reef Bay

title: Discover Bird Watching in the Virgin Islands
shortDescription: Join our Park Ranger for a tour of Francis Bay Trail and the nearby salt pond. While there you will enjoy to opportunity to view the many resident and migratory birds that call Francis Bay home.

image.altText: Two birds walking on the beach

title: Tektite Trail
shortDescription: The trailhead can be found to the right of Lameshur Road at the first switchback. The .7 mile trail begins with a moderately strenuous ascent on the Cabritte Horn Point. Hike through the desert-like terrain to reach scenic views atop coastal cliffs.

image.altText: View from Tektite Trail

title: Maho Bay
shortDescription: The perfect experience for sea turtle lovers!

image.title: Sea turtles at Maho
image.altText: A large sea turtle swims through bright turquoise water.
image.caption: Maho is a perfect place to view sea turtles!

title: Trunk Bay Underwater Snorkel Trail
shortDescription: This unique underwater trail is a great way to learn about the diverse animals of the coral reef habitat.

image.title: Unique Snorkel Opportunity
image.altText: Two young swimmers wear mask and snorkel in clear water.
image.caption: What a cool way to learn about coral reefs!

title: Annaberg Sugar Plantation
shortDescription: Take a self-guided tour of the Annaberg Sugar Plantation and immerse yourself in the time when "Sugar was King" on the island. Volunteer docents are often available during weekdays to answer questions. You are invited to tour the small country garden and learn about traditional uses of plants with Mr. Charles most weekdays,

image.title: Annaberg Sugar Plantation
image.altText: The remains of impressive stone building give a sense of the time of earlier days on St. John
image.caption: Immerse yourself in the stories of Annaberg Sugar Plantation

title: Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop And Accessible Trail
shortDescription: Cinnamon Bay Plantation was established in 1717 and was one of the earliest and most prosperous sugar plantations on the Island. In 1903, the Danish West India Plantation Company bought Cinnamon Bay and began growing bay rum trees to produce bay leaf oil, which was used in popular colognes and lotions known as St. John Bay Rum.

image.altText: Cinnamon Bay Plantation Ruins

title: Johnny Horn Trail
shortDescription: This strenuous trail leads to the remains of some beautiful stone historic sites and incredible views.

image.title: View from Johnny Horn Trail
image.altText: Distant boats dot turquoise water of varying shades on a brilliantly sunny day.
image.caption: The views make the climb worthwhile!

title: L'Esperance Trail
shortDescription: L'Esperance Trail follows a historic Danish road passing ruins of some of the earliest plantations established on St. John. View the island's only baobab, a sacred tree species that was brought to the Caribbean by enslaved Africans. From trailhead to the beach is about 2.6 miles one way. Much of the trail faces west and lacks tree shade so be sure to wear sun protection and a hat.

image.altText: L'Esperance Trail

title: Francis Bay Trail
shortDescription: Francis Bay Trail starts at the Francis Bay Sugar Factory. It continues past the Mary's Point Estate house and around a salt pond. The dry tropical forest and salt pond provide an excellent opportunity to view birds. The lower portion of the trail is an accessible boardwalk that continues through the mangroves to the two viewing platforms.
seasonDescription: Year round.

image.altText: Frances Bay Board Walk and viewing platform

title: Cinnamon Bay Trails
shortDescription: Meander through the ruins of the historic Cinnamon Bay Sugar Plantation. Smell the scent of the leaves from the bay rum trees, which were once used to make the famous St John Bay Rum Cologne. The boardwalk and nature loop are located across the road from the entrance to the Cinnamon Bay Campground. The nature loop is an easy 0.5 mile hike. For a more adventurous hike, try the strenuous 1 mile Cinnamon Bay Trail which begins east of the ruins. Hike uphill through a shaded for

image.altText: Cinnamon Bay Self Guided Trail

title: Caneel Hill Trail
shortDescription: Hiking trails in the park provide an excellent way to experience the beauty of the landscape and the rich natural and cultural history of the park/

image.title: Caneel Hill
image.altText: A wooden viewing platform at the top of the hill provides sweeping views of forest and ocean.
image.caption: The view makes the climb worthwhile!

title: Salomon/Honeymoon Bays
shortDescription: Salomon/Honeymoon Bay - These two white-sand beaches can be accessed by a short hike from Lind Point Trail that begins at the Visitor Center parking lot, from the trailhead at the Virgin Islands National Park sign off North Shore Road, or by boat.

image.altText: Salomon Bay

title: Hawksnest Bay
shortDescription: Hawksnest Bay offers three fingers of mostly Elkhorn coral reefs to snorkel. It is not advisable to snorkel directly over the reef. The Elkhorn corals are a federally protected species and extremely fragile. Snorkeling around the fingers you will see many juvenile fish and other reef creatures in and among the branches of the Elkhorn corals.

image.altText: Elkhorn and Blue Tang at Hawksnest Bay

title: Yawzi Point Trail
shortDescription: Located between Great Lameshur Bay and Little Lameshur Bay, this .3 mile trail is a good choice if looking for an easy hike. Stone ruins of homes from the Danish colonial period can be found alongside the trail. Small rocky beaches can be accessed by side trails for a quiet snorkel entry spot.

image.altText: Yawzi Trail

title: Cinnamon Bay Beach and Snorkeling
shortDescription: Cinnamon Bay offers a long gently sloping snow white beach to stick your toes in, or go for a leisurely stroll. The crystal clear waters provide many delights for even a novice snorkeler. Turtles and fish of all sizes and colors can be seen here.
seasonDescription: The beach is open year round.

image.altText: Cinnamon Bay Beach

title: Salt Pond Bay and Ram Head Trails
shortDescription: Salt Pond is perfect for someone looking for a pleasant stroll to a beautiful beach. Just a quarter mile hike from the parking area to beach, has only a slight grade.

image.altText: View from Ram Head to Salt Pond Bay

title: Hike the Lind Point Trails
shortDescription: The Lind Point Trail starts just behind the park visitor center and ends at breathtaking Honeymoon Bay or Solomon Bay. The trail offers several spurs one of which heads to the overlook. Stop and rest on the bench as you watch the boats sail by.

image.altText: Lind Point Trail Sign to Overlook

title: Windmill Tour
shortDescription: Enjoy the virtual Windmill & Plantation tour and then take a drive and see them in person.

image.altText: Catherineberg Plantation

title: Hike Blind Ash Bay Trail
shortDescription: This narrow, winding, rocky trail exposes users to the wonders of the boreal forest. This path is great for birding, it is also frequented by deer and other wildlife. From closed in forest to post card worthy views of Kabetogama Lake, this lollipop loop trail has it all.
seasonDescription:
Summer season use: Hiking
Winter season use: Snowshoeing

image.title: Overlook of Kabetogama Lake
image.altText: View overlooking Kabetogama Lake through pine trees and a few islands in the lake.
image.caption: Blind Ash Bay Trail overlook of Kabetogama Lake

title: Hike the Locator Lake Trail
shortDescription: Please note: The Cranberry Creek Portage Trail into Locator Lake from Rainy Lake has been permanently closed. Explore this two-mile, one-way hike as an afternoon adventure, or use it as a starting point for an exciting backcountry camping experience. It twists its way through forest and wetlands from Kabetogama Lake until it ends on the southern shoreline of Locator Lake - one of a series of unique interior lakes with rental canoes and reservation-only campsites.
seasonDescription: Hiking during late spring, summer, and fall.

image.title: Chain of Lakes canoe launch area
image.altText: Canoe launch area with two rack of canoes and Locator Lake in background.
image.caption: Chain of Lakes canoe launch area at end of Locator Lake Trail

title: Hike Black Bay Beaver Pond Trail
shortDescription: Take a boat one mile from the visitor center and hike this trail through northern pine country to a scenic, active beaver pond.
seasonDescription:
Summer season: Hiking
Winter Season: Snowshoeing and cross country skiing

image.title: Black Bay Beaver Pond
image.altText: View overlooking the Black Bay Beaver Pond with a beaver lodge in the middle, surround by pine trees
image.caption: View overlooking the Black Bay Beaver Pond with a beaver lodge in the middle, surround by pine trees

title: Hike Kab-Ash Trail
shortDescription: Please note: The Salmi Road entrance to the Kab-Ash Trail in the Kabetogama community is closed (click to see map). This multi-day trail connects the Kabetogama and Ash River communities through an extensive system of interconnected backcountry forests and wetlands. With multiple trailheads, you can explore smaller sections or plan an adventurous thru-hike with primitive camping opportunities along the way. Difficulty: Strenuous; Hiking Distance: 27.9 miles (44.9-km) one-wa
seasonDescription: Winter Use: Snowshoe

image.title: Meandering Daley Brook
image.altText: A narrow creek surrounded by tall, green vegetation with pine trees in the background.
image.caption: Daley Brook is a nice place to stop along the trail to look for wildlife.

title: Hike the Oberholtzer Trail
shortDescription: Wander through deciduous and conifer forest as the trail twists around the edge of a cattail filled wetland and past rocks deposited by ancient glaciers. Look for signs of wildlife as you hike to two different overlooks with marsh and lake views.
seasonDescription:
Summer Use: Hiking
Winter Use: Snowshoeing

image.title: Oberholtzer Trail Overlook
image.altText: Green cattails in foreground with lake and trees in background and blue sky with white clouds.
image.caption: Enjoy views of the marshy shoreline along the Oberholtzer Trail, keep an eye out for wading birds.

title: Hike Echo Bay Trail
shortDescription: This wide trail showcases the transition between deciduous and boreal forests as you pass through lowlands and rocky outcrops. With views of wetlands created by the engineering genius of the North American Beaver, and dense forest, the trail is popular with birders. Sightings from warblers to woodpeckers and even raptors are common.
seasonDescription:
Summer Use: Hiking
Winter Use: Cross-Country Skiing

image.title: Echo Bay Trail bridge
image.altText: A wooden bridge over a marshy area in a deciduous forest
image.caption: Echo Bay Trail passes through some marshy areas

title: Rainy Lake Recreation Trail
shortDescription: The Rainy Lake Recreation Trail offers visitors a peaceful experience as it meanders along the park road, into the woods, and around rock outcrops. This paved trail is a great option for leashed pets, bicyclists, walkers, runners, and snowshoers to take in the views of forest, lake, and marsh scenery. It is a non-strenuous, accessible trail that requires about 1.5 hours round trip to complete.

image.altText: Two visitors walk along the Rainy Lake Recreation Trail, each one with a dog on a leash.

title: Hike the Sullivan Bay Trail
shortDescription: This easy hike along an old forest road leads you through both coniferous and deciduous forest. The trail ends at a viewpoint on Sullivan Bay with a picnic table and fire ring. It treats those who are interested in geology with lots of exposed rock, created by volcanic activity over 2 billion years ago.
seasonDescription:
Summer Use: Hiking
Winter Use: Snowshoe

image.title: Sullivan Bay Picnic Site
image.altText: Picnic table and metal fire pit next to tree, overlooking lake with forest in background.
image.caption: Have a family picnic after a short hike while overlooking Sullivan Bay.

title: Hike Beaver Pond Overlook Trail
shortDescription: A short uphill hike through an aspen and pine forest leads to a rocky outcrop high above a beaver pond. Although beavers are no longer active at this pond, this trail provides great birding opportunities, and the possibility of spotting large wildlife.
seasonDescription:
Summer season use: Hiking
Winter season use: Snowshoeing

image.title: Beaver Pond Overlook
image.altText: Beaver pond surrounded by trees, reflecting a blue and cloudy sky.
image.caption: The wetlands created by beaver dams are important habitat for other wildlife.

title: Hike Voyageurs Forest Overlook Trail
shortDescription: This short trail takes you through a section of forest revealing the changes in the forest at different elevations. Growing trees have blocked the overlook that used to be at the parking area. There are picnic tables and grills by the parking area.

image.title: Voyageurs Forest Overlook
image.altText: A picnic table and raised charcoal grill in front of trees
image.caption: The picnic area at the parking area for Voyageurs Forest Overlook Trail

title: Voyageurs' Tilson Connector Trail
shortDescription: This trail accessible year-round. Once sufficient snowfall accumulates, the trail will continue be groomed for classic, cross country skiing that leads to the Tilson Bay Trails that are managed by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources.
seasonDescription: This trail is groomed from cross country skiing in the winter.

image.title: Skiing
image.altText: Two cross country skiers on a trail through the forest.
image.caption: Cross country skiing is a great way to enjoy the park in the winter.

title: Hike the Mukooda Trail
shortDescription: Accessible only by boat, the Mukooda Trail meanders through a mix of deciduous and coniferous forest and over rocky ridges, scraped bare by ancient glaciers. Take a journey through natural and cultural history on this narrow strip of land separating Sand Point Lake and the glacially carved Mukooda Lake. Look for picturesque views from high ridges and signs of wildlife as you wander through this unique and remote part of the park.

image.title: Mukooda Trail
image.altText: A large rock (glacial erratic) is next to a trail will a dead tree curving around the rock.
image.caption: Glacial erratic on the Mukooda Trail

title: Hike the Cruiser Lake Trail
shortDescription: This rugged trail crosses over the peninsula, up rocky cliffs and down into remote wetland areas. See parts of the park many people do not visit. Start your hike either at Anderson Bay on the Rainy Lake side or Lost Bay on the Kabetogama side. Reserve a backcounrty campsite to turn this into a multi-day trip. Hiking this trail increases your chances of spotting a moose or hearing the howl of a wolf.

image.title: Cruiser Lake Trail
image.altText: A view of a lake through the trees
image.caption: A view of Cruiser Lake through the trees from Cruiser Lake Trail

title: Hike Kabetogama Lake Overlook Trail
shortDescription: This short handicap accessible trail takes you through a pine forest to a viewpoint where you can sit on a bench and see Kabetogama Lake framed by the trees.

image.title: View from the Kabetogama Lake Overlook
image.altText: A view of Kabetogama Lake framed by pine trees.
image.caption: See Lake Kabetogama framed by the trees

title: Hike Anderson Bay Loop
shortDescription: This trail takes you through the forest past rocky clearings and beaver ponds to spectacular views of Rainy Lake form the shoreline and Anderson Bay from the top of the cliffs.

image.title: Anderson Bay from the top of the cliffs
image.altText: Someone stands on top of the granite outcrop at Anderson Bay looking at the bay and trees below.
image.caption: Visitor looking over Anderson Bay from the top of the cliffs

title: Go sledding on Sphunge Island
shortDescription: Visitors will find picnic tables and a fire ring at the bottom of the hill near the sledding hill parking lot. The sledding hill consists of a small hill for younger children and a larger hill for older children and adults.

image.title: Sphunge Island Sledding Hill
image.altText: Brown sign titled 'Sphunge Island Sledding Hill' in front of a hill covered with snow.
image.caption: Sphunge Island Sledding Hill

title: Stargazing at Voyageurs National Park
shortDescription: Come see the night skies at Voyageurs National Park. We have been recognized as an International Dark Sky Park because of the quality of our night skies and our commitment to protecting the sky form light pollution. The best places to view the night sky at Voyageurs are the Voyageurs Forest Overlook parking area, Kettle Falls Dam, and the Beaver Pond Overlook. If you are up by international Falls there are good viewing locations around the Rainy Lake Visitor Center.

image.title: Moonrise over Lake Kabetogama
image.altText: The moon rises over Lake Kabetogama with a jetty in the foreground
image.caption: Moonrise over Lake Kabetogama

title: Paddle through Blind Ash Bay
shortDescription: Explore the rocky shoreline and a calm bay with your canoe or kayak.  From the paddle launch head west one mile between the rocky shore and small islands before turning south to explore Blind Ash Bay. Your total trip length will be about 2.5 miles.

image.title: Kayaking near the shore
image.altText: The front of a red kayak pointing towards lily pads and reeds with a pine forest in the background.
image.caption: Kayaking near the shore

title: Watch the Northern Lights Over Voyageurs National Park
shortDescription: The Aurora Borealis, also known as northern lights, are radiant colors that light up the night sky over middle and high latitudes of the northern hemisphere, including at Voyageurs National Park.
seasonDescription: Northern lights can be seen anytime of the year, however the best chance to view them is in the winter. The smallest chance of seeing northern lights is in the summer.

image.title: Northern Lights over Lake Kabetogama
image.altText: Green waves of light shine in two waves in a dark sky, illuminated the tree line and lake below.
image.caption: Northern Lights over Lake Kabetogama

title: Become a Junior Ranger at Voyageurs National Park
shortDescription: Explore and learn about Voyageurs National Park as you become a Junior Ranger. Ask for a Junior Ranger Book at any Visitor Center. Learn about the park, its history, and animals by completing activities in the book, then explore the park on the water, on trails, or at a ranger program. The stop by the Visitor Center to be sworn in as a Junior Ranger and get your patch and badge.

image.title: Jr. Ranger swearing in
image.altText: A ranger stands in front of two children and all have their right arms raised.
image.caption: Become a Jr. Ranger at Voyageurs National Park

title: Visit Little American Island
shortDescription: Discover the past on this self guided walk Little American Island. This island was home to one of the area gold mines during the brief gold rush of the 1890s. You will see mine shafts, tailing piles, and machinery along the side of this short trail. Signs tell the story of the gold rush.

image.title: Mining gear on Little America Island
image.altText: A lichen covered rusting wheel from the mining era lies in the brush on Little America Island
image.caption: Remnants of the Little America Gold Mine can be found along the island's path.

title: Take a boat tour of Voyageurs National Park
shortDescription: See Voyageurs National Park from a boat on a tour guided by a park ranger. A variety of boat tours leave from Rainy Lake Visitor Center and Kabetogama Lake Visitor Center primarily from June to August and last from 90 to 390 minutes. This is a great way to see the park and some wildlife, especially if you don't have a boat of your own.

image.title: The Voyageur at Kettle Falls
image.altText: The park tour boat docked at Kettle Falls with trees in the background
image.caption: See the park on one of the tour boats with a park ranger.

title: Ski the Echo Bay Trail
shortDescription: Tucked amid the community of Kabetogama, the Echo Bay Ski Trail offers novice skiers another tracked ski trail.

image.title: Echo Bay Ski Trail
image.altText: A snow covered path through the forest with ski tracks.
image.caption: Echo Bay Ski Trail

title: Snowshoe the Oberholtzer Trail
shortDescription: Grab a pair of snowshoes and experience the 1.7 mile round-trip Oberholtzer Trail.

image.title: Oberholtzer Trail
image.altText: A snow covered path with snowshoe prints.
image.caption: Snowshoe the Oberholtzer Trail.

title: Visit the Ethno-botanical Garden
shortDescription: This one-acre garden of native plants restores a site that had been overtaken by invasive plants.

image.title: eb garden
image.altText: A path way in the middle of a garden.
image.caption: Take a self-guided tour of the Ethno-botanical garden

title: Recreational Fishing in Voyageurs National Park
shortDescription: Voyageurs National Park has many options for the aspiring or experienced angler.

image.title: Muskellunge
image.altText: A fish is held by one hand in a tub full of water.
image.caption: Shoepack lake contains a genetically-distinct native strain of Muskellunge (Esox masquinongy)

title: Become a Junior Ranger at Walnut Canyon
shortDescription: Join Miguel the Mule Deer in exploring the human history, geology, and wildlife of Walnut Canyon National Monument and earn a Jr. Ranger badge.

image.title: Jr. Ranger at Walnut Canyon
image.altText: A child stands on a trail above Walnut Canyon.
image.caption: Jr. Rangers get out on the trails.

title: Gold Panning at Whiskeytown NRA
shortDescription: Become a gold miner for a day! Gold pan along Clear Creek at the Clear Creek picnic area. Gold was first discovered in Clear Creek in 1848 by Pierson B. Reading. The news of the discovery brought a wave of gold rush miners to Shasta County, many of whom set up camp in what is now Whiskeytown National Recreation Area. The former community of Whiskeytown got its start as a mining town as settlers worked along Clear Creek and its tributaries.

image.altText: Ranger Lead Gold Panning Program at Whiskeytown NRA

title: Hike to Whiskeytown Falls
shortDescription: Whiskeytown Falls is a series of cascades which drop 220 feet as the east fork of Crystal Creek winds down the slope of Shasta Bally.  The falls are accessed by the James K. Carr trail, a moderately strenuous 3.4 mile round-trip path which follows old logging routes through shade and sun in a forested area that was only lightly affected by the Carr Fire of 2018.

image.title: Upper Whiskeytown Falls
image.altText: Upper Whiskeytown Falls
image.caption: Upper Whiskeytown Falls

title: Paddling on Whiskeytown Lake
shortDescription: Whiskeytown Lake is one of the premier paddle-sport areas in northern California. With almost 40 miles of shoreline there are always new areas to explore. Ranger-led kayak tours are a great way to get an introduction to kayak and paddle boarding with a fun two-hour trip through the history and unique ecosystem of Whiskeytown. These tours run between Memorial Day and Labor Day and reservations through Recreation.gov are required.

image.altText: Kayaking on Whiskeytown Lake

title: Swimming at Whiskeytown Lake
shortDescription: Whiskeytown Lake is a fantastic location to enjoy a refreshing swim on a hot day. This lake has about 37 miles of shoreline. During the summer months surface water temperatures can reach nearly 80°F. There are three main swim beaches with amenities, Brandy Creek Beach, Oak Bottom Beach and East Beach. All three of these locations have the water roped off and closed to boating. This makes them great and safe for all ages.

image.altText: Brandy Creek Beach

title: Sledding at the Roadrunner Picnic Area
shortDescription: The Roadrunner Picnic area is an excellent place to go sledding with friends and family at White Sands National Park.
seasonDescription:
Summer temperatures at White Sands National Park often average in the high 90's during the day with temperatures reaching over 100 degrees farenheit consistently. Thunderstorms are common in the park and are most frequent during July and August. Please pay attention to changing weather during your visit at the park.

Winter temperatures average in the 60's during the day and around 30 degrees at night. Please come prepared for cold temperatures.

image.title: Sledding at the Roadrunner Picnic Area
image.altText: two picnic shelters with metal toppers sit in front of a tall white dune
image.caption: Shaded picnic areas give relief from the sun while sledding at Roadrunner Picnic Area

title: Hiking the Ice Age Trail
shortDescription: This level, family-friendly trail interprets the Ice Age history of the Tularosa Basin

image.title: Ice Age Trail
image.altText: A dirt trail in the desert floor
image.caption: The Ice Age Trail interprets ancient life in the Tularosa Basin

title: Hiking Interdune Boardwalk
shortDescription: The Interdune Boardwalk is an elevated boardwalk that leads you through the fragile interdune area to a scenic view of the dune field and the Sacramento mountains.

image.title: Blue whiptail
image.altText: Close up of a large lizard with blue face and tail
image.caption: Blue whiptail lizard on the Interdune Boardwalk

title: Hiking Alkali Flat Trail
shortDescription: Imagine yourself surrounded by the spectacular views of endless dunes with few footprints. The Alkali Flat Trail takes you through the heart of the sands, up and over steep dunes to the edge of Alkali Flat.

image.title: Alkali Flat Photo
image.altText: Two people silhouetted on top of a white dune with blue sky overhead
image.caption: Alkali Flat Trail

title: Hiking Dune Life Nature Trail
shortDescription: The Dune Life Nature Trail is full of life! This family-friendly, one mile (1.6 km) loop trail is a great way to explore White Sands.

image.title: Dunes and Interdune
image.altText: White sand dune in front of plant-spotted interdune with mountains on horizon
image.caption: Yucca on the Dune Life Nature Trail

title: Hiking Backcountry Camping Trail
shortDescription: Are you looking for expansive views of snow-white gypsum dunes for miles? Hiking the Backcountry Camping Trail provides a sense of the magnitude of the world's largest gypsum dunefield.

image.title: Sunset on Backcountry Camping Trail
image.altText: A pink sky at dusk over an interdune area
image.caption: Dusk on Backcountry Camping Trail

title: Sledding at the Alkali Flat Trailhead
shortDescription: The Alkali Flat trailhead parking area has some of the tallest dunes to go sledding at White Sands.
seasonDescription:
Summer temperatures at White Sands National Park often average in the high 90's during the day with temperatures reaching over 100 degrees farenheit consistently. Thunderstorms are common in the park and are most frequent during July and August. Please pay attention to changing weather during your visit at the park.

Winter temperatures average in the 60's during the day and around 30 degrees at night. Please come prepared for cold temperatures

image.title: Sledding the Alkali Flat Trailhead Area
image.altText: sitting on top of a white dune with dunes stretching to the horizon. A trailhead sign seen below.
image.caption: Excellent sledding dunes are located just outside the Alkali Flat Trailhead parking area.

title: Picnicking at White Sands
shortDescription: White Sands National Park offers three picnic areas where people can enjoy shade, relaxation, and access to the parks incredible dunes.

image.title: Picnicking at White Sands
image.altText: a row of curved metal structures provides shade to picnic tables on a concrete pad.
image.caption: Hanging out at the park's picnic shelters is a great way to find reprieve from the hot summer sun.

title: Wind Cave Geology Driving Tour
shortDescription: The geology driving tour is a great way to see the park while learning about the rich geologic history of the Black Hills. On this 20 mile long tour, you will travel back in time and view Wind Cave's rock record to get a glimpse into its past.
seasonDescription: Periods of heavy snowfall may cause park roads to close temporarily in the winter. Winter maintenence is not performed on the gravel backcountry roads NPS 5 and 6.

image.title: Geology Driving Tour
image.altText: a gravel road winds across the prairie with rolling forested hills in the distance
image.caption: The geology driving tour allows visitors to explore the park while learning about the park's geology

title: Picnic at Wind Cave
shortDescription: Looking for a quiet place to enjoy a picnic? Whether you're looking for a good picnic spot or just a place to eat lunch while waiting for a tour, the picnic area is open year-round from sunrise to sunset.

image.title: Wind Cave Picnic Area
image.altText: a picnic area with tables and several parking spots
image.caption: The picnic area at Wind Cave features several sites with picnic tables.

title: Watch Wind Cave Wildlife
shortDescription: View some of North America's most iconic wildlife while enjoying Black Hills scenery. Wind Cave's combination of prairie and forest ecosystems allows visitors to view a number of animals in their natural environment.

image.title: Large Wildlife on Road
image.altText: three bison walk down the highway next to a sign reading: large wildlife on road next 13 miles
image.caption: Several hundred bison and many other animals call Wind Cave home.

title: Visit Wind Cave's Natural Entrance
shortDescription: You can still see the largest natural opening into Wind Cave without going on a tour. This small hole is one of the only known natural entrances into the cave. Lakota oral tradition speaks of how the first bison and humans emerged from this deeply spiritual place.

image.title: Wind Cave's Natural Entrance
image.altText: a small hole in a stone depression next to a large sign and short rock wall
image.caption: Wind Cave's natural entrance is a deeply spiritual place to many people.

title: Take a Cave Tour
shortDescription: Visit one of the world's longest and most complex caves.
seasonDescription: Cave tours occur every day of the year except Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day and New Year's Day.

image.title: Boxwork on the Fairgrounds Tour
image.altText: A young male visitor on a stairway stops to look at boxwork on the ceiling above him.
image.caption: A young visitor pauses to look at boxwork along the Fairgrounds Cave Tour route.

title: See Prairie Dogs in Their Prairie Dog Towns
shortDescription: Information about the Prairie Dog of Wind Cave National Park.

image.title: Prairie Dog
image.altText: Prairie dog standing up outside of its burrow with the edges of the photo darkened.
image.caption: Check out the main attraction at prairie dog town!

title: Pet Friendly Hikes
shortDescription: If you are traveling with a furry friend, Wind Cave has two pet friendly trails. Both are close to the visitor center and about one mile in length.

image.title: Pet Friendly Hikes
image.altText: a leashed dog on a trail in winter
image.caption: Wind Cave offers two pet friendly trails.

title: Listen For Bugling Elk
shortDescription: In September and October, male elk can be heard as they bugle to challenge each other and attract females. This haunting sound is a sure sign that fall has arrived in the West. During this time of the year, visitors may be able to join a ranger to listen for these charismatic animals.
seasonDescription: Elk typically bugle from early September through October. They may be heard as early as the end of August and as late as early November.

image.title: Elk Silhouette
image.altText: an adult male elk silhouetted far away in an open prairie at dusk
image.caption: Visitors can listen for bugling elk in September and October.

title: Horseback Riding in Wind Cave
shortDescription: The sprawling prairies and open ponderosa woodlands of Wind Cave give horseback riders thousands of acres to explore. Though there are no facilities within the park that provide horses, visitors may fill out a free day permit to bring their own horses into the park.

image.title: Horseback Riding in Wind Cave
image.altText: a group of people on horses riding into the prairie
image.caption: Horse owners are able to explore thousands of acres in the park.

title: Hiking at Wind Cave
shortDescription: View rolling prairie vistas, ponderosa forests, and see wildlife in its natural environment. Wind Cave National Park has over 30 miles of hiking trails on the surface and provides visitors the opportunity to view pristine Black Hills scenery. Find out which trail is the best for you.

image.title: Rankin Ridge Sunrise
image.altText: wide gravel path at sunrise on an open hillside with many forested hills in the distance
image.caption: Enjoy countless Black Hills views when hiking in Wind Cave.

title: Bike Wind Cave
shortDescription: Explore Wind Cave by bike. Although bikes are limited to established roads, this is a great activity for those who want to take their time to sightsee in the park.
seasonDescription: Periods of heavy snowfall may temporarily close park roads in the winter. Winter maintenance is not performed on gravel backcountry roads NPS 5 and 6.

image.title: Biking at Wind Cave
image.altText: two people in biking gear riding bikes on a dirt road in the open prairie
image.caption: Bicycling allows visitors to actively enjoy scenic park landscapes.

title: Become a Wind Cave Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Kids of all ages can become a Wind Cave Junior Ranger. Complete the activity book, learn about the park, and take the pledge to earn a Junior Ranger badge.

image.title: Wind Cave Junior Ranger Program
image.altText: a ranger showing two children an antler
image.caption: Kids of all ages can participate in the Junior Ranger program.

title: Backcountry Camping at Wind Cave
shortDescription: Experienced hikers may enjoy camping in Wind Cave's scenic backcountry. Thousands of acres of undeveloped forest and prairie provide countless sites for hikers to pitch a tent and camp.

image.title: Backcountry Camping
image.altText: a tent in a prairie overlooking the forest
image.caption: Experienced hikers may enjoy pitching a tent in the backcountry.

title: Bird Watching in Wind Cave
shortDescription: Wind Cave has many opportunities to view birds throughout the year. Although you can bird watch anywhere in the park, the Elk Mountain Campground and visitor center offer the best chances to see a diversity of species while visiting the park.
seasonDescription: Birds may be viewed in the park year round. Peak bird activity occurs during summer months and spring and fall migrations.

image.title: Western Meadowlark
image.altText: a brown bird with a yellow and black belly perched on a fence
image.caption: Western meadowlarks like to serenade the prairie from fences and tall perches.

title: Fishing at Wrangell-St. Elias
shortDescription: Sport fishing in Wrangell-St. Elias National Park offers many opportunities. Arctic grayling, dolly varden, lake trout, steelhead/rainbow trout, whitefish, sockeye salmon, coho salmon, and chinook salmon are widespread. Nothern Pike, cutthroat trout, chum salmon and pink salmon are also available in select areas. Local residents catch burbot, lake trout, rainbow trout, and whitefish through the ice in the winter.
seasonDescription: For some species, the fishing season is year-round from January 1 – December 31. Some species and some waters may have different seasons, and some regulations may vary for different management areas; consult the State ADFG Sport Regulation Brochure for the area of interest.

image.title: Person fishing at a lake
image.altText: Person fishing at a lake
image.caption: Person fishing at a lake

title: Ghost Towns
shortDescription: Ghost towns were once thriving communities that have dwindled over the decades, often created by the search for gold, copper and other valuable minerals. Some vanished entirely after the boom or were absorbed into newer settlements, but many of these towns still stand today, allowing us a nostalgic glimpse into the past. These places are where people ventured into remote areas to find their mineral fortune and endured the hardships of wilderness, wildlife and weather.
seasonDescription: Flights are dependent on weather and seaons for safety of the passengers and pilot.

image.title: Bremner Historic Mining District
image.altText: Bremner Historic Mining District
image.caption: Bremner Historic Mining District

title: Front country Hiking Trails
shortDescription: Hiking in Wrangell-St. Elias can be spectacular and we encourage you to go, but be prepared! Most of the front country hiking trails are maintained for the first few miles and then become routes into the backcountry, where route finding and navigational skills are highly recommended. There are hiking trails in the Copper Center area, on Nabesna Road and on McCarthy Road.
seasonDescription: Hiking is year-round in the park, but be prepared for extreme temperatures, especially in winter when it can be as low as 20 to 30 degrees below zero. In spring, summer and fall, be prepared for heavy rains and possible flooding. River crossing can be very dangerous, so when it doubt, turn around and return safely.

image.title: Skookum Volcano Trailhead
image.altText: Skookum Volcano Trailhead
image.caption: Skookum Volcano Trailhead

title: Backpacking in Wrangell-St Elias
shortDescription: A backpacking trip in Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve can be an exciting and rewarding experience if you are prepared for the difficulties of traveling through rugged, undeveloped land.
