image.altText: Nabesna Road

title: Crown of the Continent - Park Film
shortDescription: Soar above mountains that make their own weather and glacier-carved valleys still emerging from the Ice Age, as you return with producer John Grabowska to a place of his boyhood dreams: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve. With calving glaciers in hidden fjords, wildlife wandering a vast land and countless unnamed peaks, Wrangell-St. Elias fulfills the romantic, mythic image of Alaska.

image.altText: Park Film - Crown of the Continent

title: Flight Seeing
shortDescription: One of the best ways to experience the beauty and tremendous size of this park is from above! Fly past massive peaks, over jagged glaciers, and endless expanses of wild Alaska! There is a variety of air services available to visitors, including flightseeing excursions and air taxies for backcountry dropoffs for wilderness campers and backpackers. A wide variety of tours, trips, and itineraries are available. https://www.nps.gov/wrst/planyourvisit/air-taxis-flight-seeing.htm

image.altText: Flying over the Wrangell Mountains

title: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
shortDescription: Look out across the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone or take in the beauty of the Yellowstone River and its waterfalls.
seasonDescription: Parts of the Grand Canyon are accessible via snowmobile and guided snow coach trips in the winter.

image.title: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
image.altText: A waterfall cascades over a cliff in a canyon with pale colored walls.

title: Snow Pass Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Snow Pass Ski Trail is a 4.2 mile (6.76 km), skier-tracked, one-way, easiest to most-difficult, ski that takes skiers through a steep heavily forested area to a semi-flat wide open area with views of Swan Lake Flats.

image.title: Snow Pass Ski Trail
image.altText: Skiers follow a straight trail through a snowy forest.

title: Yellowstone River Picnic Area Trail
shortDescription: Follow the rim of the Yellowstone River valley, enjoying views of bighorn sheep, the Narrows of the Yellowstone, Overhanging Cliff, and the towers of Tower Falls.

image.title: Yellowstone River Picnic Area Trail
image.altText: A hiker stands on the edge of a canyon and looks down at the river below.

title: Yellowstone Lake Overlook Trail
shortDescription: Hike to a high mountain meadow for a commanding view of the West Thumb of Yellowstone Lake and the distant Absaroka Mountains.

image.title: Yellowstone Lake Overlook Trail
image.altText: A broad mountain rises above a forested slope.

title: West Thumb Geyser Basin Trail
shortDescription: Stroll through a geyser basin of colorful hot springs and dormant lakeshore geysers situated on the scenic shores of Yellowstone Lake.

image.title: West Thumb Geyser Basin Trail
image.altText: A turquoise hot spring pool surrounded by a boardwalk sits above a large lake.

title: Trout Lake Trail
shortDescription: Enjoy a short hill climb through Douglas-fir forest to Trout Lake.

image.title: Trout Lake Trail
image.altText: Hikers walk across a bridge at the outlet of a small lake surrounded by rolling hills.

title: Abandoned Railroad Bed Bike Trail
shortDescription: An abandoned railroad bed located near the north entrance of Yellowstone makes a beautiful bike trail.

image.title: Abandoned Railroad Bed Bike Trail
image.altText: Two people bike through a field of sagebrush in front of a mountain.

title: Storm Point Trail
shortDescription: Pass by Indian Pond and through a forest to the shores of Yellowstone Lake. Along the way, look for marmots in the rocky area near Storm Point.

image.title: Storm Point Trail
image.altText: A hiker walks across a rocky outcropping above a large lake.

title: Sepulcher Mountain Trail
shortDescription: Climb to the summit of Sepulcher Mountain while keeping an eye out for mountain goats, bighorn sheep, and moose along the way.

image.title: Sepulcher Mountain Trail
image.altText: A hiker takes in the views approaching a rocky summit.

title: Sentinel Meadows & Queen’s Laundry Trail
shortDescription: Follow the Firehole River and cross meadows until reaching a hydrothermal area. Look for the large sinter mounds of hot springs and the remains of the old, incomplete bathhouse.

image.title: Sentinel Meadows & Queen’s Laundry Trail
image.altText: A thermal area sits in a meadow in front of rolling hills.

title: Riddle Lake Trail
shortDescription: Hike through small mountain meadows and forests to the shores of a picturesque little lake. Look for elk in the meadows and for birds near the lake.

image.title: Riddle Lake Trail
image.altText: A lake covered in lily pads sits in front of a mountain.

title: Ribbon Lake Trail
shortDescription: Take a stroll out to Ribbon Lake, also passing by Lily Pad and Clear lakes.

image.title: Ribbon Lake Trail
image.altText: Lily pads cover the edge of a lake surrounded by a forest.

title: Pelican Valley Trail
shortDescription: Hike through forests, meadows, and a river valley—all of which are some of the best grizzly bear country in the lower 48 states.

image.title: Pelican Valley Trail
image.altText: People on horseback ride through a field of sagebrush with mountains in the distance.

title: Osprey Falls Trail
shortDescription: Walk along an old service road through meadows before descending into one of the deepest canyons in the park to see Osprey Falls plunge over the edge of an old lava flow.

image.title: Osprey Falls Trail
image.altText: A hiker stands at the base of a large waterfall.

title: Old Lake Road Bike Trail
shortDescription: The old roadbed near the lakeshore between Lake Hotel and where the roadbed joins the main road south of Lake Junction (1 mile) has a great views of the Yellowstone Lake.

image.title: Old Lake Road Bike Trail
image.altText: People enjoy the sunset from the shore of Yellowstone Lake.

title: Old Faithful Lower General Store to Morning Glory Pool Bike Trail
shortDescription: The paved trail in front of Old Faithful Lodge runs all the way to Morning Glory Pool. Take this short, (2 mi. round-trip) fairly level, paved-path and make stops to see geysers.

image.title: Old Faithful Bike Trail
image.altText: Two people bike on a paved trail past a geyser in a thermal basin.

title: Observation Point Trail
shortDescription: Head up switchbacks to a commanding view of the Upper Geyser Basin.

image.title: Observation Point Trail
image.altText: Water and steam erupt out of a geyser while people watch.

title: Observation Peak Trail
shortDescription: Hike to a high mountain peak for an outstanding view of the Yellowstone wilderness.

image.title: Observation Peak Trail
image.altText: A hiker approaches a fire lookout on top of a mountain.

title: Norris Geyser Basin Trails
shortDescription: Norris Geyser Basin is one of the hottest and most acidic of Yellowstone’s hydrothermal areas. It is part of one of the world’s largest active volcanoes. Many hot springs and fumaroles here have temperatures above the boiling point (200ºF / 93ºC).
seasonDescription: Norris Geyser Basin is only accessible by snowmobile during the winter months.

image.title: Norris Geyser Basin Trails
image.altText: People walk down a trail towards a steaming geyser basin.

title: Natural Bridge Trail
shortDescription: Hike through a forest and along an old service road to a natural bridge, which was cut out of a cliff of rhyolite rock by Bridge Creek.

image.title: Natural Bridge Trail
image.altText: A natural bridge formation made of rock in a forest.

title: Natural Bridge Bike Trail
shortDescription: The Natural Bridge bike trail is 2.5 mi (4km) round-trip ride and begins just south of the Bridge Bay marina off the Grand Loop Road.

image.title: Natural Bridge Trail
image.altText: A natural bridge formation made of rock in a forest.

title: Mystic Falls Trail
shortDescription: Follow a lovely creek through mixed conifer forest to Mystic Falls, over which the Little Firehole River drops from the Madison Plateau.

image.title: Mystic Falls Trail
image.altText: A waterfall cascades over a cliff and flows into a stream down a rocky creek.

title: Mud Volcano Trail
shortDescription: A loop trail leads you by turbulent pools of hot, muddy water; hillsides strewn with trees cooked by steam; strange odors; and a bizarre landscape—welcome to the Mud Volcano area.
seasonDescription: This area is accessible during the spring, summer, and fall when the main park road is open. In the winter, snowcoach tours may be able to taking tours to this area, though the trails will be covered in snow and ice.

image.title: Mud Volcano Boardwalk
image.altText: People walk down a boardwalk towards a large plume of steam.

title: Mount Washburn Spur Trail
shortDescription: A long hike from the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone and up the east side of Mount Washburn.

image.title: Mount Washburn Spur Trail
image.altText: A hiker walks on a mountain slope with a canyon and lake seen in the distance.

title: Mount Washburn Bike Trail
shortDescription: Between Canyon Village and Tower Junction hardy cyclists can ride three miles to the top of Mount Washburn. Access is from the Chittenden Road parking area to the summit of Mount Washburn.

image.altText: Two bikers on a dirt road with green trees and standing snags. Snow covers some of the landscape.

title: Mammoth Hot Springs Trails
shortDescription: Wander around large travertine terraces, built by ever-shifting hot springs.
seasonDescription: Most of the boardwalks are not maintained during the winter.

image.title: Mammoth Hot Springs Trails
image.altText: People stand on a boardwalk and admire a travertine terrace formation with water cascading down it.

title: Mallard Lake Trail
shortDescription: Cross the Firehole River, pass Pipeline Hot Springs, and climb rolling hills of partially-burned lodgepole pine and open, rocky areas to Mallard Lake.

image.title: Mallard Lake Trail
image.altText: A lake surrounded by rolling hills and forests.

title: Lost Lake Trail
shortDescription: Hike along a trail that offers views of Lost Lake, waterfowl, sagebrush hilltops, wildflowers, possibly beavers, and quite often black bears.

image.title: Lost Lake Trail
image.altText: A small lake coverd in lily pads surrounded by a forest.

title: Lone Star Geyser Trail
shortDescription: Hike this pleasant, partially paved trail beside the Firehole River to Lone Star Geyser.

image.title: Lone Star Geyser Trail
image.altText: Steam and water erupt from the tan cone of Lone Star Geyser. A rainbow appears in the mist.

title: Lone Star Geyser Bike Trail
shortDescription: The trailhead for Lone Star Geyser is east of Kepler Cascades pull-out, 3.5 miles (5.6 km) southeast of Old Faithful overpass on Grand Loop Road.

image.title: Lone Star Geyser Bike Trail
image.altText: Steam and water erupt from the tan cone of Lone Star Geyser. A rainbow appears in the mist.

title: Lewis River Channel/Dogshead Trail
shortDescription: Hike through forest to the crystal-clear waters of the Lewis River Channel. Look for eagles and osprey fishing for trout in the shallow waters.

image.title: Lewis River Channel/Dogshead Trail
image.altText: A hiker follows a trail alongside a river through a forest.

title: Howard Eaton Trail (Old Faithful Area)
shortDescription: Hike up a burned hill, continue through spruce-fir forest, and then down to Lone Star Geyser.

image.title: Howard Eaton Trail (Old Faithful Area)
image.altText: Steam and water erupt from the tan cone of Lone Star Geyser. A rainbow appears in the mist.

title: Howard Eaton Trail (Canyon Area)
shortDescription: Choose your destination on this trail that passes by four lakes, as you hike through forests, meadows, and marshes.

image.title: Howard Eaton Trail (Canyon Area)
image.altText: Two trumpeter swans float on a body of water covered in lily pads.

title: Hellroaring Trail
shortDescription: Descend down to the Yellowstone River, then continue on through a sagebrush plateau to Hellroaring Creek.

image.title: Hellroaring Trail
image.altText: Three people hike past a pond in a meadow with a forested mountain in the distance.

title: Harlequin Lake Trail
shortDescription: Follow the gentle, uphill trail to a small lake.

image.title: Harlequin Lake Trail
image.altText: Lily pads dot a lake at the base of a slopping cliff.

title: Grebe Lake Trail
shortDescription: Hike along an old fire road through meadows and forest, some of which burned in 1988.

image.title: Grebe Lake Trail
image.altText: A trail runs through the grass alongside a lake.

title: Grand Prismatic Overlook Trail
shortDescription: Hike up to an overlook of Grand Prismatic Spring.

image.title: Grand Prismatic Overlook Trail
image.altText: A large, colorful hot spring as viewed from above.

title: Garnet Hill Trail
shortDescription: Follow a stagecoach route on a meadow journey around Garnet Hill. The full route cannot be hiked due to a trail washout refer to Backcountry Conditions report.

image.title: Garnet Hill Trail
image.altText: Three people hike through a field of sagebrush in front of a hill.

title: Fountain Freight Road Bike Trail
shortDescription: Six miles north of Old Faithful, bikes are allowed on the Fountain Freight Road, an old dirt and gravel road now closed to autos.

image.altText: Five cyclists ride on a trail with steam rising from a geysers in the background.

title: Elephant Back Mountain Trail
shortDescription: Hike to the top of this mountain for panoramic views of Yellowstone Lake and the surrounding area.

image.title: Elephant Back Mountain Trail
image.altText: A hiker looks down from a vantage point across a forest to a large lake.

title: Duck Lake Trail
shortDescription: Climb a small hill for a view of Duck and Yellowstone lakes and the expanse of the 1988 fires that swept through this area.

image.altText: A small lake surrounded by conifer forest.

title: DeLacy Creek Trail
shortDescription: Hike along a forest’s edge and through open meadows to the shores of Yellowstone’s largest backcountry lake. Look for sandhill cranes, moose, and water birds.

image.title: Delacy Creek Trail
image.altText: A creek flows through a meadow surrounded by trees.

title: Bunsen Peak Trail
shortDescription: Climb to the top of this igneous peak for panoramic views of Swan Lake Flats, the Gallatin Mountain Range, and the Mammoth Hot Springs area.

image.title: Bunsen Peak Trail
image.altText: Four people hike across a talus slope with the sun setting behind a mountain in the distance.

title: Bunsen Peak Loop Bike Trail
shortDescription: The Bunsen Peak Loop is a ten mi (16 km) bike trail that circles Bunsen Peak.

image.title: Bunsen Peak Loop Bike Trail
image.altText: A person bikes on a trail through a field of sagebrush with mountains in the distance.

title: Avalanche Peak Trail
shortDescription: Experience one of the most strenuous day hikes in the park and be rewarded with stunning views of some of the park’s tallest and most remote alpine peaks.
seasonDescription: This trail is often snow-covered until early July. Grizzly bears frequent this area in the fall, seeking out whitebark pine nuts. Hiking this trail is not recommended in September and October.

image.title: Avalanche Peak Trail
image.altText: Two hikers enjoying the view of mountains in the distance from the summit of rocky mountain.

title: Chittenden Road - Mount Washburn Trail
shortDescription: Head up the shortest route to the top of Mount Washburn where you can enjoy panoramic views and interpretive exhibits.

image.title: Chittenden Road-Mount Washburn Trail
image.altText: Wildflowers bloom in an alpine meadow with mountains in the distance.

title: Slough Creek Trail
shortDescription: Follow a historic wagon trail that heads toward the Absaroka-Beartooth Wilderness beyond Yellowstone.

image.title: Slough Creek Trail
image.altText: A creek meanders past a rocky outcropping.

title: Wraith Falls Trail
shortDescription: Cross sagebrush meadows, marshland, and mixed conifer forest to the base of Wraith Falls on Lupine Creek.

image.title: Wraith Falls Trail
image.altText: Water cascades down a slope surrounded by rocky cliffs and sparse trees.

title: Seven Mile Hole Trail
shortDescription: Hike along the rim of the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, enjoy views of Silver Cord Cascade, and then descend to Seven Mile Hole.

image.title: Seven Mile Hole Trail
image.altText: A river flows through a canyon with pale, sloping walls.

title: Purple Mountain Trail
shortDescription: Hike up Purple Mountain for panoramic views of the GIbbon and Madison Rivers.

image.title: Purple Mountain Trail
image.altText: Steam from geyser basins dot a forested landscape as viewed from a mountain summit.

title: Lava Creek Trail
shortDescription: Follow Lava Creek, seeing Undine Falls and the junction with Gardner River.

image.title: Lava Creek Trail
image.altText: A two-tiered waterfall surrounded by columnar basalt as viewed from above.

title: Rescue Creek Trail
shortDescription: Climb gradually through aspens and meadows, then descend through forests to sagebrush flats that lead to a footbridge across the Gardner River.

image.title: Rescue Creek Trail
image.altText: A rocky mountain peak emerges behind rolling, grassy hills.

title: Dunraven Pass - Mount Washburn Trail
shortDescription: Starting at the Dunravenn Pass Trailhead you ascend Mount Washburn on a trail with spectacular views. The Mount Washburn Trail and trailhead parking lot at Dunraven Pass will close for improvements August 6-27, 2019.

image.title: Dunraven Pass – Mount Washburn Trail
image.altText: A trail crosses a ridgeline above forests and meadows.

title: Cascade Lake Trail
shortDescription: Hike through open meadows to Cascade Lake where wildflowers abound and wildlife is often seen.

image.title: Cascade Lake
image.altText: Lily pads sit on a lake with a reflection of the surrounding forests and a mountain in the distance.

title: Blacktail Deer Creek to Yellowstone River Trail
shortDescription: Follow Blacktail Deer Creek as it descends through rolling, grassy hills and Douglas-fir forest to a suspension bridge over the Yellowstone River.

image.title: Blacktail Deer Creek
image.altText: Two people hike through a field of yellow flowers along the side of a slope.

title: Forces of the Northern Range Self-guided Trail
shortDescription: Follow this self-guided trail along a boardwalk that winds through the grassland of Yellowstone's northern range.

image.title: Exhibit on Forces of the Northern Range
image.altText: Visitors on a boardwalk view a low profile wayside exhibit
image.caption: Visitors view a wayside exhibit on the Forces of the Northern Range Self-guided Trail

title: Brink of the Lower Falls Trail
shortDescription: Descend to the brink of the Lower Falls on this steep trail to catch a glimpse of one of Yellowstone's greatest wonders.

image.title: Brink of Lower Falls Trail
image.altText: A rainbow is cast in the mist from a waterfall over a river that cuts through a deep canyon.

title: Beaver Ponds Trail
shortDescription: Hike through forests, meadows of sage, and stands of Douglas-fir and aspen on your way to beaver ponds. You might see beavers or their sign, but you are more likely to see muskrats and water birds.

image.title: Beaver Ponds Trail
image.altText: Hikers travel along a trail through the sagebrush with a mountain peak in the distance.

title: Specimen Ridge Day Hike Trail
shortDescription: Hike up to a ridge for magnificent views of Slough Creek Valley and the Absaroka Range.

image.title: Specimen Ridge Day Hike
image.altText: A trail travels past a piece of petrified wood on a ridgeline.

title: Fountain Paint Pot Trail
shortDescription: Explore the four major types of hydrothermal features along this short, popular, boardwalk trail.
seasonDescription: This trail is accessible via snowmobile and snow coach in the winter.

image.title: Fountain Paint Pot Trail
image.altText: Steam rises from bubbling mudpots in a thermal basin.

title: Pelican Creek Nature Trail
shortDescription: Introduce yourself to a diverse assortment of Yellowstone habitats and look for birds while hike this loop trail through a forest to the shore of Yellowstone Lake.

image.title: Pelican Creek Nature Trail
image.altText: A creek spills into a large lake with mountains in the distance.

title: Fairy Falls Trail
shortDescription: Enjoy a hike to one of Yellowstone's most spectacular waterfalls.

image.title: Fairy Falls Trail
image.altText: A thin waterfall cascades down a rocky cliff.

title: Riverside Bike Trail
shortDescription: Just inside the park's West Entrance, bicyclists can travel on the Riverside trail located just north of and paralleling the main Grand Loop Road. This trail gives access to a section of the Madison River. This is a fairly level trail and mountain bikes are recommended.

image.title: Riverside Bike Trail
image.altText: Purple, pink, and orange are cast across the sky and reflect in the slowly moving water of a river.

title: Fairy Falls Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Fairy Falls Ski Trail is a 10 mile (16 km) (with ski drop) skier-tracked, round-trip, easiest to more dificult ski that provides icy views of one of Yellowstone's most popular waterfalls.

image.title: Fairy Falls Ski Trail
image.altText: A skier looks up at the ice formations surrounding a frozen waterfall.

title: Fawn Pass Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Fawn Pass Ski Trail is an 11 mile (17.7 km), one-way, more difficult ski trail that provides skiers with wide open views of the Gallatin Range.

image.title: Fawn Pass Ski Trail
image.altText: Two skiers are dwarfed by the landscape of forests and moutains in the distance.

title: Roller Coaster Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Roller Coaster Ski Trail is a more difficult 1.8 mile (2.9 km) roundtrip forested trail taking skiers on a rolling course with several steep drop-offs.

image.title: Roller Coaster Ski Trail
image.altText: A person excitedly cross-country skis down a steep hill in the forest.

title: Observation Point Loop Snowshoe Trail
shortDescription: The Observation Point Loop Snowshoe Trail is a 2.0 mile (3.2 km) snowshoe only trail that treats visitors to unobstructed views of the Upper Geyser Basin and the Firehole River.

image.title: Observation Point Loop Snowshoe Trail
image.altText: A geyser in the middle of a snowy field erupts steam and water high into the air.

title: Riverside Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Riverside Ski Trail provides several easy options to ski along the Madison River and enjoy views of both the Gallatin and Madison mountain ranges.

image.title: Riverside Ski Trail
image.altText: A lone skier makes their way along the Madison River on the Riverside Ski Trail.

title: Tower Fall Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Tower Fall Ski Trail is a 5.0 mile (8 km) round-trip easiest trail that allows skiers to enjoy canyon views of the Yellowstone River and Tower Fall.

image.title: Tower Fall Ski Trail
image.altText: Icicle formations encase a waterfall surrounded by columns of rock.

title: Bighorn Pass Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Bighorn Pass Ski Trail provides a variety of options for skiers to experience the northwest area of Yellowstone National Park.

image.altText: Glimpses of mountain views can be seen through the trees along the Divide Ski Trail.

title: Black Butte Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Black Butte Ski Trail is a 14 mile (22.6 km) roundtrip ski that follows Black Butte Creek and offers mountain views.

image.altText: Glimpses of mountain views can be seen through the trees along the Divide Ski Trail.

title: Yancey's Hole Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Yancey's Hole Ski Trail is a 2.0 mile (3.2 km) easiest ski trail with rolling terrain and wide open views of the Yancey's Hole area.

image.altText: Two skiers make their way on a slight incline through a lodgepole pine forest.

title: Bannock Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Bannock Ski Trail is a 2 mile (3.2 km) easy ski that follows the old road bed that once used to supply the mining town of Cooke City, Montana.

image.title: Bannock Ski Trail
image.altText: Ski tracks travel through a forest.

title: Barronette Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Barronette Trail is an easy 3.5 mile (5.6 km) one-way section of the Old Cooke City road and winds through conifer forest.

image.title: Barronette Ski Trail
image.altText: Skiers travel along a trail through a forest with mountain peaks rising above the trees.

title: Blacktail Plateau Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Blacktail Plateau Ski Trail is an easiest to more difficult 8 mile (12.8 km) one-way ski with two trailhead options. This trail travels open meadows and forests with great wildlife viewing opportunities in winter.

image.title: Blacktail Plateau Ski Trail
image.altText: A skier travels along a trail with a mountain peak in the distance.

title: Chittenden Loop Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Chittenden Loop Ski Trail is an easiest to more difficult 5.3 mile (8.3 km) loop providing views of Mount Washburn on clear days.

image.title: Chittenden Loop Ski Trail
image.altText: A skier travels along a trail on the edge of a canyon.

title: Lost Lake Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Lost Lake Ski Trail is a 4 mile (6.4 km) easiest to more difficult one-way trail that takes skiers by Petrified Tree, Lost Lake, and Calcite Springs Overlook.

image.title: Lost Lake Ski Trail
image.altText: Three skiers travel downhill towards mountains in the distance.

title: Mallard Lake Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Mallard Lake Ski Trail is a 6.8 mile (10.9 km) round-trip, skier-tracked, more difficult trail taking skiers on a steep climb to views of Mallard Lake.

image.title: Mallard Lake Ski Trail
image.altText: A lone skier breaks trail along the Mallard Lake Trail in the forested section near the trailhead.

title: North Rim Ski Trail
shortDescription: The North Rim Ski Trail is a 3.0 (7.24 km), easiest to more difficult forested trail that takes skiers along the North Canyon Rim providing views into the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone.

image.title: North Rim Ski Trail
image.altText: Skiers stop to admire the views of the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone from the North Rim Trail.

title: Sheepeater Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Sheepeater Ski Trail is a skier-tracked, easy, one-way 5 mile (8 km) trail that provides scenic views of Swan Lake Flats.

image.title: Sheepeater Ski Trail
image.altText: Two skiers travel across a flat meadow with mountains in the distance.

title: Pebble Creek Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Pebble Creek Ski Trail is a 13 mile (21 km) most difficult, round-trip ski that offers skilled backcountry skiers challenging terrain and beautiful views.

image.altText: Glimpses of mountain views can be seen through the trees along the Divide Ski Trail.

title: Bighorn Loop Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Bighorn Loop Ski Trail is a 5.5 mile (8.85 km), easy to more difficult trail taking skiers on a loop through rolling terrain with outstanding winter landscape views.

image.altText: Two skiers make their way on a slight incline through a lodgepole pine forest.

title: Old Canyon Bridge Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Old Canyon Bridge Ski Trail is a flat 1 mile (1.6 km) easiest ski that provides skiers a short but beautiful way to see the Yellowstone River in winter.

image.altText: A lone skier skies along the Old Canyon Bridge Ski Trial with the Chittenden Bridge seen through the

title: Ride a snowmobile or snowcoach in Yellowstone
shortDescription: Get a taste of what snowmobiling or riding a snowcoach in Yellowstone is like.

image.title: Snowmobile Tour
image.altText: A line of snowmobiles move along a snowy track that leads across a snow-covered valley.
image.caption: A line of snowmobilers head across the snowy Yellowstone landscape.

title: Watch Old Faithful Geyser Erupt
shortDescription: Old Faithful Geyser is the world's best known geyser. Its eruption intervals have varied from 40 to 126 minutes. Find out the eruption times of Old Faithful and other large geysers at the Old Faithful Visitor Education Center, following the @GeyserNPS twitter feed, or using the Geysers app.

image.title: Old Faithful Geyser
image.altText: Visitors watch an eruption of Old Faithful Geyser.

title: Canyon Rim Ski Trail
shortDescription: The Canyon Rim Ski Trail is a 4.5 mile (7.24 km), easiest to more difficult forested trail that takes skiers along the Canyon Rim providing views into the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone.

image.title: Canyon Rim Ski Trail
image.altText: A group of skiers travel on a trail along the edge of a snow-covered canyon.

title: Explore the Fort Yellowstone Historic District
shortDescription: From 1886 to 1918, the US Army managed Yellowstone National Park. Starting in 1890, the US Army constructed Fort Yellowstone as a more permanent base of operations.
seasonDescription: This tour is available year-round. Please watch for vehicles and wildlife.

image.title: Explore Fort Yellowstone
image.altText: A historic photo of a collection of buildings that make up Fort Yellowstone.

title: Watch and Listen to a Geyser
shortDescription: Experiencing the sights and sounds of geysers is a feast for the senses, whether they erupt or are between eruptions.
seasonDescription: Geysers can be viewed all year, though access to many of the geyser basins is limited to snowmobile and snowcoach tours from mid-December through mid-March. There are also road closures from early November to mid-December and mid-March to mid-April when access is unavailable.

image.title: Erupting Geyser
image.altText: Water and steam erupt up out of the ground as people stand on a boardwalk and watch.
image.caption: People watch a geyser erupt

title: Visit the Yosemite Exploration Center
shortDescription: The Yosemite Exploration Center features interactive displays and exhibits highlighting Yosemite's many stories and resources. Bring the family and learn more about Yosemite's history, the people who originally called this place home, as well as more about meadows, animals, and sequoias!

image.title: Yosemite Exploration Center
image.altText: A building with glass double doors and river rock walls surrounding both sides
image.caption: Yosemite Exploration Center

title: Watch the "Spirit of Yosemite" Film
shortDescription: The park film, The Spirit of Yosemite, is shown daily on the hour and the half hour in the theater behind the Yosemite Exploration Center. The first showing is at 9:30am, and the last showing is at 4pm.

image.title: Yosemite Exploration Center Theater
image.altText: A covered entryway leads to glass double doors; lettering above the entryway reads "theater"
image.caption: Yosemite Exploration Center Theater

title: Become a Yosemite Junior Ranger
shortDescription: Kids can become a Yosemite Junior Ranger by taking a self-guided handbook with them as they travel around the park and complete the activities that are the best fit for them. The Yosemite Junior Ranger handbook is available for free at visitor centers. When you are done, share your booklet with a park ranger at any Yosemite visitor center during operating hours to receive your badge.

image.title: Junior Ranger program with Erik
image.altText: Park Ranger looking at something in nature with kids
image.caption: Learning about the natural world of Yosemite with a Park Ranger.

title: Rock Climbing in Yosemite
shortDescription: Yosemite is one of the world's greatest climbing areas. Climbers here can enjoy an endless variety of challenges--from the sustained crack climbs of the Merced River Canyon to pinching crystals on sun-drenched Tuolumne Meadows domes to multi-day aid climbs on the big walls of the Valley. Yosemite is not just a climber's playground, however: its walls and crags are an integral part of a larger ecosystem, protected as Wilderness.

title: Scenic Driving in Yosemite
shortDescription: All of the roads in Yosemite National Park are scenic, but the most famous scenic drive is along the Tioga Road, a 46-mile (62 km) drive from Crane Flat to Tioga Pass. The road is typically open from late May or early June through sometime in November.

image.caption: Scenic Driving in Yosemite: Yosemite Valley

title: Wildlife Safety in Yosemite
shortDescription: Yosemite National Park supports more than 400 species of vertebrates including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. The high diversity of species is the result of diverse habitats in Yosemite that are largely intact. The park’s rich habitats range from thick foothill chaparral to conifer forests to expanses of alpine rock. Animals feel at home in each location.

image.title: Black Bear in Yosemite National Park
image.altText: An adult bear with a brown coat and blue ear tag walks along a log
image.caption: Bear in Yosemite National Park

title: Ride a Bike in Yosemite Valley
shortDescription: Cycling is a great way to experience the park and allows you to cover more ground during your time here. You can rent a bike, bring your own, or borrow one through the bike share program (2-hour limit). Hand-crank and tandem bicycles are also available for rent. Over 12 miles of paved bike paths are available in Yosemite Valley (speed limit is 15 mph). In addition, bicyclists can ride on regular roads (if they obey traffic laws).
seasonDescription: While you can choose to bicycle in Yosemite year-round, bike rentals are only available from spring - fall. Bicycle paths are not always cleared from snow in winter and may be difficult to impossible to ride on, depending on conditions.

title: Hiking in Yosemite
shortDescription: From a short walk to the base of a waterfall to a multi-day hike deep into the Yosemite Wilderness, taking a hike is one of the best ways to experience Yosemite's spectacular scenery. Yosemite has an extensive network of over 800 miles of hiking trails.

image.title: Lower Yosemite Fall
image.altText: Lower Yosemite Fall full of water in spring
image.caption: Lower Yosemite Fall in spring.

title: Learn Art in the Park
shortDescription: Yosemite has a long history of inspiring visitors to create art. From world-renowned artists like Ansel Adams and Chiura Obata to everyday people who love art for fun, pausing to create something beautiful is a special way to experience Yosemite's towering cliffs, dramatic waterfalls, enormous trees, and granite high country.

image.title: The Ansel Adams Gallery
image.altText: A covered porch with exposed log beams leads to a warmly lit rustic building
image.caption: The Ansel Adams Gallery

title: Visit the Yosemite History Center
shortDescription: Go back to a time of horse-drawn wagons, a covered bridge, and rustic cabins. The Yosemite History Center is a collection of historic buildings where outdoor interpretive signs tell the stories of people who moved here from around the world and shaped the park’s development. During the summer, visit exhibits inside the Chinese Laundry and the Acting Superintendent's Office, take a ride on our horse-drawn wagon, or watch blacksmiths forge iron tools on a coal forge!

image.title: Yosemite History Center
image.altText: A stage drawn by two horses outside a covered bridge
image.caption: A horse-drawn stage outside historic Wawona Covered Bridge

title: Go Skiing at Badger Pass
shortDescription: The Badger Pass Ski Area is open from mid-December through March (weather and conditions permitting). You can downhill ski, cross-country ski, go tubing, or snowshoeing all from this historic winter resort.

image.title: Badger Pass Ski Area
image.altText: Ski lift at Badger Pass with snow on the ground
image.caption: Chair lift at Badger Pass Ski Area

title: Visit the Yosemite Museum
shortDescription: Open year-round, the Yosemite Museum has displays that interpret the cultural history of Yosemite's native Miwok and Paiute people from 1850 to the present, demonstrations of stone tool making, basket-weaving, beadwork, and traditional games. In front of the museum is a cross-section of a giant sequoia tree that visitors can touch and a re-creation of an umacha, a Miwok and Paiute cedar bark house. The gallery inside the museum is open periodically with rotating exhibits.
seasonDescription: The Yosemite Museum is open year-round.

image.title: Yosemite Museum
image.altText: View of front of Yosemite Museum with dappled sunlight in fall.
image.caption: Yosemite Museum

title: Visit the Yosemite Cemetery
shortDescription: The Yosemite Cemetery is full of stories, told and untold. Some of those laid to rest here are well-known figures in the history of the park. Some spent their entire lives in Yosemite and are now almost forgotten. Others were visitors about whom very little was known, even at their time of their deaths.
seasonDescription: The Yosemite Cemetery is open year-round.

image.title: Yosemite Cemetery
image.altText: Wooden sign at entrance to Yosemite Cemetery
image.caption: Yosemite Cemetery

title: Float the Yukon River
shortDescription: A hyperlapse is a moving timelapse and, in this case, it is of the 100 mile stretch of Yukon River from Eagle, Alaska to Slaven's Roadhouse in Yukon-Charley Rivers National Preserve. Complete with notable location descriptions, this virtual tour of the Yukon River is for entertainment and basic orientation purposes.

image.altText: Boat traveling down the Yukon River with bluffs on each side

title: Yukon River Public Use Cabins
shortDescription: Take yourself back in time with a stay in one of the seven public use cabins that are available on a first come, first served basis in Yukon-Charley Rivers National Preserve. Split some wood and head inside to light a blaze in the wood stove, under the light of an oil lamp. Enjoy the warmth as your gear dries out from a long journey down the mighty Yukon River, whether it be on a recreational float or hunting trip. Please replace the firewood, but keep the memories.

image.title: Stay in a Public Use Cabin
image.altText: Yukon River view from the Glenn Creek Public Use Cabin
image.caption: Go back in time and stay in the seven public use cabins available on a first-come first-served basis

title: La Verkin Creek Trail to Kolob Arch
shortDescription: The La Verkin Creek Trail to the Kolob Arch allows hikers outstanding opportunities for solitude in a primitive area of Zion Wilderness. The trail begins at Lee Pass with stunning views of the Kolob Canyons as it crosses Timber Creek and continues to descend toward La Verkin Creek. After seven miles a spur trail leads hikers to a viewpoint where they can see the Kolob Arch.

image.title: Kolob Arch
image.altText: Looking up at an orange-red sandstone arch on a cliff-face with clear blue skies overhead.
image.caption: The Kolob Arch is one of the world's largest natural arches.

title: Upper Emerald Pools Trail
shortDescription: Upper Emerald Pools Trail is a moderate, 1 mile (1.6 km) trail that can be accessed via the Kayenta Trail, Lower Emerald Pools Trail, or Middle Emerald Pools Trail. Climb up stone steps to a sandy path that leads through pinyon-juniper woodlands to the base of towering canyon walls which boast majestic, seasonal waterfalls. The trail ends at the sandy shore of Upper Emerald Pool. No swimming.

image.title: Upper Emerald Pools in Summer
image.altText: A large group of people near a pool of water with green trees and an orange sandstone cliff face
image.caption: Upper Emerald Pools

title: Sand Bench
shortDescription: The Sand Bench Trail travels atop the remains of an ancient rockfall. This trail leads hikers along the Virgin River and then ascends a landslide that dammed the Virgin River 8,000 years ago and created a lake that extended to Angels Landing. This trail is a commercial horse trail from March to October, and it receives little shade in the hot, summer sun. Winter travel is possible, but watch for patches of ice.
seasonDescription: Seasonal commercial horse tours are available from March to October. These tours are offered through a concessioner.

image.title: Sand Bench Trail
image.altText: A cloudy blue sky over red sandstone mountains, with green foliage dotting their foothills.
image.caption: The Sand Bench Trail has excellent view of many Zion landmarks.

title: Lower Emerald Pool Trail
shortDescription: Lower Emerald Pool trail is a rough, paved trail that leads through pinyon-juniper woodland to the Lower Emerald Pool and ephemeral waterfalls.The pools are fragile and an essential water source for wildlife. Do not go into the water. Connects to the other Emerald Pools trails and the Kayenta Trail. Avoid cliff edges. Swimming is not permitted. Restrooms and water filling stations are available at the Zion Lodge.
seasonDescription: Trail may be icy in winter.

image.title: Lower Emerald Pool Trail
image.altText: A waterfall flows off of a sandstone ledge into a pool below, surrounded by foliage.
image.caption: View from the end of the Lower Emerald Pool Trail.

title: Middle Emerald Pools Trail
shortDescription: Middle Emerald Pools Trail is a moderate hike along an unpaved sandstone ledge above the Lower Emerald Pool Trail. The initial ascent is quite steep, bringing you to expansive views of main Zion Canyon below. Further along the trail, tucked into the red sandstone of the mountain, enjoy the shade and flora of pinyon-juniper woodlands. The trail then descends to emerald-colored pools of water above the small ephemeral waterfalls of Lower Emerald Pool Trail.

image.title: Middle Emerald Pools Trail
image.altText: A pool of green water on a sandstone cliff surrounded by green foliage with a mountain in the back.
image.caption: View from the end of Middle Emerald Pools Trail.

title: Angels Landing
shortDescription: On and after April 1, 2022 hikers continuing to Angels Landing from Scout Lookout are required to have a permit, obtained on recreation.gov.

image.title: Hiker on Angels Landing
image.altText: A hiker in a blue shirt holds onto chains as they traverse a sandstone cliff.
image.caption: Hiker holds onto the chains of the Angels Landing Trail.

title: West Rim to Scout Lookout
shortDescription: The strenuous West Rim Trail ascends ~1,000 ft (305 m) to Scout Lookout, high above the canyon floor. Hikers cross the Virgin River and then ascend a series of steep switchbacks along the canyon wall. The trail flattens out as it enters Refrigerator Canyon, offering relief from the heat and elevation gain of the previous segment, but resumes the climb shortly afterward at Walter’s Wiggles: a series of 21 switchbacks that leads hikers to Scout Lookout.

image.title: Scout Lookout
image.altText: A hiker with an orange backpack standing on sandstone looks at the Angels Landing peak.
image.caption: Hiker on Scout Lookout looking towards Angels Landing and the Great White Throne.

title: Kayenta Trail
shortDescription: The moderate, 2.0 mi (3.2 km) Kayenta Trail follows the Virgin River before ascending to the Lower and Upper Emerald Pool Trails. Provides panoramic views of Zion Canyon along the way. Long drop-offs are present along this trail. You can either return on the same trail, or make a loop using one of the Emerald Pools trails.  Water and restrooms are available at The Grotto.

image.title: Kayenta Trail
image.altText: A set of red sandstone stairs lined with loose rocks and green foliage leads out of frame.
image.caption: Sandstone steps of the Kayenta Trail lead you up to the Emerald Pools

title: Weeping Rock
shortDescription: Short but steep! From the parking area, you'll cross the bridge and head to the left onto a paved trail to Weeping Rock. Along the way, look for small trailside exhibits and watch for minor drop-offs. The trail ends at a set of steps leading you to a rock alcove with dripping springs.

image.title: Weeping Rock
image.altText: A large, arch shaped alcove streaked with dark shades of orange on red rock.
image.caption: View of Weeping Rock from above

title: Timber Creek Overlook
shortDescription: Follows a ridge to views of Timber Creek, Kolob Terrace, and the Pine Valley Mountains.

image.title: Timber Creek Overlook
image.altText: Red sandstone rocks with three hikers standing on them looking out over a valley. Blue, cloudy sky.
image.caption: View from the Timber Creek Overlook.

title: Taylor Creek Trail
shortDescription: Kolob Canyons hike. Follows the Middle Fork of Taylor Creek past two homestead cabins to Double Arch Alcove. Group size limit on Wilderness trails is 12 people.

image.title: Double Arch Alcove on Taylor Creek
image.altText: Red sandstone cliff face with an alcove at the bottom and an arch above.
image.caption: The Double Arch Alcove marks the end of the Traylor Creek Trail.

title: Watchman Trail
shortDescription: The Watchman trail is out-and-back. From the relatively flat beginning section of trail by the river, this unpaved trail climbs to a magnificent viewpoint of the Watchman, Temples and Towers, lower Zion Canyon, and the Town of Springdale. The terrain is sandy, rocky, and uneven, with several moderate drop-offs.
seasonDescription: This hike is accessible throughout the year. The trail may be muddy or icy during the winter and monsoon season. Limited shade in the summer.

image.title: Watchman Overlook
image.altText: View from a sandy overlook of a triangular sandstone mountain with green foliage on the foothills.
image.caption: View from the overlook at the end of Watchman Trail

title: Riverside Walk
shortDescription: The Riverside Walk is a relatively flat and paved trail in the northern end of Zion Canyon. This easy trail follows the Virgin River as the sheer sandstone walls narrow in around you. The Riverside Walk is mostly flat through the first half-mile, although paving is irregular in some sections and minor drop-offs are present.
seasonDescription: Riverside Walk is open year-round, but sections of the trail may close in winter due to icy and unsafe conditions. Check the park's current conditions before your trip.

image.title: Riverside Walk
image.altText: Two hikers in blue jackets walk along a sandy trail lined with a wooden rail and fall foliage.
image.caption: Hikers on the Riverside Walk in autumn.

title: Grotto Trail
shortDescription: The trail connects the Zion Lodge to the Grotto and is near the road most of the way. This trail is a great place to view wildlife. Restrooms are available at both the Lodge and the Grotto. When the shuttle is not in operation and the parking is full at the Grotto, this trail is a lovely alternate way to reach the Grotto.

image.title: Grotto Trail
image.altText: A tan path crossing green grass into a stand of trees. A red sandstone mountain is to the left.
image.caption: View from the Grotto Trail

title: Pa'rus Trail
shortDescription: Pa’rus is Paiute for “bubbling water.” The Pa’rus Trail follows the Virgin River and has some of the best views of the Watchman. The paved trail connects the Zion Canyon Visitor Center and Canyon Junction. It is accessible for wheelchairs, pets on leashes, and bicycles. Trailside exhibits cover a variety of subjects, including plant and animal life along the river, geology, and human history.

image.title: Pa'rus Trail
image.altText: A tan, paved trail cuts through a meadow of yellow grasses toward a triangular sandstone mountain.
image.caption: View from the Pa'rus Trail as it follows the river between Canyon Junction and the Visitor Center.

title: Canyon Overlook
shortDescription: Long drop-offs, mostly fenced. Rocky and uneven trail ends at a viewpoint for Pine Creek Canyon and lower Zion Canyon. To enter or exit the parking area just east of the tunnel, you must turn right. Parking is extremely limited, be prepared to try multiple times. Pit toilets are available in the parking area.

image.title: Canyon Overlook
image.altText: Red sandstone slickrock dotted with green foliage with mountains in the background.
image.caption: View looking towards the end of the Canyon Overlook Trail and the Towers and Temples of the Virgin

title: Stargazing in Zion
shortDescription: Zion is a great place to connect with the night sky, whether you are an avid astrophotographer or this will be your first view of the Milky Way. As an International Dark Sky Park, Zion protects our incredible dark skies for present and future generations by not degrading the night with artificial light. This means that after sunset, the park is very dark. Be prepared!

image.title: Milky Way over Bridge Mountain
image.altText: Black silhouette of a triangular mountain under a dark sky full of stars.
image.caption: The Milky Way can be seen over Zion Canyon in the summer.

title: The Narrows
shortDescription: The Narrows is a strenuous hike that follows the Virgin River through a narrow slot canyon. After 1 mile (0.6 km) on the easy, paved Riverside Walk, head down a set of stairs and into the river. The rest of your hike will take place in the Virgin River, where the flow rate can change day by day and the streambed is rocky with unstable footing. Flash flooding and hypothermia are constant dangers.
seasonDescription: The Narrows may close when the river is flowing over 140 cubic feet per second. This frequently occurs in monsoon season (late summer) and during spring runoff. Always check the weather and current conditions before beginning your hike.

image.title: The Narrows
image.altText: Red sandstone canyon walls frame the blue water of the Virgin River below.
image.caption: View in The Narrows

title: Zion Ranger-led Activities
shortDescription: Join a park ranger to learn about what makes Zion National Park such a special place! We have a variety of ranger-led activities throughout the year, and you can check the schedule on our Events Calendar. Topics range from geology and wildlife to art and human history, and everything inbetween. All ranger-led programs are free.
seasonDescription: Ranger-led programs are available throughout the year. More programs are offered in the summer than the winter months, so check the scheudle at park visitor centers or on our events calendar.

image.title: Zion Ranger-led Programs
image.altText: Four NPS rangers stand under a shade structure holding various props.
image.caption: Ranger-led programs are a great way to learn about the park

title: Climbing in Zion
shortDescription: Zion National Park's 2,000-foot sandstone cliffs are world renowned for their big wall climbs and adventurous nature. Most routes in the park are not recommended for inexperienced climbers due to difficulty and the soft nature of the rock. While areas outside of the park offer abundant sport climbing and top roping possibilities, this is rare in the park, with bolted routes often having sparse protection.
seasonDescription: The best conditions for climbing are from March through May and September through early November. Temperatures in the summer can soar over 100 degrees even on shaded walls. Additionally, summer months often bring monsoonal rainstorms. Unlike other rock types, desert sandstone is heavily weakened when wet. Avoid climbing in damp areas or after rainstorms.

image.title: Rock climbing in Zion
image.altText: Red-orange sandstone cliff-face with a rock climber in a helmet making his way up.
image.caption: Climber on Iron Messiah
